- Statement I is true. Indeed, since $A$ is a $6\times 3$ matrix and ${A}^{T}$ is a $3\times 6$ matrix, ${A}^{T}\,A$ must be a $3\times 3$ matrix: 

$$
{{A}^{T}}_{3\times 6}\times {A}_{6\times 3}={{A}^{T}\,A}_{3\times 3}
$$

Hence, $A$ has at most $3$ distinct singular values.

- Statement II is false. All singular values of any matrix are non-negative. So, $A$ can't have a negative singular value.

- Statement III is false. Since $A$ is a $4\times 5$ matrix and ${A}^{T}$ is a $5\times 4$ matrix, ${A}^{T}\,A$ must be a $5\times 5$ matrix: 

$$
{{A}^{T}}_{5\times 4}\times {A}_{4\times 5}={{A}^{T}\,A}_{5\times 5}
$$

Hence, $A$ has at most $5$ distinct singular values.

$$

Now, we solve the characteristic equation of ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ \begin{vmatrix}5-\lambda  & 4 \\ 4 & 5-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (5-\lambda )(5-\lambda )-16 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-10\lambda +25-16 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-10\lambda +9 & =0 \\ (\lambda -1)(\lambda -9) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =9,\,1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={\begin{bmatrix}3 & -2\end{bmatrix}}^{T}\begin{bmatrix}3 & -2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 & -2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}9 & -6 \\ -6 & 4\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ \begin{vmatrix}9-\lambda  & -6 \\ -6 & 4-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (9-\lambda )(4-\lambda )-36 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-9\lambda -4\lambda +36-36 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-13\lambda  & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda -13) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =13,\,0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is false. Since $A$ is a $6\times 5$ matrix and ${A}^{T}$ is a $5\times 6$ matrix, ${A}^{T}\,A$ must be a $5\times 5$ matrix: 

$$
{{A}^{T}}_{5\times 6}\times {A}_{6\times 5}={{A}^{T}\,A}_{5\times 5}
$$

Hence, $A$ has at most $5$ distinct singular values.

- Statement II is true. Indeed, since $A$ is a $8\times 9$ matrix and ${A}^{T}$ is a $9\times 8$ matrix, ${A}^{T}\,A$ must be a $9\times 9$ matrix: 

$$
{{A}^{T}}_{9\times 8}\times {A}_{8\times 9}={{A}^{T}\,A}_{9\times 9}
$$

Hence, $A$ has at most $9$ distinct singular values.

- Statement III is true.  Indeed, all singular values of any matrix are non-negative.

\\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}?$" :question/worked-solution "The singular values of the matrix $A$ are the square roots of the eigenvalues of the matrix ${A}^{T}\,A.$  

First, we calculate ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}}^{T}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the characteristic equation of ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ \begin{vmatrix}1-\lambda  & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1-\lambda  & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )\begin{vmatrix}1-\lambda  & 1 \\ 1 & 1-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )((1-\lambda )^{2}-1) & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )(1-2\lambda +{\lambda }^{2}-1) & =0 \\ -\lambda (\lambda -1)(\lambda -2) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =2,\,1,\,0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{2} \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=\sqrt{1}=1 \\ {\sigma }_{3} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{3}}=\sqrt{0}=0\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}|{A}^{T}\,A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ \begin{vmatrix}1-\lambda  & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2-\lambda  & -2 \\ 0 & -2 & 2-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )\begin{vmatrix}2-\lambda  & -2 \\ -2 & 2-\lambda \end{vmatrix} & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )((2-\lambda )(2-\lambda )-4) & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda ) & =0 \\ -\lambda (\lambda -1)(\lambda -4) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =4,\,1,\,0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the singular values of $A$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{1}}=\sqrt{4}=2 \\ {\sigma }_{2} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{2}}=\sqrt{1}=1 \\ {\sigma }_{3} & =\sqrt{{\lambda }_{3}}=\sqrt{0}=0\end{aligned}

2278} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186139556 :step/content {:db/id 17592186139635 :tutorial/content "Let's look at the three points $A,$ $B,$ and $C$ below. 

![](images/95/956f9b2c979f06897b09119b089ced903e095d72136e64b9ea52e946fba41544.png)

As indicated in the diagram, the distances between the points are

$$
\begin{aligned}AB=4\,cm,\,BC=2\,cm,\,AC=6\,cm.\end{aligned}
$$

Can we be sure that the points are collinear? To answer this, we use the **segment addition postulate**.

The postulate states the following: 

*Three points are collinear if and only if the largest distance between two of them is equal to the sum of the other two distances.*

Here, the largest distance is $AC,$ so the points $A,$ $B,$ and $C$ are collinear *if and only if*

$$
AC=AB + BC.
$$

Substituting the given information $AC=6\,\mathrm{cm},$ $AB=4\,\mathrm{cm},$ and $BC=2\,\mathrm{cm}$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}AC & =AB+BC \\ 6 & =4+2 \\ 6 & =6.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

This is a true statement, so the three points $A,$ $B,$ and $C$ are indeed collinear.

**Note:** The postulate works in both directions:

- If the points $A,$ $B,$ and $C$ are collinear then $AC= AB + BC.$

- If $AC= AB + BC$ then the points $A,$ $B,$ and $C$ are collinear." :tutorial/id #uuid "0a460529-da55-5fcc-a207-e4ae6a47f12d" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2168 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "11ec6bb7-b9b3-51ea-b1b2-5f6a0a7b75b9" :step/math-academy-id 8720 :step/next {:db/id 17592186139557}} {:db/id 17592186139557 :step/content {:db/id 17592186139636 :tutorial/content "Given two of the three distances between three collinear points, we can calculate the third distance using the segment addition postulate. 

To demonstrate, consider the collinear points $A,$ $B,$ and $C$ below.

![](images/3b/3b1bc383e8d570f9dc33346e6f4ae04377e3c5c4c0d0e53abe07b0aacd9bb3e6.png)

We are given two of the distances:

$$
\begin{aligned}AB=3\,cm,\,AC=5\,cm\end{aligned}
$$

We can calculate the third distance, $BC,$ using the segment addition postulate.

As indicated in the diagram, the distances between the points are

$$
\begin{aligned}AB=4\,cm,\,BC=2\,cm,\,AC=6\,cm.\end{aligned}
$$

Can we be sure that the points are collinear? To answer this, we use the **segment addition postulate**.

The postulate states the following: 

*Three points are collinear if and only if the largest distance between two of them is equal to the sum of the other two distances.*

Here, the largest distance is $AC,$ so the points $A,$ $B,$ and $C$ are collinear *if and only if*

$$
AC=AB + BC.
$$

Substituting the given information $AC=6\,\mathrm{cm},$ $AB=4\,\mathrm{cm},$ and $BC=2\,\mathrm{cm}$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}AC & =AB+BC \\ 6 & =4+2 \\ 6 & =6.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

This is a true statement, so the three points $A,$ $B,$ and $C$ are indeed collinear.

**Note:** The postulate works in both directions:

- If the points $A,$ $B,$ and $C$ are collinear then $AC= AB + BC.$

- If $AC= AB + BC$ then the points $A,$ $B,$ and $C$ are collinear." :tutorial/id #uuid "0a460529-da55-5fcc-a207-e4ae6a47f12d" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2168 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "11ec6bb7-b9b3-51ea-b1b2-5f6a0a7b75b9" :step/math-academy-id 8720 :step/next {:db/id 17592186139557}} {:db/id 17592186139635 :tutorial/content "Let's look at the three points $A,$ $B,$ and $C$ below.

$$
y = \sqrt[6]{x}
$$

is

$$
x \ge 0
$$

To find the domain of

$$
g(x) = -2\sqrt[6]{x+1}-2
$$

we replace $x$ with $x+1$ in the above inequality. This gives

$$
{x+1} \ge 0
$$

Solving this inequality, we get

$$
\begin{bmatrix}x + 1 & \ge 0 \\ x & \ge - 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

Therefore, the domain of $y = g(x)$ is $x \in [-1, \infty)$.

[{:db/id 17592186116231 :step/content {:db/id 17592186116535 :tutorial/content "In general, the domain of a radical function

$$
f(x)=\sqrt[n]{x}
$$

depends on whether $n$ (called the **index**) is even or odd.

If $n$ is *odd*, then the domain of $f(x)$ is *always* $x\in (-\infty, \infty)$. For example, the domain of

$$
f(x)= \sqrt[3]{x}
$$

is $x\in (-\infty, \infty)$.

We can see this in the graph below: the function

$$
f(x) = \sqrt[3]{x}
$$

extends across all values of $x$.

![](images/c6/c64950f8f253168743e8349e3f1c4f37b3bf3ad8196ccdbc7d982b7cf337e209.png)

Now, suppose that we want to find the domain of a transformed radical function, such as

$$
g(x)= -\sqrt[3]{-x+2}
$$

The domain of $\sqrt[3]{x}$ is $x\in (-\infty, \infty)$, and graph transformations will not change this interval. Therefore, we conclude that the domain of $g(x)$ is also $x \in (-\infty,\infty)$." :tutorial/id #uuid "f36b7baa-b008-5800-85a0-71c8a1713b24" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4862 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "39dca9db-2697-5a19-88ba-4bf709eab73d" :step/math-academy-id 30456 :step/next {:db/id 17592186116255}} {:db/id 17592186116232 :step/content {:db/id 17592186115314 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186115143 :question/id #uuid "bfa03caf-a95c-5ba3-aa94-94698481226d" :question/math-academy-id "e-8141"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "a4a8d54a-c034-5646-b804-0dc96f6c21d0" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050642}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186115985} {:db/id 17592186115988} {:db/id 17592186233224}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Domain of a Transformed Radical Function With an Even Index"} :step/id #uuid "35f1ec51-e7b5-54bf-b6c9-9262124c42a2" :step/math-academy-id 30457} {:db/id 17592186116254 :step/content {:db/id 17592186116537 :tutorial/content "Let's go back to considering

$$
f(x)=\sqrt[n]{x}
$$

If $n$ is *even*, then the domain of $f(x)$ is *always* $x\in [0, \infty)$. For example, the domain of

$$
f(x)= \sqrt[4]{x}\,
$$

is $x\in [0, \infty)$.

We can see this in the graph below: the function

$$
f(x) = \sqrt[4]{x}
$$

starts at $x=0$ and extends forever to the right.

![](images/eb/eb93d815dc2a981645ea5a99248cef8f8189d4990ed269b778d691a13960fc31.png)

Notice how similar this looks to the square root function! All curves of the form

$$
y=\sqrt[n]{x}
$$

for even $n$ have this shape.

Now let's consider the function

$$
g(x)= 3\sqrt[4]{x+2} -2
$$

To find the domain of

$$
g(x) = 3\sqrt[4]{x+2} -2
$$

we proceed in exactly the same way as with square roots: we set the expression under the radical sign to be greater than or equal to zero. This gives

$$
x+2 \ge 0
$$

Solving this inequality, we get

$$
x \mid \ge - 2
$$

Therefore, the domain of $y = g(x)$ is $x \in [-2, \infty)$.

We can also see that this is true from the graph of the function. The graph of $y=g(x)$ is shown below.

![](images/8c/8c0f840ea79edd03231b93156ce050b2af718b751b0f84da6b7c6dab9105e3df.png)

In general, to find the domain of a radical function of the form

$$
y = \sqrt[n]{f(x)}
$$

where $n$ is an even integer, we need to solve the inequality

$$
f(x) \geq 0
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "b35a06bf-3ad8-5d8a-899e-a094e9728c70" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5156 :tutorial/title "The Domain of a Radical Function With an Even Index"} :step/id #uuid "84378b6c-1015-5abf-b009-0b4084dc93cd" :step/math-academy-id 32413 :step/next {:db/id 17592186116232}} {:db/id 17592186116255 :step/content {:db/id 17592186115330 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186115149 :question/id #uuid "6c380798-9b3a-5d9d-96dc-d858d737e577" :question/math-academy-id "e-8720"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "d78b6269-6217-5e55-a551-aeb079c111cd" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049528}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186115984} {:db/id 17592186115987}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Domain of a Transformed Radical Function With an Odd Index"} :step/id #uuid "243ee844-2c59-5aff-9483-b018bbc24862" :step/math-academy-id 32416 :step/next {:db/id 17592186116254}}] :activity/title "The Domain of a Transformed Radical Function" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186115428} {:db/id 17592186116231 :step/content {:db/id 17592186116535 :tutorial/content "In general, the domain of a radical function

Which of the following is a fundamental matrix for the system?" :question/worked-solution "Given a linear system ${x}^{′}=Ax,$ where $A$ is an $n\times n$ matrix, a *fundamental matrix* $Φ(t)$ of the system is an $n\times n$ matrix whose columns are linearly independent solutions of the system.

In our case, we have a $2\times 2$ system. We are also given that the two linearly independent solutions of the system are the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-t}=\begin{bmatrix}2{e}^{-t} \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\ {x}_{2}(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}2t \\ 1\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-t}=\begin{bmatrix}2t{e}^{-t} \\ {e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, our fundamental could be written as

$$
Φ(t)=\begin{bmatrix}2{e}^{-t} & 2t{e}^{-t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

**Note:** The columns of $Φ$ can be written in any order."} {:db/id 17592186442556 :question/id #uuid "0f204e80-4d56-5e54-8e44-fafc75ad1af8" :question/math-academy-id "q-334325"} {:db/id A derivation showing that every solution $x(t)$ can be written in the form $x(t)=Φ(t)\,c$ for some constant vector $c=[{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}]^{T}$ is given below.

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ be the columns of $Φ(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ form a basis of solutions

$\text{L3}:\,$ $x(t)$ can be written as $x(t)={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ $Φ(t)\,c={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t)$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $x(t)=Φ(t)\,c$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L2}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L3}$ follows from line $\text{L2}$ by {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L4}$ follows from line $\text{L1}$ by the {{field-3}}." :question/worked-solution "Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}.$ Since $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ form a basis of the solution space for our system. Thus, $\text{L2}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the $\text{definition of a fundamental matrix}.$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L2}$ and $\text{L3}.$ Once ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ form a basis, every solution $x(t)$ of the system can be expressed uniquely as a linear combination

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t).
$$

Therefore, $\text{L3}$ follows from $\text{L2}$ by $\text{the definition of a basis}.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L4}.$ Since ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ are the columns of $Φ(t),$ we can write

$$
Φ(t)=\begin{bmatrix}\,| & | \\ {x}_{1}(t) & {x}_{2}(t) \\ \,| & |\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Then by the definition of matrix multiplication,

$$
Φ(t)\,c=\begin{bmatrix}\,| & | \\ {x}_{1}(t) & {x}_{2}(t) \\ \,| & |\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{bmatrix}={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t).
$$

Thus, $\text{L4}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the $\text{definition of matrix multiplication}.$"} {:db/id 17592186311648 :question/id #uuid "3d9725c1-fcc5-57a9-8b5a-bd5efbda8207" *Hint: $[a,\,b]$ denotes a matrix whose columns are vectors $a$ and $b.$*

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let $Φ(t)=[{x}_{1}(t),\,{x}_{2}(t)]$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{1}^{′}(t)=A{x}_{1}(t)$

$\text{L3}:\,$ ${x}_{2}^{′}(t)=A{x}_{2}(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}(t)=[{x}_{1}^{′}(t),\,{x}_{2}^{′}(t)]$

$\text{L5}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}(t)=[A{x}_{1}(t),\,A{x}_{2}(t)]$

$\text{L6}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}(t)=A[{x}_{1}(t),\,{x}_{2}(t)]$

$\text{L7}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}(t)=AΦ(t)$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L3}$ follows from the fact that {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L7}$ follows from line $\text{L6}$ and substitution from line {{field-3}}." :question/worked-solution "Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider line $\text{L3}.$ Since $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ are linearly independent solutions of the homogeneous system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t).$ This means that each column satisfies the differential equation. In particular, 

$$
{x}_{2}^{′}(t)=A{x}_{2}(t).
$$

Therefore, $\text{L3}$ follows from the fact that ${x}_{2}\text{ is a solution of the system}.$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L4}$ and $\text{L5}.$ By definition, the derivative of $Φ(t)$ is obtained by differentiating each column,

$$
{Φ}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}\,| & | \\ {x}_{1}^{′}(t) & {x}_{2}^{′}(t) \\ \,| & |\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Using ${x}_{1}^{′}(t)=A{x}_{1}(t)$ from $\text{L2}$ and ${x}_{2}^{′}(t)=A{x}_{2}(t)$ from $\text{L3},$ we substitute each derivative into the matrix to get

$$
{Φ}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}\,| & | \\ A{x}_{1}(t) & A{x}_{2}(t) \\ \,| & |\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Thus, $\text{L5}$ follows from $\text{L4}$ by substitution from $\text{L2}\text{ and }\text{L3}.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L6}$ and $\text{L7}.$ From $\text{L6}$ we have

$$
{Φ}^{′}(t)=A[{x}_{1}(t),\,{x}_{2}(t)].
$$

Using the definition $Φ(t)=[{x}_{1}(t),\,{x}_{2}(t)]$ from $\text{L1},$ we substitute to obtain

$$
{Φ}^{′}(t)=AΦ(t).
$$

Thus, $\text{L7}$ follows from $\text{L6}$ by substitution from $\text{L1}.$"} {:db/id 17592186391264 :question/id #uuid "49e5968a-1ea4-5510-81b8-9a383e60e6d7" :question/math-academy-id "q-333719"} </tr></tbody></table>" :question/worked-solution "Suppose $A$ is a constant $n\times n$ matrix and $x(t)$ is an $n\times 1$ column vector. The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ denoted ${Φ}_{0}(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem 

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]t+{\alpha }_{0}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & {\alpha }_{1}t \\ 0 & 2{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The only eigenvalue of $At$ is 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=2t
$$

of multiplicity two. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}r(2t)={e}^{2t} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\lambda }r(2t)={e}^{2t}\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}2t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{2t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}={e}^{2t}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- From the second equation, we get

$$
{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{2t}.
$$

- Substituting this into the first one, we get

$$
2t{e}^{2t}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{2t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{2t}(1-2t).
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}2{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =2{e}^{2t}t+{e}^{2t}(1-2t) \\  & ={e}^{2t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}t & ={e}^{2t}t \\  & =t{e}^{2t}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t} & t{e}^{2t} \\ 0 & {e}^{2t}\end{aligned}].
$$"} {:db/id 17592186221989 :question/id #uuid "5ca7cf8a-29b9-5dc9-9eb7-2eb98441be57" :question/math-academy-id "q-333713"} {:db/id 17592186308497 :question/id #uuid "eff0b088-3db3-5966-a1d7-4ea54d40635c" :question/math-academy-id "q-333715" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186221422 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "66c99cda-25a5-50f2-903b-bfb1fdc5fa10" :knowledge-point/title "Computing Fundamental Matrices Using Matrix Exponentials"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "e2ca6901-556b-5960-a3bd-8d0552587579" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "{e}^{2t}-{e}^{-2t}" :db/id 17592186307252}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "e2ca6901-556b-5960-a3bd-8d0552587579" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "{e}^{2t}-{e}^{-2t}" :db/id 17592186307252} :answer-field/id #uuid "09352193-2085-5ed0-9dac-3b45c1b2f367" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492 :db/ident :answer-field.type/blank} :db/id 17592186307553} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2961f6c2-30e1-5479-98d1-86e05fd1e48e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "{e}^{2t}-{e}^{-2t}" :db/id 17592186305541}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "2961f6c2-30e1-5479-98d1-86e05fd1e48e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "{e}^{2t}-{e}^{-2t}" :db/id 17592186305541} :answer-field/id #uuid "743ad797-c4e6-5a90-81e7-9503d1668174" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492 :db/ident :answer-field.type/blank} :db/id 17592186307887}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "$$

The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ denoted ${Φ}_{0}(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem 

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}0 & 2 \\ 2 & 0\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{\alpha }_{0} & 2{\alpha }_{1}t \\ 2{\alpha }_{1}t & {\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=-2t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=2t,
$$

both of multiplicity one. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}r(-2t) &={e}^{-2t} \\ r(2t) &={e}^{2t}\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}-2t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{-2t} \\ 2t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{2t}\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- Subtraction the second equation from the first one, we get

$$
-4t{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{-2t}-{e}^{2t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{1}=-\frac{1}{4t}({e}^{-2t}-{e}^{2t}).
$$

- Adding the first and the second equations, we get

$$
2{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-2t}+{e}^{2t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}=\frac{1}{2}({e}^{-2t}+{e}^{2t}).
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{-2t}+{e}^{2t}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{2t}+{e}^{-2t}) \\ 2{\alpha }_{1}t & =2\cdot (-\frac{1}{4t}({e}^{-4t}-{e}^{4t}))t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{2t}-{e}^{-2t})\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{2t}+{e}^{-2t} & {e}^{2t}-{e}^{-2t} \\ {e}^{2t}-{e}^{-2t} & {e}^{2t}+{e}^{-2t}\end{bmatrix}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186308609 :question/id #uuid "64533ce4-1ae9-513d-ba89-484c2cf3a62c" :question/math-academy-id "q-334382" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "5d8223f6-d576-5e04-89fc-1464abef50dd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\operatorname{sin}(5t)" :db/id 17592186306050}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186306050} :answer-field/id #uuid "0cae7130-92fe-567b-b98b-6f508a21ed99" :answer-field/key "field-3" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186307569} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "c3417787-0b37-54ba-b621-e6d55ac43b3d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{sin}(5t)" :db/id 17592186306971}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186306971} :answer-field/id #uuid "5c20d515-1f48-5aec-946c-716105bcbbf0" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186307810} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "dfed4f33-2d1f-51a1-a259-d0e2ac8c0f8d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{cos}(5t)" :db/id 17592186307224}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186307224} :answer-field/id #uuid "e6a5f5a6-0b5f-5445-b33d-5f25bda05525" :answer-field/key "field-4" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186308251} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "057dc0c1-9b91-5408-bfb2-87575fdd4609" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\operatorname{cos}(5t)" :db/id 17592186305200}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186305200} :answer-field/id #uuid "f8d91ade-2020-5dea-8c9b-3e7b3560fbbb" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186308313}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "$$

$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=-3t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=3t,
$$

both of multiplicity one. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}r(-3t) &={e}^{-3t} \\ r(3t) &={e}^{3t}\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}-3t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{-3t} \\ 3t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{3t}\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
-6t{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{-3t}-{e}^{3t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{1}=-\frac{1}{6t}({e}^{-3t}-{e}^{3t}).
$$

- Adding the first and the second equations, we get

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$
{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{5t}.

"$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 7\end{bmatrix}
$$

Consider the system of linear ODEs ${x}^{′}=Ax$ with the matrix $A$ shown above. Compute the **standard** fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ for this system.

<table align="l" cellpadding="0" rules="all">
<tbody><tr>
<td align="center" height="30px" rowspan="2">${Φ}_{0}(t)=\,\,$</td>
<td align="center" height="40px" width="5px"></td>
<td align="center" width="40px">{{field-1}}</td>
<td align="center" width="40px">{{field-2}}</td>
<td align="center" width="5px"></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td align="center"></td>
<td align="center">{{field-3}}</td>
<td align="center" width="30px">{{field-4}}</td>
<td align="center"></td>
</tr>
</tbody></table>" :question/worked-solution "Suppose $A$ is a constant $n\times n$ matrix and $x(t)$ is an $n\times 1$ column vector. The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ denoted ${Φ}_{0}(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem 

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus,

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 7\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & 0 \\ 0 & 7{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=4t\,\text{and}\,{\lambda }_{2}=7t
$$

each of multiplicity one. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}r(4t) &={e}^{4t} \\ r(7t) &={e}^{7t}\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}4t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{4t} \\ 7t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{7t}\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- Subtract the first equation from the second one, we get

$$
{\alpha }_{1}=\frac{{e}^{7t}-{e}^{4t}}{3t}.
$$

- Substituting this into the first equation, we get

$$
4t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{4t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}=\frac{7{e}^{4t}-4{e}^{7t}}{3}.
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the diagonal entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =4\cdot \frac{{e}^{7t}-{e}^{4t}}{3t}\cdot t+\frac{7{e}^{4t}-4{e}^{7t}}{3} \\  & ={e}^{4t} \\ 7{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =7\cdot \frac{{e}^{7t}-{e}^{4t}}{3t}\cdot t+\frac{7{e}^{4t}-4{e}^{7t}}{3} \\  & ={e}^{7t}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{4t} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{7t}\end{bmatrix}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186534093 :question/id #uuid "f69ba2b0-76ef-5087-a5bf-906e0adf24a4" :question/math-academy-id "q-334388" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3a54e01d-d3da-520d-a71e-fb2b3d3a8bd9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "e^{6t}+e^{-6t}" :db/id 17592186533275}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186533275} :answer-field/id #uuid "1ec158fd-889b-5066-b795-fdf52e06926c" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186533801} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "f40c120d-2ef8-574c-b604-70f11f9600d4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "e^{6t}+e^{-6t}" :db/id 17592186533740}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186533740} :answer-field/id #uuid "5ac691a2-04d5-52ef-bc49-8d3327cd84e3" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186533851}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "$$
A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 6 \\ 6 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the system of linear ODEs ${x}^{′}=Ax$ with the matrix $A$ shown above. Compute the **standard** fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ for this system.

<tbody><tr>
<td align="center" height="30px" rowspan="2">${Φ}_{0}(t)=\frac{1}{2}\,\,$</td>
<td align="center" height="40px" width="5px"></td>
<td align="center" width="80px">{{field-1}}</td>
<td align="center" width="80px">${e}^{6t}-{e}^{-6t}$</td>
<td align="center" width="5px"></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td align="center"></td>
<td align="center" width="80px">${e}^{6t}-{e}^{-6t}$</td>
<td align="center" width="80px">{{field-2}}</td>
<td align="center"></td>
</tr></tbody></table>" :question/worked-solution "Suppose $A$ is a constant $n\times n$ matrix and $x(t)$ is an $n\times 1$ column vector. The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ denoted ${Φ}_{0}(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem 

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}[\begin{aligned}0 & 6 \\ 6 & 0\end{aligned}]t+{\alpha }_{0}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} & 6{\alpha }_{1}t \\ 6{\alpha }_{1}t & {\alpha }_{0}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=-6t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=6t,
$$

each of multiplicity one. Thus, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}r(-6t)={e}^{-6t} \\ r(6t)={e}^{6t}\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}-6t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-6t} \\ 6t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{6t}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- Subtracting the second equation from the first one, we get

$$
-12t{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{-6t}-{e}^{6t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{1}=-\frac{1}{12t}({e}^{-6t}-{e}^{6t}).
$$

- Adding the first and the second equations, we get

$$
2{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-6t}+{e}^{6t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}=\frac{1}{2}({e}^{-6t}+{e}^{6t}).
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{-6t}+{e}^{6t}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{6t}+{e}^{-6t}) \\ 6{\alpha }_{1}t & =6\cdot (-\frac{1}{12t}({e}^{-6t}-{e}^{6t}))t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{6t}-{e}^{-6t})\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{6t}+{e}^{-6t} & {e}^{6t}-{e}^{-6t} \\ {e}^{6t}-{e}^{-6t} & {e}^{6t}+{e}^{-6t}\end{aligned}].
$$"} {:db/id 17592186048231} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "e2ca6901-556b-5960-a3bd-8d0552587579" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value :topic/math-academy-id 6376} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186222332 :step/content {:db/id 17592186222502 :tutorial/content "Consider the homogeneous linear system

$$
\mathbf{x}' = A\mathbf{x},
$$

where $A$ is an $n\times n$ matrix.

A **fundamental matrix** for this system is an $n\times n$ matrix $\Phi(t)$ whose columns are $n$ linearly independent solutions of the system.

If $\mathbf{x}_1(t),\dots,\mathbf{x}_n(t)$ are linearly independent solutions, then one fundamental matrix is

$$
\Phi(t)=\big[\mathbf{x}_1(t),\dots,\mathbf{x}_n(t)\big].
$$

**Note:** The columns of $\Phi(t)$ can be written in any order.

Let's see an example." :tutorial/id #uuid "a7207a24-194d-59d6-b25c-f9bb4f1b0d6e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14508 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "3b0bd285-b383-5ebb-821f-4f74a0b37719" :step/math-academy-id 594316 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222333}} {:db/id 17592186222333 :step/content {:db/id 17592186221420 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186221191 :question/id #uuid "4874a486-2cf1-5b6e-ae4f-52579f03b077" :question/math-academy-id "e-21695"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "af871f3d-da9e-5fd3-a61f-94e155ccf2b3" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049851}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186221985} {:db/id 17592186221999} {:db/id 17592186308599} {:db/id 17592186308600} {:db/id 17592186308601} {:db/id 17592186398781} {:db/id 17592186442556} {:db/id 17592186442557} {:db/id 17592186442562}] :knowledge-point/title "Constructing a Fundamental Matrix"} :step/id #uuid "aa3c7790-3ab9-5519-bad3-4f82fc8ac113" :step/math-academy-id 594317 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222334}} {:db/id 17592186222334 :step/content {:db/id 17592186222503 :tutorial/content "Again, let $\Phi(t)$ be a fundamental matrix for the linear system

$$
\mathbf{x}' = A\mathbf{x},
$$

where $A$ is an $n\times n$ matrix. The fundamental matrices have the following important properties.

1\. *Satisfies the underlying system*. Indeed, since each column of $\Phi(t)$ is a solution of the system, we have

  $$
  \Phi'(t) = A\,\Phi(t).
  $$

2\. *Invertibility*. The columns of $\Phi(t)$ are linearly independent for all $t,$ so

  $$
  \det\Phi(t)\neq 0
  $$

  for all $t.$ In particular, $\Phi(t)$ is invertible for all $t.$

3\. *Representation of solutions*. Every solution $\mathbf{x}(t)$ of the system can be written in the form

  $$
  \mathbf{x}(t)=\Phi(t)\,\mathbf{c},
  $$

  where $\mathbf{c}$ is a constant vector.

4\. *Non-uniqueness*. If $C$ is any invertible constant matrix, then

  $$
  \Psi(t)=\Phi(t)\,C
  $$

  is also a fundamental matrix for the same system.

We'll now get some practice." :tutorial/id #uuid "e2fdbc29-4542-5fdc-adbd-316c5dcb6878" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14509 :tutorial/title "Properties of the Fundamental Matrix"} :step/id #uuid "2fe7252e-7fc7-59bb-bc32-74c452b7cf73" :step/math-academy-id 594320 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222335}} {:db/id 17592186222335 :step/content {:db/id 17592186221421 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186221193 :question/id #uuid "a52a6539-60d1-557c-a042-cbce5616e94f" :question/math-academy-id "e-21697"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "0aea7503-74d6-5ba4-9411-ee53e59512d0" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186221990} {:db/id 17592186221991} {:db/id 17592186311648} {:db/id 17592186311687} {:db/id 17592186365731} {:db/id 17592186391264} {:db/id 17592186396895} {:db/id 17592186396916} {:db/id 17592186442561} {:db/id 17592186498522} {:db/id 17592186498584} {:db/id 17592186533984}] :knowledge-point/title "Proving Properties of a Fundamental Matrix"} :step/id #uuid "2b90cd12-9695-5b6b-b407-6eed6ae7fc84" :step/math-academy-id 594321 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222336}} {:db/id 17592186222336 :step/content {:db/id 17592186222504 :tutorial/content "For a linear system $\mathbf{x}' = A\mathbf{x}$ with constant $n\times n$ matrix $A,$ the **standard fundamental matrix** is the unique fundamental matrix $\Phi_0(t)$ that satisfies the initial condition

$$
\Phi_0(0)=I_n,
$$

where $I_n$ is the $n \times n$ identity matrix.

For constant matrices $A,$ the standard fundamental matrix is given by

$$
\Phi_0(t)=e^{At}.
$$

This matrix satisfies

$$
\Phi_0'(t)=A\,\Phi_0(t)
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\Phi_0(0)=I_n.
$$

**Note:** Any other fundamental matrix $\Phi(t)$ for the same system can be written in the form

$$
\Phi(t)=\Phi_0(t)\,C,
$$

$$
\mathbf{x}' = A\mathbf{x},
$$

where $A$ is an $n\times n$ matrix. The fundamental matrices have the following important properties.

1\. *Satisfies the underlying system*. Indeed, since each column of $\Phi(t)$ is a solution of the system, we have

  $$
  \Phi'(t) = A\,\Phi(t).
  $$

2\. *Invertibility*. The columns of $\Phi(t)$ are linearly independent for all $t,$ so

  $$
  \det\Phi(t)\neq 0
  $$

  for all $t.$ In particular, $\Phi(t)$ is invertible for all $t.$

3\. *Representation of solutions*. Every solution $\mathbf{x}(t)$ of the system can be written in the form

  $$
  \mathbf{x}(t)=\Phi(t)\,\mathbf{c},
  $$

  where $\mathbf{c}$ is a constant vector.

4\. *Non-uniqueness*. If $C$ is any invertible constant matrix, then

  $$
  \Psi(t)=\Phi(t)\,C
  $$

  is also a fundamental matrix for the same system.

$$
\Phi_0(0)=I_n,
$$

where $I_n$ is the $n \times n$ identity matrix.

For constant matrices $A,$ the standard fundamental matrix is given by

$$
\Phi_0(t)=e^{At}.
$$

This matrix satisfies

$$
\Phi_0'(t)=A\,\Phi_0(t)
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\Phi_0(0)=I_n.
$$

**Note:** Any other fundamental matrix $\Phi(t)$ for the same system can be written in the form

$$
\Phi(t)=\Phi_0(t)\,C,
$$

where $C$ is an invertible constant matrix.

In the next slide, we will compute the standard fundamental matrix for a specific example." :tutorial/id #uuid "4f75576c-be32-5784-9fee-e1288445728c" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14510 :tutorial/title "Fundamental Matrices and Matrix Exponentials"} :step/id #uuid "d44c84d5-4215-5318-bba2-81eb3a34ee7d" :step/math-academy-id 594325 :step/next {:db/id 17592186222337}} {:db/id 17592186222504 :tutorial/content "For a linear system $\mathbf{x}' = A\mathbf{x}$ with constant $n\times n$ matrix $A,$ the **standard fundamental matrix** is the unique fundamental matrix $\Phi_0(t)$ that satisfies the initial condition

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus,

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 7\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & 0 \\ 0 & 7{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=4t\,\text{and}\,{\lambda }_{2}=7t
$$

each of multiplicity one. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}r(4t) &={e}^{4t} \\ r(7t) &={e}^{7t}\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}4t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{4t} \\ 7t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{7t}\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- Subtract the first equation from the second one, we get

$$
{\alpha }_{1}=\frac{{e}^{7t}-{e}^{4t}}{3t}.
$$

- Substituting this into the first equation, we get

$$
4t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{4t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}=\frac{7{e}^{4t}-4{e}^{7t}}{3}.
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the diagonal entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =4\cdot \frac{{e}^{7t}-{e}^{4t}}{3t}\cdot t+\frac{7{e}^{4t}-4{e}^{7t}}{3} \\  & ={e}^{4t} \\ 7{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =7\cdot \frac{{e}^{7t}-{e}^{4t}}{3t}\cdot t+\frac{7{e}^{4t}-4{e}^{7t}}{3} \\  & ={e}^{7t}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{4t} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{7t}\end{bmatrix}.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "3ad30acf-66b9-5977-ad36-2183bb8c58c8" :step/next {:db/id 17592186498619}} {:db/id 17592186498623 :step/content {:db/id 17592186365659 :question/answer-fields $$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}0 & -6 \\ 6 & 0\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{\alpha }_{0} & -6{\alpha }_{1}t \\ 6{\alpha }_{1}t & {\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=6\text{i}t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=-6\text{i}t,
$$

which are complex conjugates. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r((6\text{i})t) & ={e}^{(6\text{i})t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}(6\text{i})t+{\alpha }_{0} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t) \\ {\alpha }_{0}+6\text{i}{\alpha }_{1}t & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we equate the real and imaginary parts, and solve for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} &=\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) \\ 6{\alpha }_{1}t &=\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} &=\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) \\ {\alpha }_{1} &=\frac{1}{6t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) \\ 6{\alpha }_{1}t & =6\cdot \frac{1}{6t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\cdot t \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) & -\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(6t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)\end{bmatrix}.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "3ea51f6a-6ea8-5162-ad6a-900689393007" :step/next {:db/id 17592186498620}} {:db/id 17592186498653 :step/content {:db/id 17592186498584 :question/answer-fields {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "d656b9e3-27c9-51a6-a70f-c9d56643be83" :question/math-academy-id "q-336108" :question/problem "Consider the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant $2\times 2$ matrix. Let $Φ(t)$ be a fundamental matrix for this system. A derivation showing that every solution $x(t)$ can be written in the form $x(t)=Φ(t)\,c$ for some constant vector $c=[{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}]^{T}$ is given below.

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ be the columns of $Φ(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ form a basis of solutions

$\text{L3}:\,$ $x(t)$ can be written as $x(t)={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ $Φ(t)\,c={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t)$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $x(t)=Φ(t)\,c$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L3}$ follows from line $\text{L2}$ by {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L4}$ follows from line $\text{L1}$ by the {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L5}$ follows from lines {{field-3}} by the transitive property of equality." :question/worked-solution "Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider lines $\text{L2}$ and $\text{L3}.$ Once ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ form a basis, every solution $x(t)$ of the system can be expressed uniquely as a linear combination

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t).
$$

Therefore, $\text{L3}$ follows from $\text{L2}$ by $\text{the definition of a basis}.$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L4}.$ Since ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ are the columns of $Φ(t),$ we can write

$$
Φ(t)=\begin{bmatrix}\,| & | \\ {x}_{1}(t) & {x}_{2}(t) \\ \,| & |\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Then by the definition of matrix multiplication,

$$
Φ(t)\,c=\begin{bmatrix}\,| & | \\ {x}_{1}(t) & {x}_{2}(t) \\ \,| & |\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{bmatrix}={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t).
$$

Thus, $\text{L4}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the $\text{definition of matrix multiplication}.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L3}$ and $\text{L4}.$ In $\text{L3}$ we have $x(t)={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t),$ and in $\text{L4}$ we have $Φ(t)c={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t).$ Since both expressions are equal to the same quantity, the transitive property of equality gives $x(t)=Φ(t)c.$ Thus, $\text{L5}$ follows from $\text{L3 and L4}.$"} :step/id #uuid \begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}0 & -6 \\ 6 & 0\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{\alpha }_{0} & -6{\alpha }_{1}t \\ 6{\alpha }_{1}t & {\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=6\text{i}t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=-6\text{i}t,
$$

which are complex conjugates. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r((6\text{i})t) & ={e}^{(6\text{i})t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}(6\text{i})t+{\alpha }_{0} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t) \\ {\alpha }_{0}+6\text{i}{\alpha }_{1}t & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we equate the real and imaginary parts, and solve for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} &=\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) \\ 6{\alpha }_{1}t &=\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} &=\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) \\ {\alpha }_{1} &=\frac{1}{6t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) \\ 6{\alpha }_{1}t & =6\cdot \frac{1}{6t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\cdot t \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6t) & -\operatorname{sin}⁡(6t) \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(6t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(6t)\end{bmatrix}.

A derivation showing that every solution $x(t)$ can be written in the form $x(t)=Φ(t)\,c$ for some constant vector $c=[{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}]^{T}$ is given below.

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ be the columns of $Φ(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ form a basis of solutions

$\text{L3}:\,$ $x(t)$ can be written as $x(t)={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ $Φ(t)\,c={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t)$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $x(t)=Φ(t)\,c$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L3}$ follows from line $\text{L2}$ by {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L4}$ follows from line $\text{L1}$ by the {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L5}$ follows from lines {{field-3}} by the transitive property of equality." :question/worked-solution "Let's justify each of the selected steps.

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t).
$$

Therefore, $\text{L3}$ follows from $\text{L2}$ by $\text{the definition of a basis}.$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L4}.$ Since ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ are the columns of $Φ(t),$ we can write

$$
Φ(t)=\begin{bmatrix}\,| & | \\ {x}_{1}(t) & {x}_{2}(t) \\ \,| & |\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Then by the definition of matrix multiplication,

$$
Φ(t)\,c=\begin{bmatrix}\,| & | \\ {x}_{1}(t) & {x}_{2}(t) \\ \,| & |\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{bmatrix}={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t).
$$

Thus, $\text{L4}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the $\text{definition of matrix multiplication}.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L3}$ and $\text{L4}.$ In $\text{L3}$ we have $x(t)={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t),$ and in $\text{L4}$ we have $Φ(t)c={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t).$ Since both expressions are equal to the same quantity, the transitive property of equality gives $x(t)=Φ(t)c.$ Thus, $\text{L5}$ follows from $\text{L3 and L4}.$"} :step/id #uuid Let $Φ(t)$ be a fundamental matrix for this system. A derivation showing that $Φ(t)$ is invertible for all $t$ is given below.

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ be the columns of $Φ(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ are linearly independent for all $t$

$\text{L3}:\,$ $det(Φ(t))\ne 0$ for all $t$

$\text{L4}:\,$ $Φ(t)$ is invertible for all $t$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L1}$ introduces the notation for the {{field-1}} of {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L2}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the {{field-3}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L4}$ follows from line {{field-4}} by the properties of invertible matrices." :question/worked-solution "Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first interpret line $\text{L1}.$ Line $\text{L1}$ introduces the notation for the $\text{columns}$ of $Φ,$ namely the functions ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t).$ These functions are the fundamental solutions of the system.

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}.$ Since $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ form a basis of the solution space for our system. Thus, $\text{L2}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the $\text{definition of a fundamental matrix}.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L3}$ and $\text{L4}.$ Recall that a square matrix is invertible when its determinant is nonzero. A=\begin{bmatrix}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 7\end{bmatrix}
$$

Consider the system of linear ODEs ${x}^{′}=Ax$ with the matrix $A$ shown above. Compute the **standard** fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ for this system.

<tbody><tr>
<td align="center" height="30px" rowspan="2">${Φ}_{0}(t)=\,\,$</td>
<td align="center" height="40px" width="5px"></td>
<td align="center" width="40px">{{field-1}}</td>
<td align="center" width="40px">{{field-2}}</td>
<td align="center" width="5px"></td>
</tr>

<td align="center">{{field-3}}</td>
<td align="center" width="30px">{{field-4}}</td>

</tbody></table>" :question/worked-solution "Suppose $A$ is a constant $n\times n$ matrix and $x(t)$ is an $n\times 1$ column vector. The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ denoted ${Φ}_{0}(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem 

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus,

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 7\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & 0 \\ 0 & 7{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=4t\,\text{and}\,{\lambda }_{2}=7t
$$

each of multiplicity one. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}r(4t) &={e}^{4t} \\ r(7t) &={e}^{7t}\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}4t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{4t} \\ 7t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{7t}\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- Subtract the first equation from the second one, we get

$$
{\alpha }_{1}=\frac{{e}^{7t}-{e}^{4t}}{3t}.
$$

- Substituting this into the first equation, we get

$$
4t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{4t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}=\frac{7{e}^{4t}-4{e}^{7t}}{3}.
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the diagonal entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =4\cdot \frac{{e}^{7t}-{e}^{4t}}{3t}\cdot t+\frac{7{e}^{4t}-4{e}^{7t}}{3} \\  & ={e}^{4t} \\ 7{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =7\cdot \frac{{e}^{7t}-{e}^{4t}}{3t}\cdot t+\frac{7{e}^{4t}-4{e}^{7t}}{3} \\  & ={e}^{7t}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{4t} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{7t}\end{bmatrix}.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "3ad30acf-66b9-5977-ad36-2183bb8c58c8" :step/next {:db/id 17592186498619}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "dae93f70-eae4-559e-a461-fdfe0abd280a" :answer/type {:db/id Let $Φ(t)$ be a fundamental matrix for this system. A derivation showing that $Φ(t)$ is invertible for all $t$ is given below.

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ be the columns of $Φ(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ are linearly independent for all $t$

$\text{L3}:\,$ $det(Φ(t))\ne 0$ for all $t$

$\text{L4}:\,$ $Φ(t)$ is invertible for all $t$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

- We first interpret line $\text{L1}.$ Line $\text{L1}$ introduces the notation for the $\text{columns}$ of $Φ,$ namely the functions ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t).$ These functions are the fundamental solutions of the system.

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}.$ Since $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ form a basis of the solution space for our system. Thus, $\text{L2}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the $\text{definition of a fundamental matrix}.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L2}$ and $\text{L3}.$ Recall that a matrix has linearly independent columns if and only if its determinant is nonzero. Since ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ are linearly independent for any particular $t,$

det(Φ(t))\ne 0.
$$

Which of the following is a fundamental matrix for the system?" :question/worked-solution "Given a linear system ${x}^{′}=Ax,$ where $A$ is an $n\times n$ matrix, a *fundamental matrix* $Φ(t)$ of the system is an $n\times n$ matrix whose columns are linearly independent solutions of the system.

In our case, we have a $2\times 2$ system. We are also given that the two linearly independent solutions of the system are the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-t}=\begin{bmatrix}2{e}^{-t} \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\ {x}_{2}(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}2t \\ 1\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-t}=\begin{bmatrix}2t{e}^{-t} \\ {e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, our fundamental could be written as

$$
Φ(t)=\begin{bmatrix}2{e}^{-t} & 2t{e}^{-t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

**Note:** The columns of $Φ$ can be written in any order."} :step/id #uuid "24523b4e-4e57-53cd-8b40-7f56c7c2589e" :step/next {:db/id 17592186534142}} {:db/id 17592186534127 :step/content {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "7179862e-a345-5508-93d4-73732015d190" :question/math-academy-id "q-333723" :question/problem "Consider the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant $2\times 2$ matrix. Let $Φ(t)$ be a fundamental matrix for this system. A derivation showing that every solution $x(t)$ can be written in the form $x(t)=Φ(t)\,c$ for some constant vector $c=[{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}]^{T}$ is given below.

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ be the columns of $Φ(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ form a basis of solutions

$\text{L3}:\,$ $x(t)$ can be written as $x(t)={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ $Φ(t)\,c={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t)$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $x(t)=Φ(t)\,c$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L2}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L3}$ follows from line $\text{L2}$ by {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L4}$ follows from line $\text{L1}$ by the {{field-3}}." :question/worked-solution "Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}.$ Since $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ form a basis of the solution space for our system. Thus, $\text{L2}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the $\text{definition of a fundamental matrix}.$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L2}$ and $\text{L3}.$ Once ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ form a basis, every solution $x(t)$ of the system can be expressed uniquely as a linear combination

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t).
$$

Therefore, $\text{L3}$ follows from $\text{L2}$ by $\text{the definition of a basis}.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L4}.$ Since ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ are the columns of $Φ(t),$ we can write

$$
Φ(t)=\begin{bmatrix}\,| & | \\ {x}_{1}(t) & {x}_{2}(t) \\ \,| & |\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Then by the definition of matrix multiplication,

$$
Φ(t)\,c=\begin{bmatrix}\,| & | \\ {x}_{1}(t) & {x}_{2}(t) \\ \,| & |\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{bmatrix}={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t).
$$

The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ denoted ${Φ}_{0}(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem 

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}-4 & 1 \\ 0 & -4\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-4{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & {\alpha }_{1}t \\ 0 & -4{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The only eigenvalue of $At$ is 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=-4t
$$

of multiplicity two. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}r(-4t) &={e}^{-4t} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\lambda }r(-4t) &={e}^{-4t}\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}-4t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{-4t} \\ {\alpha }_{1} &={e}^{-4t}\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- From the second equation, we get

$$
{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{-4t}.
$$

- Substituting this into the first one, we get

$$
-4t{e}^{-4t}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-4t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-4t}(1+4t).
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}-4{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =-4{e}^{-4t}t+{e}^{-4t}(1+4t) \\  & ={e}^{-4t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}t & ={e}^{-4t}t \\  & =t{e}^{-4t}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{-4t} & t{e}^{-4t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-4t}\end{bmatrix}.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "6372c740-c40b-54b4-b2d8-d67db30bf1d4" :step/next {:db/id 17592186534109}} {:db/id 17592186534142 :step/content {:db/id 17592186534093 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3a54e01d-d3da-520d-a71e-fb2b3d3a8bd9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "e^{6t}+e^{-6t}" :db/id 17592186533275}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186533275} :answer-field/id #uuid "1ec158fd-889b-5066-b795-fdf52e06926c" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186533801} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "f40c120d-2ef8-574c-b604-70f11f9600d4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "e^{6t}+e^{-6t}" :db/id 17592186533740}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186533740} :answer-field/id #uuid "5ac691a2-04d5-52ef-bc49-8d3327cd84e3" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186533851}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "f69ba2b0-76ef-5087-a5bf-906e0adf24a4" :question/math-academy-id "q-334388" :question/problem "$$

</tr></tbody></table>" :question/worked-solution "Suppose $A$ is a constant $n\times n$ matrix and $x(t)$ is an $n\times 1$ column vector. The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ denoted ${Φ}_{0}(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem 

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}[\begin{aligned}0 & 6 \\ 6 & 0\end{aligned}]t+{\alpha }_{0}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} & 6{\alpha }_{1}t \\ 6{\alpha }_{1}t & {\alpha }_{0}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=-6t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=6t,
$$

each of multiplicity one. Thus, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}r(-6t)={e}^{-6t} \\ r(6t)={e}^{6t}\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}-6t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-6t} \\ 6t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{6t}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- Subtracting the second equation from the first one, we get

$$
-12t{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{-6t}-{e}^{6t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{1}=-\frac{1}{12t}({e}^{-6t}-{e}^{6t}).
$$

- Adding the first and the second equations, we get

$$
2{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-6t}+{e}^{6t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}=\frac{1}{2}({e}^{-6t}+{e}^{6t}).
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{-6t}+{e}^{6t}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{6t}+{e}^{-6t}) \\ 6{\alpha }_{1}t & =6\cdot (-\frac{1}{12t}({e}^{-6t}-{e}^{6t}))t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{6t}-{e}^{-6t})\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{6t}+{e}^{-6t} & {e}^{6t}-{e}^{-6t} \\ {e}^{6t}-{e}^{-6t} & {e}^{6t}+{e}^{-6t}\end{aligned}].
$$"} :step/id #uuid "a9bd7aaf-ed47-5adf-8e37-bc1f645e1959" :step/next {:db/id 17592186534128}}] :activity/title "Fundamental Matrices" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045464 :db/ident A derivation showing that every solution $x(t)$ can be written in the form $x(t)=Φ(t)\,c$ for some constant vector $c=[{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}]^{T}$ is given below.

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ be the columns of $Φ(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ form a basis of solutions

$\text{L3}:\,$ $x(t)$ can be written as $x(t)={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ $Φ(t)\,c={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t)$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $x(t)=Φ(t)\,c$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L4}$ follows from line $\text{L1}$ by the {{field-3}}." :question/worked-solution "Let's justify each of the selected steps.

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t).
$$

Therefore, $\text{L3}$ follows from $\text{L2}$ by $\text{the definition of a basis}.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L4}.$ Since ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ are the columns of $Φ(t),$ we can write

$$
Φ(t)=\begin{bmatrix}\,| & | \\ {x}_{1}(t) & {x}_{2}(t) \\ \,| & |\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Then by the definition of matrix multiplication,

$$
Φ(t)\,c=\begin{bmatrix}\,| & | \\ {x}_{1}(t) & {x}_{2}(t) \\ \,| & |\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{c}_{1} \\ {c}_{2}\end{bmatrix}={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t).
$$

Thus, $\text{L4}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the $\text{definition of matrix multiplication}.$"} :step/id #uuid "62363ed1-22ab-56fa-9971-8c017f526c79" :step/next {:db/id 17592186534111}} {:db/id system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant $2\times 2$ matrix. Let $Φ(t)$ be a fundamental matrix for this system. A derivation showing that $Φ(t)$ is invertible for all $t$ is given below.

$\,$ Line $\text{L3}$ follows from line {{field-4}} by the properties of determinants." :question/worked-solution "Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L2}$ and $\text{L3}.$ Recall that a matrix has linearly independent columns if and only if its determinant is nonzero. Since ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ are linearly independent for any particular $t,$

Which of the following is a fundamental matrix for the system?" :question/worked-solution "Given a linear system ${x}^{′}=Ax,$ where $A$ is an $n\times n$ matrix, a *fundamental matrix* $Φ(t)$ of the system is an $n\times n$ matrix whose columns are linearly independent solutions of the system.

In our case, we have a $2\times 2$ system. We are also given that the two linearly independent solutions of the system are the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-t}=\begin{bmatrix}2{e}^{-t} \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\ {x}_{2}(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}2t \\ 1\end{bmatrix}{e}^{-t}=\begin{bmatrix}2t{e}^{-t} \\ {e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, our fundamental could be written as

$$
Φ(t)=\begin{bmatrix}2{e}^{-t} & 2t{e}^{-t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-t}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

**Note:** The columns of $Φ$ can be written in any order."} :step/id #uuid "24523b4e-4e57-53cd-8b40-7f56c7c2589e" :step/next {:db/id 17592186534142}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 6 \\ 6 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the system of linear ODEs ${x}^{′}=Ax$ with the matrix $A$ shown above. Compute the **standard** fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ for this system.

<table align="l" cellpadding="0" rules="all">
<tbody><tr>
<td align="center" height="30px" rowspan="2">${Φ}_{0}(t)=\frac{1}{2}\,\,$</td>
<td align="center" height="40px" width="5px"></td>
<td align="center" width="80px">{{field-1}}</td>
<td align="center" width="80px">${e}^{6t}-{e}^{-6t}$</td>
<td align="center" width="5px"></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td align="center"></td>
<td align="center" width="80px">${e}^{6t}-{e}^{-6t}$</td>
<td align="center" width="80px">{{field-2}}</td>
<td align="center"></td>
</tr></tbody></table>" :question/worked-solution "Suppose $A$ is a constant $n\times n$ matrix and $x(t)$ is an $n\times 1$ column vector. The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ denoted ${Φ}_{0}(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem 

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}[\begin{aligned}0 & 6 \\ 6 & 0\end{aligned}]t+{\alpha }_{0}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} & 6{\alpha }_{1}t \\ 6{\alpha }_{1}t & {\alpha }_{0}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=-6t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=6t,
$$

each of multiplicity one. Thus, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}r(-6t)={e}^{-6t} \\ r(6t)={e}^{6t}\end{aligned}\,⇒\,\{\begin{aligned}-6t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-6t} \\ 6t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{6t}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- Subtracting the second equation from the first one, we get

$$
-12t{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{-6t}-{e}^{6t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{1}=-\frac{1}{12t}({e}^{-6t}-{e}^{6t}).
$$

- Adding the first and the second equations, we get

$$
2{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-6t}+{e}^{6t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}=\frac{1}{2}({e}^{-6t}+{e}^{6t}).
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{-6t}+{e}^{6t}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{6t}+{e}^{-6t}) \\ 6{\alpha }_{1}t & =6\cdot (-\frac{1}{12t}({e}^{-6t}-{e}^{6t}))t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{6t}-{e}^{-6t})\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{6t}+{e}^{-6t} & {e}^{6t}-{e}^{-6t} \\ {e}^{6t}-{e}^{-6t} & {e}^{6t}+{e}^{-6t}\end{aligned}].
$$"} :step/id #uuid "a9bd7aaf-ed47-5adf-8e37-bc1f645e1959" :step/next {:db/id 17592186534128}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3b918900-9d47-501a-8fe9-03921f6ed92d" :answer/type {:db/id A=\begin{bmatrix}-4 & 1 \\ 0 & -4\end{bmatrix}
$$

Consider the system of linear ODEs ${x}^{′}=Ax$ with the matrix $A$ shown above. Compute the **standard** fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ for this system.

| ${Φ}_{0}(t)=\,\,$ |  | {{field-1}} | {{field-2}} |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | {{field-3}} | {{field-4}} |  |  |" :question/worked-solution "Suppose $A$ is a constant $n\times n$ matrix and $x(t)$ is an $n\times 1$ column vector. The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ denoted ${Φ}_{0}(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem 

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}-4 & 1 \\ 0 & -4\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-4{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & {\alpha }_{1}t \\ 0 & -4{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The only eigenvalue of $At$ is 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=-4t
$$

of multiplicity two. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}r(-4t) &={e}^{-4t} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\lambda }r(-4t) &={e}^{-4t}\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}-4t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{-4t} \\ {\alpha }_{1} &={e}^{-4t}\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- From the second equation, we get

$$
{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{-4t}.
$$

- Substituting this into the first one, we get

$$
-4t{e}^{-4t}+{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-4t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-4t}(1+4t).
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}-4{\alpha }_{1}t+{\alpha }_{0} & =-4{e}^{-4t}t+{e}^{-4t}(1+4t) \\  & ={e}^{-4t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}t & ={e}^{-4t}t \\  & =t{e}^{-4t}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{-4t} & t{e}^{-4t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-4t}\end{bmatrix}.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "6372c740-c40b-54b4-b2d8-d67db30bf1d4" :step/next {:db/id 17592186534109}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "5728e179-6831-5401-a928-e641db0a06b5" :answer/type {:db/id :question/problem "$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 3 \\ 3 & 0\end{bmatrix}
$$

Consider the system of linear ODEs ${x}^{′}=Ax$ with the matrix $A$ shown above. Compute the **standard** fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ for this system.

| ${Φ}_{0}(t)=\frac{1}{2}\,\,$ |  | {{field-1}} | ${e}^{3t}-{e}^{-3t}$ |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | ${e}^{3t}-{e}^{-3t}$ | {{field-2}} |  |  |" :question/worked-solution "Suppose $A$ is a constant $n\times n$ matrix and $x(t)$ is an $n\times 1$ column vector. The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ denoted ${Φ}_{0}(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem 

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}0 & 3 \\ 3 & 0\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{\alpha }_{0} & 3{\alpha }_{1}t \\ 3{\alpha }_{1}t & {\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=-3t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=3t,
$$

both of multiplicity one. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}r(-3t) &={e}^{-3t} \\ r(3t) &={e}^{3t}\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}-3t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{-3t} \\ 3t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{3t}\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- Subtracting the second equation from the first one, we get

$$
-6t{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{-3t}-{e}^{3t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{1}=-\frac{1}{6t}({e}^{-3t}-{e}^{3t}).
$$

- Adding the first and the second equations, we get

$$
2{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-3t}+{e}^{3t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}=\frac{1}{2}({e}^{-3t}+{e}^{3t}).
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{-3t}+{e}^{3t}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{3t}+{e}^{-3t}) \\ 3{\alpha }_{1}t & =3\cdot (-\frac{1}{6t}({e}^{-3t}-{e}^{3t}))t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{3t}-{e}^{-3t})\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{3t}+{e}^{-3t} & {e}^{3t}-{e}^{-3t} \\ {e}^{3t}-{e}^{-3t} & {e}^{3t}+{e}^{-3t}\end{bmatrix}.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "64943c28-d0a3-53a2-88a5-d9adefa020e7" :step/next {:db/id 17592186546015}} {:db/id 17592186545970 :step/content {:db/id 17592186365731 :question/answer-fields "9e4b9ffe-ff7e-5035-97f0-e9cfaaf038a3" :question/math-academy-id "q-336308" :question/problem "Consider the system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where $A$ is a constant $2\times 2$ matrix. Let $Φ(t)$ be a fundamental matrix for this system. A derivation showing that $Φ(t)$ satisfies the matrix differential equation ${Φ}^{′}(t)=A\,Φ(t)$ is given below.

*Hint: $[a,\,b]$ denotes a matrix whose columns are vectors $a$ and $b.$*

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let $Φ(t)=[{x}_{1}(t),\,{x}_{2}(t)]$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{1}^{′}(t)=A{x}_{1}(t)$

$\text{L3}:\,$ ${x}_{2}^{′}(t)=A{x}_{2}(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}(t)=[{x}_{1}^{′}(t),\,{x}_{2}^{′}(t)]$

$\text{L5}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}(t)=[A{x}_{1}(t),\,A{x}_{2}(t)]$

$\text{L6}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}(t)=A[{x}_{1}(t),\,{x}_{2}(t)]$

$\text{L7}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}(t)=AΦ(t)$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L3}$ follows from the fact that {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L5}$ follows from line $\text{L4}$ and substitution from lines {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L7}$ follows from line $\text{L6}$ and substitution from line {{field-3}}." :question/worked-solution "Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- We first consider line $\text{L3}.$ Since $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ are linearly independent solutions of the homogeneous system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t).$ This means that each column satisfies the differential equation. In particular, 

$$
{x}_{2}^{′}(t)=A{x}_{2}(t).
$$

Therefore, $\text{L3}$ follows from the fact that ${x}_{2}\text{ is a solution of the system}.$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L4}$ and $\text{L5}.$ By definition, the derivative of $Φ(t)$ is obtained by differentiating each column,

$$
{Φ}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}\,| & | \\ {x}_{1}^{′}(t) & {x}_{2}^{′}(t) \\ \,| & |\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Using ${x}_{1}^{′}(t)=A{x}_{1}(t)$ from $\text{L2}$ and ${x}_{2}^{′}(t)=A{x}_{2}(t)$ from $\text{L3},$ we substitute each derivative into the matrix to get

$$
{Φ}^{′}(t)=\begin{bmatrix}\,| & | \\ A{x}_{1}(t) & A{x}_{2}(t) \\ \,| & |\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Thus, $\text{L5}$ follows from $\text{L4}$ by substitution from $\text{L2}\text{ and }\text{L3}.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L6}$ and $\text{L7}.$ From $\text{L6}$ we have

$$
{Φ}^{′}(t)=A[{x}_{1}(t),\,{x}_{2}(t)].
$$

Using the definition $Φ(t)=[{x}_{1}(t),\,{x}_{2}(t)]$ from $\text{L1},$ we substitute to obtain

$$
