The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ denoted ${Φ}_{0}(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem 

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}0 & 5 \\ -5 & 0\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{\alpha }_{0} & 5{\alpha }_{1}t \\ -5{\alpha }_{1}t & {\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=5\text{i}t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=-5\text{i}t,
$$

which are complex conjugates. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r((5\text{i})t) & ={e}^{(5\text{i})t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}(5\text{i})t+{\alpha }_{0} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t) \\ {\alpha }_{0}+5\text{i}{\alpha }_{1}t & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we equate the real and imaginary parts, and solve for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} &=\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t) \\ 5{\alpha }_{1}t &=\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} &=\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t) \\ {\alpha }_{1} &=\frac{1}{5t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t) \\ 5{\alpha }_{1}t & =5\cdot \frac{1}{5t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\cdot t \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(5t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)\end{bmatrix}.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "c739f31a-33e2-5b79-9d44-a58e2e368af7" :step/next {:db/id 17592186545937}} {:db/id 17592186545985 :step/content {:db/id 17592186221988 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "4475a7f4-c95c-5c55-8109-0e9ea886a2a8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186545329}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186545329} :answer-field/id #uuid "aa786690-2dc1-59f3-a44d-639db8237f3d" :answer-field/key "field-3" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186220583} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "10f335ea-9d53-5bd8-a277-0e71096d1701" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "e^{2t}" :db/id 17592186545230}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186545230} :answer-field/id #uuid "ee77c4e2-6eb2-5db9-8618-4ba0d57d6223" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186220584} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "d4192bd6-a9b5-5e3c-a850-538acc11b68f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "e^{2t}" :db/id 17592186545587}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186545587} :answer-field/id #uuid "4f7022e0-ee16-5d5b-b4f3-9eb2d8be983b" :answer-field/key "field-4" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186220585} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "227c788b-a841-56fc-9c67-21ee4721d3f8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "te^{2t}" :db/id 17592186545272}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186545272} :answer-field/id #uuid "7c1b35ed-a68f-5e20-b0c8-7a1d98ca67ae" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186220586}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "d2008090-84f9-50fd-9af0-82b54be4b43f" :question/math-academy-id "q-333712" :question/problem "$$

$$
{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{2t}.

A derivation showing that every solution $x(t)$ can be written in the form $x(t)=Φ(t)\,c$ for some constant vector $c=[{c}_{1},\,{c}_{2}]^{T}$ is given below.

$\text{L1}:\,$ Let ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ be the columns of $Φ(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ form a basis of solutions

$\text{L3}:\,$ $x(t)$ can be written as $x(t)={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ $Φ(t)\,c={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t)$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $x(t)=Φ(t)\,c$

$\,$ Line $\text{L2}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the {{field-3}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L3}$ follows from line $\text{L2}$ by {{field-4}}." :question/worked-solution "Let's justify each of the selected steps.

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}.$ Since $Φ(t)$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ form a basis of the solution space for our system. Thus, $\text{L2}$ follows from $\text{L1}$ by the $\text{definition of a fundamental matrix}.$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L2}$ and $\text{L3}.$ Once ${x}_{1}(t)$ and ${x}_{2}(t)$ form a basis, every solution $x(t)$ of the system can be expressed uniquely as a linear combination

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{x}_{1}(t)+{c}_{2}{x}_{2}(t).
$$

A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 3 \\ 3 & 0\end{bmatrix}
$$

Consider the system of linear ODEs ${x}^{′}=Ax$ with the matrix $A$ shown above. Compute the **standard** fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ for this system.

| ${Φ}_{0}(t)=\frac{1}{2}\,\,$ |  | {{field-1}} | ${e}^{3t}-{e}^{-3t}$ |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | ${e}^{3t}-{e}^{-3t}$ | {{field-2}} |  |  |" :question/worked-solution "Suppose $A$ is a constant $n\times n$ matrix and $x(t)$ is an $n\times 1$ column vector. The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ denoted ${Φ}_{0}(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem 

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}0 & 3 \\ 3 & 0\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{\alpha }_{0} & 3{\alpha }_{1}t \\ 3{\alpha }_{1}t & {\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=-3t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=3t,
$$

both of multiplicity one. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}r(-3t) &={e}^{-3t} \\ r(3t) &={e}^{3t}\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}-3t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{-3t} \\ 3t{\alpha }_{1}+{\alpha }_{0} &={e}^{3t}\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

- Subtracting the second equation from the first one, we get

$$
-6t{\alpha }_{1}={e}^{-3t}-{e}^{3t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{1}=-\frac{1}{6t}({e}^{-3t}-{e}^{3t}).
$$

- Adding the first and the second equations, we get

$$
2{\alpha }_{0}={e}^{-3t}+{e}^{3t}\,⇒\,{\alpha }_{0}=\frac{1}{2}({e}^{-3t}+{e}^{3t}).
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{-3t}+{e}^{3t}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{3t}+{e}^{-3t}) \\ 3{\alpha }_{1}t & =3\cdot (-\frac{1}{6t}({e}^{-3t}-{e}^{3t}))t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({e}^{3t}-{e}^{-3t})\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}{e}^{3t}+{e}^{-3t} & {e}^{3t}-{e}^{-3t} \\ {e}^{3t}-{e}^{-3t} & {e}^{3t}+{e}^{-3t}\end{bmatrix}.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "64943c28-d0a3-53a2-88a5-d9adefa020e7" :step/next {:db/id 17592186546015}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2b642857-d5c7-5354-9582-e84b796c8d0c" :answer/type {:db/id :question/math-academy-id "q-334382" :question/problem "$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 5 \\ -5 & 0\end{bmatrix}
$$

Consider the system of linear ODEs ${x}^{′}=Ax$ with the matrix $A$ shown above. Compute the **standard** fundamental matrix ${Φ}_{0}(t)$ for this system.

| ${Φ}_{0}(t)=\,\,$ |  | {{field-1}} | {{field-2}} |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | {{field-3}} | {{field-4}} |  |  |" :question/worked-solution "Suppose $A$ is a constant $n\times n$ matrix and $x(t)$ is an $n\times 1$ column vector. The standard fundamental matrix of the linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ denoted ${Φ}_{0}(t),$ is the unique matrix solution of the initial value problem 

$$
{Φ}_{0}^{′}(t)=A{Φ}_{0}(t),\,{Φ}_{0}(0)={I}_{n},
$$

where ${I}_{n}$ is the identity matrix. 

Furthermore, it can be shown that ${Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}.$

We have a square matrix of dimension $n=2.$ Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{At} & ={\alpha }_{1}At+{\alpha }_{0}I \\  & ={\alpha }_{1}\begin{bmatrix}0 & 5 \\ -5 & 0\end{bmatrix}t+{\alpha }_{0}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{\alpha }_{0} & 5{\alpha }_{1}t \\ -5{\alpha }_{1}t & {\alpha }_{0}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

where ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ are constants to be determined.

Consider the polynomial $r(\lambda )={\alpha }_{1}\lambda +{\alpha }_{0}.$ The eigenvalues of $At$ are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=5\text{i}t,\,{\lambda }_{2}=-5\text{i}t,
$$

which are complex conjugates. Thus, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}r((5\text{i})t) & ={e}^{(5\text{i})t} \\ {\alpha }_{1}(5\text{i})t+{\alpha }_{0} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t) \\ {\alpha }_{0}+5\text{i}{\alpha }_{1}t & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we equate the real and imaginary parts, and solve for ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} &=\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t) \\ 5{\alpha }_{1}t &=\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} &=\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t) \\ {\alpha }_{1} &=\frac{1}{5t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${\alpha }_{1}$ and ${\alpha }_{0}$ into the expressions for the required entries of ${e}^{At},$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\alpha }_{0} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t) \\ 5{\alpha }_{1}t & =5\cdot \frac{1}{5t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\cdot t \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{Φ}_{0}(t)={e}^{At}=\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(5t) \\ -\operatorname{sin}⁡(5t) & \operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)\end{bmatrix}.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "c739f31a-33e2-5b79-9d44-a58e2e368af7" :step/next {:db/id 17592186545937}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "5d8223f6-d576-5e04-89fc-1464abef50dd" :answer/type {:db/id mass $M\,\text{kg}$ and uniform mass density occupies the region
$D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,\,0\le y\le 2\},$ where $x$ and $y$ are measured in meters. Find the moment of inertia of the plate about the origin." :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina $D$ with mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

The area of the rectangular plate $D$ is $A=1\cdot 2=2.$ 

Since the plate has uniform density, every unit of area contains the same amount of mass. Therefore, the mass density is constant and is given by the total mass divided by the total area:

$$
\lambda (x,y)=\frac{M}{A}=\frac{M}{2}.
$$

Using the formula for ${I}_{0},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{0} & ={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & =\frac{M}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}{[\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}+x{y}^{2}]}_{x=0}^{x=1}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{3}+{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{2}{[\frac{1}{3}y+\frac{1}{3}{y}^{3}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{M}{2}(\frac{2}{3}+\frac{8}{3}) \\  & =\frac{M}{2}\cdot \frac{10}{3} \\  & =\frac{5M}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia is $\frac{5M}{3}\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}.$"} {:db/id 17592186129532 :question/id #uuid "f0af98bb-12cf-5c0f-a924-a0fe039adf99" :question/math-academy-id Find the moment of inertia of the plate about the $x$-axis." :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina $D$ with mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

First, notice that $D$ is a type II region with representation

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le 3,\,\,\frac{y}{3}\le x\le 4-y\},
$$

as shown below.

![](images/47/47c897bd58a23965d9c36f683553c0817afa8bc2e37ed53a432edcd62b386e55.png)

The area of the triangular plate $D$ is 

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}\cdot 4\cdot 3=6.
$$

Since the plate has uniform density, every unit of area contains the same amount of mass. Therefore, the mass density is constant and is given by the total mass divided by the total area:

$$
\lambda (x,y)=\frac{M}{A}=\frac{M}{6}.
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{x} & ={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{y/3}^{4-y}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{\int }_{0}^{3}{y}^{2}[{\int }_{y/3}^{4-y}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{\int }_{0}^{3}{y}^{2}(4-y-\frac{1}{3}y)\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{\int }_{0}^{3}4{y}^{2}-\frac{4}{3}{y}^{3}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{[\frac{4}{3}{y}^{3}-\frac{1}{3}{y}^{4}]}_{0}^{3} \\  & =\frac{M}{6}(36-27) \\  & =\frac{3M}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186281637 :question/id #uuid "9a1f6eeb-74ef-55ae-8480-c174f3bc8d34" :question/math-academy-id "q-163219" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "839f5ece-276f-5816-96b9-c527a2493a8c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2M}{3}" :db/id 17592186279770} {:answer/id #uuid "b9e6e3da-9c21-52c4-86e6-90e111164bf1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3M}{4}" :db/id 17592186280230} {:answer/id #uuid "d898035f-95c6-5b96-a44f-c85c5e0fb62a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{M}{3}" :db/id 17592186280506} {:answer/id #uuid "f28d76a8-28fa-5a01-aefa-cb1bdd261513" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2M" :db/id 17592186280703} {:answer/id #uuid "ffd690e9-c999-5620-b45c-5474e864788b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3M" :db/id 17592186280831}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186279770} :answer-field/id #uuid "faab536c-ba69-524a-89bb-9d4a9ee45c2f" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186281279}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "![](images/c6/c683f411b11b7b353e166364c8e0fdbc0d218c07535c2f3430d832ab129702d8.png)

A triangular plate of mass $M$ and uniform mass density occupies the region $D$ enclosed between the $x$-axis and the lines $y=x$ and $y=2-x,$ as shown above. Find the moment of inertia of the plate about the $y$-axis." :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina $D$ with mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

First, notice that $D$ is a type II region with representation

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le 1,\,\,y\le x\le 2-y\},
$$

as shown below.

![](images/b1/b1ced30e4cc1fe984b56707f11e8720f2ee68c5b204b6ea7b8d607a65276acca.png)

The area of the triangular plate $D$ is 

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}\cdot 2\cdot 1=1.
$$

Since the plate has uniform density, every unit of area contains the same amount of mass. Therefore, the mass density is constant and is given by the total mass divided by the total area:

$$
\lambda (x,y)=\frac{M}{A}=M.
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & =M{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{y}^{2-y}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =M{\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}]}_{y}^{2-y}\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}(2-y)^{3}-{y}^{3}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{3}{[-\frac{1}{4}(2-y)^{4}-\frac{1}{4}{y}^{4}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-\frac{M}{12}{[(2-y)^{4}+{y}^{4}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-\frac{M}{12}(1+1-16-0) \\  & =\frac{7M}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186426168 :question/id #uuid "a005e400-255d-52bf-b2df-866a68951503" :question/math-academy-id "q-163203" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1a308805-aad8-54a7-b5b1-064462e81b88" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{22M}{3}\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186426082} {:answer/id #uuid "383fad8b-59a8-5b43-ad3d-50f07ba39230" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "13\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186426094} {:answer/id #uuid "7cd77a93-c9ac-5031-8c15-eb3b4d405d24" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "26M\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186426110} {:answer/id #uuid "b11137df-53c8-5030-b8e0-6a9bb71fdcb0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{16M}{3}\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186426131} {:answer/id #uuid "f370ad7c-77cf-51a3-8d2a-a9e647d5cb34" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{13M}{3}\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186426145}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186426145} :answer-field/id #uuid "73ed7367-47d9-5ab5-97c8-cd0c7ced1597" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186426153}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "A rectangular plate of mass $M\,\text{kg}$ and uniform mass density occupies the region

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

The area of the rectangular plate $D$ is $A=3\cdot 2=6.$ 

Since the plate has uniform density, every unit of area contains the same amount of mass. Therefore, the mass density is constant and is given by the total mass divided by the total area:

$$
\lambda (x,y)=\frac{M}{A}=\frac{M}{6}.
$$

Using the formula for ${I}_{x},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{x} & ={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{\int }_{1}^{3}{\int }_{1}^{4}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{\int }_{1}^{3}{y}^{2}[x]_{1}^{4}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{\int }_{1}^{3}3{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{[{y}^{3}]}_{1}^{3} \\  & =\frac{M}{6}(27-1) \\  & =\frac{13M}{3}.\end{aligned}

Find the moment of inertia of this lamina about the origin." :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina $D$ with mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

Using the formula for ${I}_{0},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{0} & ={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{2}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})(6-xy)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}[{\int }_{0}^{2}6{x}^{2}-{x}^{3}y+6{y}^{2}-x{y}^{3}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{[2{x}^{3}-\frac{1}{4}{x}^{4}y+6x{y}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}{y}^{3}]}_{x=0}^{x=2}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}16-4y+12{y}^{2}-2{y}^{3}\,\text{d}y \\  & =[16y-2{y}^{2}+4{y}^{3}-\frac{1}{2}{y}^{4}]_{0}^{3} \\  & =48-18+108-\frac{81}{2}-0 \\  & =97.5.\end{aligned}
$$

Find the moment of inertia of this lamina about the origin." :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina $D$ with mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

Using the formula for ${I}_{0},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{0} & ={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{3}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})(4y+1)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{3}4{x}^{2}y+{x}^{2}+4{y}^{3}+{y}^{2}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{4}{3}{x}^{3}y+\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}+4x{y}^{3}+x{y}^{2}]}_{x=0}^{x=3}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}36y+9+12{y}^{3}+3{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =[18{y}^{2}+9y+3{y}^{4}+{y}^{3}]_{0}^{1} \\  & =18+9+3+1 \\  & =31.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia of the lamina about the origin is $31\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}.$"} {:db/id 17592186281622 :question/id #uuid "566286c6-ab64-5382-ab24-0d1952795e00" :question/math-academy-id "q-163174" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1e774e3e-5483-570a-be90-3556fdfeef80" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "96" :db/id 17592186278875} {:answer/id #uuid "264c43c5-9ce5-5021-829e-191395085650" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "66" :db/id 17592186278931} {:answer/id #uuid "27a3b396-361a-5015-9461-0aae23b48259" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "88" :db/id 17592186278947} {:answer/id #uuid "4373458f-0c28-5ba9-9faf-49c7a51e957d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "124" :db/id 17592186279197} {:answer/id #uuid "aec868ad-08a2-517d-b508-f8953c729333" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "112" :db/id 17592186280137}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186280137} :answer-field/id #uuid "13ebe4cc-aac8-5388-84d5-8872f110619f" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186280865}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "![](images/a6/a6910defd242e1b65b7bdf8b580cd2f56df3ac43951a9f83f353003e00a849b4.png)

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

First, notice that $D$ is a type I region with representation

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 4,\,\,0\le y\le \sqrt{x}\},
$$

as shown below.

![](images/dd/dd5ee021dd73317a775c0ea653212f7ee5545f8c6854e6a9daabdc93b5c3b9c0.png)

If the mass density function of $D$ is given by $\lambda (x,y)=10y,$ find the moment of inertia of the lamina about the origin." :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina $D$ with mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

First, notice that $D$ is a type I region with representation

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,\,0\le y\le \sqrt{4-{x}^{2}}\},
$$

as shown below.

![](images/62/626cbf8e182d9eebb8b48026f07c5dd012c1096cc9568465f3648710ea0d07a4.png)

Using the formula for ${I}_{0},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{0} & ={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}}}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})(10y)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}[{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}}}10{x}^{2}y+10{y}^{3}\,\text{d}y]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{[5{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+\frac{5}{2}{y}^{4}]}_{y=0}^{y=\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}5{x}^{2}(4-{x}^{2})+\frac{5}{2}{(4-{x}^{2})}^{2}\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{5}{2}(4-{x}^{2})(2{x}^{2}+4-{x}^{2})\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{5}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}16-{x}^{4}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{5}{2}{[16x-\frac{{x}^{5}}{5}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{5}{2}(32-\frac{32}{5}) \\  & =64.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186426167 :question/id #uuid "780eb3bd-e477-5b2c-a046-3471aa40cca0" :question/math-academy-id "q-163195"} {:db/id 17592186426171 :question/id #uuid "c8a5bd24-d88b-5487-ab23-00b382428ad5" :question/math-academy-id "q-163175"} {:db/id 17592186426172 :question/id #uuid "d5a11202-6be7-5636-bb7a-f06e82bc2539" :question/math-academy-id "q-163145" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "080d8399-ca6e-5bfc-9948-10e6f55ec587" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3.4\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186426079} {:answer/id #uuid "52708feb-3913-5690-b2e1-2173e86cf70b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186426102} {:answer/id #uuid "591fa420-a919-5ad2-a1d5-c2c1c7db9500" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1.8\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186426103} {:answer/id #uuid "9c33f085-6253-5add-a526-e7a9b5dd2021" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1.2\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186426126} {:answer/id #uuid "a184fae6-ae92-58da-b4e6-91168995a1c8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186426128}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186426126} :answer-field/id #uuid "6289bd5c-72da-5cc5-87b8-932a6822cc65" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186426152}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "A rectangular plate occupies the region

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

Using the formula for ${I}_{x},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{x} & ={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{2}^{4}{y}^{2}\cdot x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{2}^{4}x{y}^{4}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{4}{[\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}]}_{2}^{4}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}6{y}^{4}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[\frac{6}{5}{y}^{5}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{6}{5}-0 \\  & =1.2.\end{aligned}

$$

First, notice that $D$ is a type II region with representation

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,y\le x\le 2-{y}^{2},\,\,0\le y\le 1\},

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{x} & ={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{y}^{2-{y}^{2}}{y}^{2}\cdot 12y\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{y}^{2-{y}^{2}}12{y}^{3}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[12x{y}^{3}]_{x=y}^{x=2-{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}12(2-{y}^{2}){y}^{3}-12{y}^{4}\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}24{y}^{3}-12{y}^{5}-12{y}^{4}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[6{y}^{4}-2{y}^{6}-\frac{12}{5}{y}^{5}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =6-2-\frac{12}{5} \\  & =\frac{8}{5}.\end{aligned}

{:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186281147}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "A rectangular plate of mass $M$ occupies the region
$D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,\,0\le y\le 2\}.$
The mass density at each point is proportional to its distance from the $y$-axis.
Find the moment of inertia of the lamina about the origin." :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina $D$ with mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

From the description, the mass density function can be written as

$$
\lambda (x,y)=k|x|=kx,
$$

where $k$ is a constant of proportionality. We can find an expression for $k$ in terms of $M$ by integrating the density function over the plate:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}kx\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =k({\int }_{0}^{1}x\,\text{d}x)({\int }_{0}^{2}\text{d}y) \\  & =k{[\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}]}_{0}^{1}\cdot [y]_{0}^{2} \\  & =k(\frac{1}{2}-0)(2-0) \\  & =k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $k=M$ and hence $\lambda (x,y)=kx=Mx.$
Therefore, the moment of inertia about the origin is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{0} & ={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & =M{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\cdot x\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =M{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{3}+x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =M{\int }_{0}^{2}{[\frac{1}{4}{x}^{4}+\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}{y}^{2}]}_{x=0}^{x=1}\,\text{d}y \\  & =M{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =M{[\frac{1}{4}y+\frac{1}{6}{y}^{3}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =M(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{4}{3}) \\  & =\frac{11M}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186281624 :question/id #uuid "8ba69e53-fc8f-5143-953e-05bbe8878807" :question/math-academy-id "q-163180"} {:db/id 17592186281627 :question/id #uuid Consider a plate of mass $M$ that occupies the region $D$ in the first quadrant bounded by the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=9,$ shown above. Given that the mass is distributed uniformly across the plate, find the moment of inertia of the plate about the origin." :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina $D$ with mass density function $\lambda (r,\theta ),$ we have the following definitions:

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

First, notice that the region $D$ in polar coordinates can be expressed as

$$
D=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 3,\,\,0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}\}.
$$

The area of the plate $D$ is 

$$
A=\frac{1}{4}\pi {r}^{2}=\frac{9\pi }{4}.
$$

 

Since the mass is distributed uniformly, the mass density function is given by

$$
\lambda (r,\theta )=\frac{M}{A}=\frac{4M}{9\pi }.
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the origin is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{0} & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{4M}{9\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{3}{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{4M}{9\pi }({\int }_{0}^{3}{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r)({\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\,\text{d}\theta ) \\  & =\frac{4M}{9\pi }\cdot \frac{1}{4}{r}^{4}{|}_{0}^{3}\cdot \theta {|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{4M}{9\pi }\cdot \frac{1}{4}(81-0)\cdot (\frac{\pi }{2}-0) \\  & =\frac{9M}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186129538 :question/id #uuid "41c034f9-14b4-5bc4-9351-1214f69c2032" :question/math-academy-id "q-162990" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3056ba5d-f7d1-55a3-8c91-5da94f695f90" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "9-4\sqrt{3}" :db/id 17592186426091} {:answer/id #uuid "32392a3b-31a7-5a44-8746-b4c85858d143" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5-2\sqrt{3}" :db/id 17592186426092} {:answer/id #uuid "77d105e7-3ddf-576d-b7fd-6524428a349e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4-2\sqrt{3}" :db/id 17592186426108} {:answer/id #uuid "7faf887c-1e04-5044-ade7-d44593ea0768" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8-3\sqrt{3}" :db/id 17592186426111} {:answer/id #uuid "d52f3d90-a693-584a-a56c-1a94156d2638" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "10-4\sqrt{3}" :db/id 17592186426136}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186426136} :answer-field/id #uuid "1239f0fe-7d29-5b4f-895a-1d599c74b28e" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186126725}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "![](images/0a/0a85b0be5f8e5db2cf4d1716e4afe4a2780c500d94a1ce282a9d0044f93ba084.png)

The mass density function of the plate is given by $\lambda (x,y)=\frac{6}{x}.$ Find the moment of inertia of the plate about the $y$-axis." :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina $D$ with mass density function $\lambda (r,\theta ),$ we have the following definitions:

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

First, note that the region $D$ in polar coordinates can be expressed as

$$
D=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,1\le r\le \sqrt{3},\,\,\frac{\pi }{6}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{3}\}.
$$

Also, the mass density function in polar coordinates is 

$$
\lambda (r,\theta )=\frac{6}{r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }=\frac{6}{r}\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta .
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /3}{\int }_{1}^{\sqrt{3}}(\frac{6}{r}\operatorname{sec}⁡\theta ){r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /3}{\int }_{1}^{\sqrt{3}}6{r}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =({\int }_{1}^{\sqrt{3}}6{r}^{2}\,\text{d}r)({\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta ) \\  & =2{r}^{3}{|}_{1}^{\sqrt{3}}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {|}_{\pi /6}^{\pi /3} \\  & =2(3\sqrt{3}-1)\cdot (\frac{\sqrt{3}-1}{2}) \\  & =(3\sqrt{3}-1)\cdot (\sqrt{3}-1) \\  & =10-4\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186281640 :question/id #uuid "5cf0a2c6-6793-5c24-82b1-b8c9fc0536bd" :question/math-academy-id "q-163225" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "104b5f45-a5a5-53b8-81f3-1afa7e730667" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "23" :db/id 17592186278738} {:answer/id #uuid "4f1d9c0f-74a7-5840-a8f1-946c355e9f4f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "31\sqrt{2}" :db/id 17592186279310} {:answer/id #uuid "ab1151a9-1581-5ce8-97ab-8d91464f04d4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5\sqrt{2}" :db/id 17592186280107} {:answer/id #uuid "de04ac09-2b08-5de9-947d-c33d64af0400" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{15\sqrt{2}}{2}" :db/id 17592186280549} {:answer/id #uuid "ff3ed382-97b6-5633-976b-856f4f15d75d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{21}{2}" :db/id 17592186280827}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186279310} :answer-field/id #uuid "73f8be0c-a6d9-58ec-b1bd-534c48dbccb5" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186281042}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "![](images/d1/d1ef5062d5bc045c1e1f7fa58c513315852f74aa15539c001662b0055583f01b.png)

The mass density function of the plate is given by $\lambda (x,y)=10x.$ Find the moment of inertia of the plate about the origin." :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina $D$ with mass density function $\lambda (r,\theta ),$ we have the following definitions:

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

First, note that the region $D$ in polar coordinates can be expressed as

$$
D=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,1\le r\le 2,\,\,0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}\}.
$$

Also, the mass density function in polar coordinates is 

$$
\lambda (r,\theta )=10r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the origin is

$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin, in polar coordinates, is given by

Consider a plate of mass $M$ that occupies the region $D$ bounded by the polar circles $r=1$ and $r=2,$ as shown above. The mass density at any point is proportional to its distance from the origin. Find the moment of inertia of the plate about the $y$-axis." :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina $D$ with mass density function $\lambda (r,\theta ),$ we have the following definitions:

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

First, notice that the region $D,$ in polar coordinates, can be expressed as

$$
D=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,1\le r\le 2,\,\,0\le \theta <2\pi \}.
$$

From the description, the mass density function can be written as $\lambda (r,\theta )=kr,$ where $k$ is a constant of proportionality. We can find an expression for $k$ in terms of $M$ by integrating the density function over the plate:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{1}^{2}kr\cdot r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{1}^{2}k{r}^{2}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =k({\int }_{1}^{2}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}r)({\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\text{d}\theta ) \\  & =k\cdot \frac{1}{3}{r}^{3}\,{|}_{1}^{2}\cdot \theta \,{|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =k\cdot \frac{7}{3}\cdot 2\pi  \\  & =\frac{14\pi k}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence,

$$
\lambda (r,\theta )=kr=\frac{3M}{14\pi }r.
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{3M}{14\pi }r\cdot {r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{3M}{14\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{1}^{2}{r}^{4}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{3M}{14\pi }({\int }_{1}^{2}{r}^{4}\,\text{d}r)({\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta ) \\  & =\frac{3M}{14\pi }({\int }_{1}^{2}{r}^{4}\,\text{d}r)({\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\frac{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }{2}\,\text{d}\theta ) \\  & =\frac{3M}{14\pi }\cdot \frac{1}{5}{r}^{5}\,{|}_{1}^{2}\cdot (\frac{1}{2}\theta +\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta ){|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =\frac{3M}{14\pi }\cdot \frac{31}{5}\cdot \pi  \\  & =\frac{93M}{70}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186326720 :question/id #uuid "29252808-04b0-5c9a-8f7e-a13993dbc1ba" :question/math-academy-id "q-38822"} {:db/id 17592186367867 :question/id #uuid "f466ecc5-4b24-5385-9cf8-ddb7d1c5a54a" :question/math-academy-id "q-163245"} {:db/id 17592186426163 :question/id #uuid "40276498-22d3-5917-98ab-3914446aeb38" :question/math-academy-id "q-163253"} {:db/id 17592186426164 :question/id #uuid "648c554b-c03a-5281-b06a-dd87f9becdf0" :question/math-academy-id "q-163250"} {:db/id 17592186426165 :question/id #uuid "6773c2a6-0930-567e-b7b2-ce599d9b40d9" :question/math-academy-id "q-163244"} {:db/id 17592186048585} {:db/id 17592186050741 :topic/difficulty 1.2118134338105737 :topic/encompasses [{:db/id 17592186429370 :encompassing/rationale "Initial Codex estimate from captured target-band crossing frequency. "Suppose a massless, rigid lamina rotates with angular velocity $\omega$ about a fixed axis $L.$ Attached to the lamina are a set of particles $P_1,P_2,\ldots,P_n$ of masses $m_1,m_2,\ldots,m_n$ at distances $r_1,r_2,\ldots,r_n$ from the axis, respectively. 

![](images/b4/b4eeef756faf65e7caaf5bb8dad8d803cacf3e4f17b719868b647bf7e9c9da89.png)

Let's find the total kinetic energy of this system.

Each particle $P_i$ of mass $m_i$ has linear speed $v_i = r_i\omega.$ So, its kinetic energy is

$$
\dfrac12m_iv_i^2 = \dfrac12m_i(r_i\omega)^2 = \dfrac12m_ir_i^2\omega^2.
$$

The total kinetic energy of the system is obtained by adding the energies of all the particles. So, the kinetic energy of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Total KE} & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{2}{m}_{i}{r}_{i}^{2}{\omega }^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\omega }^{2}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{m}_{i}{r}_{i}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

In other words, the total kinetic energy of the system is given by 

$$
\text{Total KE} = \dfrac12I\omega^2,
$$

where the quantity

$$
I = \sum\limits_{i=1}^n m_ir_i^2
$$

is called the **moment of inertia** of the system about the fixed axis $L.$ The units of moment of inertia are $\rm{kg}\cdot\rm{m}^2.$

The moment of inertia in angular motion is analogous to mass in linear motion:

- For linear motion, the kinetic energy is given by

$$
\text{KE} = \dfrac12 \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{M} v^2,
$$

where $M$ is the (total) mass of a system of particles.

The mass of a body measures how resistant the body is to changes in linear motion. It takes a larger force to induce a fixed change in linear motion for a large mass than for a smaller mass.

- For angular motion, the kinetic energy is given by

$$
\text{KE} = \dfrac12 \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{I} \omega^2,
$$

where $I$ is the moment of inertia of a system of particles.

The moment of inertia of a body measures how resistant the body is to changes in *angular* motion. It takes a larger force to induce a fixed change in angular motion for an object with a large moment of inertia than for a body with a smaller moment of inertia." :tutorial/id #uuid Consider a plane lamina that occupies the region $D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ with mass density function $\lambda(x,y),$ (in mass/area), which depends on the position.

By choosing a finite number of points $(x_{ij},y_{ij}),$ where $i=1,2,\ldots,m$ and $j=1,2,\ldots,n,$ we can break the region $D$ into non-overlapping boxes $B_{ij} = [x_{ij}, x_{ij} + \Delta x] \times [y_{ij}, y_{ij} + \Delta y]$ of area $\Delta x \Delta y = \Delta A.$

![](images/c5/c5ac4166ed637b4de525f069673cc6abfaeb2e8e659b3a212d6f2f4d1bf9fc11.png)

For large $m$ and $n,$ the mass density in each box, $B_{ij}$ is approximately constant and equal to the mass density of a point $(x_{ij}^*, y_{ij}^*)$ in the box. Hence, the mass of this part of the lamina is approximately the product of the mass density at this point and the area of the box:

$$
m_{ij} \approx \lambda(x_{ij}^*, y_{ij}^*) \cdot \Delta A
$$

Suppose the function $r(x,y)$ gives the distance of each point $(x,y) \in D$ from a fixed axis $L.$ Then, using the formula for the moment of inertia for a collection of masses, summing over these points, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}{m}_{i}[r({x}_{ij}^{∗},{y}_{ij}^{∗})]^{2} \\  & ≈{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}(\lambda ({x}_{ij}^{∗},{y}_{ij}^{∗})\cdot ΔA)[r({x}_{ij}^{∗},{y}_{ij}^{∗})]^{2} \\  & ≈{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}\lambda ({x}_{ij}^{∗},{y}_{ij}^{∗})[r({x}_{ij}^{∗},{y}_{ij}^{∗})]^{2}ΔA.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, taking the limit as the length and width of the boxes tend to zero, we get an exact representation of the moment of inertia as an integral:

$$
I = \lim\limits_{m,n\to \infty} \sum\limits_{i=1}^m \sum\limits_{j=1}^n \lambda(x_{ij}^*, y_{ij}^*) [r(x_{ij}^*, y_{ij}^*)]^2 \Delta A
= \iint\limits_D \lambda(x,y) [r(x,y)]^2 \:\textrm{d}A.
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about a fixed axis $L$ of a plane lamina occupying the region $D$ with mass density $\lambda(x,y)$ is

$$
I_L = \iint\limits_D \lambda(x,y) [r(x,y)]^2 \:\textrm{d}A,
$$

where $r(x,y)$ is the distance from the point $(x,y)$ to the axis $L.$

In this lesson, we'll limit the axis of rotation to the $x$- and $y$-axes. Note that the distance between a point $(x,y)$ and the $x$ and $y$ coordinate axes are $r_x(x,y) = |y|$ and $r_y(x,y) = |x|,$ respectively.

![](images/8a/8a94fcdb8bb1a97e2bc9122e88ca7bd4f441299d2ce3c7bee819e644cf4eae89.png)

Hence, the moments of inertia of a plate with respect to the coordinate axes $x$ and $y,$ denoted $I_x$ and $I_y$, respectively, are 

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{x} & ={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\ {I}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

A related concept is the **moment of inertia about the origin** (or **polar moment of inertia**), which deals with the strength of an object when it is rotating. It is defined as

$$
I_0 = \iint\limits_D (x^2+y^2)\lambda(x,y) \:\textrm dA = I_x + I_y.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "170c6cfe-d50a-5cee-b724-5409ca4c8461" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7794 :tutorial/title "Moment of Inertia of Plane Laminas"} :step/id #uuid "3f899894-d69b-5df5-8333-4e2b804563ee" :step/math-academy-id 45104 :step/next {:db/id 17592186130107}}] :activity/title "Moments of Inertia of Laminas About the Coordinate Axes" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186129369} {:db/id 17592186130105 :step/content {:db/id 17592186130411 :tutorial/content "Suppose a massless, rigid lamina rotates with angular velocity $\omega$ about a fixed axis $L.$ Attached to the lamina are a set of particles $P_1,P_2,\ldots,P_n$ of masses $m_1,m_2,\ldots,m_n$ at distances $r_1,r_2,\ldots,r_n$ from the axis, respectively. 

![](images/b4/b4eeef756faf65e7caaf5bb8dad8d803cacf3e4f17b719868b647bf7e9c9da89.png)

Let's find the total kinetic energy of this system.

Each particle $P_i$ of mass $m_i$ has linear speed $v_i = r_i\omega.$ So, its kinetic energy is

$$
\dfrac12m_iv_i^2 = \dfrac12m_i(r_i\omega)^2 = \dfrac12m_ir_i^2\omega^2.
$$

The total kinetic energy of the system is obtained by adding the energies of all the particles. So, the kinetic energy of the system is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Total KE} & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{2}{m}_{i}{r}_{i}^{2}{\omega }^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\omega }^{2}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{m}_{i}{r}_{i}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

In other words, the total kinetic energy of the system is given by 

$$
\text{Total KE} = \dfrac12I\omega^2,
$$

where the quantity

$$
I = \sum\limits_{i=1}^n m_ir_i^2
$$

is called the **moment of inertia** of the system about the fixed axis $L.$ The units of moment of inertia are $\rm{kg}\cdot\rm{m}^2.$

The moment of inertia in angular motion is analogous to mass in linear motion:

- For linear motion, the kinetic energy is given by

$$
\text{KE} = \dfrac12 \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{M} v^2,
$$

where $M$ is the (total) mass of a system of particles.

The mass of a body measures how resistant the body is to changes in linear motion. It takes a larger force to induce a fixed change in linear motion for a large mass than for a smaller mass.

- For angular motion, the kinetic energy is given by

$$
\text{KE} = \dfrac12 \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{I} \omega^2,
$$

where $I$ is the moment of inertia of a system of particles.

The moment of inertia of a body measures how resistant the body is to changes in *angular* motion. It takes a larger force to induce a fixed change in angular motion for an object with a large moment of inertia than for a body with a smaller moment of inertia." :tutorial/id #uuid "8d36ccdb-eb7d-55de-80e6-f75752dae9db" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5071 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "3933d4e7-a615-5065-8581-94f59b08025e" :step/math-academy-id 31761 :step/next {:db/id 17592186130252}} {:db/id 17592186130411 :tutorial/content "Suppose a massless, rigid lamina rotates with angular velocity $\omega$ about a fixed axis $L.$ Attached to the lamina are a set of particles $P_1,P_2,\ldots,P_n$ of masses $m_1,m_2,\ldots,m_n$ at distances $r_1,r_2,\ldots,r_n$ from the axis, respectively.

If we repeat this process for moments of inertia about the ![](images/1d/1d9b846cface9f9348e4081a0dd87dd254bf26663c12aa0d1a15aa24d2393261.svg)-axis and the origin, we obtain two more definitions. Let's summarize them below:

- The moment of inertia of ![](images/59/5914524b1d3db63c66998b75ca1d00a5dc4e294d2a8f10fe384d2b2ebf2af38e.svg) about ![](images/fc/fcc5df999e3b49fae1685ee0ab5bd03709804e1dd49f2ee722c4269eb0f5506d.svg)-axis is given by

- The moment of inertia of ![](images/59/5914524b1d3db63c66998b75ca1d00a5dc4e294d2a8f10fe384d2b2ebf2af38e.svg) about ![](images/1d/1d9b846cface9f9348e4081a0dd87dd254bf26663c12aa0d1a15aa24d2393261.svg)-axis is given by

Note that we denote ![](images/10/10b9e6b5ce99ae6bfc544d9480ac6d62cfa9d1f23f78b8b3a331c6c517e1472d.svg) the density function expressed in polar coordinates." :tutorial/id #uuid "5d1a8a74-d440-56ad-b42b-a46e22861e20" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7766 :tutorial/title "Moments of Inertia in Polar Coordinates"} {:db/id 17592186130474 :tutorial/content "Let's now find a formula for the moment of inertia of a plane lamina with continuously varying mass density.

Consider a plane lamina that occupies the region $D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^2$ with mass density function $\lambda(x,y),$ (in mass/area), which depends on the position.

By choosing a finite number of points $(x_{ij},y_{ij}),$ where $i=1,2,\ldots,m$ and $j=1,2,\ldots,n,$ we can break the region $D$ into non-overlapping boxes $B_{ij} = [x_{ij}, x_{ij} + \Delta x] \times [y_{ij}, y_{ij} + \Delta y]$ of area $\Delta x \Delta y = \Delta A.$

![](images/c5/c5ac4166ed637b4de525f069673cc6abfaeb2e8e659b3a212d6f2f4d1bf9fc11.png)

For large $m$ and $n,$ the mass density in each box, $B_{ij}$ is approximately constant and equal to the mass density of a point $(x_{ij}^*, y_{ij}^*)$ in the box. Hence, the mass of this part of the lamina is approximately the product of the mass density at this point and the area of the box:

$$
m_{ij} \approx \lambda(x_{ij}^*, y_{ij}^*) \cdot \Delta A
$$

Suppose the function $r(x,y)$ gives the distance of each point $(x,y) \in D$ from a fixed axis $L.$ Then, using the formula for the moment of inertia for a collection of masses, summing over these points, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}I & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}{m}_{i}[r({x}_{ij}^{∗},{y}_{ij}^{∗})]^{2} \\  & ≈{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}(\lambda ({x}_{ij}^{∗},{y}_{ij}^{∗})\cdot ΔA)[r({x}_{ij}^{∗},{y}_{ij}^{∗})]^{2} \\  & ≈{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}\lambda ({x}_{ij}^{∗},{y}_{ij}^{∗})[r({x}_{ij}^{∗},{y}_{ij}^{∗})]^{2}ΔA.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, taking the limit as the length and width of the boxes tend to zero, we get an exact representation of the moment of inertia as an integral:

$$
I = \lim\limits_{m,n\to \infty} \sum\limits_{i=1}^m \sum\limits_{j=1}^n \lambda(x_{ij}^*, y_{ij}^*) [r(x_{ij}^*, y_{ij}^*)]^2 \Delta A
= \iint\limits_D \lambda(x,y) [r(x,y)]^2 \:\textrm{d}A.
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about a fixed axis $L$ of a plane lamina occupying the region $D$ with mass density $\lambda(x,y)$ is

$$
I_L = \iint\limits_D \lambda(x,y) [r(x,y)]^2 \:\textrm{d}A,
$$

where $r(x,y)$ is the distance from the point $(x,y)$ to the axis $L.$

In this lesson, we'll limit the axis of rotation to the $x$- and $y$-axes. Note that the distance between a point $(x,y)$ and the $x$ and $y$ coordinate axes are $r_x(x,y) = |y|$ and $r_y(x,y) = |x|,$ respectively.

![](images/8a/8a94fcdb8bb1a97e2bc9122e88ca7bd4f441299d2ce3c7bee819e644cf4eae89.png)

Hence, the moments of inertia of a plate with respect to the coordinate axes $x$ and $y,$ denoted $I_x$ and $I_y$, respectively, are 

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{x} & ={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\ {I}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

A related concept is the **moment of inertia about the origin** (or **polar moment of inertia**), which deals with the strength of an object when it is rotating. It is defined as

$$
I_0 = \iint\limits_D (x^2+y^2)\lambda(x,y) \:\textrm dA = I_x + I_y.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "170c6cfe-d50a-5cee-b724-5409ca4c8461" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7794 :tutorial/title "Moment of Inertia of Plane Laminas"} {:activity/course {:db/id 17592186046660} :activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186435187} :activity/id #uuid "a8a272ef-3322-59e4-8457-62cd9dcd43be" :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186049331 :topic/id #uuid "ec6fdbaa-c722-5e5b-b092-5ba93bdf0c02" :topic/math-academy-id 2027} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186435185 :step/content {:db/id 17592186281611 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "00586df5-9953-5e7a-a58f-2329aa16a468" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "18\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186278586} {:answer/id #uuid "3bf84ed5-f917-50b8-8e4d-80368c472356" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "24\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186279121} {:answer/id #uuid "4237198b-add2-521b-b160-d585a0924755" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "32\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186279184} {:answer/id #uuid "58055d99-9594-5371-bd9f-20b8d761809d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "16\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186279400} {:answer/id #uuid "86941ae5-17f0-581b-91b1-2673bcdf9949" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "12\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186279793}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186279121} :answer-field/id #uuid "945c0f7a-70d5-5057-8a4c-71bc5f6f818a" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186281099}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "e73bf43d-4842-564c-b994-8b4ed88b9ee2" :question/math-academy-id "q-163146" :question/problem "A rectangular plate occupies the region

Find the moment of inertia of this lamina about the $y$-axis." :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina $D$ with mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is given by

Using the formula for ${I}_{y},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{2}{x}^{2}(x+y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}[{\int }_{0}^{2}{x}^{3}+{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{[\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}+\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}y]}_{x=0}^{x=2}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}4+\frac{8y}{3}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[4y+\frac{4{y}^{2}}{3}]}_{0}^{3} \\  & =12+12 \\  & =24.\end{aligned}

If the mass density function of $D$ is given by $\lambda (x,y)=12y,$ find the moment of inertia of the lamina about the $x$-axis." :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina $D$ with mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

First, notice that $D$ is a type II region with representation

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,y\le x\le 2-{y}^{2},\,\,0\le y\le 1\},
$$

as shown below.

![](images/7a/7a4216a2b1dc3859776c6589459d687981b79b123fa3a5eea638d31529e5cd3a.png)

Using the formula for ${I}_{x},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{x} & ={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{y}^{2-{y}^{2}}{y}^{2}\cdot 12y\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{y}^{2-{y}^{2}}12{y}^{3}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[12x{y}^{3}]_{x=y}^{x=2-{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}12(2-{y}^{2}){y}^{3}-12{y}^{4}\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}24{y}^{3}-12{y}^{5}-12{y}^{4}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[6{y}^{4}-2{y}^{6}-\frac{12}{5}{y}^{5}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =6-2-\frac{12}{5} \\  & =\frac{8}{5}.\end{aligned}

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.

$$
D=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,1\le r\le 2,\,\,0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}\}.

$$

$$

"c204945d-1cc7-5037-a46b-3df54b66b209" :question/math-academy-id "q-163183" :question/problem "![](images/dc/dc61efd6e5ef1fd46fca53f7c1e47394c6b9c95fb2455dc0c798d9936a68631b.png)

A plate occupies the region $D$ enclosed by the $x$-axis, $y$-axis, and the curve $y=\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}}$ in the first quadrant, as shown above. If the mass density function of $D$ is given by $\lambda (x,y)=10y,$ find the moment of inertia of the lamina about the origin." :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina $D$ with mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

First, notice that $D$ is a type I region with representation

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,\,0\le y\le \sqrt{4-{x}^{2}}\},
$$

as shown below.

![](images/62/626cbf8e182d9eebb8b48026f07c5dd012c1096cc9568465f3648710ea0d07a4.png)

Using the formula for ${I}_{0},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{0} & ={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}}}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})(10y)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}[{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}}}10{x}^{2}y+10{y}^{3}\,\text{d}y]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{[5{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+\frac{5}{2}{y}^{4}]}_{y=0}^{y=\sqrt{4-{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}5{x}^{2}(4-{x}^{2})+\frac{5}{2}{(4-{x}^{2})}^{2}\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{5}{2}(4-{x}^{2})(2{x}^{2}+4-{x}^{2})\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{5}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}16-{x}^{4}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{5}{2}{[16x-\frac{{x}^{5}}{5}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{5}{2}(32-\frac{32}{5}) \\  & =64.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "8cc8c4c3-672d-51c1-af40-2419b51ec4f9" :step/next {:db/id 17592186442861}} {:db/id 17592186442858 :step/content {:db/id 17592186281633 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "4c84deba-cb38-5f3b-af0e-58521ec502a3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2M}{3}\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186279280} {:answer/id #uuid "a25defa0-44b9-5bda-a10f-e6ef6a677aaa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{16M}{3}\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186280035} {:answer/id #uuid "ad5bf3b6-9c4b-50ce-879e-8ec79739fdf2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{4M}{3}\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186280127} {:answer/id #uuid "ca352098-298f-5e14-a7d7-0c7272084e0f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8M\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186280364} {:answer/id #uuid "cf1d4484-aff6-5376-8a09-a8cd9f6af638" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4M\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186280418}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186280127} :answer-field/id #uuid "8a384dc8-494e-5973-bebc-5b4d13e8a8c2" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186281085}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "095d8c09-ff9b-5528-8c3d-3967d18698a1" :question/math-academy-id "q-163204" :question/problem "A rectangular plate of mass $M\,\text{kg}$ and uniform mass density occupies the region
$D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,\,1\le y\le 3\},$ where $x$ and $y$ are measured in meters. Find the moment of inertia of the plate about the $y$-axis." :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina $D$ with mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

The area of the rectangular plate $D$ is $A=2\cdot 2=4.$ 

Since the plate has uniform density, every unit of area contains the same amount of mass. Therefore, the mass density is constant and is given by the total mass divided by the total area:

$$
\lambda (x,y)=\frac{M}{A}=\frac{M}{4}.
$$

Using the formula for ${I}_{y},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & =\frac{M}{4}{\int }_{1}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{2}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{4}{\int }_{1}^{3}{[\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}]}_{0}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{4}{\int }_{1}^{3}\frac{8}{3}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{4}{[\frac{8y}{3}]}_{1}^{3} \\  & =\frac{2M}{3}(3-1) \\  & =\frac{4M}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia is $\frac{4M}{3}\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}.$"} :step/id #uuid "9a68fb24-0279-5aa2-9378-bef9856a349d" :step/next {:db/id 17592186442859}} {:db/id 17592186442859 :step/content {:db/id 17592186281642 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "17226919-ce93-5049-994f-31d7cd5c10fb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{7\pi }{6}" :db/id 17592186278798} {:answer/id #uuid "6d3b17cc-de83-57bb-914f-013137289a03" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{5\pi }{12}" :db/id 17592186279586} {:answer/id #uuid "78cff65f-0d69-5e60-9e1c-47253821dc1b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3\pi }{8}" :db/id 17592186279669} {:answer/id #uuid "8d83c82c-bb2f-532f-ab7d-a58f6e2cc4be" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{9\pi }{4}" :db/id 17592186279853} {:answer/id #uuid "e875a915-69ff-5a94-9c30-f7fd03b5fb84" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{7\pi }{10}" :db/id 17592186280639}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186279586} :answer-field/id #uuid "bf0fe541-fc86-58e2-a9d5-645ba6b20816" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186281172}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "2726afac-54d3-5734-a6e0-8fa5ce77d367" :question/math-academy-id "q-163228" :question/problem "![](images/04/044395de3b30755d0c83d489709c38420827f6984af740bc56a3dc5bfaa33794.png)

$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .

- The moment of inertia about the origin, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.

First, note that the region $D$ in polar coordinates can be expressed as

$$
D=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,2\le r\le 3,\,\,\frac{\pi }{3}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}\}.
$$

Also, the mass density function in polar coordinates is 

$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{x} & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{2}^{3}\frac{1}{{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\cdot {r}^{3}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{2}^{3}r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =({\int }_{2}^{3}r\,\text{d}r)({\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}\text{d}\theta ) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{r}^{2}\,{|}_{2}^{3}\cdot \theta \,{|}_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(9-4)\cdot (\frac{\pi }{2}-\frac{\pi }{3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 5\cdot \frac{\pi }{6} \\  & =\frac{5\pi }{12}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "c51d9491-b808-5d51-8650-1109d5229668"} {:db/id 17592186442860 :step/content {:db/id 17592186129531 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2c5c064b-08ea-5bfd-ab69-59d08747b4f9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{4M}{3}\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186278982} {:answer/id #uuid "36add068-fc21-5310-b6d6-2c342cf02faa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2M\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186279070} {:answer/id #uuid "402db993-f88f-5fbe-94b2-191a8a4097a9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2M}{3}\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186279160} {:answer/id #uuid "a97f6f5d-dae7-50c8-b1bc-6c5e4d06a4bf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{M}{3}\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186280096} {:answer/id #uuid "bf6093ca-d163-58ee-a9e0-b840646a5e22" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{5M}{3}\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}" :db/id 17592186280274}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186280274} :answer-field/id #uuid "8415b494-bfb5-5759-9d5d-906937712b89" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186281071}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "d5a597a5-f786-5891-91b3-c78b73413f55" :question/math-academy-id "q-162905" :question/problem "A rectangular plate of mass $M\,\text{kg}$ and uniform mass density occupies the region
$D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,\,0\le y\le 2\},$ where $x$ and $y$ are measured in meters. Find the moment of inertia of the plate about the origin." :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina $D$ with mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

The area of the rectangular plate $D$ is $A=1\cdot 2=2.$ 

Since the plate has uniform density, every unit of area contains the same amount of mass. Therefore, the mass density is constant and is given by the total mass divided by the total area:

$$
\lambda (x,y)=\frac{M}{A}=\frac{M}{2}.
$$

Using the formula for ${I}_{0},$ we get

$$

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

First, note that the region $D$ in polar coordinates can be expressed as

$$
D=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,2\le r\le 3,\,\,\frac{\pi }{3}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}\}.
$$

Also, the mass density function in polar coordinates is 

$$
\lambda (r,\theta )=\frac{1}{{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }.
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{x} & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{2}^{3}\frac{1}{{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\cdot {r}^{3}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{2}^{3}r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =({\int }_{2}^{3}r\,\text{d}r)({\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}\text{d}\theta ) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{r}^{2}\,{|}_{2}^{3}\cdot \theta \,{|}_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(9-4)\cdot (\frac{\pi }{2}-\frac{\pi }{3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 5\cdot \frac{\pi }{6} \\  & =\frac{5\pi }{12}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "c51d9491-b808-5d51-8650-1109d5229668"} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "17226919-ce93-5049-994f-31d7cd5c10fb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value $$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

Using the formula for ${I}_{y},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{\int }_{2}^{4}{x}^{2}\cdot x{e}^{2y}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}[{\int }_{2}^{4}{x}^{3}{e}^{2y}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{e}^{2y}{[\frac{1}{4}{x}^{4}]}_{2}^{4}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}60{e}^{2y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =[30{e}^{2y}]_{0}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡2} \\  & =120-30 \\  & =90.\end{aligned}
$$

A triangular plate of mass $M$ and uniform mass density occupies the region $D$ enclosed between the $x$-axis and the lines $y=3x$ and $y=4-x,$ as shown above. Find the moment of inertia of the plate about the $x$-axis." :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina $D$ with mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

First, notice that $D$ is a type II region with representation

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le 3,\,\,\frac{y}{3}\le x\le 4-y\},
$$

as shown below.

![](images/47/47c897bd58a23965d9c36f683553c0817afa8bc2e37ed53a432edcd62b386e55.png)

The area of the triangular plate $D$ is 

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}\cdot 4\cdot 3=6.
$$

Since the plate has uniform density, every unit of area contains the same amount of mass. Therefore, the mass density is constant and is given by the total mass divided by the total area:

$$
\lambda (x,y)=\frac{M}{A}=\frac{M}{6}.
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{x} & ={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{y/3}^{4-y}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{\int }_{0}^{3}{y}^{2}[{\int }_{y/3}^{4-y}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{\int }_{0}^{3}{y}^{2}(4-y-\frac{1}{3}y)\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{\int }_{0}^{3}4{y}^{2}-\frac{4}{3}{y}^{3}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{[\frac{4}{3}{y}^{3}-\frac{1}{3}{y}^{4}]}_{0}^{3} \\  & =\frac{M}{6}(36-27) \\  & =\frac{3M}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "63d1ac8f-1120-57bf-a3f2-068394de0e68" :step/next {:db/id 17592186481469}} {:db/id 17592186481456 :step/content {:db/id 17592186281644 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "24eeb6dc-6a62-5d90-a207-0acfc7258433" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "15\sqrt{2}" :db/id 17592186278919} {:answer/id #uuid "349f0582-d339-5e4d-9545-b31c93cda4da" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4\sqrt{2}-1" :db/id 17592186279045} {:answer/id #uuid "538264a8-2746-5c22-950d-ad36b0c19129" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2\sqrt{2}-1}{8}" :db/id 17592186279351} {:answer/id #uuid "c7b8065a-0247-55f8-99df-fad5f0147068" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8\sqrt{2}" :db/id 17592186280342} {:answer/id #uuid "f2ebd0da-d30a-58a4-863a-0db44212f7d5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3\sqrt{2}}{4}" :db/id 17592186280710}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186279351} :answer-field/id #uuid "ec2db863-9898-51d6-ba39-8b881e966e18" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186281253}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "b6b312d9-6efa-541f-ad5d-be93b575260c" :question/math-academy-id "q-163230" :question/problem "![](images/ad/ad7c939aded3f5e5e1e2f3b5e5743609e331625479c25f6a55659be730ed1cf5.png)

The mass density function of the plate is given by $\lambda (x,y)=15y.$ Find the moment of inertia of the plate about the $y$-axis." :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina $D$ with mass density function $\lambda (r,\theta ),$ we have the following definitions:

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

First, note that the region $D$ in polar coordinates can be expressed as

$$
D=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,1\le r\le \sqrt[5]{2},\,\,\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{3}\}.
$$

Also, the mass density function in polar coordinates is 

$$
\lambda (r,\theta )=15r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /3}{\int }_{1}^{\sqrt[5]{2}}15r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot {r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /3}{\int }_{1}^{\sqrt[5]{2}}15{r}^{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =({\int }_{1}^{\sqrt[5]{2}}5{r}^{4}\,\text{d}r)({\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /3}3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta ) \\  & ={r}^{5}\,{|}_{1}^{\sqrt[5]{2}}\cdot (-{cos}^{3}⁡\theta )\,{|}_{\pi /4}^{\pi /3} \\  & =(2-1)\cdot (-\frac{1}{8}+\frac{\sqrt{2}}{4}) \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{2}-1}{8}.\end{aligned}

$$

Find the moment of inertia of the plate about the $y$-axis." :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina $D$ with mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

First, notice that $D$ is a type I region with representation

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,\,\frac{x}{2}\le y\le 3-x\},
$$

as shown below.

![](images/6c/6c2cec5e919c25623396b5ba5f052481623a868c7520aa8e3d1d3eb34f3a4a58.png)

The area of the triangular plate $D$ is 

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}\cdot 2\cdot 3=3.
$$

Since the plate has uniform density, every unit of area contains the same amount of mass. Therefore, the mass density is constant and is given by the total mass divided by the total area:

$$
\lambda (x,y)=\frac{M}{A}=\frac{M}{3}.
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & =\frac{M}{3}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{x/2}^{3-x}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{M}{3}{\int }_{0}^{2}{x}^{2}[{\int }_{x/2}^{3-x}\,\text{d}y]\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{M}{3}{\int }_{0}^{2}{x}^{2}(3-x-\frac{x}{2})\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{M}{3}{\int }_{0}^{2}3{x}^{2}-\frac{3}{2}{x}^{3}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{3}{[{x}^{3}-\frac{3}{8}{x}^{4}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{M}{3}(8-6) \\  & =\frac{2M}{3}.\end{aligned}
