:question/math-academy-id "q-3564" :question/problem "Given that 

$$
{(2{t}^{2}-3s)}^{4}=A{t}^{8}+B{t}^{6}s+C{t}^{4}{s}^{2}-216{t}^{2}{s}^{3}+81{s}^{4}
$$

where $A,B$ and $C$ are constants, determine the value of $A+B+C.$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's compare our expression with the binomial

$$
(a+b)^{n}.
$$

Here we have that $n=4,$ $a=2{t}^{2},$ and $b=-3s.$ So, the exponents of the binomial expansion must follow the pattern

$$
{a}^{4}{b}^{0},\,{a}^{3}{b}^{1},\,{a}^{2}{b}^{2},\,{a}^{1}{b}^{3},\,{a}^{0}{b}^{4}.
$$

The $4$th row in Pascal's Triangle is $(1,4,6,4,1).$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}(2{t}^{2}-3s)^{4} & =1{a}^{4}+4{a}^{3}b+6{a}^{2}{b}^{2}+4a{b}^{3}+1{b}^{4} \\  & =1{(2{t}^{2})}^{4}(-3s)^{0}+4{(2{t}^{2})}^{3}(-3s)^{1}+6{(2{t}^{2})}^{2}(-3s)^{2} \\  & \,+4{(2{t}^{2})}^{1}(-3s)^{3}+1{(2{t}^{2})}^{0}(-3s)^{4} \\  & =1(16{t}^{8})(1)+4(8{t}^{6})(-3s)+6(4{t}^{4})(9{s}^{2}) \\  & \,+4(2{t}^{2})(-27{s}^{3})+1(1)(81{s}^{4}) \\  & =16{t}^{8}-96{t}^{6}s+216{t}^{4}{s}^{2}-216{t}^{2}{s}^{3}+81{s}^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $A=16,B=-96,$ and $C=216.$ Finally,

$$
A+B+C=16-96+216=136.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "0fcd4859-f70e-5b53-af4b-3bf056bd41ce" :step/next {:db/id 17592186503841}} {:db/id 17592186503805 :step/content {:db/id 17592186503745 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0b600bcd-5006-5baf-9dca-4aab5033031d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{32}+\frac{25y}{8}+125{y}^{2}" :db/id 17592186503008} {:answer/id #uuid "4c839c43-5c26-510d-85ac-e2e3c39a216c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{32}+\frac{25y}{4}+145{y}^{2}" :db/id 17592186503128} {:answer/id #uuid "4fb998d5-d716-53e2-a50b-72e1271eb277" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{32}+\frac{25y}{8}-100{y}^{2}" :db/id 17592186503133} {:answer/id #uuid "5135b701-cd58-5dde-8d9b-989995318cb4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{32}+\frac{25y}{4}+100{y}^{2}" :db/id 17592186503136} {:answer/id #uuid "9799692b-0119-5014-ae4f-3ef5e9145c63" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{32}+\frac{25y}{8}+145{y}^{2}" :db/id 17592186503281}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186503008} :answer-field/id #uuid "ef1b5443-9d42-51aa-ac69-73ecc6958d74" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186503635}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "d6a9fa51-d96f-5308-9675-af7e9df7f105" :question/math-academy-id "q-3563" :question/problem "Find, in ascending powers of $y,$ the first three terms of the binomial expansion of ${(10y+\frac{1}{2})}^{5}.$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's compare our expression with the binomial

17592186547892}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "510f41a7-5712-55db-b50d-5c80967bb9fb" :question/math-academy-id "q-12889" :question/problem "Given that

$$
{(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+4)}^{4}=A{x}^{8}+B{x}^{6}+C{x}^{4}+128{x}^{2}+256
$$

where $A,B$ and $C$ are constants, find the value of $A+B+C.$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's compare our expression with the binomial

$$
(a+b)^{n}.
$$

Here we have that $n=4,$ $a=\frac{{x}^{2}}{2},$ and $b=4.$ So, the exponents of the binomial expansion must follow the pattern

$$
{a}^{4}{b}^{0},\,{a}^{3}{b}^{1},\,{a}^{2}{b}^{2},\,{a}^{1}{b}^{3},\,{a}^{0}{b}^{4}.
$$

The $4$th row in Pascal's Triangle is $(1,4,6,4,1).$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+4)}^{4} & =1{a}^{4}+4{a}^{3}b+6{a}^{2}{b}^{2}+4a{b}^{3}+1{b}^{4} \\  & =1{(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2})}^{4}(4)^{0}+4{(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2})}^{3}{(4)}^{1}+6{(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2})}^{2}{(4)}^{2} \\  & \,+4{(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2})}^{1}{(4)}^{3}+1{(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2})}^{0}{(4)}^{4} \\  & =1(\frac{{x}^{8}}{16})(1)+4(\frac{{x}^{6}}{8})(4)+6(\frac{{x}^{4}}{4})(16) \\  & \,+4(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2})(64)+1(1)(256) \\  & =\frac{{x}^{8}}{16}+\frac{16{x}^{6}}{8}+\frac{96{x}^{4}}{4}+\frac{256{x}^{2}}{2}+256 \\  & =\frac{{x}^{8}}{16}+2{x}^{6}+24{x}^{4}+128{x}^{2}+256.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have $A=\frac{1}{16},B=2$ and $C=24.$ So, finally

$$
A+B+C=\frac{1}{16}+2+24=\frac{417}{16}.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "a849bf07-e1b9-58de-b318-85fa4f3d86aa" :step/next {:db/id 17592186548176}} {:db/id 17592186548176 :step/content {:db/id 17592186548051 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "7869ea61-e97c-524e-a14d-1788d8383e87" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{z}^{8}-4{z}^{6}+6{z}^{4}" :db/id 17592186547577} {:answer/id #uuid "863fbced-ba48-51fa-ac1c-071cd8741980" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{z}^{8}+2{z}^{6}-6{z}^{4}" :db/id 17592186547605} {:answer/id #uuid "a2e736b8-e40c-51d3-9a0e-4ad64eae66bd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{z}^{8}-4{z}^{6}+18{z}^{4}" :db/id 17592186547671} {:answer/id #uuid "bbf1cdb0-233a-556a-92fd-fadf68dcfca7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{z}^{8}-4{z}^{6}+12{z}^{4}" :db/id 17592186547718} {:answer/id #uuid "fd90e06c-4204-5316-a4d6-0173539fd070" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{z}^{8}+2{z}^{6}-4{z}^{4}" :db/id 17592186547838}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186547577} :answer-field/id #uuid "a9807bbb-6450-5bec-9d6e-2cb5e0bc2c61" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186547924}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "c9b934c2-8c57-56f1-8a65-42f138da7b11" :question/math-academy-id "q-12891" :question/problem "Find, in descending powers of $z,$ the first three terms of the binomial expansion of ${(1-{z}^{2})}^{4}.$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's compare our expression with the binomial

$$
(a+b)^{n}.
$$

Here we have that $n=4,$ $a=1,$ and $b=-{z}^{2}.$ So, the exponents of the binomial expansion must follow the pattern

$$
{a}^{4}{b}^{0},\,{a}^{3}{b}^{1},\,{a}^{2}{b}^{2},\,{a}^{1}{b}^{3},\,{a}^{0}{b}^{4}.
$$

The $4$th row in Pascal's Triangle is $(1,4,6,4,1).$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{(1-{z}^{2})}^{4} & =1{a}^{4}+4{a}^{3}b+6{a}^{2}{b}^{2}+4a{b}^{3}+1{b}^{4} \\  & =1(1)^{4}(-{z}^{2})^{0}+4(1)^{3}(-{z}^{2})^{1}+6(1)^{2}(-{z}^{2})^{2}+4(1)^{1}(-{z}^{2})^{3}+1(1)^{0}(-{z}^{2})^{4} \\  & =1(1)(1)+4(1)(-{z}^{2})+6(1)({z}^{4})+4(1)(-{z}^{6})+1(1)({z}^{8}) \\  & =1-4{z}^{2}+6{z}^{4}-4{z}^{6}+{z}^{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

We rewrite the binomial expansion in descending powers of $z$ as follows:

$$
(1-{z}^{2})^{4}={z}^{8}-4{z}^{6}+6{z}^{4}-4{z}^{2}+1
$$

Finally, in descending powers of $z,$ the first three terms of the binomial expansion are

$$
{z}^{8}-4{z}^{6}+6{z}^{4}.

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}(2s-{u}^{2})^{4} & =1{a}^{4}{b}^{0}+4{a}^{3}b+6{a}^{2}{b}^{2}+4a{b}^{3}+1{a}^{0}{b}^{4} \\  & =1(2s)^{4}{(-{u}^{2})}^{0}+4(2s)^{3}{(-{u}^{2})}^{1}+6(2s)^{2}{(-{u}^{2})}^{2} \\  & \,+4(2s)^{1}{(-{u}^{2})}^{3}+1(2s)^{0}{(-{u}^{2})}^{4} \\  & =1(16{s}^{4})(1)+4(8{s}^{3})(-{u}^{2})+6(4{s}^{2})({u}^{4}) \\  & \,+4(2s)(-{u}^{6})+1(1)({u}^{8}) \\  & =16{s}^{4}-32{s}^{3}{u}^{2}+24{s}^{2}{u}^{4}-8s{u}^{6}+{u}^{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

We rewrite the binomial expansion in descending powers of $z$ as follows:

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

where $A,B$ and $C$ are constants, determine the value of $A+B+C.$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's compare our expression with the binomial

$$
(a+b)^{n}.
$$

Here we have that $n=4,$ $a=2s,$ and $b=-{u}^{2}.$ So, the exponents of the binomial expansion must follow the pattern

$$
{a}^{4}{b}^{0},\,{a}^{3}{b}^{1},\,{a}^{2}{b}^{2},\,{a}^{1}{b}^{3},\,{a}^{0}{b}^{4}.
$$

The $4$th row in Pascal's Triangle is $(1,4,6,4,1).$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}(2s-{u}^{2})^{4} & =1{a}^{4}{b}^{0}+4{a}^{3}b+6{a}^{2}{b}^{2}+4a{b}^{3}+1{a}^{0}{b}^{4} \\  & =1(2s)^{4}{(-{u}^{2})}^{0}+4(2s)^{3}{(-{u}^{2})}^{1}+6(2s)^{2}{(-{u}^{2})}^{2} \\  & \,+4(2s)^{1}{(-{u}^{2})}^{3}+1(2s)^{0}{(-{u}^{2})}^{4} \\  & =1(16{s}^{4})(1)+4(8{s}^{3})(-{u}^{2})+6(4{s}^{2})({u}^{4}) \\  & \,+4(2s)(-{u}^{6})+1(1)({u}^{8}) \\  & =16{s}^{4}-32{s}^{3}{u}^{2}+24{s}^{2}{u}^{4}-8s{u}^{6}+{u}^{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $A=-32,B=24,$ and $C=-8.$ Finally, then

$$
A+B+C=-32+24-8=-16.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "e88238c8-1541-5000-9ad9-0ced66e4e120"} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "209aed4f-131b-523e-a4e8-1446b6171323" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "16" To find the lowest common multiple of two small numbers, we can list all multiples of the two numbers and identify the smallest multiple that they have in common.

For example, let's find the lowest common multiple of $4$ and $6.$ We start by listing all multiples of $4$ and $6\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}4 & \,\to \,4,\,8,\,\boxed{\text{[math]12[/math]}},\,16,\,20,\,24,\,… \\ 6 & \,\to \,6,\,\boxed{\text{[math]12[/math]}},\,18,\,24,\,30,\,36,\,…\end{aligned}
$$

The smallest multiple in both lists is ![](images/92/9285d37c7b455395acb42a54f78348bedfd8c9a72ad63d6e6ab7c2426148ea0d.svg) So $12$ is our answer, and we can write

$$
\textrm{LCM}(4,6)= 12.
$$

**Note:** The lowest common multiple is also sometimes called the *least* common multiple." :tutorial/id #uuid "b16f2464-2c19-5166-bd61-97043695afcb" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5301 :tutorial/title Let's demonstrate by finding $\textrm{LCM}(10,12).$ We start by writing the prime factorization of $10$ and $12$, writing any repeating factors as powers:

$$
\begin{aligned}10 & =2\cdot 5={2}^{1}\cdot {5}^{1} \\ 12 & =2\cdot 2\cdot 3={2}^{2}\cdot {3}^{1}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we write down each unique prime factor that appears in either of our decompositions. In our case, the unique prime factors are 

$$
{\color{red}2}, \qquad {\color{red}3}, \qquad {\color{red}5}.
$$

Now, for each number in our list, we look at *both* prime factorizations and we take the *largest* power shown for each prime factor:

- The factors corresponding to ${\color{red}2}$ are ${\color{red}2}^{\color{blue}1}$ and ${\color{red}2}^{\color{blue}2}.$ Of these, the larger power is ${\color{red}2}^{\color{blue}2}.$

- There is only one factor corresponding to ${\color{red}3}.$ It is ${\color{red}3}^{\color{blue}1}.$

- There is only one factor corresponding to ${\color{red}5}.$ It is ${\color{red}5}^{\color{blue}1}.$

Finally, we multiply the largest powers of each factor together, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{LCM}(10,12) & ={2}^{2}\cdot {3}^{1}\cdot {5}^{1} \\  & =4\cdot 3\cdot 5 \\  & =60.\end{aligned}

:question/math-academy-id "q-5179" :question/problem "Given the system of equations below, what is the value of $p-q?$

$$
\{\begin{aligned}3p=15 \\ p+2q=9.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "We will isolate a variable in one of the equations and then substitute it into the other equation. It doesn't matter which equation we pick first, so we choose the easiest one. In this case, the first equation looks like the easiest.

Using the first equation, we can isolate $p$ by dividing both sides of the equation by $3:$

$$
\begin{aligned}3p & =15 \\ p & =5\end{aligned}
$$

If we now substitute $p=5$ into $p+2q=9,$ then we can find the value of $q:$

$$
\begin{aligned}p+2q & =9 \\ (5)+2q & =9 \\ 2q & =4 \\ q & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $p=5,\,q=2.$ So,

$$
p-q=5-2=3.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "0a9225c0-5f39-5569-928a-3834451e9d52" :step/next {:db/id 17592186547152}} {:db/id 17592186547152 :step/content {:db/id 17592186546991 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1b85cb2c-460d-5f91-86c0-674d13fae83e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-9" :db/id 17592186546309} {:answer/id #uuid "242eed59-c937-5dab-b478-b3a1accb9d4f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "9" :db/id 17592186546329} {:answer/id #uuid "463e0a8b-5e11-54a2-8cdd-72b176626176" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186546407} {:answer/id #uuid "6a785a85-c477-5db9-a10d-570f963f9181" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-1" :db/id 17592186546485} {:answer/id #uuid "f5ff80ce-ffb0-542a-ba50-ce8557612884" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "10" :db/id 17592186546805}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186546309} :answer-field/id #uuid "e282d81b-1bfe-5c5b-abe6-d91779057814" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186546940}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "3b789afd-79c7-56fc-b94a-f894f177dfe2" :question/math-academy-id "q-18555" :question/problem "Given the system of equations below, what is the value of $a+b?$

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2b=6a+14 \\ 5b+25=0\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "We number the equations so that we can refer to them more easily:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2b=6a+14 & \,\,(1) \\ 5b+25=0. & \,\,(2)\end{aligned}
$$

We will isolate a variable in one of the equations and then substitute it into the other equation. Using equation $(2),$ we can solve for $b$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}5b+25 & =0 \\ 5b & =-25 \\ b & =-5\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute $b=-5$ into equation $(1)$ and solve for $a:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2(-5) & =6a+14 \\ -10 & =6a+14 \\ -10-14 & =6a \\ 6a & =-24 \\ a & =-4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $a=-4,\,b=-5.$ So,

$$
a+b=-4+(-5)=-4-5=-9.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "ca7de6ad-e459-52ba-851d-06dd86cc6059" :step/next {:db/id 17592186547164}} {:db/id 17592186547164 :step/content {:db/id 17592186546971 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "25d7a53c-5916-5db7-992b-ff7a626a51c4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-5" :db/id 17592186546336} {:answer/id #uuid "51399b6f-2763-5014-9b02-635633f0dada" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "7" :db/id 17592186546427} {:answer/id #uuid "9e23c320-e17b-534f-8a91-354568ebc163" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "6" :db/id 17592186546603} {:answer/id #uuid "a3f272eb-ffc1-5fb6-b622-055a0def12d3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-1" :db/id 17592186546617} {:answer/id #uuid "d9f37f2b-79d8-5ebd-8615-8e1bcfb28380" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8" :db/id 17592186546732}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186546732} :answer-field/id #uuid "78ca5c4c-b502-5598-a6f0-d81d606b319e" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186546881}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "1ad70587-af92-55e0-95cf-31aa82c10e13" :question/math-academy-id "q-52115" :question/problem "Given the system of equations below, what is the value of $a-b?$

#uuid "3b789afd-79c7-56fc-b94a-f894f177dfe2" :question/math-academy-id "q-18555" :question/problem "Given the system of equations below, what is the value of $a+b?$

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2b=6a+14 \\ 5b+25=0\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "We number the equations so that we can refer to them more easily:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2b=6a+14 & \,\,(1) \\ 5b+25=0. & \,\,(2)\end{aligned}
$$

We will isolate a variable in one of the equations and then substitute it into the other equation. Using equation $(2),$ we can solve for $b$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}5b+25 & =0 \\ 5b & =-25 \\ b & =-5\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute $b=-5$ into equation $(1)$ and solve for $a:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2(-5) & =6a+14 \\ -10 & =6a+14 \\ -10-14 & =6a \\ 6a & =-24 \\ a & =-4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $a=-4,\,b=-5.$ So,

$$
a+b=-4+(-5)=-4-5=-9.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "ca7de6ad-e459-52ba-851d-06dd86cc6059" :step/next {:db/id 17592186547164}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1b85cb2c-460d-5f91-86c0-674d13fae83e" :answer/type {:db/id #uuid "1ad70587-af92-55e0-95cf-31aa82c10e13" :question/math-academy-id "q-52115" :question/problem "Given the system of equations below, what is the value of $a-b?$

$$
\{\begin{aligned}a=7 \\ 3a+6b=15\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "We will isolate a variable in one of the equations and then substitute it into the other equation. It so happens that the first equation is already solved for $a:$

$$
a=7
$$

If we now substitute $a=7$ into $3a+6b=15,$ then we can find the value of $b:$

$$
\begin{aligned}3a+6b & =15 \\ 3(7)+6b & =15 \\ 6b & =-6 \\ b & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $a=7,\,b=-1.$ So,

$$
a-b=7-(-1)=7+1=8.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "e5c9a09f-e906-5432-9fef-4ec9ba80344e"} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "25d7a53c-5916-5db7-992b-ff7a626a51c4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-5" :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186134779 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135012 :tutorial/content "The expression below gives the cost, in dollars, of sending a letter to Spain: 

$$
2w + 1
$$

Here, $w$ is the letter's weight in ounces.

$$
\overbrace{\:{\color{blue}2}\!\!\!{\underset{\underset{\Large\textrm{weight}}{\large\uparrow}}{w}}\!\!\!+{\color{red}1}\:}^{\large\textrm{total cost}}
$$

The coefficient of $w$ is the cost for each additional ounce of weight.

To illustrate:

- If $w=1$ (we have a $1$-ounce letter), the cost is ${\color{blue}2} \cdot 1 + {\color{red}1} = \[math]3.$

- If $w=2$ (we have a $2$-ounce letter), the cost is ${\color{blue}2} \cdot 2 + {\color{red}1} = \[/math]5.$

- If $w=3$ (we have a $3$-ounce letter), the cost is ${\color{blue}2} \cdot 3 + {\color{red}1} = \[math]7.$

Note the following:

- The number $\color{blue}2$ in this expression represents a *unit rate.* Each time we increase the letter's weight by $1$ ounce, the cost increases by $\color{blue}\[/math]2$.

- There is also a **base fee** of $\color{red}\[math]1$, which does not depend on the weight of the letter. We can think of this as the cost of sending a zero-ounce letter." :tutorial/id #uuid "4884ffa5-ca42-52e9-9661-39a00bd97ba4" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1363 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id whenever an individual or company makes a purchase. The tax is usually based on a certain percentage of the sale price.

For example, suppose a person purchases a bicycle for $\[math] 200,$ and there is a sales tax of $5\%.$ How much is this tax, and what is the total cost of the bicycle?

To determine the amount of the tax the person must pay, we multiply $200 \times 5\%$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}Tax & =\text{\[}/math]200\times 5% \\  & =\text{\[}math]200\times 0.05 \\  & =\text{\[}/math]10\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the purchaser must pay a $\[math]10$ sales tax. This means that the total amount the person needs to pay for the bicycle is

$$
\[/math]200 + \[math]10 = \[/math]210.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "683a47a7-4c0a-5da2-888c-d004b4167df5" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6218 :tutorial/title "Calculating Taxes"} :step/id #uuid "7365f275-4f44-5bdc-b64a-45158abcf6d5" :step/math-academy-id 37767 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134962}} {:db/id 17592186134962 :step/content {:db/id 17592186133947 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186133538 :question/id #uuid "93b2ed4a-45ad-5fc4-bfe8-479f5a674595" :question/math-academy-id "e-1604"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "758ce589-dcf8-5be8-8f15-ae72172050db" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049467}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186134438} {:db/id 17592186134487} {:db/id 17592186495112} {:db/id 17592186495140} {:db/id 17592186495141} {:db/id 17592186495172}] :knowledge-point/title "Constructing an Expression With a Tax Term"} :step/id #uuid "4b073ed7-15e0-5244-aa23-477855194546" :step/math-academy-id 5156 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134782}}] :activity/title "Interpreting Linear Expressions" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186134048} {:db/id 17592186134779 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135012 :tutorial/content "The expression below gives the cost, in dollars, of sending a letter to Spain:

S=\dfrac{D}{T},

$$

$$
y - y_1 = m(x-x_1).
$$

 

For example, consider the straight line graph which passes through the points $(3,1)$ and $(5,5)$, as shown below.

![](images/e7/e7838ffcb8f56ebffd384763ff761990e15031bdc5cdf3f0cc1f964ed69a4806.png)

We know that the line passes through the point $(3,1),$ so we can use $(x_1,y_1) = (3,1)$ in our point-slope formula. All that remains is to compute $m,$ and we can do this using the given points.

First, calculate the slope $m$ using the given points:

$$
\begin{aligned}m=\frac{{y}_{2}-{y}_{1}}{{x}_{2}-{x}_{1}}=\frac{5-1}{5-3}=\frac{4}{2}=2\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute $m=2$ and the point $(x_1,y_1) = (3,1)$ into the point-slope formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-1 & =2(x-3)\end{aligned}
$$

**Note:** If we simplify this point-slope formula, we obtain the slope-intercept form of the line:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-1 & =2(x-3) \\ y-1 & =2x-6 \\ y & =2x-5\end{aligned}
$$

**Watch out!** We could put $(x_1,y_1)=(5,5).$ In this case, the point-slope form will be different:

$$
y-5=2(x-5)
$$

 
But the resulting simplified slope-intercept form will be the same:

$$
y = 2x-5
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "43f9e39e-fc27-549d-8ec4-b2bf4f375a33" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8695 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "866e675a-4d40-5d4f-ab69-7850b06a40d3" :step/math-academy-id an even exponent, such as

$$
x^6 = 64?
$$

We can solve this equation by taking the $6$th root of each side and solving for $x.$ 

Since the exponent $(6)$ is even, there will be two real solutions (positive and negative):

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{6} & =64 \\ \sqrt[6]{{x}^{6}} & =\pm \sqrt[6]{64} \\ x & =\pm \sqrt[6]{{2}^{6}} \\ x & =\pm 2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions are $x=\pm 2.$

In general, we have the following rule of thumb:

*When $n$ is even, and we take the $n$th root of both sides of $x^n = a$ with $a \geq 0,$ we get two solutions (positive and negative):* 

$$
x = \pm\sqrt[n]{a}
$$

**Watch out!** If $a<0$ and $n$ is even, equation  $x^n = a$ has no solution since, in this case, $x^n \geq 0$ for any real $x.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "6a9834f3-f04b-5340-b297-793072b594d9" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4833 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "036c0d84-9bf6-5da8-986c-2ace277257a2" :step/math-academy-id 30128 :step/next {:db/id 17592186116226}}] :activity/title "Solving Equations With Even Exponents Using the Nth Root Method" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186115421} {:db/id 17592186116230 :step/content {:db/id 17592186116534 :tutorial/content "How do we solve an equation with a variable raised to an even exponent, such as

**Watch out!** If $a<0$ and $n$ is even, equation  $x^n = a$ has no solution since, in this case, $x^n \geq 0$ for any real $x.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "6a9834f3-f04b-5340-b297-793072b594d9" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4833 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:activity/expected-seconds 540.0 :activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186069792} :activity/id #uuid "2dc87c95-826a-555a-9423-36fffbf47e86" :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186051032 :topic/id #uuid "7bffda20-cdd5-5dc8-9399-950fa61fbd19" :topic/math-academy-id 382} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186069792 :step/content {:db/id 17592186069940 :tutorial/content "Sometimes, perfect square trinomials have a leading coefficient that is something other than $1.$ For example, the expression

$$
4x^2+12x+9
$$

has a leading coefficient of $4,$ and it is a perfect square trinomial because it is the square of the binomial $(2x+3)$ as we can see below:

$$
\begin{aligned}(2x+3)^{2} & = \\ (2x)^{2}+2(2x)(3)+(3)^{2} & = \\ 4{x}^{2}+12x+9 & \end{aligned}
$$

To factor a perfect square trinomial with a leading coefficient other than $1,$ we use the square of sum formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}^{2}+2ab+{b}^{2} & =(a+b)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

To illustrate, let's factor the expression $4x^2+12x+9$ using the square of sum formula. We perform the following steps:

1\. Write both the quadratic term and the constant term as perfect squares:

  $$
  \begin{aligned}4{x}^{2}+12x+9 & = \\ (2x)^{2}+12x+(3)^{2}\end{aligned}
  $$

2\. Factor a $2$ out of the linear term:

  $$
  \begin{aligned}(2x)^{2}+2(6x)+(3)^{2}\end{aligned}
  $$

3\. Write the middle parentheses $(6x)$ as a product of $2x$ and ${\color{blue}3}\mathbin{:}$

  $$
  \begin{aligned}(2x)^{2}+2(2x\cdot 3)+(3)^{2}\end{aligned}
  $$

4\. Factor the trinomial using the square of sum formula. In this case, we have $a=2x$ and $b=3\mathbin{:}$

  $$
  \begin{aligned}(2x+3)^{2}\end{aligned}
  $$

**Note:** This method works *only* when the trinomial is a perfect square! It will *not* work for every trinomial. But we will learn more general methods in the future." :tutorial/id #uuid "5d43b5e8-672e-5cdd-b7a3-8de29e6552f3" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1597 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "8854423e-52a6-5077-ab8f-c9de25d23206" :step/math-academy-id 4236 :step/next {:db/id 17592186069793}} {:db/id 17592186069793 :step/content {:db/id 17592186068847 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186068464 :question/id #uuid "99376061-f11c-50f9-8c6e-e67ad640afd1" :question/math-academy-id "e-1331"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "0f4dc7f6-d085-5ad8-8ac3-95e5b9cc337f" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049026}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186069216} {:db/id 17592186069252} {:db/id 17592186484281} {:db/id 17592186484296}] :knowledge-point/title "Factoring a Perfect Square Trinomial Generated by the Square of a Sum"} :step/id #uuid "ac3a35ba-8b05-5a52-9f06-dc5add492619" :step/math-academy-id 4237 :step/next {:db/id 17592186069898}} {:db/id 17592186069794 :step/content {:db/id 17592186068848 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186068465 :question/id #uuid "e9c8bdc9-696d-5a55-bb0d-d247008c5684" :question/math-academy-id "e-1333"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "5f64efad-73ef-5caa-b38b-060d24ce13cf" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186069219} {:db/id 17592186069220} {:db/id 17592186484210} {:db/id 17592186542225} {:db/id 17592186549989}] :knowledge-point/title "Factoring a Perfect Square Trinomial Whose Terms Have a Common Factor"} :step/id #uuid "6a2dd26d-51b3-5cc1-8396-efeb5b1b8bb7" :step/math-academy-id 4242 :step/next {:db/id 17592186069795}} {:db/id 17592186069795 :step/content {:db/id 17592186069941 :tutorial/content "How can we factor a trinomial that has a negative leading coefficient, like

$$
-25y^2 + 20y - 4\,?
$$

 
We can reduce this to a more familiar problem by factoring out $−1$ from the entire expression:

$$
-(25y^2 - 20y + 4)
$$

Now, we factor the quadratic expression inside the parentheses using the square of a difference formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}25{y}^{2}-20y+4 & = \\ (5y)^{2}-20y+{2}^{2} & = \\ (5y)^{2}-2(10y)+{2}^{2} & = \\ (5y)^{2}-2(5y\cdot 2)+{2}^{2} & = \\ (5y-2)^{2} & \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our original expression factors as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}-(25{y}^{2}-20y+4) & = \\ -(5y-2)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "757d1827-0402-5d3d-b8da-a4dc88c254bb" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1598 :tutorial/title "Factoring a Perfect Square Trinomial With a Negative Leading Coefficient"} :step/id #uuid "3464306e-5c3f-55f3-9c10-87ab309dded2" :step/math-academy-id 4244 :step/next {:db/id 17592186069796}} {:db/id 17592186069796 :step/content {:db/id 17592186068849 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186068466 :question/id #uuid "b74ed282-c54c-56f8-aa9f-8c5ef4465712" :question/math-academy-id "e-1334"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "b67de190-3b32-506e-b375-bd18d4543bf6" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186069338} {:db/id 17592186069339} {:db/id 17592186484231} {:db/id 17592186484282} {:db/id 17592186484292} {:db/id 17592186484295} {:db/id 17592186542210}] :knowledge-point/title "Factoring a Perfect Square Trinomial With a Negative Leading Coefficient"} :step/id #uuid "3222e5cc-52d3-5afd-8468-ab3d87c483b2" :step/math-academy-id 4245} {:db/id 17592186069876 :step/content {:db/id 17592186068902 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186068520 :question/id #uuid "b7141e58-61cf-5134-8443-a82d79a5506e" :question/math-academy-id "e-1593"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "69a3b7a7-1042-511a-aaff-8b0911eae499" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186069215} {:db/id 17592186069251} {:db/id 17592186484249} {:db/id 17592186484291} {:db/id 17592186542124}] :knowledge-point/title "Factoring a Perfect Square Trinomial Generated by the Square of a Difference"} :step/id #uuid "d8accb58-b4d7-5dc8-9c5e-a5ca4f3588a2" :step/math-academy-id 5059 :step/next {:db/id 17592186069794}} {:db/id 17592186069898 :step/content {:db/id 17592186069954 :tutorial/content "Other perfect square trinomials can be factored as the square of a difference:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}^{2}-2ab+{b}^{2} & =(a-b)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

To illustrate, let's factor the expression $9x^2-24x+16$ using the square of difference formula. We perform the following steps:

1\. Write both the quadratic term and the constant term as perfect squares:

  $$
  \begin{aligned}9{x}^{2}-24x+16 & = \\ (3x)^{2}-24x+(4)^{2}\end{aligned}
  $$

2\. Factor a $2$ out of the linear term:

  $$
  \begin{aligned}(3x)^{2}-24x+(4)^{2} & = \\ (3x)^{2}-2(12x)+(4)^{2}\end{aligned}
  $$

3\. Write the middle parentheses $(12x)$ as a product of $3x$ and ${\color{blue}4}\mathbin{:}$

  $$
  \begin{aligned}(3x)^{2}-2(12x)+(4)^{2} & = \\ (3x)^{2}-2(3x\cdot 4)+(4)^{2}\end{aligned}
  $$

4\. Factor the trinomial using the square of difference formula. In this case, we have $a=3x$ and $b=4\mathbin{:}$

  $$
  \begin{aligned}(3x)^{2}-2(3x\cdot 4)+(4)^{2} & = \\ (3x-4)^{2}\end{aligned}
  $$

**Note:** Once again, we note that this method works *only* when the trinomial is a perfect square! $$

To illustrate, let's factor the expression $9x^2-24x+16$ using the square of difference formula. We perform the following steps:

1\. Write both the quadratic term and the constant term as perfect squares:

  $$
  \begin{aligned}9{x}^{2}-24x+16 & = \\ (3x)^{2}-24x+(4)^{2}\end{aligned}
  $$

2\. Factor a $2$ out of the linear term:

  $$
  \begin{aligned}(3x)^{2}-24x+(4)^{2} & = \\ (3x)^{2}-2(12x)+(4)^{2}\end{aligned}
  $$

3\. Write the middle parentheses $(12x)$ as a product of $3x$ and ${\color{blue}4}\mathbin{:}$

  $$
  \begin{aligned}(3x)^{2}-2(12x)+(4)^{2} & = \\ (3x)^{2}-2(3x\cdot 4)+(4)^{2}\end{aligned}
  $$

4\. Factor the trinomial using the square of difference formula. In this case, we have $a=3x$ and $b=4\mathbin{:}$

  $$
  \begin{aligned}(3x)^{2}-2(3x\cdot 4)+(4)^{2} & = \\ (3x-4)^{2}\end{aligned}
  $$

$$
-25y^2 + 20y - 4\,?
$$

 
We can reduce this to a more familiar problem by factoring out $−1$ from the entire expression:

$$
-(25y^2 - 20y + 4)
$$

Now, we factor the quadratic expression inside the parentheses using the square of a difference formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}25{y}^{2}-20y+4 & = \\ (5y)^{2}-20y+{2}^{2} & = \\ (5y)^{2}-2(10y)+{2}^{2} & = \\ (5y)^{2}-2(5y\cdot 2)+{2}^{2} & = \\ (5y-2)^{2} & \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our original expression factors as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}-(25{y}^{2}-20y+4) & = \\ -(5y-2)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "757d1827-0402-5d3d-b8da-a4dc88c254bb" :tutorial/math-academy-id 1598 :tutorial/title "Factoring a Perfect Square Trinomial With a Negative Leading Coefficient"} :step/id #uuid "3464306e-5c3f-55f3-9c10-87ab309dded2" :step/math-academy-id 4244 :step/next {:db/id 17592186069796}} {:db/id 17592186069941 :tutorial/content "How can we factor a trinomial that has a negative leading coefficient, like

$$

$$"} :step/id #uuid "77f81baa-f622-5822-ad79-2391b7a40d19"} {:db/id 17592186542265 :step/content {:db/id 17592186542124 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2bb9bce2-0c34-585a-9786-18cdbee30507" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(3y-3)^{2}" :db/id 17592186541510} {:answer/id #uuid "41931e51-fe5c-5024-b27f-7666c39e6cec" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(y-3)^{2}" :db/id 17592186541559} {:answer/id #uuid "b7268394-d3df-50dd-aefd-a1d483bd162e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(3y-1)^{2}" :db/id 17592186541799} {:answer/id #uuid "bfc42d89-bdf4-5894-9f74-40a503a37160" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "9(y-1)^{2}" :db/id 17592186541827} {:answer/id #uuid "c4b7e90c-e93d-59fc-87e0-2091f13f04ee" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3(y-1)^{2}" :db/id 17592186541835}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186541799} :answer-field/id #uuid "bbdf1e33-0fba-578c-aaad-d0ea6db8cbc2" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186542052}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "1c00ad8d-9908-5ab2-b9e6-65ef0d5fcd94" :question/math-academy-id "q-31964" :question/problem "$9{y}^{2}-6y+1=$" :question/worked-solution "The "square of a difference" formula states that

$$

$-4{x}^{2}+4x-1.$" :question/worked-solution "Notice that the leading coefficient is negative. To reduce the expression to a more familiar form, we can factor out $-1,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}-4{x}^{2}+4x-1 & = \\ -(4{x}^{2}-4x+1)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we factor the quadratic expression inside the parentheses using the square of a difference formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{x}^{2}-4x+1 & = \\ (2x)^{2}-4x+{1}^{2} & = \\ (2x)^{2}-2\cdot (2x)+{1}^{2} & = \\ (2x-1)^{2} & \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our original expression factors as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}-(4{x}^{2}-4x+1) & = \\ -(2x-1)^{2} & \end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "bf2aa872-b9dd-51ab-a97f-7add7180d9e9" :step/next {:db/id 17592186542263}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "30bc40bd-0baa-53bc-b504-a2c240a14dc2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-(2x-1)^{2}" :db/id 17592186541522} {:answer/id #uuid "37d6615e-66de-5728-ae8f-8e2fb4faec1f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-(2x+1)^{2}" :db/id 17592186541541} {:answer/id #uuid "464d7d12-8513-5d3d-b8c3-79b6c483fb54" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-(4x-1)^{2}" :db/id 17592186541571} {:answer/id #uuid "62b93017-abd9-5aa6-a8a4-50b59a42230d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(x-2)^{2}" :db/id 17592186541625} {:answer/id #uuid "995306bc-ae35-5f95-966b-0932e6545022" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(4x-1)^{2}" :db/id 17592186541741}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186541522} :answer-field/id #uuid "d785b8b3-293e-5ba6-866c-d51249e905eb" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186542068} {:answer/id #uuid "30bc40bd-0baa-53bc-b504-a2c240a14dc2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-(2x-1)^{2}" :db/id 17592186541522} {:answer/id #uuid "37d6615e-66de-5728-ae8f-8e2fb4faec1f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-(2x+1)^{2}" :db/id 17592186541541} {:answer/id #uuid "464d7d12-8513-5d3d-b8c3-79b6c483fb54" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-(4x-1)^{2}" :db/id 17592186541571} {:answer/id #uuid "62b93017-abd9-5aa6-a8a4-50b59a42230d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(x-2)^{2}" :db/id 17592186541625} {:answer/id #uuid "995306bc-ae35-5f95-966b-0932e6545022" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(4x-1)^{2}" :db/id 17592186541741} {:db/id 17592186049088 :topic/encompasses [{:db/id 17592186428351 :encompassing/rationale "Initial Codex estimate from captured target-band crossing frequency. If $\langle x_1,x_2 \rangle$ and $\langle y_1,y_2 \rangle$ are the solutions to the systems $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}$ and $L\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{b}$ respectively, what is the value of $x_1 \cdot y_2?$" :question/worked-solution "First, notice that since $A=LU,$ we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}Ax=b\,⟹\,{{(LU)}_{⏟}}_{A}x=b.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, setting $U\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{y},$ we obtain

![](images/a1/a185a6fd91c78ed3e291b3ac8b99f9430290e5d8c1060a7d97317efc230aeb40.svg)

Now, we solve the two systems in turn.

- First, we solve $L\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{b}.$ Writing this equation in matrix form, we get
![](images/1e/1e780d384ca1fd957d742bbd047399c558ab016d187ce4cf71682546673aba35.svg)
This gives the system of equations

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} &=6 \\ -2{y}_{1}+{y}_{2} &=-8.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

The solution to this system is $y_1=6$ and $y_2=4.$ Therefore, 
![](images/58/58da62903247cf6dfdf33be86293c181ef5184048ca7cd6c921360e5d202f353.svg)

- Next, we solve $U\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{y}.$ Writing this equation in matrix form, we get
![](images/e0/e0563dde4944ecbe2ccb98bc91246fa18c7a808df96ab77f9f8efb5510084677.svg)
This gives the system of equations

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}7{x}_{1}+4{x}_{2} &=6 \\ -2{x}_{2} &=4.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

$$
A={{\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 4 & 1\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{L}{{\begin{bmatrix}2 & -1 \\ 0 & 4\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{U},\,b=\begin{bmatrix}6 \\ 20\end{bmatrix}.
$$

If $⟨{x}_{1},{x}_{2}⟩$ and $⟨{y}_{1},{y}_{2}⟩$ are the solutions to the systems $Ax=b$ and $Ly=b$ respectively, what is the value of ${x}_{2}\cdot {y}_{2}?$" :question/worked-solution "First, notice that since $A=LU,$ we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}Ax=b\,⟹\,{{(LU)}_{⏟}}_{A}x=b.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, setting $Ux=y,$ we obtain

$$
L{{(Ux)}_{⏟}}_{y}=b\,⟹\,\left\{\begin{aligned}Ly &=b \\ Ux &=y.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Now, we solve the two systems in turn.

- First, we solve $Ly=b.$ Writing this equation in matrix form, we get

$$
\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 4 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{y}_{1} \\ {y}_{2}\end{bmatrix}=b=\begin{bmatrix}6 \\ 20\end{bmatrix}.
$$

This gives the system of equations

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} &=6 \\ 4{y}_{1}+{y}_{2} &=20.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

The solution to this system is ${y}_{1}=6$ and ${y}_{2}=-4.$ Therefore, 

$$
y=\begin{bmatrix}6 \\ -4\end{bmatrix}.
$$

- Next, we solve $Ux=y.$ Writing this equation in matrix form, we get

$$
\begin{bmatrix}2 & -1 \\ 0 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}=y=\begin{bmatrix}6 \\ -4\end{bmatrix}.
$$

This gives the system of equations

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}-{x}_{2} &=6 \\ 4{x}_{2} &=-4.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

The solution to this system is ${x}_{2}=-1$ and ${x}_{1}=\frac{5}{2}.$ Therefore, 

$$
x=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{5}{2} \\ -1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}Ly &=b \\ Ux &=y\end{aligned}\right.
$$

is equivalent to $Ax=b.$" :question/worked-solution "First, notice that since $A=LU,$ we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}Ax=b\,⟹\,{{(LU)}_{⏟}}_{A}x=b.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, setting $Ux=y,$ we obtain

$$
L{{(Ux)}_{⏟}}_{y}=b\,⟹\,\left\{\begin{aligned}Ly &=b \\ Ux &=y.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We now solve $Ly=b.$ Writing this equation in matrix form, we get

$$
\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -2 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{y}_{1} \\ {y}_{2} \\ {y}_{3}\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

This gives the system of equations

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} &=1 \\ -2{y}_{1}+{y}_{2} &=-2 \\ -{y}_{1}+{y}_{2}+{y}_{3} &=2.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We can compute the solution to this system using forward substitution, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & =1, \\ {y}_{2} & =-2+2{y}_{1} \\  & =-2+2(1) \\  & =0, \\ {y}_{3} & =2+{y}_{1}-{y}_{2} \\  & =2+(1)-(0) \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 
$y=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}.$"} {:db/id 17592186479090 :question/id #uuid "53971d39-ffaa-5c20-9081-d54743d61b0a" :question/math-academy-id "q-32579" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id $$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ -3 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{y}_{1} \\ {y}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

This gives the system of equations

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} &=2 \\ -3{y}_{1}+{y}_{2} &=-2.\end{aligned}\right.

:activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186120663 :step/content {:db/id 17592186121031 :tutorial/content "There is an algorithm that uses $LU$ factorization to solve systems of equations of the form 

$$
A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b} .
$$

For example, let's solve the following equation:

![](images/77/77bbf7683a8ecfbd6864ce82eede96dcab60480e9f5395ac38eae88218af8fde.svg)

Since the LU factorization of $A$ is

![](images/d7/d704b00f3e25fdd85fcf123baf0340f87b82125ae2ce0718891102c9da9968f2.svg)
our equation $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}$ can be written as

![](images/14/1481be73064ba910f27931cba3f6a252123090c055ed3d4eb3657fd9b9084c58.svg)

i.e., 

$$
LU\mathbf{x}= \mathbf{b}.
$$

Now, suppose we set $U\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{y}.$ Substituting this into the above, we have

$$
L\mathbf{y}= \mathbf{b}.
$$

In other words, we can reduce the problem to the following system of matrix equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}Ly &=b \\ Ux &=y\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Since $L$ and $U$ are both triangular, each of these equations is easily solvable using back and forward substitution.

- First, we solve $L\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{b}.$ Let's assume that ![](images/46/46e89549c82a3571050bf103d9f539cfd82c197c6c0ffef9161ed3c67cdbb4c0.svg) Then, we have
![](images/af/af1f7463d07d4ddf3f25b8ae1cff3d658f8c0d2a9ab8295c5ea1e0e9c69d2fe6.svg)
which gives the system of equations

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} &=-1 \\ -{y}_{1}+{y}_{2} &=0.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Solving this equation using *forward* substitution, we get the solution
![](images/5b/5bb589d79fbb718f91b5df14ae4c7ac0a3767cb625c2079c0b16562b74484491.svg)

- Finally, we solve $U\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{y}.$ We have
![](images/4a/4a54f9bbd8830b3be687a168c8d9548466124669f8e7309ee18e1f05904fd084.svg)
which gives the system of equations

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-3{x}_{2} &=-1 \\ -{x}_{2} &=-1.\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}

17592186120663 :step/content {:db/id 17592186121031 :tutorial/content "There is an algorithm that uses $LU$ factorization to solve systems of equations of the form 

$$
A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b} .
$$

For example, let's solve the following equation:

![](images/77/77bbf7683a8ecfbd6864ce82eede96dcab60480e9f5395ac38eae88218af8fde.svg)

Since the LU factorization of $A$ is

![](images/d7/d704b00f3e25fdd85fcf123baf0340f87b82125ae2ce0718891102c9da9968f2.svg)
our equation $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}$ can be written as

![](images/14/1481be73064ba910f27931cba3f6a252123090c055ed3d4eb3657fd9b9084c58.svg)

i.e., 

$$
LU\mathbf{x}= \mathbf{b}.
$$

Now, suppose we set $U\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{y}.$ Substituting this into the above, we have

$$
L\mathbf{y}= \mathbf{b}.
$$

In other words, we can reduce the problem to the following system of matrix equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}Ly &=b \\ Ux &=y\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Since $L$ and $U$ are both triangular, each of these equations is easily solvable using back and forward substitution.

- First, we solve $L\mathbf{y} = \mathbf{b}.$ Let's assume that ![](images/46/46e89549c82a3571050bf103d9f539cfd82c197c6c0ffef9161ed3c67cdbb4c0.svg) Then, we have
![](images/af/af1f7463d07d4ddf3f25b8ae1cff3d658f8c0d2a9ab8295c5ea1e0e9c69d2fe6.svg)
which gives the system of equations

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} &=-1 \\ -{y}_{1}+{y}_{2} &=0.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Solving this equation using *forward* substitution, we get the solution
![](images/5b/5bb589d79fbb718f91b5df14ae4c7ac0a3767cb625c2079c0b16562b74484491.svg)

- Finally, we solve $U\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{y}.$ We have
![](images/4a/4a54f9bbd8830b3be687a168c8d9548466124669f8e7309ee18e1f05904fd084.svg)
which gives the system of equations

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-3{x}_{2} &=-1 \\ -{x}_{2} &=-1.\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this equation using *back* substitution, we get the solution

17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "For the function of two variables 
$f(x,y)={e}^{x-2y},$
the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $(0,0)$ is given by

$$
f(x,y)=1+x+a\,y+\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+bxy+c{y}^{2}.
$$

Find the value of $a+b+c.$" :question/worked-solution "If the function $f(x,y)$ is twice differentiable at $(x,y)=(0,0),$ then the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $(0,0)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈\overset{\text{Linear approximation}}{\overset{⏞}{f(0,0)+{f}_{x}(0,0)\cdot x+{f}_{y}(0,0)\cdot y}} \\  & \,\,+{{\frac{1}{2}({f}_{xx}(0,0)\cdot {x}^{2}+2{f}_{xy}(0,0)\cdot xy+{f}_{yy}(0,0)\cdot {y}^{2})}_{⏟}}_{\text{Quadratic part}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the terms of our Taylor polynomial.

- Calculating the value of the function, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0,0) & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

- Calculating the first derivatives, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & ={e}^{x-2y}, & \,{f}_{y}(x,y) & =-2{e}^{x-2y} \\ {f}_{x}(0,0) & =1, & \,{f}_{y}(0,0) & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

- Calculating the second derivatives, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xx}(x,y) & ={e}^{x-2y}, & \,{f}_{xx}(0,0) & =1 \\ {f}_{xy}(x,y) & =-2{e}^{x-2y}, & \,{f}_{xy}(0,0) & =-2 \\ {f}_{yy}(x,y) & =4{e}^{x-2y}, & \,{f}_{yy}(0,0) & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the second-degree Taylor polynomial is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈1+1\cdot x+(-2)\cdot y+\frac{1}{2}(1\cdot {x}^{2}+2(-2)\cdot xy+4\cdot {y}^{2}) \\  & =1+x+(-2)y+\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+(-2)xy+2{y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
a+b+c=(-2)+(-2)+2=-2.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186198655 :question/id #uuid "6e6d1ba4-7501-5c84-a8cd-0bbe2d40c544" :question/math-academy-id "q-163113" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186198434 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "e74c46c7-7f57-5adc-8acb-ea91958d8725" :knowledge-point/title "Finding a Quadratic Taylor Polynomial"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "02574b50-c710-5a8f-8229-9eaa00044a04" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186278603} {:answer/id #uuid "10420ffa-1165-5942-a0ff-b3580c576eab" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-1" :db/id 17592186278737} {:answer/id #uuid "3c91efce-0927-5416-b18a-4ba2ceaf7a3f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186279126} {:answer/id #uuid "908df91a-4453-5800-be38-08e07668caab" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186279879} {:answer/id #uuid "e37ae8eb-1e3b-558b-bcf1-ab48ef85e453" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{3}{2}" :db/id 17592186280599}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "908df91a-4453-5800-be38-08e07668caab" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-\frac{1}{2}" :db/id 17592186279879} :answer-field/id #uuid "71592c6a-fdb5-5942-ae34-39eaef90dabf" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186281033}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "For the function of two variables 
$f(x,y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-2y),$
the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $(0,0)$ is given by

$$
f(x,y)=1+a{x}^{2}+bxy+c{y}^{2}.
$$

Find the value of $a+b+c.$" :question/worked-solution "If the function $f(x,y)$ is twice differentiable at $(x,y)=(0,0),$ then the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $(0,0)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈\overset{\text{Linear approximation}}{\overset{⏞}{f(0,0)+{f}_{x}(0,0)\cdot x+{f}_{y}(0,0)\cdot y}} \\  & \,\,+{{\frac{1}{2}({f}_{xx}(0,0)\cdot {x}^{2}+2{f}_{xy}(0,0)\cdot xy+{f}_{yy}(0,0)\cdot {y}^{2})}_{⏟}}_{\text{Quadratic part}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the terms of our Taylor polynomial.

- Calculating the value of the function, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0,0) & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

- Calculating the first derivatives, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-2y), & \,{f}_{y}(x,y) & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-2y) \\ {f}_{x}(0,0) & =0, & \,{f}_{y}(0,0) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

- Calculating the second derivatives, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xx}(x,y) & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-2y), & \,{f}_{xx}(0,0) & =-1 \\ {f}_{xy}(x,y) & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-2y), & \,{f}_{xy}(0,0) & =2 \\ {f}_{yy}(x,y) & =-4\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-2y), & \,{f}_{yy}(0,0) & =-4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the second-degree Taylor polynomial is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈1+0\cdot x+0\cdot y+\frac{1}{2}(-1\cdot {x}^{2}+2(2)\cdot xy+(-4)\cdot {y}^{2}) \\  & =1+(-\frac{1}{2}){x}^{2}+2xy+(-2){y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
a+b+c=(-\frac{1}{2})+2+(-2)=-\frac{1}{2}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186281594 :question/id #uuid "40019177-315b-5f8c-afeb-29b9f1c22ad3" :question/math-academy-id "q-163088" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186198434 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "e74c46c7-7f57-5adc-8acb-ea91958d8725" :knowledge-point/title "Finding a Quadratic Taylor Polynomial"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "03c1228e-2050-56a2-b557-e042a94e13ad" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{3}{2}" :db/id 17592186278617} {:answer/id #uuid "65bcf28f-9665-53c8-ad9d-52494b8f71a0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186279517} {:answer/id #uuid "867433f2-e62a-5149-8f65-89ea1338e1a0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186279791} {:answer/id #uuid "b0ef3ec5-904b-5bac-aaf1-4b133a5204b2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{5}{4}" :db/id 17592186280159} {:answer/id #uuid "f8c774d0-0b8d-5b1a-aac1-8ea3a6aa6f9a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186280777}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "867433f2-e62a-5149-8f65-89ea1338e1a0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186279791} :answer-field/id #uuid "2b371790-c15b-5ab7-8f10-3eae5d762331" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186280912}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "For the function of two variables

$$
f(x,y)=a+bxy.
$$

Find the value of $a+b.$" :question/worked-solution "If the function $f(x,y)$ is twice differentiable at $(x,y)=(0,0),$ then the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $(0,0)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈\overset{\text{Linear approximation}}{\overset{⏞}{f(0,0)+{f}_{x}(0,0)\cdot x+{f}_{y}(0,0)\cdot y}} \\  & \,\,+{{\frac{1}{2}({f}_{xx}(0,0)\cdot {x}^{2}+2{f}_{xy}(0,0)\cdot xy+{f}_{yy}(0,0)\cdot {y}^{2})}_{⏟}}_{\text{Quadratic part}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the terms of our Taylor polynomial.

- Calculating the value of the function, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0,0) & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

- Calculating the first derivatives, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =y{e}^{xy}, & \,{f}_{y}(x,y) & =x{e}^{xy} \\ {f}_{x}(0,0) & =0, & \,{f}_{y}(0,0) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

- Calculating the second derivatives, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xx}(x,y) & ={y}^{2}{e}^{xy}, & \,{f}_{xx}(0,0) & =0 \\ {f}_{xy}(x,y) & =(1+xy){e}^{xy}, & \,{f}_{xy}(0,0) & =1 \\ {f}_{yy}(x,y) & ={x}^{2}{e}^{xy}, & \,{f}_{yy}(0,0) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the second-degree Taylor polynomial is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈1+0\cdot x+0\cdot y+\frac{1}{2}(0\cdot {x}^{2}+2(1)\cdot xy+0\cdot {y}^{2}) \\  & =1+1xy.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
a+b=1+1=2.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186281595 :question/id #uuid "27445c9b-7e4a-5e28-a2d1-3fc7a72547b8" :question/math-academy-id "q-163089" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "259e5a02-0c0f-55f3-bd6c-0425cc1b2fca" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186278926} {:answer/id #uuid "5764bf31-2e34-5139-b5af-336d908fb12d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0" :db/id 17592186279392} {:answer/id #uuid "b8015639-eca8-56a2-ba22-50eb0b6beb73" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-3" :db/id 17592186280209} {:answer/id #uuid "cceb0541-bef3-574b-9eaf-de3916b0c09d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2" :db/id 17592186280395} {:answer/id #uuid "f640ccfa-97c4-5abd-9713-fdd182bc2d62" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186280750}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186278926} :answer-field/id #uuid "28d25be3-23d4-5ea5-b1b7-1033574afeb4" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186280907}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "For the function of two variables

$$
f(x,y)=2+ax-2y+b{x}^{2}+cxy+{y}^{2}.
$$

Find the value of $a+b+c.$" :question/worked-solution "If the function $f(x,y)$ is twice differentiable at $(x,y)=(0,0),$ then the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $(0,0)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈\overset{\text{Linear approximation}}{\overset{⏞}{f(0,0)+{f}_{x}(0,0)\cdot x+{f}_{y}(0,0)\cdot y}} \\  & \,\,+{{\frac{1}{2}({f}_{xx}(0,0)\cdot {x}^{2}+2{f}_{xy}(0,0)\cdot xy+{f}_{yy}(0,0)\cdot {y}^{2})}_{⏟}}_{\text{Quadratic part}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the terms of our Taylor polynomial.

- Calculating the value of the function, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0,0) & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

- Calculating the first derivatives, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =2{e}^{x-y}, & \,{f}_{y}(x,y) & =-2{e}^{x-y} \\ {f}_{x}(0,0) & =2, & \,{f}_{y}(0,0) & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

- Calculating the second derivatives, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xx}(x,y) & =2{e}^{x-y}, & \,{f}_{xx}(0,0) & =2 \\ {f}_{xy}(x,y) & =-2{e}^{x-y}, & \,{f}_{xy}(0,0) & =-2 \\ {f}_{yy}(x,y) & =2{e}^{x-y}, & \,{f}_{yy}(0,0) & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the second-degree Taylor polynomial is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈2+2\cdot x+(-2)\cdot y+\frac{1}{2}(2\cdot {x}^{2}+2(-2)\cdot xy+2\cdot {y}^{2}) \\  & =2+2x-2y+1{x}^{2}+(-2)xy+{y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
a+b=2+1+(-2)=1.

- Calculating the value of the function, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0,0) & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

- Calculating the first derivatives, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =2x{e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}, & \,{f}_{y}(x,y) & =2y{e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\ {f}_{x}(0,0) & =0, & \,{f}_{y}(0,0) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xx}(x,y) & =2(1+2{x}^{2}){e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}, & \,{f}_{xx}(0,0) & =2 \\ {f}_{xy}(x,y) & =4xy{e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}, & \,{f}_{xy}(0,0) & =0 \\ {f}_{yy}(x,y) & =2(1+2{y}^{2}){e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}, & \,{f}_{yy}(0,0) & =2\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈1+0\cdot x+0\cdot y+\frac{1}{2}(2\cdot {x}^{2}+2(0)\cdot xy+2\cdot {y}^{2}) \\  & =1+1{x}^{2}+1{y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$

- Calculating the value of the function, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0,0) & =2.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y) & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x+y+4}}, & \,{f}_{y}(x,y) & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x+y+4}} \\ {f}_{x}(0,0) & =\frac{1}{4}, & \,{f}_{y}(0,0) & =\frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

- Calculating the second derivatives, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xx}(x,y) & =-\frac{1}{4\sqrt{(x+y+4)^{3}}}, & \,{f}_{xx}(0,0) & =-\frac{1}{32} \\ {f}_{xy}(x,y) & =-\frac{1}{4\sqrt{(x+y+4)^{3}}}, & \,{f}_{xy}(0,0) & =-\frac{1}{32} \\ {f}_{yy}(x,y) & =-\frac{1}{4\sqrt{(x+y+4)^{3}}}, & \,{f}_{yy}(0,0) & =-\frac{1}{32}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the second-degree Taylor polynomial is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈2+\frac{1}{4}\cdot x+\frac{1}{4}\cdot y+\frac{1}{2}(-\frac{1}{32}\cdot {x}^{2}+2(-\frac{1}{32})\cdot xy+(-\frac{1}{32})\cdot {y}^{2}) \\  & =2+\frac{1}{4}x+\frac{1}{4}y-\frac{1}{64}{x}^{2}+(-\frac{1}{32})xy+(-\frac{1}{64}){y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
a+b+c=\frac{1}{4}+(-\frac{1}{32})+(-\frac{1}{64})=\frac{13}{64}.

"For the function $f:{R}^{2}\to R,$ defined as

$$
f(x,y)={x}^{3}y+x{y}^{3}+{y}^{2},
$$

the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $a=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$ is given by

$$
f(x,y)≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}{\begin{bmatrix}∗ \\ y\end{bmatrix}}^{T}\begin{bmatrix}0 & ∗ \\ 3 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}∗ \\ y\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Find the sum of the three missing expressions." :question/worked-solution "Suppose that the function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ is defined by 

$$
f:\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{bmatrix}⟶z
$$

 

and is twice differentiable at $x=a.$ Then, the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $a$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(a)(x-a),\end{aligned}
$$

where

$$
{f}^{′}(a)={\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{bmatrix}|}_{x=a}
$$

and

$$
{f}^{″}(a)={\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}}_{x=a}
$$

In this case, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{bmatrix}, & \,{f}^{″}(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Calculating the first derivative, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}3{x}^{2}y+{y}^{3} & {x}^{3}+3x{y}^{2}+2y\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Calculating the second derivative, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}6xy & 3{x}^{2}+3{y}^{2} \\ 3{x}^{2}+3{y}^{2} & 6xy+2\end{bmatrix} \\ {f}^{″}(1,0) & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & 3 \\ 3 & 2\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the second-degree Taylor polynomial is given by

$$
f(x)≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}{\begin{bmatrix}x-1 \\ y\end{bmatrix}}^{T}\begin{bmatrix}0 & 3 \\ 3 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x-1 \\ y\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Finally, the sum of the missing expressions is

$$
(x-1)+3+(x-1)=2x+1.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186198643 :question/id #uuid "2ec5ff3d-fd4d-5171-8304-f2a9e9fbb4f6" :question/math-academy-id "q-162989"} {:db/id 17592186281602 :question/id #uuid "c7c75fe7-9dcd-544f-9c7d-b36cf94f46b9" :question/math-academy-id "q-163102"} {:db/id 17592186281603 :question/id #uuid "b07db089-383d-5673-822f-6a5d7846d04c" :question/math-academy-id "q-163104"} {:db/id 17592186281607 :question/id #uuid "e7670cca-4082-532e-925a-af41e094c0c3" :question/math-academy-id "q-163122" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0488d7ff-b23d-57ca-ac1f-3b003b1d4cad" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x-2\pi " :db/id 17592186278628} {:answer/id #uuid "19abce14-7fbc-5539-b049-f6588065cc58" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2x-\frac{3\pi }{2}" :db/id 17592186278820} {:answer/id #uuid "1b20a70e-e52e-59a8-a425-efc1714f3b05" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2x" :db/id 17592186278843} {:answer/id #uuid "4be49a5e-04bf-5a10-ba8f-0ff99825ca37" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x-\frac{\pi }{2}" :db/id 17592186279271} {:answer/id #uuid "f7c391e8-39ad-5fb2-9766-ec1eb8cec68c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2x-\pi " :db/id 17592186280763}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186278820} :answer-field/id #uuid "11825cc6-3e2c-51ee-8c64-1a71cc1b22e6" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186280861}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "For the function $f:{R}^{2}\to R,$ defined as

In this case, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{bmatrix}, & \,{f}^{″}(x) & =\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}

$$

$$

 

and is twice differentiable at $x=a.$ Then, the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $a$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(a)(x-a),\end{aligned}

where

$$
{f}^{′}(a)={[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{aligned}]|}_{x=a}

and

$$
{f}^{″}(a)={[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{aligned}]}_{x=a}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{aligned}], & \,{f}^{″}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

$$

Use the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $a=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}$ to approximate the value of $f(1,0,0).$" :question/worked-solution "Suppose that the function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ is defined by 

$$
f:\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{bmatrix}⟶z
$$

 

and is twice differentiable at $x=a.$ Then, the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $a$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(a)(x-a),\end{aligned}
$$

where

$$
{f}^{′}(a)={\begin{bmatrix}\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{bmatrix}|}_{x=a}
$$

and

$$
{f}^{″}(a)={\begin{bmatrix}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{bmatrix}}_{x=a}
$$

In this case, we have $a=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix},$ and the following data:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(a) & =4, & \,{f}^{′}(a) & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 2 & 2\end{bmatrix}, & \,{f}^{″}(a) & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 2 & -1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the second-degree Taylor polynomial is given by

$$
f(x)≈4+\begin{bmatrix}3 & 2 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x-2 \\ y+1 \\ z+1\end{bmatrix}+\frac{1}{2}{\begin{bmatrix}x-2 \\ y+1 \\ z+1\end{bmatrix}}^{T}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 2 & -1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x-2 \\ y+1 \\ z+1\end{bmatrix}
$$

Finally, evaluating the polynomial at $x=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{bmatrix},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1,0,0) & ≈4+\begin{bmatrix}3 & 2 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1-2 \\ 0+1 \\ 0+1\end{bmatrix}+\frac{1}{2}{\begin{bmatrix}1-2 \\ 0+1 \\ 0+1\end{bmatrix}}^{T}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 2 & -1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1-2 \\ 0+1 \\ 0+1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =4+\begin{bmatrix}3 & 2 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}+\frac{1}{2}{\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}}^{T}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 2 & -1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =4+1+\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ -2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =5+\frac{1}{2}(-3) \\  & =\frac{7}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186049676} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1e54e1c9-205f-5069-a26e-144f61699b11" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-2" :db/id :topic/math-academy-id 4171} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186199372 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199501 :tutorial/content "Recall that the quadratic Taylor polynomial of a function $f(x)$ at the point $x=a$ is given by

$$
f(x) \approx  \overbrace{f(a) + f'(a)(x-a)}^{\text{Linear approximation}} + \underbrace{\dfrac{1}{2}f''(a)(x-a)^2}_{\textrm{Quadratic part}}.
$$

We can extend the concept of Taylor polynomials to multivariable functions. 

Given a twice-differentiable function $f(x,y),$ the **quadratic Taylor polynomial** of $f$ about the point $(a,b)$ is given by 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈\overset{\text{Linear approximation}}{\overset{⏞}{f(a,b)+{f}_{x}(a,b)\cdot (x-a)+{f}_{y}(a,b)\cdot (y-b)}} \\  & \,\,+{{\frac{1}{2}({f}_{xx}(a,b)\cdot (x-a)^{2}+2{f}_{xy}(a,b)\cdot (x-a)(y-b)+{f}_{yy}(a,b)\cdot (y-b)^{2})}_{⏟}}_{\text{Quadratic part}}.\end{aligned}
$$

In particular, the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f(x,y)$ about the origin $O$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈f(0,0)+{f}_{x}(0,0)\cdot x+{f}_{y}(0,0)\cdot y \\  & \,\,+\frac{1}{2}({f}_{xx}(0,0)\cdot {x}^{2}+2{f}_{xy}(0,0)\cdot xy+{f}_{yy}(0,0)\cdot {y}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

Later in the lesson, we will develop some intuition for why the quadratic part looks the way it does. But before we do that, let's get some practice working with this formula." :tutorial/id #uuid "31dda75b-f239-5680-b7b4-0dce1ba5e51f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7846 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "0b4dea87-c57c-5435-9e3b-1027840f045c" :step/math-academy-id 45308 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199373}} {:db/id 17592186199373 :step/content {:db/id 17592186198434 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186198076 :question/id #uuid "6c5e3d93-e244-52da-845b-365bb94bd19d" :question/math-academy-id "e-12562"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "e74c46c7-7f57-5adc-8acb-ea91958d8725" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049019}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186198645} {:db/id 17592186198655} {:db/id 17592186281594} {:db/id 17592186281595} {:db/id 17592186281596} {:db/id 17592186281599} {:db/id 17592186281604} {:db/id 17592186432370} {:db/id 17592186432374} {:db/id 17592186520486} {:db/id 17592186520510}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding a Quadratic Taylor Polynomial"} :step/id #uuid "b898729c-517e-588b-8fc2-30ad336c09b1" :step/math-academy-id 45309 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199374}} {:db/id 17592186199374 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199502 :tutorial/content "It's possible to derive Taylor polynomials for functions of more than two variables. However, increasing the number of variables significantly increases the number of terms in the Taylor polynomial. 

Ideally, we'd like a compact expression for the quadratic Taylor polynomial that works for all twice-differentiable functions $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R.$ This can be achieved using matrix notation. 

To see how, let's consider the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f(x,y)$ about $(a,b){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈\overset{\text{Linear approximation}}{\overset{⏞}{f(a,b)+{f}_{x}(a,b)\cdot (x-a)+{f}_{y}(a,b)\cdot (y-b)}} \\  & \,\,+{{\frac{1}{2}({f}_{xx}(a,b)\cdot (x-a)^{2}+2{f}_{xy}(a,b)\cdot (x-a)(y-b)+{f}_{yy}(a,b)\cdot (y-b)^{2})}_{⏟}}_{\text{Quadratic part}}.\end{aligned}
$$

If we denote ![](images/6f/6fe1832d2f4ae2b36446386e5d0ec7c41f898f4e575af9238695c37f7c427250.svg) and ![](images/49/496eacb98651e3fab4c0d0a7b44ab283fadad1c07243da485aeb0c4a059d5712.svg) then the total derivative of $f(x,y)=f(\mathbf{x})$ at $(a,b)=\mathbf{a}$ is given by

![](images/d6/d696700e295d9f43111ac53602b936a991b7766af654cedaa5afdae21b088a59.svg)

With that in mind, we can rewrite the linear part of the approximation as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Linear approximation} & =f(a,b)+{f}_{x}(a,b)\cdot (x-a)+{f}_{y}(a,b)\cdot (y-b) \\  & =f(a)+[\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(a,b) & {f}_{y}(a,b)\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}x-a \\ y-b\end{aligned}] \\  & =f(a)+[\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(a,b) & {f}_{y}(a,b)\end{aligned}]\cdot ([\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]) \\  & =f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that this is just our usual linear approximation of a function $f.$

The second derivative of $f$ at $\mathbf x = \mathbf a$ is given by

![](images/de/de2a75a6681e1e393b21b60de9d7aeee748a8e6d04010ab713b40f0f41f239cf.svg)

Therefore, using the fact that $f_{xy} = f_{yx},$ we can rewrite the quadratic part of the approximation using matrix multiplication as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Quadratic part} & =\frac{1}{2}({f}_{xx}(a,b)\cdot (x-a)^{2}+2{f}_{xy}(a,b)\cdot (x-a)(y-b)+{f}_{yy}(a,b)\cdot (y-b)^{2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}x-a & y-b\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}{f}_{xx}(a) & {f}_{xy}(a) \\ {f}_{yx}(a) & {f}_{yy}(a)\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}x-a \\ y-b\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}([\begin{aligned}x & y\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}a & b\end{aligned}])\cdot [\begin{aligned}{f}_{xx}(a) & {f}_{xy}(a) \\ {f}_{yx}(a) & {f}_{yy}(a)\end{aligned}]\cdot ([\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(a)(x-a)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our quadratic Taylor polynomial can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ≈\overset{\text{Linear approximation}}{\overset{⏞}{f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)}}+{{\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(a)(x-a)}_{⏟}}_{\text{Quadratic part}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that this formula is more compact and has clear similarity with the corresponding formula for functions with one variable:

$$
f(x) \approx  \overbrace{f(a) + f'(a)(x-a)}^{\text{Linear approximation}} + \underbrace{\dfrac{1}{2}f''(a)(x-a)^2}_{\textrm{Quadratic part}}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "81df7b3f-d26d-54e0-baa0-de20a949b348" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7847 :tutorial/title "The Quadratic Taylor Polynomial in Matrix Form"} :step/id #uuid "3baad2a8-726c-5a26-b651-c058c266b286" :step/math-academy-id 45312 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199375}} {:db/id 17592186199375 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199503 :tutorial/content "The formula derived earlier works for multivariable functions with a finite number of variables. 

Suppose that the function $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ is defined by 

![](images/2e/2eaa4da1b90a317a7570670566b2a81bb636701680d6a2ca2224b5ef60e80230.svg) 

and is twice differentiable at $\mathbf x = \mathbf a.$ Then, the quadratic Taylor approximation of $f$ about $\mathbf a$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(a)(x-a),\end{aligned}
$$

where the first derivative is 

![](images/08/08b2f366456caf4c7c8db85d08a8494e50c3098f148eb9c9075da748801cb574.svg)

Suppose that the function $f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined by

![](images/df/dfa82e503eeaa38943edddc7d6982cf4893c73fd2f6d075dd390f51cd0450091.svg)

and is twice differentiable at $\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{a}.$
By restricting $\mathbf x$ to a line through $\mathbf{a},$ we can consider $f$ as a function of one variable. Then, we'll use the second-degree Taylor polynomial of a single-variable function to derive the formula.

Let $\mathbf{x}_0$ be a constant vector in $\mathbb{R}^n.$ Then, the line through $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{x}_0$ is given by

$$
\mathbf{x}(t) = \mathbf{a} + t(\mathbf{x}_0 - \mathbf{a}), \qquad t \in (-\infty, \infty),
$$

where $\mathbf{x}(0) = \mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{x}(1) = \mathbf{x}_0.$

Now, we define a function $F: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ by restricting the domain of $f$ to this line:

$$
F(t)
= f(\mathbf{x}(t))
%= f(\mathbf{a} + t(\mathbf{x}_0 - \mathbf{a}))
$$

The second-degree Taylor polynomial of this single-variable function about $t=0$ is given by

$$
F(t) \approx F(0) + F'(0)t + \dfrac12F''(0)t^2.
$$

We can find the first derivative of $F$ using the chain rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}F}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(a+t({x}_{0}-a)) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}\cdot ({x}_{0}-a)\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\dfrac{\textrm{d}f}{\textrm{d}\mathbf{x}}$ is a row vector and $(\mathbf{x}_0 - \mathbf{a})$ is a column vector, this is a scalar quantity and, hence, equal to its transpose:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}F}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}\cdot ({x}_{0}-a) \\  & ={(\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}\cdot ({x}_{0}-a))}^{T} \\  & =({x}_{0}-a)^{T}{(\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x})}^{T}\end{aligned}
$$

With this, we can find the second derivative of $F{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}F}{\text{d}{t}^{2}} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{\text{d}F}{\text{d}t}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(({x}_{0}-a)^{T}{(\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x})}^{T}) \\  & =({x}_{0}-a)^{T}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}{(\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x})}^{T} \\  & =({x}_{0}-a)^{T}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}{(\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x})}^{T}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \\  & =({x}_{0}-a)^{T}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}f}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}({x}_{0}-a)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the first and second derivatives are given by

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(t) &={f}^{′}(x(t))({x}_{0}-a) \\ {F}^{″}(t) &=({x}_{0}-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(x(t))({x}_{0}-a).\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Evaluating the function and its derivatives at $t=0$ and using the fact that $\mathbf{x}(0) = \mathbf{a},$ we have

![](images/ba/ba4825ec7e9bb46e08df09c8b46b941c36a69ffd6e72081d09cd1ef6134a54d8.svg)

Putting these values into the second-degree Taylor polynomial of a single-variable function about $t=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}F(t) & ≈F(0)+{F}^{′}(0)t+\frac{1}{2}{F}^{″}(0){t}^{2} \\  & ≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)({x}_{0}-a)t+\frac{1}{2}({x}_{0}-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(a)({x}_{0}-a){t}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, using this polynomial to approximate the value of $F(1),$ and the fact that $F(1) = f(\mathbf{x}(1)) = f(\mathbf{x}_0),$ we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}F(1) & ≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)({x}_{0}-a)\cdot 1+\frac{1}{2}({x}_{0}-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(a)({x}_{0}-a)\cdot {1}^{2} \\ f({x}_{0}) & ≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)({x}_{0}-a)+\frac{1}{2}({x}_{0}-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(a)({x}_{0}-a).\end{aligned}
$$

However, $\mathbf{x}_0 \in \mathbb{R}^n$ is an arbitrary constant. Therefore, we can relax the assumption that $\mathbf{x}_0$ is fixed and replace it with a general point $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n$ near $\mathbf{a}$ to obtain the formula for the second-degree Taylor polynomial of a multivariable function in vector form:

$$
f(\mathbf{x}) \approx f(\mathbf{a}) + \boldsymbol{f}'(\mathbf{a})(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a}) + \dfrac{1}{2} (\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a})^T \boldsymbol{f}''(\mathbf{a}) (\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{a})
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "de526622-dda2-5168-9ec1-6b123e04fa54" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7862 :tutorial/title "Deriving the Quadratic Taylor Polynomial in Matrix Form"} :step/id #uuid "b64ce030-6e67-5cb0-926b-59488cada120" :step/math-academy-id 45339} {:db/id 17592186199378 :step/content {:db/id 17592186198436 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186198078 :question/id #uuid "137d7caf-b232-5e21-9583-14d907a98624" :question/math-academy-id "e-12564"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "b19cc766-bdc5-5ab2-aa4d-ebddf8311116" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186198678} {:db/id 17592186198679} {:db/id 17592186284521} {:db/id 17592186284522} {:db/id 17592186284523} {:db/id 17592186284524} {:db/id 17592186284530} {:db/id 17592186284531} {:db/id 17592186367901} {:db/id 17592186367908} {:db/id 17592186432371} {:db/id 17592186432373}] :knowledge-point/title "Approximating a Multivariable Function at a Point Using a Quadratic Taylor Polynomial"} :step/id #uuid "ac6cf855-2b6f-5681-9ea0-41408d0715ca" :step/math-academy-id 45340 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199377}}] :activity/title "Second-Degree Taylor Polynomials of Multivariable Functions" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186198498} {:db/id 17592186199372 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199501 :tutorial/content "Recall that the quadratic Taylor polynomial of a function $f(x)$ at the point $x=a$ is given by

Given a twice-differentiable function $f(x,y),$ the **quadratic Taylor polynomial** of $f$ about the point $(a,b)$ is given by

$$

In particular, the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f(x,y)$ about the origin $O$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈f(0,0)+{f}_{x}(0,0)\cdot x+{f}_{y}(0,0)\cdot y \\  & \,\,+\frac{1}{2}({f}_{xx}(0,0)\cdot {x}^{2}+2{f}_{xy}(0,0)\cdot xy+{f}_{yy}(0,0)\cdot {y}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

Later in the lesson, we will develop some intuition for why the quadratic part looks the way it does. However, increasing the number of variables significantly increases the number of terms in the Taylor polynomial. 

Ideally, we'd like a compact expression for the quadratic Taylor polynomial that works for all twice-differentiable functions $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R.$ This can be achieved using matrix notation. 

To see how, let's consider the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f(x,y)$ about $(a,b){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈\overset{\text{Linear approximation}}{\overset{⏞}{f(a,b)+{f}_{x}(a,b)\cdot (x-a)+{f}_{y}(a,b)\cdot (y-b)}} \\  & \,\,+{{\frac{1}{2}({f}_{xx}(a,b)\cdot (x-a)^{2}+2{f}_{xy}(a,b)\cdot (x-a)(y-b)+{f}_{yy}(a,b)\cdot (y-b)^{2})}_{⏟}}_{\text{Quadratic part}}.\end{aligned}
$$

If we denote ![](images/6f/6fe1832d2f4ae2b36446386e5d0ec7c41f898f4e575af9238695c37f7c427250.svg) and ![](images/49/496eacb98651e3fab4c0d0a7b44ab283fadad1c07243da485aeb0c4a059d5712.svg) then the total derivative of $f(x,y)=f(\mathbf{x})$ at $(a,b)=\mathbf{a}$ is given by

![](images/d6/d696700e295d9f43111ac53602b936a991b7766af654cedaa5afdae21b088a59.svg)

With that in mind, we can rewrite the linear part of the approximation as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Linear approximation} & =f(a,b)+{f}_{x}(a,b)\cdot (x-a)+{f}_{y}(a,b)\cdot (y-b) \\  & =f(a)+[\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(a,b) & {f}_{y}(a,b)\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}x-a \\ y-b\end{aligned}] \\  & =f(a)+[\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(a,b) & {f}_{y}(a,b)\end{aligned}]\cdot ([\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]) \\  & =f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that this is just our usual linear approximation of a function $f.$

The second derivative of $f$ at $\mathbf x = \mathbf a$ is given by

![](images/de/de2a75a6681e1e393b21b60de9d7aeee748a8e6d04010ab713b40f0f41f239cf.svg)

Therefore, using the fact that $f_{xy} = f_{yx},$ we can rewrite the quadratic part of the approximation using matrix multiplication as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Quadratic part} & =\frac{1}{2}({f}_{xx}(a,b)\cdot (x-a)^{2}+2{f}_{xy}(a,b)\cdot (x-a)(y-b)+{f}_{yy}(a,b)\cdot (y-b)^{2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}x-a & y-b\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}{f}_{xx}(a) & {f}_{xy}(a) \\ {f}_{yx}(a) & {f}_{yy}(a)\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}x-a \\ y-b\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}([\begin{aligned}x & y\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}a & b\end{aligned}])\cdot [\begin{aligned}{f}_{xx}(a) & {f}_{xy}(a) \\ {f}_{yx}(a) & {f}_{yy}(a)\end{aligned}]\cdot ([\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}a \\ b\end{aligned}]) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(a)(x-a)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our quadratic Taylor polynomial can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ≈\overset{\text{Linear approximation}}{\overset{⏞}{f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)}}+{{\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(a)(x-a)}_{⏟}}_{\text{Quadratic part}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that this formula is more compact and has clear similarity with the corresponding formula for functions with one variable:

$$
f(x) \approx  \overbrace{f(a) + f'(a)(x-a)}^{\text{Linear approximation}} + \underbrace{\dfrac{1}{2}f''(a)(x-a)^2}_{\textrm{Quadratic part}}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "81df7b3f-d26d-54e0-baa0-de20a949b348" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7847 :tutorial/title "The Quadratic Taylor Polynomial in Matrix Form"} :step/id #uuid "3baad2a8-726c-5a26-b651-c058c266b286" :step/math-academy-id 45312 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199375}} {:db/id 17592186199502 :tutorial/content "It's possible to derive Taylor polynomials for functions of more than two variables.
