$$
x(t)={{{e}^{A(t-{t}_{0})}\,x({t}_{0})}_{⏟}}_{\text{homogeneous part}}+{{{\int }_{{t}_{0}}^{t}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s)\,\text{d}s}_{⏟}}_{\text{particular solution}},
$$

where $x({t}_{0})$ is the initial condition vector. 

Let's evaluate each part separately:

- First, we find the homogeneous part. We are given that ${e}^{At}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(6t) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(6t) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(6t) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(6t)\end{aligned}].$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-1)}\,x(1) & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(6(t-1)) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(6(t-1)) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(6(t-1)) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(6(t-1))\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{cosh}⁡(6(t-1))+\operatorname{sinh}⁡(6(t-1)) \\ 2\operatorname{sinh}⁡(6(t-1))+\operatorname{cosh}⁡(6(t-1))\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we find the particular solution. Notice that 

$$
{e}^{A(t-s)}=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(6(t-s)) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(6(t-s)) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(6(t-s)) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(6(t-s))\end{aligned}].
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{A(t-s)}g(s) & =[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(6(t-s)) & \operatorname{sinh}⁡(6(t-s)) \\ \operatorname{sinh}⁡(6(t-s)) & \operatorname{cosh}⁡(6(t-s))\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ {e}^{6s}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{6s}\operatorname{sinh}⁡(6(t-s)) \\ {e}^{6s}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(6(t-s))\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =[\begin{aligned}2\operatorname{cosh}⁡(6(t-1))+\operatorname{sinh}⁡(6(t-1)) \\ 2\operatorname{sinh}⁡(6(t-1))+\operatorname{cosh}⁡(6(t-1))\end{aligned}]+{\int }_{1}^{t}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{6s}\operatorname{sinh}⁡(6(t-s)) \\ {e}^{6s}\operatorname{cosh}⁡(6(t-s))\end{aligned}]\text{d}s.\end{aligned}

$f(n+1) = f(n) -6, \quad f(1) = 1, \quad n\geq 1$." :question/worked-solution "Starting with the first term

$$
f(1)=1
$$

we compute the next terms using the recursive rule until we reach the fourth term $f(4)$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
f(1) &= 1 \\
f(2) &= f(1) - 6 = 1 - 6 =-5 \\
f(3) &= f(2) - 6 =-5 - 6 =-11 \\
f(4) &= f(3) - 6 =-11 - 6 =-17
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the fourth term is

$$
f(4)=-17
$$"} {:db/id 17592186049579} {:db/id 17592186050380} {:db/id 17592186180129 :question/id #uuid "cf42428e-d1bc-5459-93fa-165d93fdb0b9" :question/math-academy-id "q-214153"} {:db/id 17592186180201 :question/id #uuid "17e3c368-1c20-570a-bdde-2b4d6562eb29" :question/math-academy-id "q-44796"} {:db/id 17592186179638 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186179481 :question/id #uuid "1fa96efe-9a81-5c09-b172-fd0ca6d6a2e3" :question/math-academy-id "e-14380"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "25aaf48f-f1ca-50a5-8fae-aa4f9508cfba" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186180130 :question/id #uuid "3fe59f93-ea77-5aca-9fa0-fe70029276b9" :question/math-academy-id "q-214155"} {:db/id 17592186180200 :question/id #uuid "e18dc692-a288-5ddd-8ee7-6bbf8a007a02" :question/math-academy-id "q-44795"}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding a Recursive Formula"} {:db/id 17592186179481 :question/id #uuid "1fa96efe-9a81-5c09-b172-fd0ca6d6a2e3" :question/math-academy-id "e-14380" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186179638 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "25aaf48f-f1ca-50a5-8fae-aa4f9508cfba" :knowledge-point/title "Finding a Recursive Formula"}] :question/problem "What is the recursive formula for the following arithmetic sequence?
$4,\: 9,\: 14,\: \ldots$" :question/worked-solution "The recursive formula for an arithmetic sequence with common difference $d$ is

$$
a_{n+1} =a_n+d
$$

In our case, the common difference is

$$
\begin{aligned}
d &= a_{2} - a_{1} \\
&= 9 - 4 \\
&= 5
\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, the recursive formula for this sequence is

$$
a_{n+1}= a_n + 5, \quad a_1=4, \quad n\geq 1\,
$$"} {:db/id 17592186180130 :question/id #uuid "3fe59f93-ea77-5aca-9fa0-fe70029276b9" :question/math-academy-id "q-214155"} {:db/id 17592186180200 :question/id #uuid "e18dc692-a288-5ddd-8ee7-6bbf8a007a02" :question/math-academy-id "q-44795"} {:db/id 17592186049399} {:activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186180329} :activity/id #uuid "77e3ae57-98b5-5d38-9772-30811dbaca9c" :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186049305 :topic/id #uuid "eb169cdb-9ded-599f-b8d4-23b30958ff03" :topic/math-academy-id 3695} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186180329 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180786 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have the following arithmetic sequence with first term

$$
a_1 = {\color{red}4}
$$

and common difference

$$
d={\color{blue}{3}}
$$

$$
{\color{red}{4}},7,10,13,16,\ldots
$$

Each term is ${\color{blue}{3}}$ more than the previous, starting with ${\color{red}{4}}$. Therefore, we can express this sequence recursively:

$$
a_{n+1} = a_n + {\color{blue}{3}}, \quad a_1 = {\color{red}{4}}, \quad n\geq 1
$$

We can also express the sequence using function notation:

$$
f(n+1) = f(n) + {\color{blue}{3}}, \quad f(1) = {\color{red}{4}}, \quad n\geq 1

:answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186163840}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "Consider the vector field $F$ and the surface $S$ with unit normal vector $n,$ where

$$
F(x,y,z)=⟨2z,\,x+y,\,y-z⟩\,,\,n(x,y,z)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨1,\,-1,\,1⟩\,.
$$

If the flux of $F$ across $S$ with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}{∬}_{S}\boxed{}\,\text{d}S,
$$

what is the missing expression?" :question/worked-solution "If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Calculating the dot product, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨2z,\,x+y,\,y-z⟩\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨1,\,-1,\,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨2z,\,x+y,\,y-z⟩\cdot ⟨1,\,-1,\,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}(2z-(x+y)+(y-z)) \\  & =\frac{z-x}{\sqrt{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the flux can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}\frac{z-x}{\sqrt{3}}\,\text{d}S \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}{∬}_{S}z-x\,\text{d}S.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186278420 :question/id #uuid "e0855a1e-4e9d-5aec-ac2d-5bafc7bc5253" :question/math-academy-id "q-161199" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "30c26cb1-a78b-546d-9346-a3292a576ab9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "xy-3{e}^{z}" :db/id 17592186275910} {:answer/id #uuid "751cc22b-1310-5836-99ad-05300271a000" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3{e}^{z}+xy+3" :db/id 17592186276537} {:answer/id #uuid "7e59aef0-444f-52b9-ac9d-43083f4f8de6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "xy-3-{e}^{z}" :db/id 17592186276626} {:answer/id #uuid "e9be6646-27fa-5451-b505-31251d5e0a9e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "xy+{e}^{z}" :db/id 17592186277520} {:answer/id #uuid "fbfb7733-23eb-5b42-b8e0-72a48ba55123" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "xy+6" :db/id 17592186277687}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186275910} :answer-field/id #uuid "902a8b32-2004-52a8-a453-ce38efbc95fa" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186277980}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "Consider the vector field $F$ and the surface $S$ with unit normal vector $n,$ where

$$

$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}x\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}x\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}x\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\text{d}y{\int }_{0}^{1}x\,\text{d}x \\  & =1\cdot {[\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}

17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨x,\,y,\,z+3⟩$ and a finite region $S$ of the plane $z=x+y$ such that $\text{Area}(S)=\sqrt{3}.$ Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S$ with respect to the upward-pointing unit normal vector $n.$" :question/worked-solution "If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that our surface $z=x+y$ can be written using the dot product as 

$$
⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨-1,\,-1,\,1⟩}_{⏟}}_{\overset{~}{n}}=0,\,\text{or}\,⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨1,\,1,\,-1⟩}_{⏟}}_{-\overset{~}{n}}=0.
$$

Since we require an upward-pointing normal vector to our surface $S,$ we must select one where the $z$-component is positive. This gives us the normal vector

$$
\overset{~}{n}=⟨-1,\,-1,\,1⟩.
$$

Normalizing this vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{\overset{~}{n}}{‖\overset{~}{n}‖} \\  & =\frac{⟨-1,\,-1,\,1⟩}{\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨-1,\,-1,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that $z=x+y$ on $S,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨x,\,y,\,z+3⟩\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨-1,\,-1,\,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨x,\,y,\,x+y+3⟩\cdot ⟨-1,\,-1,\,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}(-x-y+(x+y+3)) \\  & =\frac{3}{\sqrt{3}} \\  & =\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across $S$ as follows:

"Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨x,\,y,\,2z⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined in Cartesian coordinates as $z=2x+3y$ for $0\le x\le 1$ and $0\le y\le 1.$ Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S$ with respect to the upward-pointing unit normal vector $n.$

*Hint: You're given that the fundamental vector product of $S$ with respect to its canonical parametrization is $||{r}_{x}\times {r}_{y}||=\sqrt{14}.$*" :question/worked-solution "If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that our surface $z=2x+3y$ can be written using the dot product as 

$$
⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨-2,\,-3,\,1⟩}_{⏟}}_{\overset{~}{n}}=0,\,\text{or}\,⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨2,\,3,\,-1⟩}_{⏟}}_{-\overset{~}{n}}=0.
$$

Since we require an upward-pointing normal vector to our surface $S,$ we must select one where the $z$-component is positive. This gives us the normal vector

$$
\overset{~}{n}=⟨-2,\,-3,\,1⟩.
$$

Normalizing this vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{\overset{~}{n}}{‖\overset{~}{n}‖} \\  & =\frac{⟨-2,\,-3,\,1⟩}{\sqrt{(-2)^{2}+(-3)^{2}+{1}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{14}}⟨-2,\,-3,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that $z=2x+3y$ on $S,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨x,\,y,\,2z⟩\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{14}}⟨-2,\,-3,\,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{14}}⟨x,\,y,\,4x+6y⟩\cdot ⟨-2,\,-3,\,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{14}}(-2x-3y+4x+6y) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{14}}(2x+3y).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}\frac{1}{\sqrt{14}}(2x+3y)\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{1}{\sqrt{14}}(2x+3y)\cdot ||{r}_{x}\times {r}_{y}||\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{1}{\sqrt{14}}(2x+3y)\cdot \sqrt{14}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{1}{\cancel{\sqrt{14}}}(2x+3y)\cdot \cancel{\sqrt{14}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2x+3y\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}2x+3y\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[{x}^{2}+3xy]}_{x=0}^{x=1}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}1+3y\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[y+\frac{3}{2}{y}^{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{5}{2}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186167130 :question/id #uuid "07582355-f319-5419-a760-27151ce99dcb" :question/math-academy-id "q-161244"} {:db/id 17592186278417 :question/id #uuid $$

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}\frac{1}{\sqrt{11}}(4y-4x)\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{1}{\sqrt{11}}(4y-4x)\cdot ||{r}_{x}\times {r}_{y}||\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{1}{\sqrt{11}}(4y-4x)\cdot \sqrt{11}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{1}{\cancel{\sqrt{11}}}(4y-4x)\cdot \cancel{\sqrt{11}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(4y-4x)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}(4y-4x)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{[4xy-2{x}^{2}]}_{x=0}^{x=1}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(4y-2)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[2{y}^{2}-2y]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =4\end{aligned}

\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{\overset{~}{n}}{‖\overset{~}{n}‖} \\  & =\frac{⟨1,\,2,\,-1⟩}{\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{2}^{2}+(-1)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}⟨1,\,2,\,-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that $z=x+2y+1$ on $S,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨z+5,\,x-2y,\,3x-2y⟩\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}⟨1,\,2,\,-1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}⟨x+2y+6,\,x-2y,\,3x-2y⟩\cdot ⟨1,\,2,\,-1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}((x+2y+6)+2(x-2y)-(3x-2y)) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}(x+2y+6+2x-4y-3x+2y) \\  & =\frac{6}{\sqrt{6}} \\  & =\sqrt{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}\sqrt{6}\,\text{d}S \\  & =\sqrt{6}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S \\  & =\sqrt{6}\cdot \text{Area}(S) \\  & =\sqrt{6}\cdot \sqrt{2} \\  & =2\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186444619 :question/id #uuid "627a222e-9363-5b8b-b1ec-0730c89cfcbe" :question/math-academy-id "q-161193" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2e7ca8ec-891f-5ccc-985b-4e4a85531ac2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2" :db/id 17592186444602} {:answer/id #uuid "3ccaaf5e-0e10-5c99-a0bc-d8a834cb86f3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{3}" :db/id 17592186444604} {:answer/id #uuid "a5039a5b-f9d4-5a06-b32c-4be440d0e059" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-1" :db/id 17592186444609} {:answer/id #uuid "c73e0516-826a-57fd-99ad-0e6ddc957f95" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-3" :db/id 17592186444611} {:answer/id #uuid "f817a54c-d2b8-5a8f-9b28-dbefeb579916" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\sqrt{3}" :db/id 17592186444615}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186444611} :answer-field/id #uuid "5c6a2aa9-7d14-5b93-966f-5ef76762e118" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186444616}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨z,\,y,\,x⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined in Cartesian coordinates as $z=x+y$ for $0\le x\le 3$ and $0\le y\le 1.$ Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S$ with respect to the upward-pointing unit normal vector $n.$

*Hint: You're given that the fundamental vector product of $S$ with respect to its canonical parametrization is $||{r}_{x}\times {r}_{y}||=\sqrt{3}.$*" :question/worked-solution "If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that our surface $z=x+y$ can be written using the dot product as 

$$
⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨-1,\,-1,\,1⟩}_{⏟}}_{\overset{~}{n}}=0,\,\text{or}\,⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨1,\,1,\,-1⟩}_{⏟}}_{-\overset{~}{n}}=0.
$$

Since we require an upward-pointing normal vector to our surface $S,$ we must select one where the $z$-component is positive. This gives us the normal vector

$$
\overset{~}{n}=⟨-1,\,-1,\,1⟩.
$$

Normalizing this vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{\overset{~}{n}}{‖\overset{~}{n}‖} \\  & =\frac{⟨-1,\,-1,\,1⟩}{\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨-1,\,-1,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that $z=x+y$ on $S,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨z,\,y,\,x⟩\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨-1,\,-1,\,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨x+y,\,y,\,x⟩\cdot ⟨-1,\,-1,\,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}(-(x+y)-y+x) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}(-2y) \\  & =-\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\,y.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}(-\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\,y)\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\,y)\cdot ||{r}_{x}\times {r}_{y}||\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}y\cdot \sqrt{3}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}-\frac{2}{\cancel{\sqrt{3}}}y\cdot \cancel{\sqrt{3}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}-2y\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{3}-2y\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{1}2y\,\text{d}y\cdot {\int }_{0}^{3}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-[{y}^{2}]_{0}^{1}\cdot [x]_{0}^{3} \\  & =-1\cdot 3 \\  & =-3\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186048185} {:db/id 17592186049315} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "83738cc5-1219-53e4-93d6-345faec69645" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} 3178} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186167782 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168144 :tutorial/content "Consider the vector field $\mathbf F$ and the surface $S$ with unit normal vector $\mathbf n,$ where

$$
\mathbf{F}(x,y,z) = \left\langle xz + y,\: x^2,\: 2y-z^2 \right\rangle\!, 
\qquad 
\mathbf{n}(x,y,z) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt5}\left\langle 2,\: 0,\: -1 \right\rangle\!.
$$

Let's construct a surface integral representing the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $S$ with respect to $\mathbf{n}.$

First, we recall that if $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $\mathbf n,$ and $\mathbf F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $\mathbf n$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}
=
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}S.
$$

Calculating the dot product, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨xz+y,\,{x}^{2},\,2y-{z}^{2}⟩\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}⟨2,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}⟨xz+y,\,{x}^{2},\,2y-{z}^{2}⟩\cdot ⟨2,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}((xz+y)\cdot 2+{x}^{2}\cdot 0+(2y-{z}^{2})\cdot (-1)) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}(2xz+2y-2y+{z}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{2xz+{z}^{2}}{\sqrt{5}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral representing the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $S$ with respect to $\mathbf n$ can be written as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}\frac{2xz+{z}^{2}}{\sqrt{5}}\,\text{d}S \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}{∬}_{S}2xz+{z}^{2}\,\text{d}S\end{aligned}
$$

We can then evaluate this integral using the usual methods." :tutorial/id #uuid "c936101d-fbb9-594d-888c-2327d0908e71" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7632 :tutorial/title "A Worked Example"} :step/id #uuid :tutorial/content "Recall that the flux of a two-dimensional vector field $\mathbf F(x,y)$ across a curve $C$ with respect to a unit normal vector $\mathbf n(x,y)$ is given by the line integral

$$
\int\limits_C \mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n\,\textrm d s.
$$

The flux measures the total flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C,$ as depicted below.

![](images/23/2392d6c27fc6767c78172936d6df37b3dfec8b2198abbdf9e22b87d4337ed9da.png)

Flux is always measured with respect to a preselected unit normal vector $\mathbf n,$ and we have two choices of orientation for this vector. If we measure the flux relative to the unit normal pointing in the *opposite* direction, our flux will have the *same* magnitude but *opposite* sign.

![](images/e4/e451548a5d9874b9eff9d61c2d423696dc76a3f560e2936eb7bdb3a9cbfbed49.png)

This lesson aims to extend the concept of flux to three-dimensional vector fields. But first, we need a brief discussion on surface orientations." :tutorial/id #uuid "8a17f47e-f50d-578f-a41c-9e537ded3620" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7725 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "507e9c0b-b2be-5bf9-a53c-e763d7e4315b" :step/math-academy-id 657075 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167787}} {:db/id 17592186167786 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168146 :tutorial/content "In three dimensions, flux measures the total flow of a vector field $\mathbf F(x,y,z)$ *through an orientable surface.*

Suppose that $\mathbf F(x,y,z)$ is a three-dimensional vector field, and $S$ is an orientable surface with the choice of orientation given by the unit normal vector $\mathbf n(x,y,z),$ as shown below.

![](images/99/9976f35dcf348da89c15a40aad43ab5a1d3edea75558ef5539f9421ed9b75f4e.png)

 

The **flux of $\mathbf F$ across $\boldsymbol{S}$** with respect to $\mathbf n,$ which we write as 

$$
\iint\limits_S \mathbf F \cdot \textrm d \mathbf S
$$

 is given by the surface integral

$$
\iint\limits_S  \mathbf F \cdot \mathbf n \,\textrm d S.
$$

It's worth taking a moment to compare this to the flux formula for two-dimensional vector fields: 

- The quantity $\mathbf F \cdot \mathbf n$ evaluated at a point $P$ on $S$ measures the projection of $\mathbf F$ in the direction of $\mathbf n$ at $P.$

- By summing (integrating) the quantity $\mathbf F \cdot \mathbf n$ over the entire surface, we get the total flow of $\mathbf F$ through $S.$

Our flux depends on our choice of orientation. If we were to select the *opposite* orientation, we'd get a result with the same magnitude but opposite sign." :tutorial/id #uuid "5a72f9c0-0bf4-59dd-be49-827f9e278fa3" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7727 :tutorial/title "Flux in Three-Dimensional Vector Fields"} :step/id #uuid "4b9873f3-a548-5ea9-a86b-7682d0efa06b" :step/math-academy-id 657077 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167782}} {:db/id 17592186167787 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168147 :tutorial/content "A surface is **orientable** if it has two distinct sides. So, for example, the surface $S$ shown below is orientable.

![](images/29/29be1e415eaf0072aea7f4093e71665f5996b29804702a37a4d4493e0b0002d4.png)

 

If a unit vector $\mathbf n(x,y,z)$ to our orientable surface varies continuously over $S,$ we say that $S$ is **oriented** and the choice of $\mathbf n$ gives an **orientation** of $S.$

We can choose the opposite orientation for our surface by selecting a vector that points in the opposite direction, as shown below.

![](images/40/40268c448b7c4ac99acf356e9f1e2702112a0d46dc1b6e6afd98d5c95e5ea317.png)

 

When dealing with two-sided (i.e., orientable) surfaces, we must always be clear about our chosen orientation. 

Note that some surfaces are *not* orientable. This means they do not have two distinct sides. An example of a non-orientable surface is a Möbius strip, shown below.

![](images/27/277ffb9e1594e64f3411b0c5063841616aaa433ccc4915bc96e2c9ab865ece95.png)

 

A Möbius strip can be made by taking a long rectangular piece of paper, twisting one of its ends by $180^\circ$ and gluing the two ends together. 

A Möbius strip does not have two distinct sides because if you were to start at a point $P$ on the strip and move along it (following the dark blue curve shown), you'd eventually end up at the same point but on the opposite side! Thus, a Möbius strip only has one distinct side. 

In the work that follows, we will only consider orientable surfaces." :tutorial/id #uuid "e93caa6c-3516-5696-8b97-769b20ec4ac0" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7728 :tutorial/title "Orientable vs. Non-Orientable Surfaces"} :step/id #uuid "15c5dca7-7c90-57e5-be91-60bf5e44e76b" :step/math-academy-id 657076 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167786}} {:db/id 17592186167788 :step/content {:db/id 17592186166882 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186166487 :question/id #uuid "35c3c9ba-60b0-5bcf-8e9c-2862ece44e7e" :question/math-academy-id "e-12454"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "f9a62365-4278-557f-ba76-caa31abe7869" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186167129} {:db/id 17592186167130} {:db/id 17592186167131} {:db/id 17592186278417} {:db/id 17592186278418} {:db/id 17592186281387} {:db/id 17592186281388} {:db/id 17592186281492} {:db/id 17592186281494} {:db/id 17592186281496} {:db/id 17592186369894} {:db/id 17592186369908} {:db/id 17592186421235} {:db/id 17592186421237} {:db/id 17592186421241} {:db/id 17592186444618} {:db/id 17592186444619}] :knowledge-point/title "Computing the Flux of a Vector Field Through a Tilted Plane"} :step/id #uuid "99f84857-19d8-532f-b1f8-974d1ed142df" :step/math-academy-id 657087} {:db/id 17592186167789 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168148 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have the horizontal plane $z=k,$ where $k$ is a fixed parameter. 

The magnitude of the fundamental vector product is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}||{r}_{x}\times {r}_{y}|| & =\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂k}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂k}{∂y})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+{0}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, in such cases, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,f(x,y,z)\text{d}S\, & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,z)\cdot ||{r}_{x}\times {r}_{y}||\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,z)\cdot 1\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Restating, we have

$$
\iint\limits_S f(x,y,z)\, \textrm d S = \iint\limits_D f(x,y,z)  \,\textrm d A.
$$

We arrive at a similar result when considering vertical planes parallel to the $xz$- or $yz$-axes.

This observation can help provide a shortcut when calculating the flux of a vector field through a horizontal plane. Let's see an example." :tutorial/id #uuid "3a45ce20-02a0-56e8-9b38-add2ba9480d1" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7733 :tutorial/title "The Fundamental Vector Product for a Horizontal Plane"} :step/id #uuid "e8905e0e-c7f6-5708-9e74-d2d69c659271" :step/math-academy-id 657082 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167784}} {:db/id 17592186362446 :step/content {:db/id 17592186362413 :tutorial/content "If we wish to find the flux through a tilted plane, we should first calculate the unit normal vector to this plane.

For example, consider the vector field $\mathbf F(x,y,z) = \langle x,\: 1-x+y,\: 2y+8\rangle$ and a finite region $S$ of the plane $z=2x+2y-1$ such that $\textrm{Area}(S) = 2.$ 
Assume that we need to find the flux of $\mathbf F$ through $S$ with respect to the upward-pointing unit normal vector $\mathbf n.$

If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $\mathbf n,$ and $\mathbf F$ is a continuous vector field, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $\mathbf n$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}
=
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}S.
$$

Notice that our surface $z = 2x+2y-1$ can be written using the dot product as 

$$
\langle x,\: y,\: z\rangle \cdot \underbrace{\langle -2,\: -2, \: 1\rangle}_{\widetilde{\mathbf n}} = -1, \quad \textrm{or}\quad \langle x,\: y,\: z\rangle \cdot \underbrace{\langle 2,\: 2, \: -1\rangle}_{-\widetilde{\mathbf n}}= 1.
$$

Since we require an upward-pointing normal vector to our surface $S,$ we must select one where the $z$-component is positive. This gives us the normal vector

$$
\widetilde{\mathbf n} = \langle -2,\, -2,\, 1\rangle.
$$

Normalizing this vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{\overset{~}{n}}{‖\overset{~}{n}‖} \\  & =\frac{⟨-2,\,-2,\,1⟩}{\sqrt{(-2)^{2}+(-2)^{2}+{1}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}⟨-2,\,-2,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨x,\,1-x+y,\,2y+8⟩\cdot \frac{1}{3}⟨-2,\,-2,\,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}⟨x,\,1-x+y,\,2y+8⟩\cdot ⟨-2,\,-2,\,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(-2x-2(1-x+y)+2y+8) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(-2x-2+2x-2y+2y+8) \\  & =\frac{6}{3} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}2\,\text{d}S \\  & =2{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S \\  & =2\cdot \text{Area}(S) \\  & =2\cdot 2 \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "48c45790-f4c7-562f-9a3f-46bf6009dd4e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 15974 :tutorial/title "Computing the Flux of a Vector Field Through a Tilted Plane"} :step/id #uuid "81d0dc6b-4e76-5f80-934b-e300c50b0201" :step/math-academy-id 657086 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167788}}] :activity/title "Flux in Three-Dimensional Vector Fields" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186166981} {:db/id 17592186167785 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168145 :tutorial/content "Recall that the flux of a two-dimensional vector field $\mathbf F(x,y)$ across a curve $C$ with respect to a unit normal vector $\mathbf n(x,y)$ is given by the line integral

$$
\int\limits_C \mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n\,\textrm d s.
$$

The flux measures the total flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C,$ as depicted below.

![](images/23/2392d6c27fc6767c78172936d6df37b3dfec8b2198abbdf9e22b87d4337ed9da.png)

Flux is always measured with respect to a preselected unit normal vector $\mathbf n,$ and we have two choices of orientation for this vector. If we measure the flux relative to the unit normal pointing in the *opposite* direction, our flux will have the *same* magnitude but *opposite* sign.

![](images/e4/e451548a5d9874b9eff9d61c2d423696dc76a3f560e2936eb7bdb3a9cbfbed49.png)

This lesson aims to extend the concept of flux to three-dimensional vector fields. But first, we need a brief discussion on surface orientations." :tutorial/id #uuid "8a17f47e-f50d-578f-a41c-9e537ded3620" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7725 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "507e9c0b-b2be-5bf9-a53c-e763d7e4315b" :step/math-academy-id 657075 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167787}} {:db/id 17592186167782 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168144 :tutorial/content "Consider the vector field $\mathbf F$ and the surface $S$ with unit normal vector $\mathbf n,$ where

$$
\mathbf{F}(x,y,z) = \left\langle xz + y,\: x^2,\: 2y-z^2 \right\rangle\!, 
\qquad 
\mathbf{n}(x,y,z) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt5}\left\langle 2,\: 0,\: -1 \right\rangle\!.
$$

Let's construct a surface integral representing the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $S$ with respect to $\mathbf{n}.$

First, we recall that if $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $\mathbf n,$ and $\mathbf F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $\mathbf n$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}
=
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}S.
$$

Calculating the dot product, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨xz+y,\,{x}^{2},\,2y-{z}^{2}⟩\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}⟨2,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}⟨xz+y,\,{x}^{2},\,2y-{z}^{2}⟩\cdot ⟨2,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}((xz+y)\cdot 2+{x}^{2}\cdot 0+(2y-{z}^{2})\cdot (-1)) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}(2xz+2y-2y+{z}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{2xz+{z}^{2}}{\sqrt{5}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral representing the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $S$ with respect to $\mathbf n$ can be written as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}\frac{2xz+{z}^{2}}{\sqrt{5}}\,\text{d}S \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}{∬}_{S}2xz+{z}^{2}\,\text{d}S\end{aligned}
$$

We can then evaluate this integral using the usual methods." :tutorial/id #uuid "c936101d-fbb9-594d-888c-2327d0908e71" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7632 :tutorial/title "A Worked Example"} :step/id #uuid "88355efb-c547-50b1-b76e-a290fd494387" :step/math-academy-id 657078 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167783}} {:db/id 17592186168144 :tutorial/content "Consider the vector field $\mathbf F$ and the surface $S$ with unit normal vector $\mathbf n,$ where

$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}2\,\text{d}S \\  & =2{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S \\  & =2\cdot \text{Area}(S) \\  & =2\cdot 2 \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "48c45790-f4c7-562f-9a3f-46bf6009dd4e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 15974 :tutorial/title "Computing the Flux of a Vector Field Through a Tilted Plane"} :step/id #uuid "81d0dc6b-4e76-5f80-934b-e300c50b0201" :step/math-academy-id 657086 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167788}} {:db/id 17592186168145 :tutorial/content "Recall that the flux of a two-dimensional vector field $\mathbf F(x,y)$ across a curve $C$ with respect to a unit normal vector $\mathbf n(x,y)$ is given by the line integral

$$
\int\limits_C \mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n\,\textrm d s.
$$

The flux measures the total flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C,$ as depicted below.

![](images/23/2392d6c27fc6767c78172936d6df37b3dfec8b2198abbdf9e22b87d4337ed9da.png)

Flux is always measured with respect to a preselected unit normal vector $\mathbf n,$ and we have two choices of orientation for this vector. If we measure the flux relative to the unit normal pointing in the *opposite* direction, our flux will have the *same* magnitude but *opposite* sign.

![](images/e4/e451548a5d9874b9eff9d61c2d423696dc76a3f560e2936eb7bdb3a9cbfbed49.png)

This lesson aims to extend the concept of flux to three-dimensional vector fields. But first, we need a brief discussion on surface orientations." :tutorial/id #uuid "8a17f47e-f50d-578f-a41c-9e537ded3620" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7725 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186167787 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168147 :tutorial/content "A surface is **orientable** if it has two distinct sides. So, for example, the surface $S$ shown below is orientable.

![](images/29/29be1e415eaf0072aea7f4093e71665f5996b29804702a37a4d4493e0b0002d4.png)

 

If a unit vector $\mathbf n(x,y,z)$ to our orientable surface varies continuously over $S,$ we say that $S$ is **oriented** and the choice of $\mathbf n$ gives an **orientation** of $S.$

We can choose the opposite orientation for our surface by selecting a vector that points in the opposite direction, as shown below.

![](images/40/40268c448b7c4ac99acf356e9f1e2702112a0d46dc1b6e6afd98d5c95e5ea317.png)

 

When dealing with two-sided (i.e., orientable) surfaces, we must always be clear about our chosen orientation. 

Note that some surfaces are *not* orientable. This means they do not have two distinct sides. An example of a non-orientable surface is a Möbius strip, shown below.

![](images/27/277ffb9e1594e64f3411b0c5063841616aaa433ccc4915bc96e2c9ab865ece95.png)

 

A Möbius strip can be made by taking a long rectangular piece of paper, twisting one of its ends by $180^\circ$ and gluing the two ends together. 

A Möbius strip does not have two distinct sides because if you were to start at a point $P$ on the strip and move along it (following the dark blue curve shown), you'd eventually end up at the same point but on the opposite side! Thus, a Möbius strip only has one distinct side. 

In the work that follows, we will only consider orientable surfaces." :tutorial/id #uuid "e93caa6c-3516-5696-8b97-769b20ec4ac0" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7728 :tutorial/title "Orientable vs. Non-Orientable Surfaces"} :step/id #uuid "15c5dca7-7c90-57e5-be91-60bf5e44e76b" :step/math-academy-id 657076 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167786}} {:db/id 17592186167786 :step/content {:db/id 17592186168146 :tutorial/content "In three dimensions, flux measures the total flow of a vector field $\mathbf F(x,y,z)$ *through an orientable surface.*

Suppose that $\mathbf F(x,y,z)$ is a three-dimensional vector field, and $S$ is an orientable surface with the choice of orientation given by the unit normal vector $\mathbf n(x,y,z),$ as shown below.

![](images/99/9976f35dcf348da89c15a40aad43ab5a1d3edea75558ef5539f9421ed9b75f4e.png)

 

The **flux of $\mathbf F$ across $\boldsymbol{S}$** with respect to $\mathbf n,$ which we write as 

$$
\iint\limits_S \mathbf F \cdot \textrm d \mathbf S
$$

 is given by the surface integral

$$

It's worth taking a moment to compare this to the flux formula for two-dimensional vector fields: 

- The quantity $\mathbf F \cdot \mathbf n$ evaluated at a point $P$ on $S$ measures the projection of $\mathbf F$ in the direction of $\mathbf n$ at $P.$

- By summing (integrating) the quantity $\mathbf F \cdot \mathbf n$ over the entire surface, we get the total flow of $\mathbf F$ through $S.$

Our flux depends on our choice of orientation. If we were to select the *opposite* orientation, we'd get a result with the same magnitude but opposite sign." :tutorial/id #uuid "5a72f9c0-0bf4-59dd-be49-827f9e278fa3" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7727 :tutorial/title "Flux in Three-Dimensional Vector Fields"} :step/id #uuid "4b9873f3-a548-5ea9-a86b-7682d0efa06b" :step/math-academy-id 657077 :step/next {:db/id 17592186167782}} {:db/id 17592186168146 :tutorial/content "In three dimensions, flux measures the total flow of a vector field $\mathbf F(x,y,z)$ *through an orientable surface.*

The magnitude of the fundamental vector product is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}||{r}_{x}\times {r}_{y}|| & =\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂k}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂k}{∂y})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+{0}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, in such cases, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,f(x,y,z)\text{d}S\, & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,z)\cdot ||{r}_{x}\times {r}_{y}||\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,z)\cdot 1\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Restating, we have

$$
\iint\limits_S f(x,y,z)\, \textrm d S = \iint\limits_D f(x,y,z)  \,\textrm d A.
$$

We arrive at a similar result when considering vertical planes parallel to the $xz$- or $yz$-axes.

This observation can help provide a shortcut when calculating the flux of a vector field through a horizontal plane. Let's see an example." :tutorial/id #uuid "3a45ce20-02a0-56e8-9b38-add2ba9480d1" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7733 :tutorial/title "The Fundamental Vector Product for a Horizontal Plane"} {:db/id 17592186362413 :tutorial/content "If we wish to find the flux through a tilted plane, we should first calculate the unit normal vector to this plane.

For example, consider the vector field $\mathbf F(x,y,z) = \langle x,\: 1-x+y,\: 2y+8\rangle$ and a finite region $S$ of the plane $z=2x+2y-1$ such that $\textrm{Area}(S) = 2.$ 
Assume that we need to find the flux of $\mathbf F$ through $S$ with respect to the upward-pointing unit normal vector $\mathbf n.$

If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $\mathbf n,$ and $\mathbf F$ is a continuous vector field, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $\mathbf n$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}
=
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}S.
$$

Notice that our surface $z = 2x+2y-1$ can be written using the dot product as 

$$
\langle x,\: y,\: z\rangle \cdot \underbrace{\langle -2,\: -2, \: 1\rangle}_{\widetilde{\mathbf n}} = -1, \quad \textrm{or}\quad \langle x,\: y,\: z\rangle \cdot \underbrace{\langle 2,\: 2, \: -1\rangle}_{-\widetilde{\mathbf n}}= 1.
$$

Since we require an upward-pointing normal vector to our surface $S,$ we must select one where the $z$-component is positive. This gives us the normal vector

$$
\widetilde{\mathbf n} = \langle -2,\, -2,\, 1\rangle.
$$

Normalizing this vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{\overset{~}{n}}{‖\overset{~}{n}‖} \\  & =\frac{⟨-2,\,-2,\,1⟩}{\sqrt{(-2)^{2}+(-2)^{2}+{1}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}⟨-2,\,-2,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨x,\,1-x+y,\,2y+8⟩\cdot \frac{1}{3}⟨-2,\,-2,\,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}⟨x,\,1-x+y,\,2y+8⟩\cdot ⟨-2,\,-2,\,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(-2x-2(1-x+y)+2y+8) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(-2x-2+2x-2y+2y+8) \\  & =\frac{6}{3} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}2\,\text{d}S \\  & =2{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S \\  & =2\cdot \text{Area}(S) \\  & =2\cdot 2 \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "48c45790-f4c7-562f-9a3f-46bf6009dd4e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 15974 :tutorial/title "Computing the Flux of a Vector Field Through a Tilted Plane"} {:activity/course {:db/id 17592186046660} :activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186444620} :activity/id #uuid "0bdff687-f8d4-5855-9373-b5ab9e4534b8" :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186050188 :topic/id #uuid "34eb87b9-7036-55c0-88eb-1b1efbd11584" :topic/math-academy-id 3178} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186444620 :step/content {:db/id 17592186167127 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "51f5f2fd-94a6-51c3-ac48-99d59a93e907" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x+2y+z" :db/id 17592186444605} {:answer/id #uuid "8524a039-125d-5c28-8aaa-2b417ce25d91" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "y+z" :db/id 17592186444606} {:answer/id #uuid "a0cc803d-28d2-5c8a-ad4d-e88ee6c149ca" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-y-z" :db/id 17592186444608} {:answer/id #uuid "ad810e29-dc47-543e-aeb1-8297ce882407" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "z-x" :db/id 17592186444610} {:answer/id #uuid "e9761621-383d-53ec-8615-e110f65c1ad5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x+y+2z" :db/id 17592186444613}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186444610} :answer-field/id #uuid "63f86b8b-b32a-5de1-8bfa-b93d1b01899d" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186163840}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "44a48f57-f74b-5294-bb24-4cee5d89d1d4" :question/math-academy-id "q-161149" :question/problem "Consider the vector field $F$ and the surface $S$ with unit normal vector $n,$ where

$$
F(x,y,z)=⟨2z,\,x+y,\,y-z⟩\,,\,n(x,y,z)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨1,\,-1,\,1⟩\,.
$$

If the flux of $F$ across $S$ with respect to $n$ is given by

{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}{∬}_{S}\boxed{}\,\text{d}S,
$$

what is the missing expression?" :question/worked-solution "If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Calculating the dot product, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨2z,\,x+y,\,y-z⟩\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨1,\,-1,\,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨2z,\,x+y,\,y-z⟩\cdot ⟨1,\,-1,\,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}(2z-(x+y)+(y-z)) \\  & =\frac{z-x}{\sqrt{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the flux can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}\frac{z-x}{\sqrt{3}}\,\text{d}S \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}{∬}_{S}z-x\,\text{d}S.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "03b4b191-1c32-5328-8c44-46701817acdf" :step/next {:db/id 17592186444623}} {:db/id 17592186444621 :step/content {:db/id 17592186444618 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "23676b92-59ce-549e-bb44-0ce2c22aff60" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186444601} {:answer/id #uuid "30a14e60-74d3-59a0-9d7c-8bfb0dc4a3c2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{6}" :db/id 17592186444603} {:answer/id #uuid "8c7915a4-09c6-54d8-8b86-d3abcf6997b3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\sqrt{6}" :db/id 17592186444607} {:answer/id #uuid "ca06b212-b30b-58a7-bceb-f7e5db8c00f0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2\sqrt{3}" :db/id 17592186444612} {:answer/id #uuid "f6e593f7-c2c1-5fc5-8a3d-c699694f0c1d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\sqrt{3}" :db/id 17592186444614}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186444614} :answer-field/id #uuid "6ac4cbf3-d6da-5e60-8eb4-cf067330135d" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186444617}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "2ae7b222-1017-5e06-9f85-8323117b3184" :question/math-academy-id "q-162158" :question/problem "Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨z+5,\,x-2y,\,3x-2y⟩$ and a finite region $S$ of the plane $z=x+2y+1$ such that $\text{Area}(S)=\sqrt{2}.$ Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S$ with respect to the *downward*-pointing unit normal vector $n.$" :question/worked-solution "If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that our surface $z=x+2y+1$ can be written using the dot product as 

$$
⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨-1,\,-2,\,1⟩}_{⏟}}_{\overset{~}{n}}=1,\,\text{or}\,⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨1,\,2,\,-1⟩}_{⏟}}_{-\overset{~}{n}}=-1.
$$

Since we require a downward-pointing normal vector to our surface $S,$ we must select one where the $z$-component is negative. This gives us the normal vector

$$
\overset{~}{n}=⟨1,\,2,\,-1⟩.
$$

Normalizing this vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{\overset{~}{n}}{‖\overset{~}{n}‖} \\  & =\frac{⟨1,\,2,\,-1⟩}{\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{2}^{2}+(-1)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}⟨1,\,2,\,-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that $z=x+2y+1$ on $S,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨z+5,\,x-2y,\,3x-2y⟩\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}⟨1,\,2,\,-1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}⟨x+2y+6,\,x-2y,\,3x-2y⟩\cdot ⟨1,\,2,\,-1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}((x+2y+6)+2(x-2y)-(3x-2y)) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}(x+2y+6+2x-4y-3x+2y) \\  & =\frac{6}{\sqrt{6}} \\  & =\sqrt{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}\sqrt{6}\,\text{d}S \\  & =\sqrt{6}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S \\  & =\sqrt{6}\cdot \text{Area}(S) \\  & =\sqrt{6}\cdot \sqrt{2} \\  & =2\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "0ad1dc8f-1c73-5500-a47a-c0fda9ab766e"} {:db/id 17592186444622 :step/content {:db/id 17592186278421 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2720bb2d-ef3c-5bd3-b5d1-47e2a36e5b59" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "xy+yz+xz" :db/id 17592186275834} {:answer/id #uuid "30f13b93-277e-5c15-b9c8-932581f5f992" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "xy-2yz+xz" :db/id 17592186275912} {:answer/id #uuid "3b883b06-8332-53dc-bb7f-68fb90e59ae4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3xz-yz" :db/id 17592186275997} {:answer/id #uuid "74a4ce69-d793-5db1-9424-5b3b421ad0a2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2{x}^{2}{y}^{2}{z}^{2}" :db/id 17592186276532} {:answer/id #uuid "8f857f74-c7bf-534b-90d2-dc5735bc9d12" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "xy-yz+2xz" :db/id 17592186276777}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186276777} :answer-field/id #uuid "74b1826a-ee9f-5272-9977-4058c1ea92ea" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186277932}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "fe4ccf73-c8f1-5e87-8e15-f27def60e911" :question/math-academy-id "q-161200" :question/problem "Consider the vector field $F$ and the surface $S$ with unit normal vector $n,$ where

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S$ with respect to the upward-pointing unit normal vector $n.$" :question/worked-solution "If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that our surface $z=x-y$ can be written using the dot product as 

$$
⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨-1,\,1,\,1⟩}_{⏟}}_{\overset{~}{n}}=0,\,\text{or}\,⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨1,\,-1,\,-1⟩}_{⏟}}_{-\overset{~}{n}}=0.
$$

Since we require an upward-pointing normal vector to our surface $S,$ we must select one where the $z$-component is positive. This gives us the normal vector

$$
\overset{~}{n}=⟨-1,\,1,\,1⟩.
$$

Normalizing this vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{\overset{~}{n}}{‖\overset{~}{n}‖} \\  & =\frac{⟨-1,\,1,\,1⟩}{\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨-1,\,1,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that $z=x-y$ on $S,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨x+3,\,x+y,\,z-x+6⟩\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨-1,\,1,\,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨x+3,\,x+y,\,6-y⟩\cdot ⟨-1,\,1,\,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}(-(x+3)+(x+y)+(6-y)) \\  & =\frac{3}{\sqrt{3}} \\  & =\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}\sqrt{3}\,\text{d}S \\  & =\sqrt{3}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S \\  & =\sqrt{3}\cdot \text{Area}(S) \\  & =\sqrt{3}\cdot \sqrt{6} \\  & =3\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "76294a87-9654-50ec-a44d-a6393dfb7851"} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0ec4eec9-d885-5e59-95b5-8276383a1984" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "q-162551" :question/problem "Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨3x,\,2z,\,y-2⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined in Cartesian coordinates as $z=2x-y+1$ for $0\le x\le 4$ and $0\le y\le 1.$ Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S$ with respect to the *downward*-pointing unit normal vector $n.$

*Hint: You're given that the fundamental vector product of $S$ with respect to its canonical parametrization is $||{r}_{x}\times {r}_{y}||=\sqrt{6}.$*" :question/worked-solution "If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that our surface $z=2x-y+1$ can be written using the dot product as 

$$
⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨-2,\,1,\,1⟩}_{⏟}}_{-\overset{~}{n}}=1,\,\text{or}\,⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨2,\,-1,\,-1⟩}_{⏟}}_{\overset{~}{n}}=-1.
$$

Since we require a downward-pointing normal vector to our surface $S,$ we must select one where the $z$-component is negative. This gives us the normal vector

$$
\overset{~}{n}=⟨2,\,-1,\,-1⟩.
$$

Normalizing this vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{\overset{~}{n}}{‖\overset{~}{n}‖} \\  & =\frac{⟨2,\,-1,\,-1⟩}{\sqrt{{2}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+(-1)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}⟨2,\,-1,\,-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that $z=2x-y+1$ on $S,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨3x,\,2z,\,y-2⟩\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}⟨2,\,-1,\,-1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}⟨3x,\,4x-2y+2,\,y-2⟩\cdot ⟨2,\,-1,\,-1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}(6x-(4x-2y+2)-(y-2)) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}(2x+y).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}(2x+y)\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}(2x+y)\cdot ||{r}_{x}\times {r}_{y}||\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}(2x+y)\cdot \sqrt{6}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{1}{\cancel{\sqrt{6}}}(2x+y)\cdot \cancel{\sqrt{6}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2x+y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{4}(2x+y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[{x}^{2}+xy]}_{x=0}^{x=4}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(4y+16)\,\text{d}y \\  & =[2{y}^{2}+16y]_{0}^{1} \\  & =18\end{aligned}

*Hint: You're given that the fundamental vector product of $S$ with respect to its canonical parametrization is $||{r}_{x}\times {r}_{y}||=\sqrt{11}.$*" :question/worked-solution "If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that our surface $z=3x-y$ can be written using the dot product as 

$$
⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨-3,\,1,\,1⟩}_{⏟}}_{-\overset{~}{n}}=0,\,\text{or}\,⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨3,\,-1,\,-1⟩}_{⏟}}_{\overset{~}{n}}=0.
$$

Since we require a downward-pointing normal vector to our surface $S,$ we must select one where the $z$-component is negative. This gives us the normal vector

$$
\overset{~}{n}=⟨3,\,-1,\,-1⟩.
$$

Normalizing this vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{\overset{~}{n}}{‖\overset{~}{n}‖} \\  & =\frac{⟨3,\,-1,\,-1⟩}{\sqrt{{3}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+(-1)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{11}}⟨3,\,-1,\,-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that $z=3x-y$ on $S,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨y,\,x,\,z⟩\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{11}}⟨3,\,-1,\,-1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{11}}⟨y,\,x,\,3x-y⟩\cdot ⟨3,\,-1,\,-1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{11}}(3y-x-(3x-y)) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{11}}(4y-4x).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}\frac{1}{\sqrt{11}}(4y-4x)\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{1}{\sqrt{11}}(4y-4x)\cdot ||{r}_{x}\times {r}_{y}||\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{1}{\sqrt{11}}(4y-4x)\cdot \sqrt{11}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{1}{\cancel{\sqrt{11}}}(4y-4x)\cdot \cancel{\sqrt{11}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(4y-4x)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}(4y-4x)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{[4xy-2{x}^{2}]}_{x=0}^{x=1}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(4y-2)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[2{y}^{2}-2y]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "1f385f05-45d4-59c1-9f32-a7029261c4c3" :step/next {:db/id 17592186549078}} {:db/id 17592186549109 :step/content {:db/id 17592186370846 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "8eb87a35-5ced-5a5e-b4ba-6ed8f43fa65b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{5}{2}" :db/id 17592186370848} {:answer/id #uuid "ed0b221a-37f0-59c2-9ebf-9e2be6f4943a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{5}{2}" :db/id 17592186370849} {:answer/id #uuid "f449e0d2-71cb-570a-b7f8-b46a261c1889" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-\frac{3}{2}" :db/id 17592186370850} {:answer/id #uuid "efe12eb7-f752-5e10-9617-78e76fdbdf10" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{2}" :db/id 17592186370851} {:answer/id #uuid "574d87f2-9154-53de-97ba-85268e66a98b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-2" :db/id 17592186370852}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186370848} :answer-field/id #uuid "4ba53699-98f1-5f44-bc12-18afd01851f4" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186370847}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "41a56a15-fd44-52b0-9c06-c58863771399" :question/math-academy-id "q-365881" :question/problem "Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨y,\,z,\,2x-y⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined in Cartesian coordinates as $z=3$ for $1\le x\le 2$ and $0\le y\le 1.$ Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S$ with respect to the *downward*-pointing unit normal vector $n.$" :question/worked-solution "If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is a continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$

Notice that our surface $z=2x-y+1$ can be written using the dot product as 

$$

$$

Since we require a downward-pointing normal vector to our surface $S,$ we must select one where the $z$-component is negative. This gives us the normal vector

$$
\overset{~}{n}=⟨2,\,-1,\,-1⟩.
$$

Normalizing this vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{\overset{~}{n}}{‖\overset{~}{n}‖} \\  & =\frac{⟨2,\,-1,\,-1⟩}{\sqrt{{2}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+(-1)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}⟨2,\,-1,\,-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨3x,\,2z,\,y-2⟩\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}⟨2,\,-1,\,-1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}⟨3x,\,4x-2y+2,\,y-2⟩\cdot ⟨2,\,-1,\,-1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}(6x-(4x-2y+2)-(y-2)) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}(2x+y).\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}(2x+y)\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}(2x+y)\cdot ||{r}_{x}\times {r}_{y}||\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}(2x+y)\cdot \sqrt{6}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{1}{\cancel{\sqrt{6}}}(2x+y)\cdot \cancel{\sqrt{6}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2x+y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{4}(2x+y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[{x}^{2}+xy]}_{x=0}^{x=4}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(4y+16)\,\text{d}y \\  & =[2{y}^{2}+16y]_{0}^{1} \\  & =18\end{aligned}

mass $M$ and uniform mass density occupies the region
$D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,\,1\le y\le 3\}.$ Find the radius of gyration of the plate about the origin." :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina in the shape of a region $D$ with mass $M$ and mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{x}$ about the $x$-axis is given by
${R}_{x}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{x}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{x}$ is the moment of inertia about the $x$-axis.

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{y}$ about the $y$-axis is given by
${R}_{y}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{y}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{y}$ is the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis.

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{0}$ about the origin is given by
${R}_{0}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{0}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{0}$ is the moment of inertia about the origin.

The moment of inertia about the origin is defined as

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}\lambda (x,y)({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A,
$$

where $\lambda (x,y)$ is the mass density function.

The area of the rectangular plate $D$ is $A=2\cdot 2=4.$ Since the plate has uniform density, the mass density function is given by

$$
\lambda (x,y)=\frac{M}{A}=\frac{M}{4}.
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the origin is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{0} & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (x,y)({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & =\frac{M}{4}{\int }_{1}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{2}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{4}{\int }_{1}^{3}{[\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}+x{y}^{2}]}_{x=0}^{x=2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{4}{\int }_{1}^{3}\frac{8}{3}+2{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{2}{\int }_{1}^{3}\frac{4}{3}+{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{2}{[\frac{4}{3}y+\frac{1}{3}{y}^{3}]}_{1}^{3} \\  & =\frac{M}{2}(4+9-(\frac{4}{3}+\frac{1}{3})) \\  & =\frac{M}{2}(13-\frac{5}{3}) \\  & =\frac{M}{2}\cdot \frac{34}{3} \\  & =\frac{17M}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
{R}_{0}^{2}=\frac{17}{3}\,⇒\,{R}_{0}=\sqrt{\frac{17}{3}}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186198665 :question/id #uuid "2496e287-b250-5877-a40c-af954399de62" :question/math-academy-id "q-163612" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186198417 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "2bfe2e3e-9d7b-5c53-8de8-2717237d3e9c" :knowledge-point/title "Calculating the Radius of Gyration of a Uniform Rectangular Laminar"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1e41b76a-dabb-5807-a6bb-5779e0a43c8c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}" :db/id 17592186278869} {:answer/id #uuid "59d4646c-a8cc-5cc4-8c20-a790ad2f4d3f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\sqrt{\frac{3}{5}}" :db/id 17592186279413} {:answer/id #uuid "74959f37-361c-597f-97f4-79fda9c4ad64" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\sqrt{\frac{2}{3}}" :db/id 17592186279642} {:answer/id #uuid "ed79e371-e80a-5031-880e-b39448d43e87" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}" :db/id 17592186280675} {:answer/id #uuid "ee046b1f-ca21-54a9-88ec-7eeb4e214626" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}" :db/id 17592186280677}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "ed79e371-e80a-5031-880e-b39448d43e87" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}" :db/id 17592186280675} :answer-field/id #uuid "ee676f82-5c11-53e9-9b1a-845255b4b041" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186281256}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "A rectangular plate of mass $M$ and uniform mass density occupies the region
$D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,\,4\le y\le 6\}.$ Find the radius of gyration of the plate about the $y$-axis." :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina in the shape of a region $D$ with mass $M$ and mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{x}$ about the $x$-axis is given by
${R}_{x}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{x}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{x}$ is the moment of inertia about the $x$-axis.

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{y}$ about the $y$-axis is given by
${R}_{y}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{y}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{y}$ is the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis.

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{0}$ about the origin is given by
${R}_{0}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{0}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{0}$ is the moment of inertia about the origin.

The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is defined as

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A,
$$

where $\lambda (x,y)$ is the mass density function.

The area of the rectangular plate $D$ is $A=1\cdot 2=2.$ Since the plate has uniform density, the mass density function is given by

$$
\lambda (x,y)=\frac{M}{A}=\frac{M}{2}.
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & =\frac{M}{2}{\int }_{4}^{6}{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{2}{\int }_{4}^{6}{[\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}]}_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{2}{\int }_{4}^{6}\frac{1}{3}(1-0)\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{\int }_{4}^{6}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{6}[y]_{4}^{6} \\  & =\frac{M}{6}(6-4) \\  & =\frac{M}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
{R}_{y}^{2}=\frac{1}{3}\,⇒\,{R}_{y}=\sqrt{\frac{1}{3}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186235554 :question/id #uuid "12d7be9e-b12c-5440-971b-269b8c57642f" :question/math-academy-id "q-169104"} {:db/id 17592186281676 :question/id #uuid "c58b6231-e237-5de8-8e27-d0ade4f5cce7" :question/math-academy-id "q-163576" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "28052605-ef85-5d61-b60d-35c652016958" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3}" :db/id 17592186278950} {:answer/id #uuid "30e535dc-d841-51b2-9346-6dd8f8151f9e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{\frac{7}{5}}" :db/id 17592186279019} {:answer/id #uuid "7d4a7fcf-e348-50c3-a268-aaa5fcf0d810" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{\frac{3}{2}}" :db/id 17592186279712} {:answer/id #uuid "cd62681a-f336-57f7-9271-562c7877f73a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{5}}{2}" :db/id 17592186280402} {:answer/id #uuid "e5cb850d-af3a-58fe-9a74-754886c3ca4d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}" :db/id 17592186280620}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186280620} :answer-field/id #uuid "2fb299df-44bd-5725-bf66-0524bf139842" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186280921}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "A rectangular plate of mass $M$ and uniform mass density occupies the region
$D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,\,0\le y\le 3\}.$ Find the radius of gyration of the plate about the $y$-axis." :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina in the shape of a region $D$ with mass $M$ and mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{x}$ about the $x$-axis is given by
${R}_{x}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{x}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{x}$ is the moment of inertia about the $x$-axis.

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{y}$ about the $y$-axis is given by
${R}_{y}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{y}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{y}$ is the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis.

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{0}$ about the origin is given by
${R}_{0}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{0}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{0}$ is the moment of inertia about the origin.

The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is defined as

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A,
$$

where $\lambda (x,y)$ is the mass density function.

The area of the rectangular plate $D$ is $A=2\cdot 3=6.$ Since the plate has uniform density, the mass density function is given by

$$
\lambda (x,y)=\frac{M}{A}=\frac{M}{6}.
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{2}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{\int }_{0}^{3}{[\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}]}_{0}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{1}{3}(8-0)\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{4M}{9}[y]_{0}^{3} \\  & =\frac{4M}{9}\cdot 3 \\  & =\frac{4M}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}\lambda (x,y)({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A,
$$

The area of the rectangular plate $D$ is $A=1\cdot 3=3.$ Since the plate has uniform density, the mass density function is given by

$$
\lambda (x,y)=\frac{M}{A}=\frac{M}{3}.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{0} & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (x,y)({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & =\frac{M}{3}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{3}{\int }_{0}^{3}{[\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}+x{y}^{2}]}_{x=0}^{x=1}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{3}{\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{1}{3}+{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{3}{[\frac{1}{3}y+\frac{1}{3}{y}^{3}]}_{0}^{3} \\  & =\frac{M}{3}(1+9) \\  & =\frac{10M}{3}.\end{aligned}

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A,
$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{x} & ={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{\int }_{1}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{3}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{\int }_{1}^{3}[x{y}^{2}]_{x=0}^{x=3}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{\int }_{1}^{3}3{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{6}[{y}^{3}]_{1}^{3} \\  & =\frac{M}{6}(27-1) \\  & =\frac{13M}{3}.\end{aligned}

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{x}$ about the $x$-axis is given by
${R}_{x}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{x}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{x}$ is the moment of inertia about the $x$-axis.

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{y}$ about the $y$-axis is given by
${R}_{y}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{y}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{y}$ is the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis.

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{0}$ about the origin is given by
${R}_{0}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{0}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{0}$ is the moment of inertia about the origin.

The moment of inertia about the origin is defined as

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}\lambda (x,y)({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A,
$$

where $\lambda (x,y)$ is the mass density function.

The area of the rectangular plate $D$ is $A=3\cdot 2=6.$ Since the plate has uniform density, the mass density function is given by

$$
\lambda (x,y)=\frac{M}{A}=\frac{M}{6}.
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the origin is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{0} & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (x,y)({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{\int }_{1}^{3}{\int }_{1}^{4}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{\int }_{1}^{3}{[\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}+x{y}^{2}]}_{x=1}^{x=4}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{\int }_{1}^{3}(\frac{64}{3}+4{y}^{2}-\frac{1}{3}-{y}^{2})\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{\int }_{1}^{3}21+3{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{6}{[21y+{y}^{3}]}_{1}^{3} \\  & =\frac{M}{6}(63+27-21-1) \\  & =\frac{M}{6}\cdot 68 \\  & =\frac{34M}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
{R}_{0}^{2}=\frac{34}{3}\,⇒\,{R}_{0}=\sqrt{\frac{34}{3}}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186444169 :question/id #uuid "ae31463b-0937-5dcb-a149-ee8482b71924" :question/math-academy-id "q-163579" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1e358496-a583-59a6-b4e0-5fcf99d9cafa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{3}" :db/id 17592186444157} {:answer/id #uuid "2ca9c9b8-05e4-5eb3-8122-ad72c6a359f7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{7}}{3}" :db/id 17592186444158} {:answer/id #uuid "688f7ffe-b0fd-57c9-821e-0495e33a6fae" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{\frac{17}{5}}" :db/id 17592186444161} {:answer/id #uuid "9bbfff91-ca90-559f-ae5d-5fd328a1f1e9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{7}" :db/id 17592186444163} {:answer/id #uuid "bb7abb37-0de9-58cb-8a76-9f11aa3adea3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{\frac{21}{2}}" :db/id 17592186444165}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186444163} :answer-field/id #uuid "02ef48a6-5de2-5aeb-b94d-50e269438d16" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186444166}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "A rectangular plate of mass $M$ and uniform mass density occupies the region
$D=\{(x,y)\,:\,1\le x\le 4,\,\,2\le y\le 5\}.$ Find the radius of gyration of the plate about the $y$-axis." :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina in the shape of a region $D$ with mass $M$ and mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{x}$ about the $x$-axis is given by
${R}_{x}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{x}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{x}$ is the moment of inertia about the $x$-axis.

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{y}$ about the $y$-axis is given by
${R}_{y}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{y}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{y}$ is the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis.

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{0}$ about the origin is given by
${R}_{0}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{0}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{0}$ is the moment of inertia about the origin.

The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is defined as

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A,
$$

where $\lambda (x,y)$ is the mass density function.

The area of the rectangular plate $D$ is $A=3\cdot 3=9.$ Since the plate has uniform density, the mass density function is given by

$$
\lambda (x,y)=\frac{M}{A}=\frac{M}{9}.
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & =\frac{M}{9}{\int }_{2}^{5}{\int }_{1}^{4}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{9}{\int }_{2}^{5}{[\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}]}_{1}^{4}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{9}{\int }_{2}^{5}(\frac{64}{3}-\frac{1}{3})\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{M}{9}{\int }_{2}^{5}21\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{7M}{3}{\int }_{2}^{5}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{7M}{3}[y]_{2}^{5} \\  & =\frac{7M}{3}(5-2) \\  & =7M.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{R}_{y}^{2}=7\,⇒\,{R}_{y}=\sqrt{7}.

"![](images/5b/5b8ddb36e814517af21d790374e1fb192141bd6ef0fd99e83a147c6ed5a62aea.png)

A plate of mass $M$ occupies the region $D$ in the first quadrant bounded by the circles ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1,$ ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=4,$ and the coordinate axes, as shown above. Its mass density at any point is given by $\lambda (x,y)=\frac{3}{7}My.$ Find the radius of gyration of the plate about the $y$-axis." :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina in the shape of a region $D$ with mass $M$ and mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{x}$ about the $x$-axis is given by
${R}_{x}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{x}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{x}$ is the moment of inertia about the $x$-axis.

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{y}$ about the $y$-axis is given by
${R}_{y}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{y}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{y}$ is the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis.

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{0}$ about the origin is given by
${R}_{0}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{0}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{0}$ is the moment of inertia about the origin.

In polar coordinates, the region occupied by the plate is given by

$$
D=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,1\le r\le 2,\,\,0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}\}.
$$

The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis, in polar coordinates, is defined as

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta ){r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ,
$$

where $\lambda (r,\theta )$ is the mass density function.

Also, the mass density in terms of polar coordinates is $\lambda (r,\theta )=\frac{3}{7}Mr\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .$
Therefore, the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta ){r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{3}{7}M{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{1}^{2}{r}^{4}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{3}{7}M({\int }_{1}^{2}{r}^{4}\,\text{d}r)({\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta ) \\  & =\frac{3}{7}M\cdot \frac{1}{5}{r}^{5}{|}_{1}^{2}\cdot {[-\frac{{cos}^{3}⁡\theta }{3}]}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{3}{7}M\cdot (\frac{32}{5}-\frac{1}{5})\cdot (-0+\frac{1}{3}) \\  & =\frac{3}{7}M\cdot \frac{31}{5}\cdot \frac{1}{3} \\  & =\frac{31M}{35}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the radius of gyration about the $x$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{R}_{y} & =\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{y}}{M}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{31M}{35}\cdot \frac{1}{M}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{31}{35}}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186198957 :question/id #uuid "b6fbab0f-40fd-5c65-87d5-1b56f0245d59" :question/math-academy-id "q-38825"} {:db/id 17592186281681 :question/id #uuid region $D$ with mass $M$ and mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{x}$ about the $x$-axis is given by
${R}_{x}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{x}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{x}$ is the moment of inertia about the $x$-axis.

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{y}$ about the $y$-axis is given by
${R}_{y}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{y}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{y}$ is the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis.

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{0}$ about the origin is given by
${R}_{0}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{0}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{0}$ is the moment of inertia about the origin.

In polar coordinates, the region occupied by the plate is given by

$$
D=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,1\le r\le 2,\,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi \}.
$$

The moment of inertia about the origin, in polar coordinates, is defined as

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta ){r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta ,
$$

where $\lambda (r,\theta )$ is the mass density function.

Also, the mass density in terms of polar coordinates is $\lambda (r,\theta )=\frac{4M}{15\pi }{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta .$
Therefore, the moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{0} & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta ){r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{4M}{15\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{1}^{2}{r}^{5}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{4M}{15\pi }({\int }_{1}^{2}{r}^{5}\,\text{d}r)({\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta ) \\  & =\frac{4M}{15\pi }\cdot \frac{1}{6}{r}^{6}{|}_{1}^{2}({\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\frac{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta }{2}\,\text{d}\theta ) \\  & =\frac{4M}{15\pi }\cdot \frac{21}{2}\cdot {[\frac{\theta }{2}+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta }{4}]}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =\frac{14M}{5\pi }\cdot \pi  \\  & =\frac{14M}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the radius of gyration about the $x$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{R}_{0} & =\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{0}}{M}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{14M}{5}\cdot \frac{1}{M}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{14}{5}}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186284397 :question/id #uuid "2bedf3e3-7671-5f19-9c93-56fbbbe7e210" :question/math-academy-id "q-163658"} {:db/id 17592186369922 :question/id #uuid 17592186280897}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "A plate of mass $M$ occupies the region $D$ enclosed by the lines $y=x,$ $x=2,$ and the $x$-axis. Its mass density at any point on the plate is given by $\lambda (x,y)=\frac{3}{4}My.$ Find the radius of gyration of the plate about the $y$-axis." :question/worked-solution "For a plane lamina in the shape of a region $D$ with mass $M$ and mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{x}$ about the $x$-axis is given by
${R}_{x}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{x}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{x}$ is the moment of inertia about the $x$-axis.

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{y}$ about the $y$-axis is given by
${R}_{y}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{y}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{y}$ is the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis.

- The radius of gyration ${R}_{0}$ about the origin is given by
${R}_{0}=\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{0}}{M}},$
where ${I}_{0}$ is the moment of inertia about the origin.

The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is defined as

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A,
$$

where $\lambda (x,y)$ is the mass density function. The region $D$ is a type I region with representation

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,\,0\le y\le x\}.
$$

Hence, the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{x}{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{3}{4}My\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3M}{4}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{x}{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3M}{4}{\int }_{0}^{2}{[\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}{y}^{2}]}_{y=0}^{y=x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3M}{4}{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{2}{x}^{4}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3M}{4}{[\frac{1}{10}{x}^{5}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{3M}{4}\cdot \frac{16}{5} \\  & =\frac{12M}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the radius of gyration about the $y$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{R}_{y} & =\sqrt{\frac{{I}_{y}}{M}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{12M}{5}\cdot \frac{1}{M}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{12}{5}} \\  & =2\sqrt{\frac{3}{5}}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186198956 :question/id #uuid "2db88b84-fe57-56b2-8d78-b4ac01dd1164" :question/math-academy-id "q-38824"} {:db/id 17592186281682 :question/id #uuid "ad1b682f-b157-528a-b0f7-855122eb923c" :question/math-academy-id "q-163600"} {:db/id 17592186281684 :question/id #uuid "fd3dc29c-e508-5e62-812f-85ffd3f21aae" :question/math-academy-id "q-163609" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "01f9db5c-e164-5da8-8198-fa6bb66ab5d8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{2}" :db/id 17592186278599} {:answer/id #uuid "1a4abe59-3a00-5413-9a13-f76e53a05f56" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{\frac{14}{5}}" :db/id 17592186278827} {:answer/id #uuid "27295108-8d28-5e44-bd4c-fd9f5f5c1dc6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186278939} {:answer/id #uuid "2a222fa5-d9c5-5841-9ffa-a9c00a82be6b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3\sqrt{5}" :db/id 17592186278965} {:answer/id #uuid "9a04f08e-efba-5b0c-ad94-d016db6f7419" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{7}}{2}" :db/id 17592186279952}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186278827} :answer-field/id #uuid "a1724ad2-5623-51fe-a835-78c2ea54e619" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186281118}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "A plate of mass $M$ occupies the region $D$ enclosed by the lines $y=3x,$ $x=1,$ $x=2,$ and the $x$-axis.
