$=1.$" :question/worked-solution "The Cartesian equation of a horizontal hyperbola centered at the origin is

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=1.
$$

Therefore, to write the equation of the hyperbola in standard form, we need to divide both sides of the equation by $126$ and then simplify, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}14{x}^{2}-21{y}^{2} & =126 \\ \frac{14{x}^{2}}{126}-\frac{21{y}^{2}}{126} & =\frac{126}{126} \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{9}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{6} & =1\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186299875 :question/id #uuid "54b5fd86-3d2b-5b48-84c2-d1b54392706a" :question/math-academy-id "q-320675" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2f0cc90b-e38c-506a-8a4c-6a2e8028c58f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{{x}^{2}}{3}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{27}" :db/id 17592186297751}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186297751} :answer-field/id #uuid "01a3424d-fe0a-549a-8dea-0f4f6a36be2c" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186298650}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "The equation of the hyperbola $45{x}^{2}-5{y}^{2}=135$ in standard form is{{field-1}}
$=1.$" :question/worked-solution "The Cartesian equation of a horizontal hyperbola centered at the origin is

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}-\frac{{y}^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=1.
$$

Therefore, to write the equation of the hyperbola in standard form, we need to divide both sides of the equation by $135$ and then simplify, as follows:

$B=\begin{bmatrix}\sqrt{5} & 4 & 1 \\ -3 & 2\sqrt{2} & -3.2 \\ 0 & 1 & -\sqrt{3}\end{bmatrix}.$" :question/worked-solution "Notice that $A$ is the $2$nd *row* of the identity matrix ${I}_{3}.$

Since we're multiplying the $3\times 3$ matrix $B$ by the $2$nd *row* of the identity matrix ${I}_{3}$ on the *left*, the result must be the $2$nd *row* of $B.$ Therefore,

$$
AB=\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 2\sqrt{2} & -3.2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Let's check the long way:

$$
\begin{aligned}AB & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}\sqrt{5} & 4 & 1 \\ -3 & 2\sqrt{2} & -3.2 \\ 0 & 1 & -\sqrt{3}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 2\sqrt{2} & -3.2\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}

$$
x=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,\,\,y=3\operatorname{cos}⁡2t,\,t\in [0,2\pi ).
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's make the trigonometric functions the subject of each equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}x=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\, & ⇒\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t=\frac{x}{2} \\ y=3\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\, & ⇒\,\operatorname{cos}⁡2t=\frac{y}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using double angle formula for cosine and the Pythagorean identity, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡2t & ={cos}^{2}⁡t-{sin}^{2}⁡t \\  & =(1-{sin}^{2}⁡t)-{sin}^{2}⁡t \\  & =1-2{sin}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\operatorname{sin}⁡t=\frac{x}{2}$ and $\operatorname{cos}⁡2t=\frac{y}{3}$ into this formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{y}{3} & =1-2{(\frac{x}{2})}^{2} \\ \frac{y}{3} & =1-2(\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}) \\ \frac{y}{3} & =1-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2} \\ y & =3(1-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

So the Cartesian equation of the given curve is $y=3(1-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}).$"} {:db/id 17592186290552 :question/id #uuid "50632a56-05a3-5b2c-a470-4387daec2008" :question/math-academy-id "q-24574"} {:db/id 17592186290553 :question/id #uuid "ca1f80dd-221f-5c68-b74a-e39a400a3763" :question/math-academy-id "q-24575"} {:db/id 17592186290554 :question/id #uuid "fd03cb1f-af7d-59db-bf84-fa1a13cb0a30" :question/math-academy-id "q-24576"} {:db/id 17592186299922 :question/id #uuid "4923000b-5c5c-55b7-9b95-5a7082500328" :question/math-academy-id "q-320946"} {:db/id 17592186302048 :question/id #uuid "746bed7b-e090-56a7-9ad1-4c0bfac39908" :question/math-academy-id "q-321314"} {:db/id 17592186302049 :question/id #uuid "3eac432e-a9f4-5e40-ae91-1f28e72debdf" :question/math-academy-id "q-321318"} {:db/id 17592186375624 :question/id #uuid "8b4d7dbc-be4c-5d12-8115-af652723cf38" :question/math-academy-id "q-102677"} {:db/id 17592186377082 :question/id #uuid "1c9558ce-37ee-554b-ae06-97c014ed01c5" :question/math-academy-id "q-319828"} {:db/id 17592186377088 :question/id #uuid "e0deecc2-15f7-5c26-991c-e45282132b63" :question/math-academy-id "q-321315"} {:db/id 17592186377091 :question/id #uuid "6f647799-4d25-58ea-a46d-69aef277766e" :question/math-academy-id "q-321400"} {:db/id 17592186048858} {:db/id 17592186048918} {:db/id 17592186049212} {:db/id 17592186050722} {:db/id 17592186050745} {:db/id 17592186050769} {:db/id 17592186050356 :topic/difficulty 1.224438375983708 :topic/encompasses [{:db/id 17592186428207 :encompassing/rationale "Initial Codex estimate from captured target-band crossing frequency. :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "Find the values of $x$ for which the function $f(x)=2{x}^{3}-3{x}^{2}+8$ is strictly increasing." :question/worked-solution "The function is strictly increasing where ${f}^{′}(x)>0.$ Differentiating $f(x),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =2\cdot 3{x}^{2}-3\cdot 2x \\  & =6{x}^{2}-6x,\end{aligned}
$$

so we need to solve the inequality

$$
\begin{aligned}6{x}^{2}-6x & >0.\end{aligned}
$$

The above inequality factors as

$$
6x(x-1)>0.
$$

The graph of $y=6x(x-1)$ has roots at $x=0$ and $x=1,$ as shown below:

![](images/ec/ec7ea6baa82d60a6cf472c904460190042d889d86cb092b19d9809111bd93b36.png)

Therefore, we conclude that the function is strictly increasing on the intervals $x\in (-\infty ,0)\cup (1,\infty ).$"} {:db/id 17592186235361 :question/id #uuid "11d48983-8d2c-5031-ab51-9f45fb7ab1a7" :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186341692}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Consider the system of linear equations

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}2x-6y &=10 \\ -x+3y &=-5.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce the augmented matrix $M$ of the system to row echelon form, and then find the general solution of the linear system." :question/worked-solution "First, we set up the augmented matrix for the system:

$$
M=\begin{bmatrix}2 & -6 & 10 \\ -1 & 3 & -5\end{bmatrix}
$$

Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & -6 & 10 \\ -1 & 3 & -5\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{1} & :=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -3 & 5 \\ -1 & 3 & -5\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -3 & 5 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

The corresponding system is now

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-3y &=5 \\ 0x+0y &=0.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Since any pair of numbers $x,y$ is a solution of the final equation $0x+0y=0,$ we can remove this equation from the system. So, our system now consists of a single equation

$$
x-3y=5.
$$

The first variable $(x)$ is the basic variable, and the second variable $(y)$ is the free variable. Solving for the basic variable $(x)$ in terms of the free variable $(y),$ we get $x=5+3y,$ and the general solution is

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=5+3y \\ y &=y\end{aligned}\right.
$$

where $y$ is an arbitrary number. 

In vector form, the general solution can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}5+3y \\ y\end{bmatrix},\,y\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186379994 :question/id #uuid "a9a9e509-4293-5590-b2bf-432eea2f6134" :question/math-academy-id "q-73749"} {:db/id 17592186390395 :question/id #uuid "1766ca49-3fde-5817-b4dd-1d97ee2424fc" :question/math-academy-id "q-20965"} {:db/id 17592186392481 :question/id #uuid "653d2739-ff74-51ff-bc93-114e79b1a15b" :question/math-academy-id "q-42153"} {:db/id 17592186393355 :question/id #uuid "79d64547-fc54-5cd3-a6ec-b00c0e085729" :question/math-academy-id "q-73750"} {:db/id 17592186414183 :question/id #uuid "2dc4858f-be36-5c29-9f4f-6c819c499765" :question/math-academy-id "q-20961"} {:db/id 17592186414185 :question/id #uuid "e2f37bf7-c408-5d68-a145-8a36082b4969" :question/math-academy-id "q-42163"} {:db/id 17592186414186 :question/id #uuid "f4b75945-9982-5318-bfc3-2aef2116e166" :question/math-academy-id "q-42154"} {:db/id 17592186050178} {:db/id 17592186048819 :topic/difficulty 0.679502246147745 :topic/encompasses [{:db/id 17592186428234 :encompassing/rationale "Initial Codex estimate from captured target-band crossing frequency. 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** $v=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}$ is an eigenvector of $A=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & -2 \\ 3 & 4\end{bmatrix}$ that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-1.$

- **II.** $v=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}$ is an eigenvector of $A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 4 \\ 3 & 0\end{bmatrix}$ that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-3.$

- **III.** If $v$ is an eigenvector of a matrix $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-2,$ then $3v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ corresponding to $\lambda =-6.$" :question/worked-solution "Remember that the eigenvectors of $A$ are the non-zero vectors $v$ such that $Av=\lambda v.$ With that in mind, let's examine the statements one by one.

- Statement I is false. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}Av & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 & -2 \\ 3 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =1\cdot \begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =1v.\end{aligned}
$$

 
Since $Av=v,$ we conclude that $v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ and the corresponding eigenvalue is $\lambda =1$ (but not $-1$).

- Statement II is true. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}Av & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 4 \\ 3 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ -3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =-3\cdot \begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =-3v.\end{aligned}
$$

 
Since $Av=-3v,$ we conclude that $v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ and the corresponding eigenvalue is $\lambda =-3.$

- Statement III is false. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}A(3v)=3Av=3(-2v)=-2(3v).\end{aligned}
$$

Since, $A(3v)=-2(3v),$ and $3v\ne 0,$ this implies that $3v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ and the corresponding eigenvalue is $\lambda =-2$ (but not $-6$).

**Note:** In general, any non-zero multiple of an eigenvector is again an eigenvector, and the corresponding eigenvalue is the same.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only"."} {:db/id 17592186323843 :question/id #uuid "187c7a1d-e687-5fd7-b36a-8bd4869c300f" :question/math-academy-id "q-36678"} {:db/id 17592186323858 :question/id to have a common base. To do this, we rewrite the equation using $16={2}^{4}$ and $8={2}^{3},$ as follows:

$$
{({2}^{4})}^{2n}={({2}^{3})}^{n+1}\,
$$

Then, we apply the power rule of exponents. This gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{2}^{8n} & ={2}^{3(n+1)}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since both sides of the equation share the same base $(2)$, we equate the exponents and solve for $n:$

$$
\begin{aligned}8n & =3(n+1) \\ 8n & =3n+3 \\ 5n & =3 \\ n & =\frac{3}{5}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186547999 :question/id #uuid "49bb96bd-7826-5c22-b9da-330c6f2a3a6b" :question/math-academy-id "q-66881"} {:db/id 17592186049784} {:db/id 17592186048589 :topic/id #uuid "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186546845}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "Which of the following probabilities could be approximated using the normal approximation of the binomial distribution?

I. The probability that a student correctly solves $4$ questions in a $5$-question math test if the student has a $75%$ probability of correctly answering each question.

II. The probability that $42$ flights out of $120$ arrive early at an airport if the probability of a single flight arriving early is $0.45$ for each flight.

III. The probability of getting $4$ ones on $10$ rolls of a $4$-sided die." :question/worked-solution "Given a binomial random variable $X∼B(n,p),$ if 

- $np>5,$ and

- $n(1-p)>5,$

we can approximate $X$ as a normal random variable $Y$ with mean $\mu =np$ and variance ${\sigma }^{2}=np(1-p),$ that is, 

$$
Y∼N(np,np(1-p)).
$$

Let's now examine each situation.

- In situation I, we have $n=5$ and $p=0.75.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}np & =5\cdot 0.75 \\  & =3.75 \\  & ≯5.\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

So, we *cannot* use the normal approximation of the binomial distribution.

- In situation II, we have $n=120$ and $p=0.45.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}np & =120\cdot 0.45 \\  & =54 \\  & >5\,✓ \\ n(1-p) & =120\cdot (1-0.45) \\  & =66 \\  & >5.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can use the normal approximation of the binomial distribution.

- In situation III, we have $n=10$ and $p=\frac{1}{4}.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}np & =10\cdot \frac{1}{4} \\  & =2.5 \\  & ≯5.\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

So, we *cannot* use the normal approximation of the binomial distribution.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only.""} {:db/id 17592186115316 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186115145 :question/id #uuid "4c4e12c4-1593-500d-873d-863b4a825e91" approximation to the binomial distribution to approximate $P(X=50).$ Give your final answer to three decimal places

*Hint: The data below is taken from the table of values of the cumulative distribution function $Φ(z)$ for the standard normal distribution. *

| $z$ | $\,0.04\,$ | $\,0.05\,$ | $\,0.06\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\,1.9\,$ | $\,0.9738\,$ | $\,0.9744\,$ | $\,0.9750\,$ |
| $\,2.0\,$ | $\,0.9793\,$ | $\,0.9798\,$ | $\,0.9803\,$ |
| $\,2.1\,$ | $\,0.9838\,$ | $\,0.9842\,$ | $\,0.9846\,$ |
| $\,2.2\,$ | $\,0.9875\,$ | $\,0.9878\,$ | $\,0.9881\,$ |
| $\,2.3\,$ | $\,0.9904\,$ | $\,0.9906\,$ | $\,0.9909\,$ |" :question/requires-calculator true :question/worked-solution "Given a binomial random variable $X∼B(n,p),$ if 

- $np>5,$ and

- $n(1-p)>5,$

we can approximate $X$ as a normal random variable $Y$ with mean $\mu =np$ and variance ${\sigma }^{2}=np(1-p),$ that is, 

$$
Y∼N(np,np(1-p)).
$$

Here, we have $n=100$ and $p=0.4.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}np & =100\cdot 0.4 \\  & =40 \\  & >5\,✓ \\ n(1-p) & =100\cdot (1-0.4) \\  & =60 \\  & >5.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can approximate our binomial random variable $X$ with a normal random variable $Y$ with mean

$$
\mu =np=(100)(0.4)=40
$$

and variance

$$
{\sigma }^{2}=np(1-p)=(100)(0.4)(1-0.4)=24.
$$

That is, we can approximate $X$ by $Y∼N(40,24).$

Now, we can approximate the desired probability $P(X=50).$ Using a continuity correction, we have

$$
P(X=50)≈P(49.5\le Y\le 50.5).
$$

To compute this probability, we transform to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(49.5\le Y\le 50.5) & =P(\frac{49.5-40}{\sqrt{24}}\le Z\le \frac{50.5-40}{\sqrt{24}}) \\  & ≈P(1.94\le Z\le 2.14) \\  & =P(Z\le 2.14)-P(Z<1.94) \\  & =P(Z\le 2.14)-P(Z\le 1.94) \\  & =Φ(2.14)-Φ(1.94) \\  & =0.9838-0.9738 \\  & =0.010\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
P(X=50)≈0.010.
$$

Note: Using a software package for the approximation gives a probability of $0.0102.$"} {:db/id 17592186115992 :question/id #uuid "1c656830-cd06-512a-9850-cdb6ac44625c" :question/math-academy-id "q-95746" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "846b0a24-fd02-5b82-a38e-3133b9c4e7c5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.133" :db/id 17592186114890} {:answer/id #uuid "dcc7c66a-d184-5463-9399-88208cbe2ab6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.211" :db/id 17592186114891} {:answer/id #uuid "fb1f9f0d-16fe-5b9a-9bc6-de5e149b666c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.102" :db/id 17592186114892} {:answer/id #uuid "38aa6d6d-24a6-5498-a798-156dd186cf8b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.112" :db/id 17592186114893} {:answer/id #uuid "586f4bec-7011-58e8-8061-da5c682ca9f7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.311" :db/id 17592186114894}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186114890} :answer-field/id #uuid "790c6c63-5981-55a0-b734-56731235ce58" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186114889}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Using the normal approximation to the binomial distribution, approximate the probability that a student gets $14$ correct answers on a true/false quiz with $25$ questions if the student answers all questions at random. *Hint: The data below is taken from the table of values of the cumulative distribution function $Φ(z)$ for the standard normal distribution. *

| $\,0.8\,$ | $\,0.7881\,$ | $\,0.7910\,$ | $\,0.7939\,$ |" :question/requires-calculator true :question/worked-solution "Given a binomial random variable $X∼B(n,p),$ if 

- $np>5,$ and

- $n(1-p)>5,$

we can approximate $X$ as a normal random variable $Y$ with mean $\mu =np$ and variance ${\sigma }^{2}=np(1-p),$ that is, 

$$
Y∼N(np,np(1-p)).
$$

Here, we have $n=25$ and $p=0.5.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}np & =25\cdot 0.5 \\  & =12.5 \\  & >5\,✓ \\ n(1-p) & =25\cdot (1-0.5) \\  & =12.5 \\  & >5.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can approximate our binomial random variable $X$ with a normal random variable $Y$ with mean

$$
\mu =np=(25)(0.5)=12.5
$$

and variance

$$
{\sigma }^{2}=np(1-p)=(25)(0.5)(1-0.5)=6.25.
$$

That is, we can approximate $X$ by $Y∼N(12.5,6.25).$

Now, we can approximate the desired probability $P(X=14).$ Using a continuity correction, we have

$$
P(X=14)≈P(13.5\le Y\le 14.5).
$$

To compute this probability, we transform to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(13.5\le Y\le 14.5) & =P(\frac{13.5-12.5}{\sqrt{6.25}}\le Z\le \frac{14.5-12.5}{\sqrt{6.25}}) \\  & ≈P(0.40\le Z\le 0.80) \\  & =P(Z\le 0.80)-P(Z<0.40) \\  & =P(Z\le 0.80)-P(Z\le 0.40) \\  & =Φ(0.80)-Φ(0.40) \\  & =0.7881-0.6554 \\  & =0.1327\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
P(X=14)≈0.133.
$$

$$
Y∼N(np,np(1-p)).
$$

Here, we have $n=200$ and $p=0.43.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}np & =200\cdot 0.43 \\  & =86 \\  & >5\,✓ \\ n(1-p) & =200\cdot (1-0.43) \\  & =114 \\  & >5.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can approximate our binomial random variable $X$ with a normal random variable $Y$ with mean

$$
\mu =np=(200)(0.43)=86
$$

and variance

$$
{\sigma }^{2}=np(1-p)=(200)(0.43)(1-0.43)=49.02.
$$

That is, we can approximate $X$ by $Y∼N(86,49.02).$

Now, we can estimate the desired probability $P(80<X<105).$ Using a continuity correction, we have

$$
P(80<X<105)=P(81\le X\le 104)≈P(80.5\le Y\le 104.5).
$$

To compute this probability, we transform to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(80.5\le Y<104.5) & =P(\frac{80.5-86}{\sqrt{49.02}}\le Z\le \frac{104.5-86}{\sqrt{49.02}}) \\  & ≈P(-0.79\le Z\le 2.64) \\  & =P(Z\le 2.64)-P(Z<-0.79) \\  & =P(Z\le 2.64)-P(Z\le -0.79) \\  & =Φ(2.64)-Φ(-0.79) \\  & =0.9959-0.2148 \\  & =0.7811\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
P(80<X<105)≈0.781.
$$

Here, we have $n=80$ and $p=0.4.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}np & =80\cdot 0.4 \\  & =32 \\  & >5\,✓ \\ n(1-p) & =80\cdot (1-0.4) \\  & =48 \\  & >5.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can approximate our binomial random variable $X$ with a normal random variable $Y$ with mean

$$
\mu =np=(80)(0.4)=32
$$

and variance

$$
{\sigma }^{2}=np(1-p)=(80)(0.4)(1-0.4)=19.2.
$$

That is, we can approximate $X$ by $Y∼N(32,19.2).$

$$

$$

$$

$$

Therefore,

$$
P(25<X<35)≈0.646.

17592186045487} :question/problem "Given that $det(A)=3$, which of the following statements are true? 
- **I.** $-4\text{det}({A}^{T})+2\text{det}(I)=3$
- **II.** $2\text{det}({A}^{T})=6$
- **III.** $\text{det}({A}^{T})-\text{det}(I)=1$

Select all that apply. If none apply, leave all boxes unchecked." :question/worked-solution "From the properties of determinants, we know that 

$$
\text{det}({A}^{T})=\text{det}(A)=3
$$

and

$$
det(I)=1.
$$

With that in mind, let's analyze each statement in turn.

- Statement I is false. Indeed,

$$
-4\text{det}({A}^{T})+2\text{det}(I)=-4\cdot 3+2\cdot 1=-10\ne 3.
$$

- Statement II is true. We have

$$
2\text{det}({A}^{T})=2\cdot 3=6.
$$

- Statement III is false. We have

$$
\text{det}({A}^{T})-\text{det}(I)=3-1=2\ne 1.
$$

In conclusion, the correct answer is "II only.""} {:db/id 17592186329655 :question/id #uuid "4524ce2c-6b42-5e23-be24-247fd51db7f6" :question/math-academy-id "q-42482"} {:db/id 17592186329689 :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "Given that $det(A)=14$, and $I$ is the $3\times 3$ identity matrix, which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** $\text{det}(A)-\text{det}(3I)=-13$

- **II.** $-\text{det}({A}^{T})+\text{det}(I)=-13$

- **III.** $\text{det}(A)-\text{det}({A}^{T})=-28$" :question/worked-solution "From the properties of determinants, we know that 

$$
\text{det}({A}^{T})=\text{det}(A)=14
$$

and

$$
det(I)=1.
$$

Now, notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}3I & =3\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

The determinant of a diagonal matrix is equal to the product of the entries on the main diagonal. Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{vmatrix}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{vmatrix} & ={3}^{3}=27.\end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's analyze each statement in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed,

$$
\text{det}(A)-\text{det}(3I)=14-27=-13
$$

- Statement II is true. Indeed,

$$
-\text{det}({A}^{T})+\text{det}(I)=-14+1=-13
$$

- Statement III is false. We have

$$
\text{det}(A)-\text{det}({A}^{T})=14-14=0\ne -28
$$

In conclusion, the correct answer is "I and II only"."} {:db/id 17592186119932 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186119506 :question/id #uuid "a67e620f-6380-5754-81db-7e593cdf4336" 17592186274708}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Calculate the volume of the $4$-dimensional parallelepiped spanned by the vectors

$$
a=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -2 \\ 0 \\ -3\end{bmatrix},\,b=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 7 \\ 5 \\ 5\end{bmatrix},\,c=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 10 \\ 0 \\ 7\end{bmatrix},\,d=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 3 \\ 4 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's construct the matrix $M,$ whose columns are the coordinates of our vectors $a,$ $b,$ $c,$ and  $d:$

$$
M=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 2 & 0 & 0 \\ -2 & 7 & 10 & 3 \\ 0 & 5 & 0 & 4 \\ -3 & 5 & 7 & 2\end{bmatrix}
$$

The volume of the parallelepiped spanned by these vectors equals the absolute value of the determinant of $M:$

$$
V=|det(M)|
$$

Notice that the $1$st row of the determinant contains three zeros. So, using Laplace expansion along the $1$st row, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}det(M) & =\begin{vmatrix}0 & 2 & 0 & 0 \\ -2 & 7 & 10 & 3 \\ 0 & 5 & 0 & 4 \\ -3 & 5 & 7 & 2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =2\cdot (-1)^{1+2}\begin{vmatrix}-2 & 10 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 4 \\ -3 & 7 & 2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-2\begin{vmatrix}-2 & 10 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 4 \\ -3 & 7 & 2\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the $2$nd row of the $3\times 3$ determinant contains two zeros. So, using Laplace expansion along the $2$nd row, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}det(M) & =-2\begin{vmatrix}-2 & 10 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 4 \\ -3 & 7 & 2\end{vmatrix} \\  & =-2\cdot 4\cdot (-1)^{2+3}\begin{vmatrix}-2 & 10 \\ -3 & 7\end{vmatrix} \\  & =8\begin{vmatrix}-2 & 10 \\ -3 & 7\end{vmatrix} \\  & =8(-14+30) \\  & =128.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the volume is

$$
V=|det(M)|=|128|=128.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186369845 :question/id #uuid "9fc304b0-a53d-5a62-b8cd-1ca341a43179" :question/math-academy-id "q-158367"} {:db/id 17592186369852 :question/id #uuid $$

If $r=⟨x,y,z⟩,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨x,y,z⟩\cdot ⟨2,-5,4⟩ & =20 \\ 2x-5y+4z & =20 \\ 4z & =20-2x+5y \\ z & =5-\frac{1}{2}x+\frac{5}{4}y.\end{aligned}
$$

Setting $x=2$ and $y=4,$ we get 

$$
z=5-\frac{1}{2}(2)+\frac{5}{4}(4)=9.
$$

So, the point $Q(2,4,9)$ lies on the plane. 

Now, we find

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PQ} & =⟨2,4,9⟩-⟨-2,11,1⟩ \\  & =⟨4,-7,8⟩.\end{aligned}

To do that, we simply substitute some concrete values for $x$ and $y$ into the equation and solve for $z.$ Let's choose $x=2$ and $y=3$ (though it doesn't really matter what values we choose). Solving for $z,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}3x+2y+7z & =-9 \\ 3(2)+2(3)+7z & =-9 \\ 7z & =-21 \\ z & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we get the point $Q(2,3,-3)$ which lies on the plane.

Computing $\overset{\to }{PQ},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PQ} & =⟨2,3,-3⟩-⟨5,9,-6⟩ \\  & =⟨-3,-6,3⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

We also need a normal vector to the plane. For any Cartesian equation of a plane $ax+by+cz=d,$ the normal vector is $n=⟨a,b,c⟩.$ So, for the plane $Π,$ we have $n=⟨3,2,7⟩.$ 

Finally, the shortest distance from the point $P$ to the plane $Π$ is the absolute value of the scalar projection of $\overset{\to }{PQ}$ onto the normal vector of the plane:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =|{\text{comp}}_{n}\,\overset{\to }{PQ}| \\  & =\frac{|\overset{\to }{PQ}\cdot n|}{|n|} \\  & =\frac{|(-3)\cdot 3+(-6)\cdot 2+3\cdot 7|}{\sqrt{{3}^{2}+{2}^{2}+{7}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{|-9-12+21|}{\sqrt{9+4+49}} \\  & =\frac{|\,0\,|}{\sqrt{62}} \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

:question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Which of the three sequences below are geometric sequences?

I. $5,\,10,\,15,\,…$

II. ${a}_{n+1}=6{a}_{n},\,{a}_{1}=18,\,n\ge 1$

III. $f(n+1)=2f(n)+3,\,f(1)=1,\,n\ge 1$

Select all that apply." :question/worked-solution "A sequence is geometric if there is a common ratio between its terms. Let's check each sequence in turn.

- Sequence I is not geometric because not every pair of consecutive terms has the same ratio. To see this, we only need to go up to the third term:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{f(2)}{f(1)}=\frac{10}{5} & =2 \\ \frac{f(3)}{f(2)}=\frac{15}{10} & =\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

- Sequence II is a geometric sequence. The recursive rule ${a}_{n+1}=6{a}_{n}$ tells us that each term is $6$ times the previous term, so the common ratio is $r=6.$

- Sequence III is not a geometric sequence. To see this, we can calculate the first $3$ terms of the sequence and then compute the ratios of consecutive terms:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1) & =1 \\ f(2) & =2\cdot 1+3=5 \\ f(3) & =2\cdot 5+3=13\end{aligned}
$$

So, the first two pairs of consecutive terms have different ratios:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{f(2)}{f(1)}=\frac{5}{1} & =5 \\ \frac{f(3)}{f(2)}=\frac{13}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

In conclusion, only sequence II is a geometric sequence."} {:db/id 17592186548984 :question/id #uuid "1faddb6e-7103-543e-9a46-6187e7487263" :question/math-academy-id "q-109811"} {:db/id 17592186549046 :question/id #uuid "baaafa36-2999-5769-af9b-da0e59cba7b8" :question/math-academy-id "q-101443"} {:db/id 17592186050067} {:db/id 17592186048499 :topic/difficulty 0.4417760528545274 :topic/encompasses [{:db/id 17592186428389 :encompassing/rationale "Initial Codex estimate from captured target-band crossing frequency. $$

$$
{a}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix},\,{a}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -3 \\ 5\end{bmatrix},\,b=\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 1 \\ -4\end{bmatrix}.
$$

If ${x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2}=b,$ then what is ${x}_{1}+{x}_{2}?$" :question/worked-solution "If ${x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2}=b$, then we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -2 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -3 \\ 5\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 1 \\ -4\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ -2{x}_{1} \\ 3{x}_{1}\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}2{x}_{2} \\ -3{x}_{2} \\ 5{x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 1 \\ -4\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2} \\ -2{x}_{1}-3{x}_{2} \\ 3{x}_{1}+5{x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 1 \\ -4\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Equating the corresponding components, we get the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2} &=-3 \\ -2{x}_{1}-3{x}_{2} &=1 \\ 3{x}_{1}+5{x}_{2} &=-4\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Multiplying the first equation by $2$ and adding the resulting equations, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & =-5,\end{aligned}
$$

which we substitute into the second equation to get 

$$
\begin{aligned}-2{x}_{1}-3{x}_{2}=1 \\ -2{x}_{1}-3(-5) & =1 \\ -2{x}_{1} & =-14 \\ {x}_{1} & =7.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute ${x}_{1}=7$ and ${x}_{2}=-5$ into the third equation and obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}3{x}_{1}+5{x}_{2}=-4 \\ 3(7)+5(-5) & =-4 \\ -4 & =-4,\end{aligned}
$$

which gives a true statement. 

So the solution of the system is ${x}_{1}=7$ and ${x}_{2}=-5,$ which means

$$
7{a}_{1}-5{a}_{2}=b.
$$

Consequently, 

$$
{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=7+(-5)=2.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186240991 :question/id #uuid "d5149dd7-ead1-5d7c-a754-e514e2e6e606" :question/math-academy-id "q-105167"} {:db/id 17592186317259 :question/id #uuid "8179ffc2-2381-5ec9-a386-111d6e4cae85" :question/math-academy-id "q-34242"} {:db/id 17592186342116 :question/id #uuid "0008ebd1-cf28-5d38-a9cd-5c6dde0f95a6" :question/math-academy-id "q-73951"} {:db/id 17592186342117 :question/id #uuid "eec4fe83-c254-5d51-9484-b88391578898" :question/math-academy-id "q-73952"} {:db/id 17592186342118 :question/id #uuid "abf235b3-2d59-5bfb-aea0-aa237461f6b8" :question/math-academy-id "q-73954"} {:db/id 17592186342123 :question/id #uuid "3c67076c-502b-504a-869c-d6e3549e0a05" :question/math-academy-id "q-73981"} {:db/id 17592186435825 :question/id #uuid "e9e20ff9-23b3-5457-a430-304f98c0d839" :question/math-academy-id "q-73950" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0fdd8247-3e99-5680-9837-f81ce2e4daa8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186435812} {:answer/id #uuid "6588aecf-5be8-5075-92ab-05e2c0bd205f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "No solution" :db/id 17592186435816} {:answer/id #uuid "877b327c-7099-5b51-a1a0-e54f12c801d5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-3" :db/id 17592186435818} {:answer/id #uuid "9a314fbe-bce0-5c72-becd-d86fdd89cb4c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186435819} {:answer/id #uuid "b6573507-37c6-5328-ab6e-7644606e55a7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-4" :db/id 17592186435821}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186435819} :answer-field/id #uuid "50ab6af3-7838-5baf-b926-7d20ec2e1151" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186435822}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Consider the vectors

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 4 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 3 \\ -3\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-11 \\ 8 \\ -14\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}3{x}_{1} \\ 4{x}_{1} \\ 2{x}_{1}\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}-2{x}_{2} \\ 3{x}_{2} \\ -3{x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-11 \\ 8 \\ -14\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}3{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2} \\ 4{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2} \\ 2{x}_{1}-3{x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}-11 \\ 8 \\ -14\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding components, we get the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}3{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2} &=-11 \\ 4{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2} &=8 \\ 2{x}_{1}-3{x}_{2} &=-14\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Adding the second and the third equations we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}6{x}_{1} & =-6 \\ {x}_{1} & =-1,\end{aligned}
$$

which we substitute into the second equation to get 

$$
\begin{aligned}4{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2} & =8 \\ 4(-1)+3{x}_{2} & =8 \\ 3{x}_{2} & =12 \\ {x}_{2} & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute ${x}_{1}=-1$ and ${x}_{2}=4$ into the first equation to get

$$
\begin{aligned}3{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2} & =-11 \\ 3(-1)-2(4) & =-11 \\ -11 & =-11,\end{aligned}
$$

which gives a true statement. 

So the solution of the system is ${x}_{1}=-1$ and ${x}_{2}=4,$ which means

$$
-{a}_{1}+4{a}_{2}=b.
$$

Consequently, 

$$
{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=-1+4=3.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186119854 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186119669 :question/id #uuid "d9beff9d-db58-540f-811e-a07fb77d3d92" :question/math-academy-id "e-6191"} :knowledge-point/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Consider the vectors

$$
{a}_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3 \\ -2\end{bmatrix},\,{a}_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ -8 \\ 6\end{bmatrix},\,{a}_{3}=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 5 \\ -3\end{bmatrix},\,b=\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

If ${x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2}+{x}_{3}{a}_{3}=b,$ then what is ${x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}?$" :question/worked-solution "If ${x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2}+{x}_{3}{a}_{3}=b$, then we have  

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ -8 \\ 6\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{3}\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 5 \\ -3\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ 3{x}_{1} \\ -2{x}_{1}\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}-3{x}_{2} \\ -8{x}_{2} \\ 6{x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}2{x}_{3} \\ 5{x}_{3} \\ -3{x}_{3}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1}-3{x}_{2}+2{x}_{3} \\ 3{x}_{1}-8{x}_{2}+5{x}_{3} \\ -2{x}_{1}+6{x}_{2}-3{x}_{3}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding components, we get the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-3{x}_{2}+2{x}_{3} &=2 \\ 3{x}_{1}-8{x}_{2}+5{x}_{3} &=1 \\ -2{x}_{1}+6{x}_{2}-3{x}_{3} &=2\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We will solve this system using Gaussian elimination. First, we write the augmented matrix for this system:

$$
M=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -3 & 2 & 2 \\ 3 & -8 & 5 & 1 \\ -2 & 6 & -3 & 2\end{bmatrix}
$$

Row-reducing the augmented matrix, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -3 & 2 & 2 \\ 3 & -8 & 5 & 1 \\ -2 & 6 & -3 & 2\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-3){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -3 & 2 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & -5 \\ -2 & 6 & -3 & 2\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -3 & 2 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & -5 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 6\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now 

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-3{x}_{2}+2{x}_{3} &=2 \\ {x}_{2}-{x}_{3} &=-5 \\ {x}_{3} &=6.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

From the third equation, we get ${x}_{3}=6.$ Substituting ${x}_{3}=6$ into the second equation, we obtain

$$
{x}_{2}-6=-5\,⟹\,{x}_{2}=1.
$$

Now, substituting ${x}_{2}=1$ and ${x}_{3}=6$ into the first equation, we obtain

$$
{x}_{1}-3(1)+2(6)=2\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=-7.
$$

So, the solution of the system is ${x}_{1}=-7$, ${x}_{2}=1$, and ${x}_{3}=6,$ which means 

$$
-7{a}_{1}+{a}_{2}+6{a}_{3}=b.
$$

Consequently,

$$

$$

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2} &=-2 \\ -{x}_{2}-{x}_{3} &=5 \\ {x}_{1}-{x}_{2}-3{x}_{3} &=1\end{aligned}\right.
$$

$$

$$

$$

The system is now 

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2} &=-2 \\ {x}_{2}+{x}_{3} &=-5 \\ 0 &=-12.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

$$

If ${x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2}+{x}_{3}{a}_{3}=b,$ then what is ${x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}?$" :question/worked-solution "If ${x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2}+{x}_{3}{a}_{3}=b$, then we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{3}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ -11 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}5 \\ -18 \\ -1\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ 0 \\ {x}_{1}\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{2} \\ -2{x}_{2} \\ 2{x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}3{x}_{3} \\ -11{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}5 \\ -18 \\ -1\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+3{x}_{3} \\ -2{x}_{2}-11{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}5 \\ -18 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding components, we get the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+3{x}_{3} &=5 \\ -2{x}_{2}-11{x}_{3} &=-18 \\ {x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}+{x}_{3} &=-1\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We will solve this system using Gaussian elimination. First, we write the augmented matrix for this system:

$$
M=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 3 & 5 \\ 0 & -2 & -11 & -18 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 & -1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Row-reducing the augmented matrix, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 3 & 5 \\ 0 & -2 & -11 & -18 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 & -1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 3 & 5 \\ 0 & -2 & -11 & -18 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 & -6\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & ↔{R}_{3} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 3 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 & -6 \\ 0 & -2 & -11 & -18\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+2{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 3 & 5 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 & -6 \\ 0 & 0 & -15 & -30\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :=-\frac{1}{15}{R}_{3} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 & 3 & 5 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 & -6 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

The system is now 

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+3{x}_{3} &=5 \\ {x}_{2}-2{x}_{3} &=-6 \\ {x}_{3} &=2.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

 

From the third equation, we get ${x}_{3}=2.$ Substituting this value into  the second equation, we get

$$
{x}_{2}-2(2)=-6\,⟹\,{x}_{2}=-2.
$$

 

Finally, by substituting ${x}_{2}=-2$ and ${x}_{3}=2$ into the first equation, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+3{x}_{3} & =5 \\ {x}_{1}+(-2)+3(2) & =5 \\ {x}_{1}+4 & =5 \\ {x}_{1} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the solution of the system is ${x}_{1}=1$, ${x}_{2}=-2$, and ${x}_{3}=2,$ which means 

$$
{a}_{1}-2{a}_{2}+2{a}_{3}=b.
$$

Consequently, 

$$
{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}=1+(-2)+2=1.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186342134 :question/id #uuid "118e9ea0-84b3-5e8f-866f-104da032b6d7" :question/math-academy-id "q-74035"} {:db/id 17592186342138 :question/id #uuid "a8d414ab-92e5-5218-83d9-6fd3ed558d87" :question/math-academy-id "q-74046"} {:db/id 17592186371499 :question/id #uuid "1eebc51b-6af1-57eb-9255-9e266158abc7" :question/math-academy-id "q-105171"} {:db/id 17592186048315} {:db/id 17592186049045} {:db/id 17592186051046} {:db/id 17592186048729 :topic/difficulty 0.3044184119898127 :topic/encompasses [{:db/id 17592186428448 :encompassing/rationale "Initial Codex estimate from captured target-band crossing frequency. :question/problem "Find the parametric equations of the line that passes through the points $P(2,-5,4)$ and $Q(3,-2,2).$" :question/worked-solution "We need to find a direction vector that is parallel to the given line. We can use the vector $\overset{\to }{PQ}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\overset{\to }{PQ} \\  & =\overset{\to }{OQ}-\overset{\to }{OP} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -5 \\ 4\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the vector equation of the line is

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =p+tv \\ r & =\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -5 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}+t\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3 \\ -2\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -5 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}t \\ 3t \\ -2t\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}2+t \\ -5+3t \\ 4-2t\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$ And finally, the parametric equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=2+t \\ y &=-5+3t \\ z &=4-2t\end{aligned}\right.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186262696 :question/id #uuid "a6414901-e420-59fa-9f01-37ad745b6f9d" :question/math-academy-id "q-127048"} {:db/id 17592186262703 :question/id #uuid point $B(0,1).$" :question/worked-solution "The directional derivative ${f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)$ of a function $f(x,y)$ at the point $(a,b)$ in the direction of the vector $v$ is given by

$$
{f}_{u}^{′}(a,b)=∇f(a,b)\cdot u
$$

where $u$ is a unit vector in the direction of $v.$

First, we find the direction vector and the corresponding unit vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB} & =⟨0,1⟩-⟨1,0⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,1⟩ \\ u & =\frac{\overset{\to }{AB}}{‖\overset{\to }{AB}‖} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}}}⟨-1,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟨-1,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the gradient $∇f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $A(1,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{e}^{y}+{x}^{2}y),\,\frac{∂}{∂y}(x{e}^{y}+{x}^{2}y)⟩ \\  & =⟨{e}^{y}+2xy,\,x{e}^{y}+{x}^{2}⟩ \\ ∇\,f(1,0) & =⟨{e}^{0}+2\cdot 1\cdot 0,\,1\cdot {e}^{0}+{1}^{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the directional derivative is:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{u}^{′}(1,0) & =∇f(1,0)\cdot u \\  & =⟨1,\,2⟩\cdot ⟨-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}},\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}⟩ \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186354470 :question/id #uuid "f8f45df0-069c-5e4a-a4d7-bdd2e15f5467" :question/math-academy-id "q-86429"} {:db/id 17592186446241 :question/id #uuid the direction of the vector $v=⟨1,-\sqrt{2}⟩?$" :question/worked-solution "The rate of change of $g(x,y)$ at the point $(-1,1)$ in the direction of $v$ is equal to the directional derivative ${g}_{u}^{′}(-1,1).$ 

First, we find the unit vector $u$ in the direction of $v:$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖v‖ & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+(-\sqrt{2})^{2}}=\sqrt{3} \\ u & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨1,-\sqrt{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find the gradient $∇g(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $(-1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇g(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{x}{y}+\frac{y}{x}),\,\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{x}{y}+\frac{y}{x})⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{y}-\frac{y}{{x}^{2}},\,\frac{1}{x}-\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}⟩ \\ ∇g(-1,1) & =⟨\frac{1}{1}-\frac{1}{(-1)^{2}},\frac{1}{(-1)}-\frac{(-1)}{{1}^{2}}⟩ \\  & =⟨0,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the directional derivative ${g}_{u}^{′}(-1,1)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}_{u}^{′}(-1,1) & =∇g(-1,1)\cdot u \\  & =⟨0,0⟩\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨1,-\sqrt{2}⟩ \\  & =\frac{0(1)+0(-\sqrt{2})}{\sqrt{3}} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186323791 :question/id #uuid "a13cba05-5f4a-5d75-8f65-f72eb54e0d73" :question/math-academy-id "q-36300" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0f931965-4230-53c9-9c4e-51f593f9d015" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{10}" :db/id 17592186321267} {:answer/id #uuid "57f67efd-2b45-5e67-a5e4-4b0fd709ba1b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{8}" :db/id 17592186321837} {:answer/id #uuid "7b1a8d46-fbc3-5f92-8b69-6709f7023c5a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{80}" :db/id 17592186322114} {:answer/id #uuid "cda4641b-3880-5a2f-a60a-2d4b84c1090a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "9" :db/id 17592186322750} {:answer/id #uuid "d4216551-4828-50f1-870a-15d1ba740ddb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{82}" :db/id 17592186322802}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186322802} :answer-field/id #uuid "9e6c5b32-a96f-564b-b174-aa4099e65f9a" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186323476}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "Consider the function $f(x,y)=2xy+{e}^{3x-y}.$ What is the rate of change of $f(x,y)$ at the point $(1,3)$ in the direction in which the function decreases most rapidly?" :question/worked-solution "At a given point, a function $f(x,y)$ decreases most rapidly in the opposite direction of its gradient at that point.

In our case, we compute $-∇f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $(1,3):$

$$
\begin{aligned}-∇\,f(x,y) & =-\frac{∂}{∂x}(2xy+{e}^{3x-y})\text{ }i-\frac{∂}{∂y}(2xy+{e}^{3x-y})\text{ }j \\  & =-(2y+3{e}^{3x-y})\text{ }i-(2x-{e}^{3x-y})\text{ }j \\ -∇\,f(1,3) & =-(2\cdot 3+3\cdot {e}^{3\cdot 1-3})\text{ }i-(2\cdot 1-{e}^{3\cdot 1-3})\text{ }j \\  & =-9\text{ }i-\text{ }j\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the rate of change of $f(x,y)$ at the point $(1,3)$ in the direction of $-∇f(1,3)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}‖-∇\,f(1,3)‖ & =‖-9\text{ }i-\text{ }j‖ \\  & =\sqrt{(-9)^{2}+(-1)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{82}.\end{aligned}

In our case, we compute $-∇f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $(2,-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}-∇\,f(x,y) & =-\frac{∂}{∂x}((x+y)\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y))\text{ }i-\frac{∂}{∂y}((x+y)\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y))\text{ }j \\  & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)+1)\text{ }i+(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)+1)\text{ }j \\ -∇\,f(2,-1) & =-(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2-1)+1)i-(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2-1)+1)j \\  & =-i-j\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the rate of change of $f(x,y)$ at the point $(2,-1)$ in the direction of $-∇f(2,-1)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}‖-∇\,f(2,-1)‖ & =‖-i-j‖ \\  & =\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+(-1)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186351520 :question/id #uuid "e60c4cce-b8b4-5a37-8e5f-19c98e4b5e86" :question/math-academy-id "q-83608"} {:db/id 17592186351521 :question/id #uuid :question/problem "Consider the function $g(x,y)=\frac{{e}^{y}}{yx}.$ What is the rate of change of $g(x,y)$ at the point $(1,1)$ in the direction of the vector $v=⟨2,4⟩?$" :question/worked-solution "The rate of change of $g(x,y)$ at the point $(1,1)$ in the direction of $v$ is equal to the directional derivative ${g}_{u}^{′}(1,1).$ 

First, we find the unit vector $u$ in the direction of $v:$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖v‖ & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{4}^{2}}=\sqrt{20}=2\sqrt{5} \\ u & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{5}}⟨2,4⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}⟨1,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find the gradient $∇g(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $(1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇g(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{{e}^{y}}{yx}),\,\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{{e}^{y}}{yx})⟩ \\  & =⟨-\frac{{e}^{y}}{{x}^{2}y},\,\frac{{e}^{y}(y-1)}{x{y}^{2}}⟩ \\ ∇g(1,1) & =⟨-\frac{{e}^{1}}{{1}^{2}\cdot 1},\,\frac{{e}^{1}\cdot (1-1)}{1\cdot {1}^{2}}⟩ \\  & =⟨-e,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the directional derivative ${g}_{u}^{′}(1,1)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}_{u}^{′}(1,1) & =∇g(1,1)\cdot u \\  & =⟨-e,0⟩\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}⟨1,2⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}(-e\cdot 1+0\cdot 2) \\  & =-\frac{e}{\sqrt{5}} \\  & =-\frac{e\sqrt{5}}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186048413 :topic/encompasses [{:db/id 17592186428526 :encompassing/rationale "Initial Codex estimate from captured target-band crossing frequency. 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "Let $R=[5,6]\times [1,3]$ be a region in the $xy$-plane, and let $f(x,y)$ be a function defined over $R.$
The lower and upper Riemann sums corresponding to an arbitrary partition $P$ of $R$ are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}L(f,P) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}(2{x}_{i-1}-3{y}_{j})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}, \\ U(f,P) & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}(2{x}_{i}-3{y}_{j-1})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the definition of the double integral in terms of $L(f,P)$ and $U(f,P),$ compute ${∬}_{R}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A.$

*Hint: You may wish to make use of the following result:*

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({x}_{i-1}+{x}_{i})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}=({x}_{m}^{2}-{x}_{0}^{2})({y}_{n}-{y}_{0})\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "For a function $f(x,y),$ the double integral of $f$ over a rectangular region $R$ is the unique number $I$ (if it exists) such that

$$
L(f,P)\le I\le U(f,P)
$$

over all partitions $P$ of $R.$

First, notice that ${\overset{¯}{x}}_{i}=\frac{1}{2}({x}_{i-1}+{x}_{i})$ will always lie between ${x}_{i-1}$ and ${x}_{i}$, and similarly ${\overset{¯}{y}}_{j}=\frac{1}{2}({y}_{j-1}+{y}_{j})$ will always lie between ${y}_{j-1}$ and ${y}_{j}.$ Therefore,

$$
2{x}_{i-1}-3{y}_{j}\le 2\cdot \frac{1}{2}({x}_{i-1}+{x}_{i})-3\cdot \frac{1}{2}({y}_{j-1}+{y}_{j})\le 2{x}_{i}-3{y}_{j-1}
$$

which simplifies to

$$
2{x}_{i-1}-3{y}_{j}\le ({x}_{i-1}+{x}_{i})-\frac{3}{2}({y}_{j-1}+{y}_{j})\le 2{x}_{i}-3{y}_{j-1}.
$$

Multiplying this by $Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}$ and applying the double summation gives:

$$
L(f,P)\le {\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}[({x}_{i-1}+{x}_{i})-\frac{3}{2}({y}_{j-1}+{y}_{j})]Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}\le U(f,P)
$$

Separating the sums using the addition and constant multiple rules, we get

$$
L(f,P)\le {\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({x}_{i-1}+{x}_{i})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}-\frac{3}{2}{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({y}_{j-1}+{y}_{j})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j}\le U(f,P).
$$

Using the hint, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({x}_{i-1}+{x}_{i})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j} & =({6}^{2}-{5}^{2})(3-1)=22 \\ \frac{3}{2}{\sum }_{i=1}^{m}{\sum }_{j=1}^{n}({y}_{j-1}+{y}_{j})Δ{x}_{i}Δ{y}_{j} & =\frac{3}{2}({3}^{2}-{1}^{2})(6-5)=12\end{aligned}
$$

Finally then:

$$
\begin{aligned}L(f,P)\le 22-12\le U(f,P)\,⟹\,L(f,P)\le 10\le U(f,P)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that 

$$
{∬}_{R}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A=10.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186371686 :question/id #uuid "e22927a0-203d-5f08-b005-006aad6d8afd" :question/math-academy-id "q-123859"} {:db/id 17592186544806 :question/id #uuid :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "![](images/bc/bc3809e55e601738d56be6885475ed442dec1fb3a0d2e19da14be045510f73dc.png)

The above scatter plot shows the relationship between age and years of experience of a group of professional soccer players. 

Given that none of the points overlap, which of the following statements are true?

I. Only one player has exactly $10$ years of experience.

II. There are two players aged $21.$

III. None of the players has fewer than $6$ years of experience.

Select all that apply." :question/worked-solution "Let's examine our scatter plot.

- Statement I is true. The scatter plot has only one dot whose vertical coordinate equals $10,$ namely, $(21,10).$ This means only one of the players has exactly $10$ years of experience.

![](images/20/209759f5d70fd8587740d1da840f9da838a3c9a055a0d1e962f76c1cd6341fd3.png)

- Statement II is true. The scatter plot has two dots whose horizontal coordinate equals $21,$ namely, $(21,10)$ and $(21,12).$ This means that two players are $21$ years old.

![](images/75/753c503d6751363b1c7d2dc449f1c5f11baec159b1e938e8c807938512111750.png)

- Statement III is false. From the scatter plot, one player has fewer than $6$ years of experience. The dot below the horizontal line represents this player.

![](images/66/66facd1a0683f420aa2ac3d7bfd54290bdb009850bc66cc7523ee569ec81daea.png)

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only.""} {:db/id 17592186268966 :question/id #uuid "7b463b24-e0d7-56c4-b957-08fba1ac548b" :question/math-academy-id "q-134105"} {:db/id 17592186268967 $$
\text{E}[\overset{―}{X}]=\mu ,\,\text{Var}[\overset{―}{X}]=\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n},
$$

and the standard error is given by

$$
\text{SE}[\overset{―}{X}]=\sqrt{\text{Var}[\overset{―}{X}]}=\frac{\sigma }{\sqrt{n}}.
$$

We're told that the nails in the population have lengths $5\,\text{cm}$ and $\text{10}\,\text{cm},$ and these are distributed in the ratio $4:1.$ Therefore, to compute the population mean and variance, we can consider a population consisting of $4+1=5$ nails only with the following lengths:

$$
5\,\text{cm},\,5\,\text{cm},\,5\,\text{cm},\,5\,\text{cm}\,10\,\text{cm}.
$$

Therefore, the population mean is

$$
\begin{aligned}\mu  & =\frac{1}{5}{\sum }_{i}{x}_{i} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}(4\cdot 5+10) \\  & =\frac{1}{5}(20+10) \\  & =\frac{30}{5} \\  & =6\,\text{cm},\end{aligned}
$$

and the population variance is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }^{2} & =\frac{1}{5}{\sum }_{i}{x}_{i}^{2}-{\mu }^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}(4\cdot {5}^{2}+{10}^{2})-{6}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}(200)-36 \\  & =40-36 \\  & =4\,{\text{cm}}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the sample size $n=3,$ we have

$$
\text{Var}[\overset{―}{X}]=\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n}=\frac{4}{3}\,{\text{cm}}^{2}.
$$

Finally,

$$
\text{SE}[\overset{―}{X}]=\sqrt{\frac{4}{3}}≈1.15\,\text{cm}
$$

Since the sample size is $n=4,$ we have

$$
\text{E}[\overset{―}{X}]=\mu ,\,\text{Var}[\overset{―}{X}]=\frac{{\sigma }^{2}}{n},
$$

and the standard error is given by

$$
\text{SE}[\overset{―}{X}]=\sqrt{\text{Var}[\overset{―}{X}]}=\frac{\sigma }{\sqrt{n}}.
$$

We're told that the employees in the population have working hours $38\,\text{h/week}$ and $40\,\text{h/week},$ and these are distributed in the ratio $3:1.$ Therefore, to compute the population's mean and variance, we can consider a population consisting of $3+1=4$ employees only with the following working hours:

$$
38\,\text{h/week},\,38\,\text{h/week},\,38\,\text{h/week},\,40\,\text{h/week}.
$$

Therefore, the population mean is

$$
\begin{aligned}\mu  & =\frac{1}{4}{\sum }_{i}{x}_{i} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(3\cdot 38+40) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(114+40) \\  & =\frac{154}{4} \\  & =38.5\,\text{h/week},\end{aligned}
$$

and the population variance is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }^{2} & =\frac{1}{4}{\sum }_{i}{x}_{i}^{2}-{\mu }^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(3\cdot {38}^{2}+{40}^{2})-{38.5}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(5\,932)-1\,482.25 \\  & =1\,483-1\,482.25 \\  & =0.75\,{(\text{h/week})}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the population standard deviation is $\sigma =\sqrt{0.75},$ and we have that 

$$
\text{SE}[\overset{―}{X}]=\sqrt{\frac{0.75}{n}}.
$$

We require that the standard error is less than $0.5\,\text{h/week}.$ Therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{\frac{0.75}{n}} & <0.5 \\ \sqrt{n} & >\frac{\sqrt{0.75}}{0.5} \\ \sqrt{n} & >\sqrt{\frac{0.75}{{0.5}^{2}}} \\ \sqrt{n} & >\sqrt{\frac{0.75}{0.25}} \\ \sqrt{n} & >\sqrt{3} \\ n & >3.\end{aligned}
$$

A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -10 & 4 \\ -3 & 2 & -6 \\ -2 & 5 & -2\end{bmatrix}
$$

$$
B=\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 0 & 0 \\ 3 & -13 & 0 \\ -2 & 5 & -2\end{bmatrix}
$$

By applying elementary row operations of the form ${R}_{i}:={R}_{i}+k{R}_{3},$ the matrix $A$ can be transformed into the matrix $B.$ What are the elementary row operations?" :question/worked-solution "To transform $A$ into $B,$ we need to make the entries above ${a}_{33}=-2$ equal to $0.$

To do this, we can apply the following elementary row operations:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -10 & 4 \\ -3 & 2 & -6 \\ -2 & 5 & -2\end{bmatrix} &  & \,\begin{aligned}{R}_{1}: &={R}_{1}+2{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 0 & 0 \\ -3 & 2 & -6 \\ -2 & 5 & -2\end{bmatrix} &  & \,\begin{aligned}{R}_{2}: &={R}_{2}-3{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 0 & 0 \\ 3 & -13 & 0 \\ -2 & 5 & -2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =B\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the elementary row operations are

$\,$ ${R}_{1}:={R}_{1}+2{R}_{3}\,$ and $\,{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}-3{R}_{3}.$"} {:db/id 17592186404517 :question/id #uuid "26e3c3e9-0f2f-55d8-b677-4d51648ddadf" :question/math-academy-id "q-91159"} {:db/id <p></p></th></tr></tbody></table>" :question/worked-solution "Two discrete random variables $X$ and $Y$ with joint probability mass function $f(x,y)$ are independent if and only if 

$$
f(x,y)={f}_{X}(x)\cdot {f}_{Y}(y)
$$

 

for all possible values $x$ and $y,$ where ${f}_{X}(x)$ and ${f}_{Y}(y)$ are the marginal probability mass functions for $X$ and $Y,$ respectively.

Therefore, since our discrete random variables are independent, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(4,3) & ={f}_{X}(4)\cdot {f}_{Y}(3) \\  & =0.2\cdot 0.15 \\  & =0.03.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186426031 :question/id #uuid "651363c2-d60f-536f-b27c-718f157b1a2e" :question/math-academy-id "q-143322"} {:db/id 17592186426032 :question/id #uuid to $1[5\in B]?$" :question/worked-solution "The indicator function $1[P]$ equals $1$ if the predicate $P$ is true and $0$ if $P$ is false.

$$
1[P]=\{\begin{aligned}1, & \text{if }P\text{ is true}, \\ 0, & \text{if }P\text{ is false}.\end{aligned}
$$

Recall that the indicator function ${1}_{A}(x)$ of a set $A$ equals $1$ if $x\in A$ and $0$ if $x\notin A.$ This can be written using Iverson bracket notation as

$$
{1}_{A}(x)=1[x\in A].
$$

Here, the Iverson bracket expression $1[5\in B]$ has $x=5$ and $A=B.$ Therefore, converting back to set indicator notation, we have

$$
1[5\in B]={1}_{B}(5).
$$"} {:db/id 17592186521491 :question/id #uuid "45172067-6fd8-53b2-8b3e-3767eb3b99d5" :question/math-academy-id "q-346661"} {:db/id 17592186521492 :question/id #uuid "4946e8ca-eef4-5bca-ab77-2e318993cb3a" :question/math-academy-id "q-346664"} {:db/id 17592186521551 :question/id #uuid "d217e754-13bb-55c1-bf52-1609c0455dd0" :question/math-academy-id "q-351127"} {:db/id 17592186521564 :question/id #uuid "e8d6c64e-e665-50e4-b8dc-09f085134af3" :question/math-academy-id "q-351130"} {:db/id 17592186521566 :question/id #uuid "ee0e20b3-c728-5a30-b95b-8f191603cec6" :question/math-academy-id "q-351129"} {:db/id 17592186554590 :question/id #uuid "7ecead24-f472-509d-9b09-182eae6554e7" :question/math-academy-id "q-346663" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "34d52dde-78fc-56d2-a22f-16743942f394" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1[\{0,5,10\}\in 7]" :db/id 17592186553963} {:answer/id #uuid "3e5a4ce9-38a3-50c2-ab37-2b31fa255565" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1[7=D]" :db/id 17592186553982} {:answer/id #uuid "3f98e784-15fe-5da6-bf43-5d7bde990e34" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1[D\in \{0,5,10\}]" :db/id 17592186553984} {:answer/id #uuid "929abffe-450c-5006-a4e0-9188f9b6910d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1[7\in \{0,5,10\}]" :db/id 17592186554193} {:answer/id #uuid "caeec9e3-866d-5050-ab7c-4b6736d7497b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1[7\notin \{0,5,10\}]" :db/id 17592186554316}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186554193} :answer-field/id #uuid "cd8b1eb9-905f-5eaa-b94d-45d4a5b08f18" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186554515}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "Let $D=\{0,5,10\}.$ Which of the following is equivalent to ${1}_{D}(7)?$" :question/worked-solution "The indicator function $1[P]$ equals $1$ if the predicate $P$ is true and $0$ if $P$ is false.

$$
1[P]=\{\begin{aligned}1, & \text{if }P\text{ is true}, \\ 0, & \text{if }P\text{ is false}.\end{aligned}
$$

For $x=-5,$ we evaluate each indicator function:

- $1[x\ge 0]=1[-5\ge 0]=0$ (since $-5\ge 0$ is false)

- $1[-3\le x<0]=1[-3\le -5<0]=0$ (since $-3\le -5$ is false)

- $1[x<-3]=1[-5<-3]=1$ (since $-5<-3$ is true)

Substituting into the expression for $p(x),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}p(-5) & =0\cdot 25+0\cdot 1+1\cdot (-2(-5)) \\  & =10.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that the indicator functions act as a "switch": since $x=-5<-3,$ only the third term contributes to the result."} {:db/id 17592186521515 :question/id #uuid "7ce60c02-eb25-536f-a376-c9d5685f21ea" :question/math-academy-id "q-347932"} {:db/id 17592186521549 :question/id #uuid "cde00f71-de2d-5ff7-ae71-1ddcfa0a1b1f" :question/math-academy-id "q-347433"} {:db/id 17592186521550 :question/id #uuid "ce2c0db9-ad0b-5196-91d2-2f4a888aa062" :question/math-academy-id "q-346669"} {:db/id 17592186521559 :question/id #uuid "e022df96-ab83-5f54-81a6-300069e7bfc3" :question/math-academy-id "q-346680"} {:db/id 17592186521570 :question/id #uuid "f9506abb-49a9-5357-8f1d-b8154670131b" :question/math-academy-id "q-346673"} {:db/id 17592186554626 :question/id #uuid "e3d61585-203e-5ae2-ba7d-32b154b3cecc" :question/math-academy-id "q-347438" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "dd697bf3-bab3-5be7-93b9-af592dc078ba" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "24" :db/id 17592186554352}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186554352} :answer-field/id #uuid "edb32b44-fa3a-53b5-9c67-b4cbe35e057e" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186554530}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "$$
{x}_{1}=-6,\,{x}_{2}=-1,\,{x}_{3}=0,\,{x}_{4}=4,\,{x}_{5}=7
$$

$$
1[P]=\{\begin{aligned}1, & \text{if }P\text{ is true}, \\ 0, & \text{if }P\text{ is false}.\end{aligned}
$$

The expression $1[{x}_{i}\ge 0]\cdot (2{x}_{i})+1[{x}_{i}<0]\cdot 1$ equals $2{x}_{i}$ when ${x}_{i}\ge 0$ and equals $1$ when ${x}_{i}<0.$ Thus, the sum

$$
{\sum }_{i=1}^{5}1[{x}_{i}\ge 0]\cdot (2{x}_{i})+1[{x}_{i}<0]\cdot 1
$$

adds $2{x}_{i}$ for nonnegative values and $1$ for negative values.

We evaluate the indicator function for each ${x}_{i}:$

- $1[{x}_{1}\ge 0]=1[-6\ge 0]=0,$ $1[{x}_{1}<0]=1$

- $1[{x}_{2}\ge 0]=1[-1\ge 0]=0,$ $1[{x}_{2}<0]=1$

- $1[{x}_{3}\ge 0]=1[0\ge 0]=1,$ $1[{x}_{3}<0]=0$

- $1[{x}_{4}\ge 0]=1[4\ge 0]=1,$ $1[{x}_{4}<0]=0$

- $1[{x}_{5}\ge 0]=1[7\ge 0]=1,$ $1[{x}_{5}<0]=0$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{5}1[{x}_{i}\ge 0]\cdot (2{x}_{i})+1[{x}_{i}<0]\cdot 1 & =1+1+2\cdot 0+2\cdot 4+2\cdot 7 \\  & =1+1+0+8+14 \\  & =24.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186554636 :question/id #uuid "f030361e-8a29-5e63-bca8-4e28e1ba5da0" :question/math-academy-id "q-346677" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "156a71be-c9a4-5ae7-9a2c-02e2f98c3a59" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "15" :db/id 17592186553911}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186553911} :answer-field/id #uuid "034b7137-7dce-507f-82b0-3f725c6f8c4a" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186554429}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "$$

{\sum }_{i=1}^{5}1[{x}_{i}>0]\cdot {x}_{i}

- $1[{x}_{5}>0]=1[2>0]=1$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{i=1}^{5}1[{x}_{i}>0]\cdot {x}_{i} & =1\cdot 9+0\cdot (-8)+0\cdot (-1)+1\cdot 4+1\cdot 2 \\  & =9+0+0+4+2 \\  & =15.\end{aligned}

"Using the cumulative distribution function table of the Poisson random variable $X∼\text{Po}(11)$ given below, compute $P(X<10).$

| $\,x\,$ | $7$ | $8$ | $9$ | $10$ | $11$ | $12$ | $13$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $P(X\le x)$ | $\,0.1432\,$ | $\,0.2320\,$ | $\,0.3405\,$ | $\,0.4599\,$ | $\,0.5793\,$ | $\,0.6887\,$ | $\,0.7813\,$ |" :question/worked-solution "The cumulative distribution function of a discrete random variable $X$ is a function $F(x)$ such that

$$
F(x)=P(X\le x).
$$

Therefore, we have

P(X>a)=1-P(X\le a)=1-F(a).

$$
P(X\ge 7)=P(X>6).

:answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186549819}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "The disjoint union ${A}_{1}⊔{A}_{2}⊔{A}_{3}⊔{A}_{4}$ of events ${A}_{1},{A}_{2},{A}_{3},{A}_{4}$ covers the entire sample space. Compute $P({A}_{2}|B)$ given the following probabilities:

$$
\begin{aligned} & P(B|{A}_{1})=0.25, & P({A}_{1})=0.28 \\  & P(B|{A}_{2})=0.3, &  \\  & P(B|{A}_{3})=0.28, & P({A}_{3})=0.18 \\  & P(B|{A}_{4})=0.1, & P({A}_{4})=0.22\end{aligned}
$$

Round your answer to $3$ decimal places." :question/worked-solution "If the disjoint union ${A}_{1}⊔{A}_{2}⊔…⊔{A}_{n}$ covers the entire sample space, Bayes' theorem combined with the law of total probability gives us the following:

$$
P({A}_{k}|B)=\frac{P(B|{A}_{k})P({A}_{k})}{P(B)}=\frac{P(B|{A}_{k})P({A}_{k})}{{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}P(B|{A}_{i})P({A}_{i})}
$$

where $k=1,2,…,n.$

In our case, $n=4,$ and ${A}_{1}⊔{A}_{2}⊔{A}_{3}⊔{A}_{4}$ covers the entire sample space. Consequently, we have

$$
P({A}_{1})+P({A}_{2})+P({A}_{3})+P({A}_{4})=1.
$$

As a result,

$$
\begin{aligned}P({A}_{2}) & =1-(P({A}_{1})+P({A}_{3})+P({A}_{4})) \\  & =1-(0.28+0.18+0.22) \\  & =0.32.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P({A}_{2}|B) & =\frac{P(B|{A}_{2})P({A}_{2})}{{\sum }_{i=1}^{4}P(B|{A}_{i})P({A}_{i})} \\  & =\frac{P(B|{A}_{2})P({A}_{2})}{P(B|{A}_{1})P({A}_{1})+P(B|{A}_{2})P({A}_{2})+P(B|{A}_{3})P({A}_{3})+P(B|{A}_{4})P({A}_{4})} \\  & =\frac{(0.3)(0.32)}{(0.25)(0.28)+(0.3)(0.32)+(0.28)(0.18)+(0.1)(0.22)} \\  & =\frac{0.096}{0.2384} \\  & ≈0.403.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186166848 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186166698 :question/id #uuid "284f5029-19eb-53d4-a3b7-0f66d33b9cc9" :question/math-academy-id "e-8912"} :knowledge-point/id split among three classes, class $1,$ class $2,$ and class $3.$

- Class $1$ contains $25%$ of the students in the school, and $55%$ of those students take biology.

- Class $2$ contains $35%$ of the students in the school, and $40%$ of those students take biology.

- Class $3$ contains $40%$ of the students in the school.

If $45%$ of students in the entire school are female, $80%$ of female students take biology, and $70%$ of biology students are female, what is the probability that a randomly selected student from class $3$ takes biology? Round your answer to $3$ decimal places." :question/requires-calculator true :question/worked-solution "Let $F$ be the event that a student is female, $B$ be the event that a student takes biology, and ${C}_{1},{C}_{2},{C}_{3}$ be the event that a student is in class $1,$ $2,$ or $3,$ respectively. 

Let's break down the information given in the problem statement:

- From the bullet points, we have the following information:

$$
\begin{aligned} & P({C}_{1})=0.25 &  & P(B|{C}_{1})=0.55 \\  & P({C}_{2})=0.35 &  & P(B|{C}_{2})=0.4 \\  & P({C}_{3})=0.4\end{aligned}
$$

The disjoint union ${C}_{1}⊔{C}_{2}⊔{C}_{3}$ covers the entire sample space, and we have

$$
P({C}_{1})+P({C}_{2})+P({C}_{3})=0.25+0.35+0.4=1.
$$

- Since $45%$ of students in the entire school are female, we have

$$
P(F)=0.45.
$$

- Since $80%$ of females take biology, we have

$$
P(B|F)=0.8.
$$

- Since $70%$ of biology students are female, we have

$$
P(F|B)=0.7.
$$

We want to find the probability that a randomly chosen student from class $3$ takes biology, which is represented as $P(B|{C}_{3}).$ 

Using Bayes' theorem combined with the law of total probability, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(F|B) & =\frac{P(B|F)P(F)}{P(B)} \\ P(F|B) & =\frac{P(B|F)P(F)}{P(B|{C}_{1})P({C}_{1})+P(B|{C}_{2})P({C}_{2})+P(B|{C}_{3})P({C}_{3})} \\ 0.7 & =\frac{(0.8)(0.45)}{(0.55)(0.25)+(0.4)(0.35)+P(B|{C}_{3})(0.4)} \\ 0.7 & =\frac{0.36}{0.2775+0.4P(B|{C}_{3})}.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this equation for $P(B|{C}_{3}),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}0.7(0.2775+0.4P(B|{C}_{3})) & =0.36 \\ 0.2775+0.4P(B|{C}_{3}) & =\frac{0.36}{0.7} \\ 0.2775+0.4P(B|{C}_{3}) & =\frac{18}{35} \\ 0.4P(B|{C}_{3}) & =\frac{18}{35}-0.2775 \\ P(B|{C}_{3}) & =\frac{1}{0.4}(\frac{18}{35}-0.2775) \\ P(B|{C}_{3}) & ≈0.592\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to three decimal places."} {:db/id 17592186167119 :question/id #uuid "5b92de6f-2dd5-5916-8078-94243b8290b0" :question/math-academy-id "q-148674"} {:db/id 17592186275200 :question/id #uuid "cbae7601-74f3-53d4-af26-b2c79a262289" :question/math-academy-id "q-148669" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186166848 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "3a4fee2d-88c3-5381-bd55-98990abc7df3" :knowledge-point/title "Solving for an Unknown Conditional Probability"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "55719c9a-dcbc-577a-8d18-ef15b0b142fc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0.923" :db/id 17592186273114} {:answer/id #uuid "5c2b6301-9863-588c-afcf-a1135853ff30" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0.872" :db/id 17592186273178} {:answer/id #uuid "afce45e8-dac9-5cec-af05-43e0ae761b82" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0.943" :db/id 17592186273907} {:answer/id #uuid "b30dcdf1-6ef0-5b34-9ff8-48cae2cd50c4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0.664" :db/id 17592186273933} {:answer/id #uuid "d2736c69-c89a-5244-a3d8-660d1d7a9be2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0.885" :db/id 17592186274228}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "b30dcdf1-6ef0-5b34-9ff8-48cae2cd50c4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "0.664" :db/id 17592186273933} :answer-field/id #uuid "c2759a57-ee5d-532e-a24f-4499af67035f" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186274975}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "A local newspaper is sold by three distributors, $1,$ $2,$ and $3.$

- Distributor $1$ gets $36%$ of the copies.

- Distributor $2$ gets $23%$ of the copies, and $92%$ of those copies are sold.

- Distributor $3$ gets $41%$ of the copies, and $95%$ of those copies are sold.

If $3%$ of all copies have some printing defect, $70%$ of defective copies are sold, and $2.5%$ of sold copies are defective, what is the probability that a randomly chosen copy bought by distributor $1$ is sold? Round your answer to $3$ decimal places." :question/worked-solution "Let $R$ be the event that a copy has a printing defect, $S$ be the event that a copy is sold, and ${D}_{1},{D}_{2},{D}_{3}$ be the event that a copy is given to distributor $1,$ $2,$ or $3,$ respectively.

Let's break down the information given in the problem statement:

- From the bullet points, we have the following information:

$$
\begin{aligned} & P({D}_{1})=0.36 \\  & P({D}_{2})=0.23 &  & P(S|{D}_{2})=0.92 \\  & P({D}_{3})=0.41 &  & P(S|{D}_{3})=0.95\end{aligned}
$$

The disjoint union ${D}_{1}⊔{D}_{2}⊔{D}_{3}$ covers the entire sample space, and we have

$$
P({D}_{1})+P({D}_{2})+P({D}_{3})=0.36+0.23+0.41=1.
$$

- Since $3%$ of all copies has some printing defect, we have

$$
P(R)=0.03.
$$

- Since $70%$ of defective copies are sold, we have

$$
P(S|R)=0.7.
$$

- Since $2.5%$ of sold copies are defective, we have

$$
P(R|S)=0.025.
$$

We want to find the probability that a randomly chosen copy bought by distributor $1$ is sold, which is represented as $P(S|{D}_{1}).$ 

Using Bayes' theorem combined with the law of total probability, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(R|S) & =\frac{P(S|R)P(R)}{P(S)} \\ P(R|S) & =\frac{P(S|R)P(R)}{P(S|{D}_{1})P({D}_{1})+P(S|{D}_{2})P({D}_{2})+P(S|{D}_{3})P({D}_{3})} \\ 0.025 & =\frac{(0.7)(0.03)}{P(S|{D}_{1})(0.36)+(0.92)(0.23)+(0.95)(0.41)} \\ 0.025 & =\frac{0.021}{0.36P(S|{D}_{1})+0.6011}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this equation for $P(S|{D}_{1}),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}0.025(0.36P(S|{D}_{1})+0.6011) & =0.021 \\ 0.36P(S|{D}_{1})+0.6011 & =\frac{0.021}{0.025} \\ 0.36P(S|{D}_{1})+0.6011 & =\frac{21}{25} \\ 0.36P(S|{D}_{1}) & =\frac{21}{25}-0.6011 \\ P(S|{D}_{1}) & =\frac{1}{0.36}(\frac{21}{25}-0.6011) \\ P(S|{D}_{1}) & ≈0.664\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to three decimal places."} {:db/id 17592186487319 :question/id #uuid "42158c74-7958-54df-8e89-80fc77114095" :question/math-academy-id "q-148270"} {:db/id 17592186487354 :question/id #uuid "9b22d29b-922e-508b-b541-5acf3087f769" :question/math-academy-id "q-148523"} {:db/id 17592186487355 :question/id #uuid "9c74ed7c-bf09-54d6-a2a8-5c3ba0194b49" :question/math-academy-id "q-170685"} {:db/id 17592186487367 :question/id #uuid "ad4190f4-bdf3-5375-9c0a-f6bde72a3f1c" :question/math-academy-id "q-148273"} {:db/id 17592186487403 :question/id #uuid "fa54d1c3-840f-55dc-9c9a-7cb1c9435baf" :question/math-academy-id "q-159358"} {:db/id 17592186493912 :question/id #uuid "39f657eb-aa97-5394-b0e6-ecba3bf80018" :question/math-academy-id "q-148666" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "08123d50-e1d2-5e75-87c8-dc4ecec898fa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.05" :db/id 17592186493402} {:answer/id #uuid "2315c5ef-ec06-536c-af7c-d82e621541c3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.03" :db/id 17592186493448} {:answer/id #uuid "68e491ab-da9f-5329-9aaa-a11a1bebb3d6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.047" :db/id 17592186493547} {:answer/id #uuid "75ac382e-a141-5c83-ade6-7dc3a4ffc925" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.035" :db/id 17592186493566} {:answer/id #uuid "e67f42bf-f74e-5283-955d-76c3d0573b19" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.040" :db/id 17592186493760}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186493760} :answer-field/id #uuid "f3f4b001-3f5d-563e-a82a-efaf92b09aad" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186493885}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "A manufacturing company has three sites, factory $1,$ factory $2,$ and factory $3.$ They all produce two types of light bulbs: A and B.

- Factory $2$ produces $45%$ of the entire production.

- Factory $3$ produces $10%$ of the entire production, and $1%$ of those bulbs are defective.

Round your answer to $3$ decimal places." :question/worked-solution "Let $A$ be the event that a light bulb is of type A, $D$ be the event that a light bulb is defective, and ${F}_{1},{F}_{2},{F}_{3}$ be the event that a light bulb is produced in factory $1,$ $2,$ or $3,$ respectively. 

Let's break down the information given in the problem statement:

- From the bullet points, we have the following information:

$$
\begin{aligned} & P({F}_{1})=0.45 &  & P(D|{F}_{1})=0.05 \\  & P({F}_{2})=0.45 \\  & P({F}_{3})=0.1 &  & P(D|{F}_{3})=0.01\end{aligned}
$$

The disjoint union ${F}_{1}⊔{F}_{2}⊔{F}_{3}$ covers the entire sample space, and we have

$$
P({F}_{1})+P({F}_{2})+P({F}_{3})=0.45+0.45+0.1=1.
$$

- Since $57%$ of all light bulbs are of type A, we have

$$
P(A)=0.57.
$$

- Since $3%$ of type A light bulbs are defective, we have

$$
P(D|A)=0.03.
$$

- Since $41%$ of defective light bulbs are of type A, we have

$$
P(A|D)=0.41
$$

We want to find the probability that a randomly chosen light bulb from factory $2$ is defective, which is represented as $P(D|{F}_{2}).$ 

Using Bayes' theorem combined with the law of total probability, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(A|D) & =\frac{P(D|A)P(A)}{P(D)} \\ P(A|D) & =\frac{P(D|A)P(A)}{P(D|{F}_{1})P({F}_{1})+P(D|{F}_{2})P({F}_{2})+P(D|{F}_{3})P({F}_{3})} \\ 0.41 & =\frac{(0.03)(0.57)}{(0.05)(0.45)+P(D|{F}_{2})(0.45)+(0.01)(0.1)} \\ 0.41 & =\frac{0.0171}{0.0235+0.45P(D|{F}_{2})}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this equation for $P(D|{F}_{2}),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}0.41(0.0235+0.45P(D|{F}_{2})) & =0.0171 \\ 0.0235+0.45P(D|{F}_{2}) & =\frac{0.0171}{0.41} \\ 0.0235+0.45P(D|{F}_{2}) & =\frac{171}{4100} \\ 0.45P(D|{F}_{2}) & =\frac{171}{4100}-0.0235 \\ P(D|{F}_{2}) & =\frac{1}{0.45}(\frac{171}{4100}-0.0235) \\ P(D|{F}_{2}) & ≈0.040\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to three decimal places."} {:db/id 17592186493967 :question/id #uuid "deb0627a-b1f4-5ecd-95e2-372ffa642f2c" :question/math-academy-id "q-149493" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "aad9a2ec-8c38-50c5-a148-e148cf1a201f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.307" :db/id 17592186493659} {:answer/id #uuid "cb08ac4c-bcdb-5bf3-803d-48abd3c44b23" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.546" :db/id 17592186493717} {:answer/id #uuid "db3514aa-7da2-58cd-a765-4883b4c73d8a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.135" :db/id 17592186493736} {:answer/id #uuid "e44bfd71-59f5-5456-8e29-b331fc4b994f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.398" :db/id 17592186493751} {:answer/id #uuid "e5ca70ca-440e-5d09-bd91-1a12c84d2bf9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.252" :db/id 17592186493758}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186493751} :answer-field/id #uuid "b2b5eda7-fc54-5354-9c43-01751b2546c8" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186493866}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "A volleyball school for children splits the players into three teams, team $1$, team $2,$ and team $3.$ 

- $44%$ of children are in team $1,$ and $23%$ of children in this team have been playing for over two years.

- $32%$ of children are in team $2,$ and $26%$ of children in this team have been playing for over two years.

- $24%$ of children are in team $3.$

If $7%$ of all children can play in the blocker position, $40%$ of children who can play as blockers have been playing for over two years, and $10%$ of children who have been playing for over two years can play as blockers, what is the probability that a randomly chosen child in team $3$ has been playing for over two years? Round your answer to $3$ decimal places." :question/worked-solution "Let $B$ be the event that a child can play in the blocker position, $I$ be the event that a child has been playing for over two years, and ${T}_{1},{T}_{2},{T}_{3}$ be the events that a child is in team $1,$ $2,$ or $3,$ respectively. 

Let's break down the information given in the problem statement:

- From the bullet points, we have the following information:

$$
\begin{aligned} & P({T}_{1})=0.44 &  & P(I|{T}_{1})=0.23 \\  & P({T}_{2})=0.32 &  & P(I|{T}_{2})=0.26 \\  & P({T}_{3})=0.24\end{aligned}
$$

The disjoint union ${T}_{1}⊔{T}_{2}⊔{T}_{3}$ covers the entire sample space, and we have

$$
P({T}_{1})+P({T}_{2})+P({T}_{3})=0.44+0.32+0.24=1.
$$

- Since $7%$ of children can play in the blocker position, we have

$$
P(B)=0.07.
$$

- Since $40%$ of children who can play as blockers have been playing for over two years, we have

$$
P(I|B)=0.4.
$$

- Since $10%$ of children who have been playing for over two years can play as blockers, we have

$$
P(B|I)=0.1.
$$

We want to find the probability that a randomly chosen child in team 3 has been playing for over two years, which is represented as $P(I|{T}_{3}).$

Using Bayes' theorem combined with the law of total probability, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(B|I) & =\frac{P(I|B)P(B)}{P(I)} \\ P(B|I) & =\frac{P(I|B)P(B)}{P(I|{T}_{1})P({T}_{1})+P(I|{T}_{2})P({T}_{2})+P(I|{T}_{3})P({T}_{3})} \\ 0.1 & =\frac{(0.4)(0.07)}{(0.23)(0.44)+(0.26)(0.32)+P(I|{T}_{3})(0.24)} \\ 0.1 & =\frac{0.028}{0.1844+0.24P(I|{T}_{3})}.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this equation for $P(I|{T}_{3}),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}0.1(0.1844+0.24P(I|{T}_{3})) & =0.028 \\ 0.1844+0.24P(I|{T}_{3}) & =\frac{0.028}{0.1} \\ 0.1844+0.24P(I|{T}_{3}) & =\frac{7}{25} \\ 0.24P(I|{T}_{3}) & =\frac{7}{25}-0.1844 \\ P(I|{T}_{3}) & =\frac{1}{0.24}(\frac{7}{25}-0.1844) \\ P(I|{T}_{3}) & ≈0.398\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to three decimal places."} {:db/id 17592186549938 :question/id #uuid "1787d264-9d95-57d2-8330-7eec4c052cfe" :question/math-academy-id "q-148271" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "50e9c58b-4fb9-5497-9482-e8f285727015" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.055" :db/id 17592186549479} {:answer/id #uuid "5b9c5c15-f6a2-5b4a-a895-22168d05307d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.095" :db/id 17592186549499} {:answer/id #uuid "8a26048a-fd81-56ee-8af6-bd08ebb325b0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.047" :db/id 17592186549578} {:answer/id #uuid "a2ac414e-15b9-5ce9-93e3-a7f2a6d829da" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.019" :db/id 17592186549625} {:answer/id #uuid "c97eb869-625e-551f-be3b-c0ff2ec27876" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.028" :db/id 17592186549690}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186549690} :answer-field/id #uuid "2d9e6faf-9e8f-5d9c-aa84-79845b127ed4" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186549823}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "A medical center is investigating the correlation between scoliosis and sports practice in a sample of children.
