$$
T:u⟶Au+b,
$$

where $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix and $u$ and $b$ are $2\times 1$ column vectors, we have one of the following three possibilities:

- If $T$ is non-singular, i.e., when $det(A)\ne 0,$ then the image of a two-dimensional object is a two-dimensional object. In particular, the image of a polygon with $n$ vertices is a polygon with $n$ vertices.

- If $T$ is singular, i.e., when $det(A)=0,$ we have two additional subcases:

- If $A$ has at least one nonzero entry, then the image of a two-dimensional object is a one-dimensional line segment.

- If $A$ is the zero matrix, then the image of a two-dimensional object is a point on the plane.

With that in mind, let's examine our transformation.

Notice that the matrix representation of the linear transformation associated with $T$ is 
$A=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 2 \\ -4 & 8\end{bmatrix}.$

Computing the determinant of $A,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}det(T) & =\begin{vmatrix}-1 & 2 \\ -4 & 8\end{vmatrix} \\  & =(-1)\cdot 8-(-4)\cdot 2 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a singular nonzero matrix.

17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "e92cb69b-a679-593b-8882-9cab8d26a8fb" :question/math-academy-id "q-124289" :question/problem "The affine transformation $T$ is defined as

$$
x=u-v-1,\,y=3v-2u-6.
$$

Given that the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ of $T$ is

$$
u=ax+y+9,\,v=bx+y+c,
$$

what is the value of $a+b+c?$" :question/worked-solution "An affine transformation $T:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2}$ is a function of the form

$$
x=Au+b,
$$

where $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Reversing the action of $T,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}Au+b & =x \\ Au & =x-b \\ u & ={A}^{-1}(x-b).\end{aligned}
$$

So, writing our transformation in matrix form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}u-v-1 \\ 3v-2u-6\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}u-v \\ -2u+3v\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ -6\end{bmatrix} \\  & ={{\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ -2 & 3\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ -6\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we calculate the inverse of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{3\cdot 1-(-1)\cdot (-2)}\begin{bmatrix}3 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{{\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{u} & ={{\begin{bmatrix}3 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{A}^{-1}}\cdot ({{\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{x}-{{\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ -6\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{b}) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x+1 \\ y+6\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3\cdot (x+1)+1\cdot (y+6) \\ 2\cdot (x+1)+1\cdot (y+6)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3x+y+9 \\ 2x+y+8\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding components, the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ in coordinate form is

$$
u=3x+y+9,\,v=2x+y+8.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a+b+c=3+2+8=13.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "b7332e33-ee2f-5908-9f85-c258b5d80b5d" :step/next {:db/id 17592186406972}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3f998697-e815-585e-b0b5-3820b9ab9a03" :answer/type {:db/id $$
\begin{aligned}Au+b & =x \\ Au & =x-b \\ u & ={A}^{-1}(x-b).\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}2u-3v+2 \\ 6v-3u-4\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2u-3v \\ -3u+6v\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -4\end{bmatrix} \\  & ={{\begin{bmatrix}2 & -3 \\ -3 & 6\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -4\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{6\cdot 2-(-3)\cdot (-3)}\begin{bmatrix}6 & 3 \\ 3 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}6 & 3 \\ 3 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 1 & \frac{2}{3}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
x=2-u-v,\,y=3u+4v-1.
$$

Given that the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ of $T$ is

$$
u=7+ax-y,\,v=bx+y+c,
$$

what is the value of $a+b+c?$" :question/worked-solution "An affine transformation $T:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2}$ is a function of the form

$$
x=Au+b,
$$

where $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Reversing the action of $T,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}Au+b & =x \\ Au & =x-b \\ u & ={A}^{-1}(x-b).\end{aligned}
$$

So, writing our transformation in matrix form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}2-u-v \\ 3u+4v-1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-u-v \\ 3u+4v\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & ={{\begin{bmatrix}-1 & -1 \\ 3 & 4\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we calculate the inverse of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{4\cdot (-1)-(-1)\cdot 3}\begin{bmatrix}4 & 1 \\ -3 & -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{-1}\begin{bmatrix}4 & 1 \\ -3 & -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-4 & -1 \\ 3 & 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{{\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{u} & ={{\begin{bmatrix}-4 & -1 \\ 3 & 1\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{A}^{-1}}\cdot ({{\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{x}-{{\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{b}) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-4 & -1 \\ 3 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x-2 \\ y+1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-4\cdot (x-2)+(-1)\cdot (y+1) \\ 3\cdot (x-2)+1\cdot (y+1)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}7-4x-y \\ 3x+y-5\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding components, the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ in coordinate form is

$$
u=7+(-4)x-y,\,v=3x+y+(-5).
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a+b+c=-4+3+(-5)=-6.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "d9eae084-1f11-516b-9c30-618279f69755" :step/next {:db/id 17592186412070}} {:db/id 17592186412072 :step/content {:db/id 17592186179995 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0086e1d8-f0ee-53c6-8443-35f56170d9d8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-11" :db/id 17592186256787} {:answer/id #uuid "0d67fff4-252d-5baa-b919-6e2e71d71094" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "7" :db/id 17592186256912} {:answer/id #uuid "80d9c10d-d8ce-5ef8-9f6d-73c22d791bad" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "11" :db/id 17592186257926} {:answer/id #uuid "d0f2b7b2-0f28-5166-96d2-007456d5faee" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-9" :db/id 17592186258602} {:answer/id #uuid "d1a8a822-04f8-5fb6-8bb9-09b853fcf229" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-8" :db/id 17592186258608}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186258602} :answer-field/id #uuid "79824dff-905f-590c-af91-7c9745e11bfb" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186259237}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "24203ad0-c666-584c-ace2-35e7e7f927ec" :question/math-academy-id "q-124117" :question/problem "The matrix form of the affine transformation $T$ is given by

- If $A$ has at least one nonzero entry, then the image of a two-dimensional object is a one-dimensional line segment.

\begin{aligned}det(T) & =\begin{vmatrix}-1 & 2 \\ -4 & 8\end{vmatrix} \\  & =(-1)\cdot 8-(-4)\cdot 2 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}

"The affine transformation $T$ is defined as

$$
x=2u-3v+2,\,y=6v-3u-4.
$$

Given that the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ of $T$ is

$$
u=2x+y+a,\,v=x+by+c,
$$

what is the value of $a+b+c?$" :question/worked-solution "An affine transformation $T:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2}$ is a function of the form

$$
x=Au+b,
$$

where $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Reversing the action of $T,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}Au+b & =x \\ Au & =x-b \\ u & ={A}^{-1}(x-b).\end{aligned}
$$

So, writing our transformation in matrix form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}2u-3v+2 \\ 6v-3u-4\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2u-3v \\ -3u+6v\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -4\end{bmatrix} \\  & ={{\begin{bmatrix}2 & -3 \\ -3 & 6\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -4\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we calculate the inverse of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{6\cdot 2-(-3)\cdot (-3)}\begin{bmatrix}6 & 3 \\ 3 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}6 & 3 \\ 3 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 1 & \frac{2}{3}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{{\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{u} & ={{\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 1 & \frac{2}{3}\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{A}^{-1}}\cdot ({{\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{x}-{{\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -4\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{b}) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 1 & \frac{2}{3}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x-2 \\ y+4\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2\cdot (x-2)+1\cdot (y+4) \\ 1\cdot (x-2)+(\frac{2}{3})\cdot (y+4)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2x+y \\ x+\frac{2}{3}y+\frac{2}{3}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding components, the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ in coordinate form is

$$
u=2x+y+0,\,v=x+\frac{2}{3}y+\frac{2}{3}.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a+b+c=0+\frac{2}{3}+\frac{2}{3}=\frac{4}{3}.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "7e79ca9f-a884-5f7c-a928-03d9e0201c9a" :step/next {:db/id 17592186412069}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "23580040-99be-5f75-be43-adefd3cbfade" :answer/type {:db/id :question/math-academy-id "q-124280" :question/problem "The affine transformation $T$ is defined as

$$
x=2-u-v,\,y=3u+4v-1.
$$

u=7+ax-y,\,v=bx+y+c,

$$
x=Au+b,
$$

where $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Reversing the action of $T,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}Au+b & =x \\ Au & =x-b \\ u & ={A}^{-1}(x-b).\end{aligned}
$$

So, writing our transformation in matrix form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}2-u-v \\ 3u+4v-1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-u-v \\ 3u+4v\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & ={{\begin{bmatrix}-1 & -1 \\ 3 & 4\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we calculate the inverse of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{4\cdot (-1)-(-1)\cdot 3}\begin{bmatrix}4 & 1 \\ -3 & -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{-1}\begin{bmatrix}4 & 1 \\ -3 & -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-4 & -1 \\ 3 & 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{{\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{u} & ={{\begin{bmatrix}-4 & -1 \\ 3 & 1\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{A}^{-1}}\cdot ({{\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{x}-{{\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{b}) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-4 & -1 \\ 3 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x-2 \\ y+1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-4\cdot (x-2)+(-1)\cdot (y+1) \\ 3\cdot (x-2)+1\cdot (y+1)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}7-4x-y \\ 3x+y-5\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding components, the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ in coordinate form is

$$
u=7+(-4)x-y,\,v=3x+y+(-5).
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a+b+c=-4+3+(-5)=-6.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "d9eae084-1f11-516b-9c30-618279f69755" :step/next {:db/id 17592186412070}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0086e1d8-f0ee-53c6-8443-35f56170d9d8" :answer/type {:db/id $$

"The affine transformation $T$ is defined as

$$
x=2u-3v+2,\,y=6v-3u-4.
$$

Given that the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ of $T$ is

$$
u=2x+y+a,\,v=x+by+c,
$$

what is the value of $a+b+c?$" :question/worked-solution "An affine transformation $T:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2}$ is a function of the form

$$
x=Au+b,
$$

where $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Reversing the action of $T,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}Au+b & =x \\ Au & =x-b \\ u & ={A}^{-1}(x-b).\end{aligned}
$$

So, writing our transformation in matrix form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}2u-3v+2 \\ 6v-3u-4\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2u-3v \\ -3u+6v\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -4\end{bmatrix} \\  & ={{\begin{bmatrix}2 & -3 \\ -3 & 6\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -4\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we calculate the inverse of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{6\cdot 2-(-3)\cdot (-3)}\begin{bmatrix}6 & 3 \\ 3 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix}6 & 3 \\ 3 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 1 & \frac{2}{3}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{{\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{u} & ={{\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 1 & \frac{2}{3}\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{A}^{-1}}\cdot ({{\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{x}-{{\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ -4\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{b}) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 1 & \frac{2}{3}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x-2 \\ y+4\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2\cdot (x-2)+1\cdot (y+4) \\ 1\cdot (x-2)+(\frac{2}{3})\cdot (y+4)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2x+y \\ x+\frac{2}{3}y+\frac{2}{3}\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding components, the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ in coordinate form is

$$
u=2x+y+0,\,v=x+\frac{2}{3}y+\frac{2}{3}.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a+b+c=0+\frac{2}{3}+\frac{2}{3}=\frac{4}{3}.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "7c2cc732-641c-57e5-95b3-542bab8f0800"} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "709e3e28-43f0-5774-9967-f2a77296b518" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "11" "q-124315" :question/problem "The affine transformation $T$ is defined as

$$
x=5u-9v-2,\,y=4u-8v+4.
$$

Given that the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ of $T$ is

$$
u=ax-\frac{9}{4}y+b,\,v=cx-\frac{5}{4}y+7.
$$

what is the value of $a+b+c?$" :question/worked-solution "An affine transformation $T:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2}$ is a function of the form

$$
x=Au+b,
$$

where $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Reversing the action of $T,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}Au+b & =x \\ Au & =x-b \\ u & ={A}^{-1}(x-b).\end{aligned}
$$

So, writing our transformation in matrix form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}5u-9v-2 \\ 4u-8v+4\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}5u-9v \\ 4u-8v\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 4\end{bmatrix} \\  & ={{\begin{bmatrix}5 & -9 \\ 4 & -8\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we calculate the inverse of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{-8\cdot 5-(-9)\cdot 4}\begin{bmatrix}-8 & 9 \\ -4 & 5\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\frac{1}{-4}\begin{bmatrix}-8 & 9 \\ -4 & 5\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & -\frac{9}{4} \\ 1 & -\frac{5}{4}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{{\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{u} & ={{\begin{bmatrix}2 & -\frac{9}{4} \\ 1 & -\frac{5}{4}\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{A}^{-1}}\cdot ({{\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{x}-{{\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{b}) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & -\frac{9}{4} \\ 1 & -\frac{5}{4}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x+2 \\ y-4\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2\cdot (x+2)-\frac{9}{4}\cdot (y-4) \\ 1\cdot (x+2)+(-\frac{5}{4})\cdot (y-4)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2x-\frac{9}{4}y+13 \\ x-\frac{5}{4}y+7\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding components, the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ in coordinate form is

$$
u=2x-\frac{9}{4}y+13,\,v=1x-\frac{5}{4}y+7.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}2u-v+1 \\ 9u-4v+3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2u-v \\ 9u-4v\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & ={{\begin{bmatrix}2 & -1 \\ 9 & -4\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{-4\cdot 2-(-1)\cdot 9}\begin{bmatrix}-4 & 1 \\ -9 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-4 & 1 \\ -9 & 2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{{\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{u} & ={{\begin{bmatrix}-4 & 1 \\ -9 & 2\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{A}^{-1}}\cdot ({{\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{x}-{{\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{b}) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-4 & 1 \\ -9 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x-1 \\ y-3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-4\cdot (x-1)+1\cdot (y-3) \\ -9\cdot (x-1)+2\cdot (y-3)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}y-4x+1 \\ 2y-9x+3\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}

\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 6 \\ 1 & -3\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

 
What would be the image of the square shown above under the action of $T?$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that for any affine transformation 

$$
T:u⟶Au+b,
$$

where $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix and $u$ and $b$ are $2\times 1$ column vectors, we have one of the following three possibilities:

- If $T$ is non-singular, i.e., when $det(A)\ne 0,$ then the image of a two-dimensional object is a two-dimensional object. In particular, the image of a polygon with $n$ vertices is a polygon with $n$ vertices.

- If $T$ is singular, i.e., when $det(A)=0,$ we have two additional subcases:

- If $A$ has at least one nonzero entry, then the image of a two-dimensional object is a one-dimensional line segment.

- If $A$ is the zero matrix, then the image of a two-dimensional object is a point on the plane.

With that in mind, let's examine our transformation.

Notice that the matrix representation of the linear transformation associated with $T$ is 
$A=\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 6 \\ 1 & -3\end{bmatrix}.$

Computing the determinant of $A,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}det(T) & =\begin{vmatrix}-2 & 6 \\ 1 & -3\end{vmatrix} \\  & =(-2)\cdot (-3)-6\cdot 1 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a singular nonzero matrix. 

Therefore, $T$ is non-invertible and the image of the square under the action of $T$ is a line segment."} :step/id #uuid "31efd4db-96ca-5899-a79c-9be17347f5b5" :step/next {:db/id 17592186445239}} {:db/id 17592186445239 :step/content {:db/id 17592186389257 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "e04b870d-e25b-5d96-b606-28a110148002" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "A square" :db/id 17592186389259} {:answer/id #uuid "062427a9-0f48-53fc-94f1-c6c3d5e866d8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "A point" :db/id 17592186389260} {:answer/id #uuid "b7b5ad5a-830d-59fb-be20-4b48087915f5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "A triangle" :db/id 17592186389261} {:answer/id #uuid "4003098a-783e-5e93-bb25-5f94f36652a5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "A pentagon" :db/id 17592186389262} {:answer/id #uuid "1f7e5e40-3f3f-5c2d-abac-4a9137d31956" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "A line segment" :db/id 17592186389263}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186389262} :answer-field/id #uuid "d1250926-eea3-55ee-b530-0094a4347a99" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186389258}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "b31d6cdc-6f82-507f-838b-9eddf7b3f11a" :question/math-academy-id "q-162215" :question/problem "![](images/1f/1f550963f047a3860566564abc2cb1e9f3939125895912762ff751767ca55c57.png)

$$
T:u⟶Au+b,
$$

where $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix and $u$ and $b$ are $2\times 1$ column vectors, we have one of the following three possibilities:

- If $T$ is non-singular, i.e., when $det(A)\ne 0,$ then the image of a two-dimensional object is a two-dimensional object. In particular, the image of a polygon with $n$ vertices is a polygon with $n$ vertices.

- If $T$ is singular, i.e., when $det(A)=0,$ we have two additional subcases:

- If $A$ has at least one nonzero entry, then the image of a two-dimensional object is a one-dimensional line segment.

- If $A$ is the zero matrix, then the image of a two-dimensional object is a point on the plane.

With that in mind, let's examine our transformation.

The given transformation can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}2u-v \\ 4u-v+2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2u-v \\ 4u-v\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & -1 \\ 4 & -1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

$A=\begin{bmatrix}2 & -1 \\ 4 & -1\end{bmatrix}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(T) & =\begin{vmatrix}2 & -1 \\ 4 & -1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =2\cdot (-1)-4\cdot (-1) \\  & =2 \\  & \ne 0.\end{aligned}

transformation $T$ is defined as

$$
x=2u-v+1,\,y=9u-4v+3.
$$

Given that the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ of $T$ is

$$
u=y-4x+a,\,v=by+cx+3,
$$

what is the value of $a+b+c?$" :question/worked-solution "An affine transformation $T:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2}$ is a function of the form

$$
x=Au+b,
$$

where $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Reversing the action of $T,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}Au+b & =x \\ Au & =x-b \\ u & ={A}^{-1}(x-b).\end{aligned}
$$

So, writing our transformation in matrix form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}2u-v+1 \\ 9u-4v+3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2u-v \\ 9u-4v\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & ={{\begin{bmatrix}2 & -1 \\ 9 & -4\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we calculate the inverse of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{-4\cdot 2-(-1)\cdot 9}\begin{bmatrix}-4 & 1 \\ -9 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-4 & 1 \\ -9 & 2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{{\begin{bmatrix}u \\ v\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{u} & ={{\begin{bmatrix}-4 & 1 \\ -9 & 2\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{A}^{-1}}\cdot ({{\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{x}-{{\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{b}) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-4 & 1 \\ -9 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x-1 \\ y-3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-4\cdot (x-1)+1\cdot (y-3) \\ -9\cdot (x-1)+2\cdot (y-3)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}y-4x+1 \\ 2y-9x+3\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding components, the inverse transformation ${T}^{-1}$ in coordinate form is

$$
u=y-4x+1,\,v=2y+(-9)x+3.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a+b+c=1+2+(-9)=-6.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "33e812b7-0a19-5479-b824-948d87ff1605" :step/next {:db/id 17592186445235}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "04abb601-17e0-5fec-b990-97706ac5a596" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186199051 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199525 :tutorial/content "Let $T_P$ and $T_Q$ be the truth sets of the predicates $P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)$ and $Q(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n),$ respectively. Note that we're assuming our predicates have the same universal set.

The **implication** of the predicates $P$ and $Q$ is a new predicate that we denote as follows:

$$
P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n) \Rightarrow Q(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)
$$

This implication is false whenever $P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)$ is true *and* $Q(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)$ is false for a specific set of respective variable assignments $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n.$

Now, recall the following logical equivalence:

$$
P\Rightarrow Q \equiv \lnot P \lor Q
$$

Therefore, the truth set of $P \Rightarrow Q$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}_{P⇒Q} & ={T}_{¬P∨Q} \\  & ={T}_{¬P}\cup {T}_{Q} \\  & ={\overset{―}{T}}_{P}\cup {T}_{Q}.\end{aligned}
$$

For example, suppose we have the following universal set:

$$
U = \big\{ 1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9 \big\}
$$

Let's define the following predicates over $U{:}$

- $P(x):$ $x$ is prime

- $Q(x):$ $9$ is divisible by $x$

To find the truth set of $P(x) \Rightarrow Q(x),$ we note the following:

- The truth set of $P(x)$ is $T_P = \left\{ 2,3,5,7 \right\}.$ As a result, the complement is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\overset{―}{T}}_{P}=\overset{―}{\{2,3,5,7\}}=\{1,4,6,8,9\}.\end{aligned}
$$

- The truth set of $Q(x)$ is 

$$
T_Q = \big\{ 1,3,9 \big\}.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}_{P⇒Q} & ={\overset{―}{T}}_{P}\cup {T}_{Q} \\  & =\{1,4,6,8,9\}\cup \{1,3,9\} \\  & =\{1,3,4,6,8,9\}.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "06a295ff-82fc-5afe-8aa1-b24421f2c474" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7992 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "49a55e7b-da8f-5b9b-aca0-ea5672a75f90" :step/math-academy-id 144906 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199052}} {:db/id 17592186199052 :step/content {:db/id 17592186198259 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186198108 :question/id #uuid "662bda92-63ee-5d5c-a45f-7219b160e08d" :question/math-academy-id "e-12740"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "264cfe66-691e-550e-97ad-b71924332f21" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049170} {:db/id 17592186049546} {:db/id 17592186049805}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186198712} {:db/id 17592186198713} {:db/id 17592186381637} {:db/id 17592186381644} {:db/id 17592186381651} {:db/id 17592186381658} {:db/id 17592186407605} {:db/id 17592186415189} {:db/id 17592186434447} {:db/id 17592186500321}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Truth Set of an Implication"} :step/id #uuid "5bf2cacb-1ce2-5c76-9cc6-0e6f2a29dc49" :step/math-academy-id 144907 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199053}} {:db/id 17592186199053 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199527 :tutorial/content "Let $T_P$ and $T_Q$ be the truth sets of the predicates $P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)$ and $Q(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n),$ respectively. Again, we're assuming our predicates have the same universal set.

The **equivalence** of the predicates $P$ and $Q$ is a new predicate that we denote as follows:

$$
P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n) \Leftrightarrow Q(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)
$$

This predicate is true when $P$ and $Q$ have the same truth values for a specific set of variable assignments $x_1,x_2,\ldots, x_n.$

$$
P \Leftrightarrow Q \equiv \big(P \land Q\big) \lor \big(\neg P \land \neg Q\big)
$$

Let's look at some examples. Assume $x\in\mathbb R$ throughout.

- The following statement is an equivalence (i.e., it is true).

$$
x + 2 = 5 \quad\Leftrightarrow\quad x=3
$$

This statement is true because 

$$
\left(x+2=5\quad\Rightarrow\quad x=3\right)\qquad\textrm{and}\qquad \left(x=3\quad\Rightarrow\quad x+2 = 5\right).
$$

- The following statement is **not** an equivalence (i.e., it is false).

$$
x^2 = 4 \quad\Leftrightarrow\quad x=2
$$

This statement is false because 

$$
\left(x=2 \quad \Rightarrow\quad  x^2 = 4\right) \qquad \textrm{and} \qquad \left(x^2=4\quad \not\Rightarrow\quad x=2\right).
$$

However, the following statement is true:

$$
x^2 = 4 \quad\Leftrightarrow\quad x=\pm 2
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "5e9f21f0-8dbb-5442-968e-b1fb4425fef7" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7995 :tutorial/title "Equivalence of Predicates"} :step/id #uuid "62147a48-4a50-55e4-a548-b950bc9af5a9" :step/math-academy-id 144910 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199054}} {:db/id 17592186199054 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199603 :tutorial/content "For predicates $P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)$ and $Q(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n),$ the equivalence $P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)\Leftrightarrow Q(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)$ is true when $P$ and $Q$ have the same truth value.  

$$
P \Leftrightarrow Q \equiv \big(P \land Q\big) \lor \big(\neg P \land \neg Q\big)
$$

It follows that the truth set of $P \Leftrightarrow Q$ can be found using

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}_{P⇔Q}=({T}_{P}\cap {T}_{Q})\cup ({\overset{―}{T}}_{P}\cap {\overset{―}{T}}_{Q}).\end{aligned}
$$

Let's find the truth set of $P(x) \Leftrightarrow Q(x)$ given the following predicates defined over the universal set $\mathbb{R}{:}$

- $P(x):$ $1-5x  < 11$

- $Q(x):$ $x \geq -1$

Note the following:

- To find the the truth set of $P(x),$ we solve the corresponding inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}1-5x & <11 \\ -5x & <10 \\ x & >-2\end{aligned}
$$

So, the truth set of $P(x)$ is $T_P = (-2, \infty)$ and its complement is $\overline{T}_P = (-\infty,-2].$

- The truth set of $Q(x)$ is $T_Q = [-1, \infty)$ and its complement is $\overline{T}_Q = (-\infty,-1).$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}_{P}\cap {T}_{Q} & =(-2,\infty )\cap [-1,\infty ) \\  & =[-1,\infty ) \\ {\overset{―}{T}}_{P}\cap {\overset{―}{T}}_{Q} & =(-\infty ,-2]\cap (-\infty ,-1) \\  & =(-\infty ,-2] \\ {T}_{P⇔Q} & =({T}_{P}\cap {T}_{Q})\cup ({\overset{―}{T}}_{P}\cap {\overset{―}{T}}_{Q}) \\  & =[-1,\infty )\cup (-\infty ,-2] \\  & =(-\infty ,-2]\cup [-1,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

Let's see another example." :tutorial/id #uuid "196ed409-81bb-5e86-bf1c-5e34aa4fb041" :tutorial/math-academy-id 9146 :tutorial/title "Truth Sets of Equivalences"} :step/id #uuid "2f2be205-1493-56f5-8512-a42f382c50fa" :step/math-academy-id 144911 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199055}} {:db/id 17592186199055 :step/content {:db/id 17592186198260 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186198106 :question/id #uuid "a2ae75f0-e1bd-5f07-b728-7d574b892786" :question/math-academy-id "e-12738"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "8c5f2a86-209a-5bb3-a3f2-77d679adb0a4" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050882}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186198714} {:db/id 17592186198715} {:db/id 17592186381423} {:db/id 17592186381686} {:db/id 17592186390177} {:db/id 17592186390184} {:db/id 17592186407603} {:db/id 17592186407604} {:db/id 17592186431925} {:db/id 17592186434446} {:db/id 17592186443911} {:db/id 17592186500377}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Truth Set of an Equivalence"} :step/id #uuid "4e2b4e61-5f88-5898-bcf9-9d4fae86c41e" :step/math-academy-id 144912 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199056}} {:db/id 17592186199056 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199526 :tutorial/content "Since implication and equivalence of predicates are simply generalizations of logical operations on statements, all the properties of these operations can be translated to the corresponding operations on predicates.

In particular, for predicates $P(x_1,x_2\ldots,x_n)$ and $Q(y_1,y_2\ldots,y_m),$ we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}P⇒Q & ≡¬P∨Q \\ P⇔Q & ≡(P⇒Q)∧(Q⇒P) \\  & ≡(¬P∨Q)∧(¬Q∨P) \\  & ≡(¬P∧¬Q)∨(P∧Q)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, let's remind ourselves of the grammatical constructions for implications and biconditionals that we've encountered so far:

For conditional statements, the following are equivalent:

- $P\Rightarrow Q$

- *If $P,$ then $Q$*

- *$P$ implies $Q$*

For biconditional statements, the following are equivalent:

- $P\Leftrightarrow Q$

- *$P$ is equivalent to $Q$*

- *$P$ if and only if $Q$*

- *If $P$ then $Q,$ and if $Q$ then $P$*" :tutorial/id #uuid "599dc11e-cbd2-596c-bb72-4f73b83034ab" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7993 :tutorial/title "Logical Laws Involving Implications and Equivalences With Predicates"} :step/id #uuid "b35ba584-56c8-537f-b6d7-15de6671592a" :step/math-academy-id 144915 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199057}} {:db/id 17592186199057 :step/content {:db/id 17592186198261 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186198107 :question/id #uuid "316efd8a-8618-58b9-a41c-7507942f15b4" :question/math-academy-id "e-12739"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "0d6db336-845a-506a-b020-cced1b38e23a" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186198710} {:db/id 17592186198711} {:db/id 17592186381665} {:db/id 17592186381672} {:db/id 17592186381679} {:db/id 17592186401749} {:db/id 17592186407606} {:db/id 17592186415187} {:db/id 17592186415188} {:db/id 17592186431924} {:db/id 17592186431926} {:db/id 17592186527924}] :knowledge-point/title "Using Laws Involving Implications and Equivalences"} :step/id #uuid "bc5d356c-d8d2-517d-839c-18b823820728" :step/math-academy-id 144916}] :activity/title "Conditional Statements With Predicates" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186198516} {:db/id 17592186199051 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199525 :tutorial/content "Let $T_P$ and $T_Q$ be the truth sets of the predicates $P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)$ and $Q(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n),$ respectively. Note that we're assuming our predicates have the same universal set.

The **implication** of the predicates $P$ and $Q$ is a new predicate that we denote as follows:

$$
P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n) \Rightarrow Q(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)
$$

This implication is false whenever $P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)$ is true *and* $Q(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)$ is false for a specific set of respective variable assignments $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n.$

Now, recall the following logical equivalence:

$$
P\Rightarrow Q \equiv \lnot P \lor Q
$$

Therefore, the truth set of $P \Rightarrow Q$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}_{P⇒Q} & ={T}_{¬P∨Q} \\  & ={T}_{¬P}\cup {T}_{Q} \\  & ={\overset{―}{T}}_{P}\cup {T}_{Q}.\end{aligned}
$$

For example, suppose we have the following universal set:

$$
U = \big\{ 1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9 \big\}
$$

Let's define the following predicates over $U{:}$

- $P(x):$ $x$ is prime

- $Q(x):$ $9$ is divisible by $x$

To find the truth set of $P(x) \Rightarrow Q(x),$ we note the following:

- The truth set of $P(x)$ is $T_P = \left\{ 2,3,5,7 \right\}.$ As a result, the complement is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\overset{―}{T}}_{P}=\overset{―}{\{2,3,5,7\}}=\{1,4,6,8,9\}.\end{aligned}
$$

- The truth set of $Q(x)$ is 

$$
T_Q = \big\{ 1,3,9 \big\}.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}_{P⇒Q} & ={\overset{―}{T}}_{P}\cup {T}_{Q} \\  & =\{1,4,6,8,9\}\cup \{1,3,9\} \\  & =\{1,3,4,6,8,9\}.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "06a295ff-82fc-5afe-8aa1-b24421f2c474" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7992 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "49a55e7b-da8f-5b9b-aca0-ea5672a75f90" :step/math-academy-id 144906 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199052}} {:db/id 17592186199525 :tutorial/content "Let $T_P$ and $T_Q$ be the truth sets of the predicates $P(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)$ and $Q(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n),$ respectively. - $x\in Z$ if and only if $-x\in Z.$

- $x\in Z$ is equivalent to $-x\in Z.$

- If $x\in Z$ then $-x\in Z$, and if $-x\in Z$ then $x\in Z.$

Which of the following is logically equivalent to the conditional predicate above?" :question/worked-solution "Let's denote by $P(x)$ and $Q(x)$ the following predicates:

- $P(x):$ $x$ is a multiple of $10.$

- $Q(x):$ $x$ is a multiple of $5.$

Then, our initial sentence can be written as $P(x)⇒Q(x),$ which is logically equivalent to 

$$
¬P(x)∨Q(x).
$$

The negation of $P(x)$ can be written as

- $¬P(x):$ $x$ is not is a multiple of $10.$

Therefore, the given sentence is logically equivalent to the following:

$\,$ $x$ is not a multiple of $10,$ or $x$ is a multiple of $5.$"} :step/id #uuid "079b11ff-7cb7-562a-8580-d39e3f97c28c" :step/next {:db/id 17592186415191}} {:db/id 17592186415191 :step/content {:db/id 17592186415187 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "80e50955-37f8-51bc-83cc-cb950145c252" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186472820} {:answer/id #uuid "495a8b40-49df-5a56-9235-6ebb943146aa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186472821}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186472821} :answer-field/id #uuid "33d25ffd-2c6e-5b5b-99df-560a24530be3" :answer-field/key "I" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186473805} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1322f1f2-f4c5-54d8-87cc-355df640d02d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186472822} {:answer/id #uuid "33f4cad9-66cd-545d-9ac0-97d5414f12cd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186472823}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186472823} :answer-field/id #uuid "8aeb8409-1020-570b-8cec-0822b2e40889" :answer-field/key "II" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186473806} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0ff70513-8053-559e-b6b1-7a97e4aa128d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186472824} {:answer/id #uuid "78ab4291-cd70-5529-b069-e726e0430998" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186472825}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186472824} :answer-field/id #uuid "aebe7e6e-372c-5557-a0e2-e163a4bed7dd" :answer-field/key "III" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186473807}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "4d6a13d3-ad69-5578-b6a3-a3b3842749f5" :question/math-academy-id "q-183354" :question/problem "Consider the following predicates.

Which of the following is equivalent to the biconditional predicate $A(x)⇔B(x)?$
- **I.** If $x\ge 2$ then $-x\le -2,$ and if $-x\le -2$ then $x\ge 2.$
- **II.** $x\ge 2$ is equivalent to $-x\le -2.$
- **III.** If $x\ge 2$ then $-x\le -2,$ or if $-x\le -2$ then $x\ge 2.$

Select all that apply." :question/worked-solution "A biconditional expression $P⇔Q≡(P⇒Q)∧(Q⇒P)$ can be read as shown below:

- $P$ if and only if $Q$

- $P$ is equivalent to $Q$

- If $P$ then $Q,$ and if $Q$ then $P$

So, $A⇔B$ translates into the following sentences:

- $x\ge 2$ if and only if $-x\le -2.$

- $x\ge 2$ is equivalent to $-x\le -2.$

- If $x\ge 2$ then $-x\le -2,$ and if $-x\le -2$ then $x\ge 2.$

- $P(x):$ $2x+1\le 7$

- $Q(x):$ $x>1$" :question/worked-solution "Since we have that

$$
P(x)⇔Q(x)≡(P(x)∧Q(x))∨(¬P(x)∧¬Q(x)),
$$

 

the corresponding truth set can be found as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}_{P⇔Q}=({T}_{P}\cap {T}_{Q})\cup ({\overset{―}{T}}_{P}\cap {\overset{―}{T}}_{Q})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we note the following:

- To find the the truth set of $P(x),$ we solve the inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}2x+1 & \le 7 \\ 2x & \le 6 \\ x & \le 3\end{aligned}
$$

So, the truth set of $P(x)$ is
${T}_{P}=(-\infty ,3]$
and its complement is
${\overset{―}{T}}_{P}=(3,\infty ).$

- The truth set of $Q(x)$ is 
${T}_{Q}=(1,\infty )$ 
and its complement is
${\overset{―}{T}}_{Q}=(-\infty ,1].$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}_{P}\cap {T}_{Q} & =(-\infty ,3]\cap (1,\infty ) \\  & =(1,3] \\ {\overset{―}{T}}_{P}\cap {\overset{―}{T}}_{Q} & =(3,\infty )\cap (-\infty ,1] \\  & =∅ \\ {T}_{P⇔Q} & =({T}_{P}\cap {T}_{Q})\cup ({\overset{―}{T}}_{P}\cap {\overset{―}{T}}_{Q}) \\  & =(1,3]\cup ∅ \\  & =(1,3].\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "d6c757aa-5130-5319-8a06-731523e17e08" :step/next {:db/id 17592186415193}} {:db/id 17592186415193 :step/content {:db/id 17592186415189 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "387aad0d-bb8f-5b82-9e3e-546a38a316a5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(-\infty ,-3)\cup (2,\infty )" :db/id 17592186415167} {:answer/id #uuid "593a82e8-9e86-54b3-98d9-66e1b119d3aa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(3,\infty )" :db/id 17592186415171} {:answer/id #uuid "9ef73a8c-ede8-54cc-8ecc-ab3bcf027fd6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[-3,\infty )" :db/id 17592186415174} {:answer/id #uuid "acc753ba-6cdc-5e6f-a65f-cf4670d35ffc" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[-3,2]" :db/id 17592186415175} {:answer/id #uuid "f6a5945c-de3e-54a9-85e3-ea79b0853ec9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "R" :db/id 17592186415180}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186415167} :answer-field/id #uuid "c0c1a066-5f9e-50ca-b88c-ecae2c88919a" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186415186}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "f02a6ca7-3a4a-592a-bdf2-d7236cdc3430" :question/math-academy-id "q-183319" :question/problem "Find the truth set of $P(x)⇒Q(x)$ given the following predicates defined over the universal set $R:$

$\,$ $A(x):$ $x\ge 2.$ $\,$ $B(x):$ $-x\le -2.$

Which of the following is equivalent to the biconditional predicate $A(x)⇔B(x)?$
- **I.** If $x\ge 2$ then $-x\le -2,$ and if $-x\le -2$ then $x\ge 2.$
- **II.** $x\ge 2$ is equivalent to $-x\le -2.$
- **III.** If $x\ge 2$ then $-x\le -2,$ or if $-x\le -2$ then $x\ge 2.$

Select all that apply." :question/worked-solution "A biconditional expression $P⇔Q≡(P⇒Q)∧(Q⇒P)$ can be read as shown below:

- $P$ if and only if $Q$

- $P$ is equivalent to $Q$

- If $P$ then $Q,$ and if $Q$ then $P$

So, $A⇔B$ translates into the following sentences:

- $x\ge 2$ if and only if $-x\le -2.$

- $x\ge 2$ is equivalent to $-x\le -2.$

- If $x\ge 2$ then $-x\le -2,$ and if $-x\le -2$ then $x\ge 2.$

"q-183319" :question/problem "Find the truth set of $P(x)⇒Q(x)$ given the following predicates defined over the universal set $R:$

$$

Now, we note the following:

- To find the the truth set of $P(x),$ we solve the inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2} & \le 9 \\ -3 & \le x\le 3\end{aligned}
$$

So, the truth set of $P(x)$ is 
${T}_{P}=[-3,3].$ 
As a result, the complement is
${\overset{―}{T}}_{P}=(-\infty ,-3)\cup (3,\infty ).$

- To find the the truth set of $Q(x),$ we solve the inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}5x-3 & >7 \\ 5x & >10 \\ x & >2\end{aligned}
$$

So, the truth set of $Q(x)$ is
${T}_{Q}=(2,\infty ).$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}_{P⇒Q} & ={\overset{―}{T}}_{P}\cup {T}_{Q} \\  & =((-\infty ,-3)\cup (3,\infty ))\cup (2,\infty ) \\  & =(-\infty ,-3)\cup (2,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "d9ff112c-b10d-58ef-9019-76fb899420e4" :step/next {:db/id 17592186415190}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "387aad0d-bb8f-5b82-9e3e-546a38a316a5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "db5f04ef-3cc1-58de-87ac-cce7945d8e35" :question/math-academy-id "q-183355" :question/problem "Consider the following predicates.

$\,$ $A(x):$ $x\in Z.$ $\,$ $B(x):$ $-x\in Z.$

Which of the following is equivalent to the biconditional predicate $A(x)⇔B(x)?$

I. If $x\in Z$ then $-x\in Z$, and if $-x\in Z$ then $x\in Z.$

II. $x\in Z$ is equivalent to $-x\in Z.$

III. $x\in Z$ if and only if $-x\in Z.$

- $P$ if and only if $Q$

- $P$ is equivalent to $Q$

- If $P$ then $Q,$ and if $Q$ then $P$

So, $A⇔B$ translates into the following sentences:

- $x\in Z$ if and only if $-x\in Z.$

- $x\in Z$ is equivalent to $-x\in Z.$

- If $x\in Z$ then $-x\in Z$, and if $-x\in Z$ then $x\in Z.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III.""} :step/id #uuid "427c4899-8f2f-5df5-bfb1-7ef58c544fcd" :step/next {:db/id 17592186443915}} {:db/id 17592186443915 :step/content {:db/id 17592186381679 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "38d82c66-da81-5da6-99b2-f8009487d231" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186471233} {:answer/id #uuid "6cfd2ce4-c861-572f-be91-5a67f9259251" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186471234}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186471233} :answer-field/id #uuid "9bf3be5b-830f-58c9-a573-942a40eae3d7" :answer-field/key "I" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186472122} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "a3951911-eb29-5274-9d8c-cca561b05b9b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186471235} {:answer/id #uuid "15f517a1-1be6-5193-a806-cc5eb0a13364" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186471236}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186471235} :answer-field/id #uuid "0990f9ff-8884-566c-89d3-36080e85cb1c" :answer-field/key "II" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186472123} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "90c29c97-3228-56b1-859a-71e6720b678f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186471237} {:answer/id #uuid "3e5acb9a-b1ff-54fa-9112-bdbc02b6fd10" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186471238}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186471238} :answer-field/id #uuid "cfcc4a68-2133-54c2-b0a0-3c81584244b4" :answer-field/key "III" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186472124}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "9aa776da-0143-5b4b-9d08-2751ea2726a2" :question/math-academy-id "q-183357" :question/problem "Consider the following predicates.

$$
P(x)⇔Q(x)≡(P(x)∧Q(x))∨(¬P(x)∧¬Q(x)),

the corresponding truth set can be found as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}_{P⇔Q}=({T}_{P}\cap {T}_{Q})\cup ({\overset{―}{T}}_{P}\cap {\overset{―}{T}}_{Q})\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that:

- The truth set of $P(x)$ is 

$$
{T}_{P}=\{2,3,5,7\}
$$

and its complement is

$$
{\overset{―}{T}}_{P}=\{4,6,8,9\}.
$$

- The truth set of $Q(x)$ is 

$$
{T}_{Q}=\{3,6,9\}
$$

 
and its complement is

$$
{\overset{―}{T}}_{Q}=\{2,4,5,7,8\}.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}_{P}\cap {T}_{Q} & =\{2,3,5,7\}\cap \{3,6,9\} \\  & =\{3\} \\ {\overset{―}{T}}_{P}\cap {\overset{―}{T}}_{Q} & =\{4,6,8,9\}\cap \{2,4,5,7,8\} \\  & =\{4,8\} \\ {T}_{P⇔Q} & =({T}_{P}\cap {T}_{Q})\cup ({\overset{―}{T}}_{P}\cap {\overset{―}{T}}_{Q}) \\  & =\{3\}\cup \{4,8\} \\  & =\{3,4,8\}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "bad485c1-18f8-57ef-850a-fe161c531db2" :step/next {:db/id 17592186443912}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "45fbefc3-395f-553e-8152-7832975cb2b4" :answer/type {:db/id - **II.** $x\ge 2$ is equivalent to $-x\le -2.$

variable $X$ defined over a set $S$ is a function $f(x)$ that satisfies the following conditions:

- $f(x) \geq 0$ for all $x$ in $S$

- $\displaystyle \int_{S} f(x) \, \textrm dx = 1$

The probability that $X$ lies in the interval $[a,b]$ is given by

$$
P(a \leq X \leq b) = \int_a^b f(x) \, \textrm dx.
$$

This probability can be interpreted as the area bounded between $f(x)$ and the $x$-axis over the interval $x\in [a,b],$ as shown below.

![](images/e6/e6c21e69a0dbd15ce32d18c2e74d8fcab0276e82bc55b354eaa5140adff610e6.png)

Also, remember that for continuous random variables, we get the same answer whether or not we include the endpoints of an interval $[a,b].$ In other words,

$$
P(a \leq X \leq b) = P(a < X < b)  = P(a < X \leq b) = P(a \leq X < b).
$$

In this lesson, we'll get some practice at computing probabilities with continuous random variables." :tutorial/id #uuid "a6c7afdc-da68-55d5-aaa4-9ff1c77b6740" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6926 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "167eafc7-5e80-5952-9c5c-541b7d78828f" :step/math-academy-id 41930 :step/next {:db/id 17592186193611}} {:db/id 17592186193667 :step/content {:db/id 17592186192789 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186192513 :question/id #uuid "4baa68f1-2f68-5df5-936a-aff56605ed8e" :question/math-academy-id "e-11038"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "17408f35-ef57-5eb2-8cb6-3a946194d2d3" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050215}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186193177} {:db/id 17592186193180} {:db/id 17592186275473} {:db/id 17592186275474} {:db/id 17592186275475} {:db/id 17592186275477} {:db/id 17592186278184} {:db/id 17592186278185} {:db/id 17592186278187} {:db/id 17592186278189} {:db/id 17592186406920} {:db/id 17592186419853}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating Probabilities With Piecewise PDFs"} :step/id #uuid "c5ab4c4d-fb97-5d7e-a711-dca2df3d7318" :step/math-academy-id 41936}] :activity/title "Calculating Probabilities With Continuous Random Variables" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186192912} {:db/id 17592186193666 :step/content {:db/id 17592186193886 :tutorial/content "Recall that the **probability density function** (or **pdf**) of a continuous random variable $X$ defined over a set $S$ is a function $f(x)$ that satisfies the following conditions:

"Recall that the **probability density function** (or **pdf**) of a continuous random variable $X$ defined over a set $S$ is a function $f(x)$ that satisfies the following conditions:

- $f(x) \geq 0$ for all $x$ in $S$

- $\displaystyle \int_{S} f(x) \, \textrm dx = 1$

The probability that $X$ lies in the interval $[a,b]$ is given by

$$
P(a \leq X \leq b) = \int_a^b f(x) \, \textrm dx.
$$

This probability can be interpreted as the area bounded between $f(x)$ and the $x$-axis over the interval $x\in [a,b],$ as shown below.

![](images/e6/e6c21e69a0dbd15ce32d18c2e74d8fcab0276e82bc55b354eaa5140adff610e6.png)

Also, remember that for continuous random variables, we get the same answer whether or not we include the endpoints of an interval $[a,b].$ In other words,

$$
P(a \leq X \leq b) = P(a < X < b)  = P(a < X \leq b) = P(a \leq X < b).
$$

In this lesson, we'll get some practice at computing probabilities with continuous random variables." :tutorial/id #uuid "a6c7afdc-da68-55d5-aaa4-9ff1c77b6740" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6926 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:activity/course {:db/id 17592186046659} :activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186426232} :activity/id #uuid "fb0c4ffb-c4f5-5d37-8b97-09041215ffb0" :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186048744 :topic/id #uuid "ba8cd959-4cba-5c60-858b-f7ee86680552" :topic/math-academy-id 4043} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186426230 :step/content {:db/id 17592186426229 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "05e8a10c-8bca-5b60-94fa-c58a19413d8f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{7}{20}" :db/id 17592186426223} {:answer/id #uuid "57650fd3-48dd-55d0-ac9f-7d32e8ecc4b8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{7}{10}" :db/id 17592186426224} {:answer/id #uuid "c0132ea6-fdc2-5a17-acb2-a6b30862b933" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{10}" :db/id 17592186426225} {:answer/id #uuid "c404deb2-b7c8-573d-8c43-7e7ec28f3b65" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{5}" :db/id 17592186426226} {:answer/id #uuid "f1b44f8c-0f09-5979-a51a-7558f4d266c3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{3}{20}" :db/id 17592186426227}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186426225} :answer-field/id #uuid "e2057c9f-e99d-5d1c-a575-837b0893982e" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186426228}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "0ee0de2e-5389-59ac-b881-e7c459d89539" :question/math-academy-id "q-158461" :question/problem "Compute $P(X\le 0)$ given that the random variable $X$ has the probability density function

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{20}(3{x}^{2}+2x+1),\, & -2\le x\le 2, \\ 0,\, & \text{otherwise.}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "If a continuous random variable $X$ has the probability density function $f(x),$ then 

$$
P(a\le X\le b)={\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le 0) & ={\int }_{-2}^{0}f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{0}\frac{1}{20}(3{x}^{2}+2x+1)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{20}{\int }_{-2}^{0}3{x}^{2}+2x+1\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{20}{[{x}^{3}+{x}^{2}+x]}_{-2}^{0} \\  & =\frac{1}{20}([{0}^{3}+{0}^{2}+0]-[(-2)^{3}+(-2)^{2}+(-2)]) \\  & =\frac{1}{20}(0-[-8+4-2]) \\  & =\frac{1}{20}\cdot 6 \\  & =\frac{3}{10}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "24093c17-aaf6-5f14-99d2-b70a36b04680"} {:db/id 17592186426231 :step/content {:db/id 17592186419853 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "384b21df-8a7c-5b30-9125-1330da362a5b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{5}{24}" :db/id 17592186419836} {:answer/id #uuid "3e21377a-680e-57d6-80e2-410c96b326e9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{7}{24}" :db/id 17592186419837} {:answer/id #uuid "6c20cdc4-8968-5346-8c22-76a6ecf55625" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{7}{36}" :db/id 17592186419839} {:answer/id #uuid "e2afce84-edf6-5026-8a56-a45c4ffb8701" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{11}{36}" :db/id 17592186419843} {:answer/id #uuid "f1943a76-0ce9-5efd-8b74-da642c9f9e88" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{5}{18}" :db/id 17592186419845}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186419839} :answer-field/id #uuid "d0b9338f-ce76-54a7-9f1b-a16c716aaa54" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186419852}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "a05ac3ca-da7d-5bdc-b9ed-2ee65cee279b" :question/math-academy-id "q-158421" :question/problem "Compute $P(-1<X<0)$ given that the random variable $X$ has the probability density function

17592186199073 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199555 :tutorial/content "Recall that a set is **finite** if it contains a finite number of elements and is **infinite** if it has infinitely many elements.

In this lesson, we'll determine whether a set given in set-builder notation is finite or infinite.

For example, let's determine which of the following sets are finite and which are infinite:

$$
\begin{aligned}A={n\in Z\,:\,|2n|\le 8},\,B={q\in Q\,:\,|2q|\le 8},\,C={x\in R\,:\,|2x|\le 8}\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that all three sets are defined using a conditional definition with the same restricting inequality defined over different universal sets ($\mathbb{Z},$ $\mathbb{Q},$ and $\mathbb{R}$).

Firstly, since $\mathbb Z\subset \mathbb Q \subset \mathbb R,$ we start by solving the restricting inequality $|2x| \leq 8$ for $x\in \mathbb R{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}|2x|\le 8 \\ 2|x|\le 8 \\ |x|\le 4\end{aligned}
$$

This inequality has the solution

$$
-4 \leq x \leq 4.
$$

For convenience, we'll express our solution in interval notation as $x\in I,$ where $I=\left[-4,4\right].$ 

Now, before we analyze our sets, we need to state a couple of theorems:

 ** *Theorem 1* **: *Every real interval of nonzero length contains infinitely many rational numbers.*

 ** *Theorem 2* **: *If $X$ is infinite and $X\subseteq Y,$ then $Y$ is infinite.*

We're now ready to determine whether $A, B,$ and $C$ are finite or infinite:

- Set $A$ is finite. If $n \in \mathbb{Z},$ the solutions to the inequality $|2n| \leq 8$ are all the *integers* that lie in the interval $I.$ Therefore, 

$$
A = \{0,\pm 1, \pm 2, \pm 3, \pm 4\}.
$$

Consequently, $|A| = 9,$ which is finite.

- Set $B$ is infinite. If $q \in \mathbb{Q},$ the solutions to $|2q| \leq 8$ are all the *rational* numbers in the interval $I.$ Since any real interval of nonzero length contains infinitely many rational numbers (by Theorem 1), it follows that $B$ is infinite.

- Set $C$ is infinite. Since $B$ is infinite, and $B \subset C,$ it follows that $C$ is infinite (by Theorem 2).

Therefore, we conclude that $A$ is finite, while $B$ and $C$ are infinite.

{:db/id 17592186199073 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199555 :tutorial/content "Recall that a set is **finite** if it contains a finite number of elements and is **infinite** if it has infinitely many elements.

In this lesson, we'll determine whether a set given in set-builder notation is finite or infinite.

For example, let's determine which of the following sets are finite and which are infinite:

$$
\begin{aligned}A={n\in Z\,:\,|2n|\le 8},\,B={q\in Q\,:\,|2q|\le 8},\,C={x\in R\,:\,|2x|\le 8}\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that all three sets are defined using a conditional definition with the same restricting inequality defined over different universal sets ($\mathbb{Z},$ $\mathbb{Q},$ and $\mathbb{R}$).

Firstly, since $\mathbb Z\subset \mathbb Q \subset \mathbb R,$ we start by solving the restricting inequality $|2x| \leq 8$ for $x\in \mathbb R{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}|2x|\le 8 \\ 2|x|\le 8 \\ |x|\le 4\end{aligned}
$$

This inequality has the solution

$$
-4 \leq x \leq 4.
$$

For convenience, we'll express our solution in interval notation as $x\in I,$ where $I=\left[-4,4\right].$ 

Now, before we analyze our sets, we need to state a couple of theorems:

 ** *Theorem 1* **: *Every real interval of nonzero length contains infinitely many rational numbers.*

 ** *Theorem 2* **: *If $X$ is infinite and $X\subseteq Y,$ then $Y$ is infinite.*

We're now ready to determine whether $A, B,$ and $C$ are finite or infinite:

- Set $A$ is finite. If $n \in \mathbb{Z},$ the solutions to the inequality $|2n| \leq 8$ are all the *integers* that lie in the interval $I.$ Therefore, 

$$
A = \{0,\pm 1, \pm 2, \pm 3, \pm 4\}.
$$

Consequently, $|A| = 9,$ which is finite.

- Set $B$ is infinite. If $q \in \mathbb{Q},$ the solutions to $|2q| \leq 8$ are all the *rational* numbers in the interval $I.$ Since any real interval of nonzero length contains infinitely many rational numbers (by Theorem 1), it follows that $B$ is infinite.

- Set $C$ is infinite. Since $B$ is infinite, and $B \subset C,$ it follows that $C$ is infinite (by Theorem 2).

Therefore, we conclude that $A$ is finite, while $B$ and $C$ are infinite. 

Let's see some more examples." :tutorial/id #uuid "32f4b216-b9df-5b0b-a06c-f22d30a51693" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8231 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "9618b821-6d6c-5a8b-b57f-4d5b54ebec92" :step/math-academy-id 152952 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199074}} {:db/id 17592186199555 :tutorial/content "Recall that a set is **finite** if it contains a finite number of elements and is **infinite** if it has infinitely many elements.

:tutorial/content "As previously seen, we can define sets using so-called *constructive definitions* of the form

$$
\big\{ {\color{blue}\textrm{rule}} \: : \: {\color{blue}\textrm{base set}} \big\}
$$

 

where the ${\color{blue}\textrm{rule}}$ is an expression (or formula) that depends on a variable that *constructs* elements of our set when the variable runs over some ${\color{blue}\textrm{base set}}.$ 

For example, the set $A,$ given by

$$
A = \big\{ 2n+1\, : \, n\in\mathbb N_0 \big \}
$$

is defined constructively and contains all positive odd numbers:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={2n+1\,:\,n\in {N}_{0}} \\  & ={2(0)+1,\,2(1)+1,\,2(2)+1,\,2(3)+1,\,…} \\  & ={1,3,5,7,…}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Sometimes, it's helpful to write a set using a constructive definition. For example, how might we express the following set constructively?

$$
B = \big\{ 4, 7, 10, 13, \ldots \big\}
$$

First, notice that the elements of our set 

$$
4,\quad 7,\quad 10,\quad 13,\quad \ldots
$$

form an arithmetic sequence with common difference $d=3{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =3 \\  & =7-4 \\  & =10-7 \\  & =13-10 \\  & ⋮\end{aligned}
$$

So, the $n$th term $a_n$ of our sequence for $n\in\mathbb N$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}+(n-1)\cdot d \\  & =4+(n-1)\cdot 3 \\  & =4+3n-3 \\  & =3n+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can define our set constructively as follows:

$$
B = \big\{ 3n+1 \: : \: n \in \mathbb{N} \big\}
$$

The expression $3n+1$ generates the elements of our set when $n$ runs over $\mathbb{N}.$ 

Note the following:

- A bar "$\mid$" is just as acceptable as a colon to separate the rule from the base set. So, we could also express our set as follows:

$$
B=\big\{ 3n+1 \: \mid \: n \in \mathbb{N} \big\}
$$

- The constructive definition of a given set is typically not unique. For example, we could also define $B$ as follows:

$$
B=\big\{ 3n+4 \: :\: n \in \mathbb{N}_0 \big\}
$$

Notice that we used $\mathbb N_0$ as the base set.

This definition does indeed generate all elements of $B{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{3n+4\,:\,n\in {N}_{0}} & ={3(0)+4,\,3(1)+4,\,3(2)+4,\,3(3)+4,\,…} \\  & ={4,\,7,\,10,\,13,\,…} \\  & =B.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "57358da7-7aa7-5201-b3bd-e43581b18a41" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8307 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "95633ec2-0a87-53d4-9845-589ad5e2c472" :step/math-academy-id 67909 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199426}} {:db/id 17592186199426 :step/content {:db/id 17592186198463 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186198166 :question/id #uuid "231da77b-8370-543a-abf0-effb78e50802" :question/math-academy-id "e-13186"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "1c5b3eb6-187f-5f16-a32e-66b0842adfe9" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050157} {:db/id 17592186050367}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186198843} {:db/id 17592186198872} {:db/id 17592186287858} {:db/id 17592186287860} {:db/id 17592186396282} {:db/id 17592186396295}] :knowledge-point/title "Expressing a Given Set Using an Arithmetic Sequence"} :step/id #uuid "d31b48cd-0396-5a79-94df-84872a357ae8" :step/math-academy-id 67910 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199427}} {:db/id 17592186199427 :step/content {:db/id 17592186198464 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186198164 :question/id #uuid "e81a9a3f-3dbb-5244-8ea0-9b967bb5a46f" :question/math-academy-id "e-13184"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "9df722a8-2db6-5bb8-a69c-b81b33037ab2" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050067}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186198844} {:db/id 17592186198873} {:db/id 17592186287862} {:db/id 17592186287863} {:db/id 17592186287864} {:db/id 17592186287865} {:db/id 17592186396308}] :knowledge-point/title "Expressing a Given Set Using a Geometric Sequence"} :step/id #uuid "01644308-2657-5bfc-bdad-7c6353f7293a" :step/math-academy-id 67913 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199428}} {:db/id 17592186199428 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199552 :tutorial/content "We can also define sets using so-called *conditional definitions* of the form

$$
\{ {\color{blue}\textrm{base set}} \: : \: {\color{blue}\textrm{conditions}} \}
$$

where our set contains only those elements of the ${\color{blue}\textrm{base set}}$ that satisfy the given ${\color{blue}\textrm{conditions}}$ (or restrictions).

For example, the set $A,$ given by

$$
A = \{n\in \mathbb Z \::\: -2\leq n\leq 2\}
$$

is defined conditionally and contains all integers between $-2$ and $2$ inclusive:

$$
A = \{-2,-1,0,1,2\}
$$

It's often helpful to describe sets using conditional definitions. For example, let's rewrite the following set using a conditional definition.

$$
S = \big\{50,51,52,53,\ldots\big\}
$$

The set $S$ contains all natural numbers greater than or equal to $50,$ which we can write as follows:

$$
S = \{n\in \mathbb N \::\: n\geq 50\}
$$

The conditional definition of a set is not unique. We can write down an equivalent definition of $S$ as follows:

$$
S = \{n\in \mathbb N \::\: n\gt 49\}
$$

Under this definition, $S$ contains all natural numbers greater than $49,$ *excluding* $49.$ 

Although $\mathbb N$ is the most natural base set in this instance, we can also define $S$ using the set of integers $\mathbb Z$ as the base set. For example,

$$
S = \{n\in \mathbb Z \::\: n\geq 50\}.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "a5b5e889-bdb2-5707-90ab-be875064cc73" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8228 :tutorial/title "Conditional Definitions of Sets"} :step/id #uuid "82de79d7-d2f1-5a78-845b-a3a4a47ee4c5" \begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}+(n-1)\cdot d \\  & =4+(n-1)\cdot 3 \\  & =4+3n-3 \\  & =3n+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can define our set constructively as follows:

$$
B = \big\{ 3n+1 \: : \: n \in \mathbb{N} \big\}
$$

The expression $3n+1$ generates the elements of our set when $n$ runs over $\mathbb{N}.$ 

Note the following:

- A bar "$\mid$" is just as acceptable as a colon to separate the rule from the base set. So, we could also express our set as follows:

$$
B=\big\{ 3n+1 \: \mid \: n \in \mathbb{N} \big\}
$$

- The constructive definition of a given set is typically not unique. For example, we could also define $B$ as follows:

$$
B=\big\{ 3n+4 \: :\: n \in \mathbb{N}_0 \big\}
$$

Notice that we used $\mathbb N_0$ as the base set.

This definition does indeed generate all elements of $B{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{3n+4\,:\,n\in {N}_{0}} & ={3(0)+4,\,3(1)+4,\,3(2)+4,\,3(3)+4,\,…} \\  & ={4,\,7,\,10,\,13,\,…} \\  & =B.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "57358da7-7aa7-5201-b3bd-e43581b18a41" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8307 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186199426 :step/content {:db/id 17592186198463 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186198166 :question/id #uuid "231da77b-8370-543a-abf0-effb78e50802" :question/math-academy-id "e-13186"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "1c5b3eb6-187f-5f16-a32e-66b0842adfe9" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050157} {:db/id 17592186050367}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186198843} {:db/id 17592186198872} {:db/id 17592186287858} {:db/id 17592186287860} {:db/id 17592186396282} {:db/id 17592186396295}] :knowledge-point/title "Expressing a Given Set Using an Arithmetic Sequence"} :step/id #uuid "d31b48cd-0396-5a79-94df-84872a357ae8" :step/math-academy-id 67910 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199427}} {:db/id 17592186199427 :step/content {:db/id 17592186198464 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186198164 :question/id #uuid "e81a9a3f-3dbb-5244-8ea0-9b967bb5a46f" :question/math-academy-id "e-13184"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "9df722a8-2db6-5bb8-a69c-b81b33037ab2" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050067}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186198844} {:db/id 17592186198873} {:db/id 17592186287862} {:db/id 17592186287863} {:db/id 17592186287864} {:db/id 17592186287865} {:db/id 17592186396308}] :knowledge-point/title "Expressing a Given Set Using a Geometric Sequence"} :step/id #uuid "01644308-2657-5bfc-bdad-7c6353f7293a" :step/math-academy-id 67913 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199428}} {:db/id 17592186199428 :step/content {:db/id 17592186199552 :tutorial/content "We can also define sets using so-called *conditional definitions* of the form

$$
\{ {\color{blue}\textrm{base set}} \: : \: {\color{blue}\textrm{conditions}} \}
$$

where our set contains only those elements of the ${\color{blue}\textrm{base set}}$ that satisfy the given ${\color{blue}\textrm{conditions}}$ (or restrictions).

For example, the set $A,$ given by

$$
A = \{n\in \mathbb Z \::\: -2\leq n\leq 2\}
$$

is defined conditionally and contains all integers between $-2$ and $2$ inclusive:

$$
A = \{-2,-1,0,1,2\}
$$

It's often helpful to describe sets using conditional definitions. For example, let's rewrite the following set using a conditional definition.

$$
S = \big\{50,51,52,53,\ldots\big\}
$$

The set $S$ contains all natural numbers greater than or equal to $50,$ which we can write as follows:

$$
S = \{n\in \mathbb N \::\: n\geq 50\}
$$

The conditional definition of a set is not unique. We can write down an equivalent definition of $S$ as follows:

$$
S = \{n\in \mathbb N \::\: n\gt 49\}
$$

Under this definition, $S$ contains all natural numbers greater than $49,$ *excluding* $49.$ 

Although $\mathbb N$ is the most natural base set in this instance, we can also define $S$ using the set of integers $\mathbb Z$ as the base set. For example,

$$
S = \{n\in \mathbb Z \::\: n\geq 50\}.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "a5b5e889-bdb2-5707-90ab-be875064cc73" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8228 :tutorial/title "Conditional Definitions of Sets"} :step/id #uuid "82de79d7-d2f1-5a78-845b-a3a4a47ee4c5" :step/math-academy-id 67916 :step/next {:db/id 17592186199429}} {:db/id 17592186199552 :tutorial/content "We can also define sets using so-called *conditional definitions* of the form

*Hint: Take ${a}_{1}=6$ in the sequence that generates the elements of $S.$*

$$
S=\{{{field-1}}\,:\,n\in {{field-2}}\}
$$" :question/worked-solution "Notice that the elements of our set

$$
…,\,3,\,6,\,12,\,24,\,48,\,…
$$

form a two-way infinite geometric sequence with a common ratio $r=2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =2 \\  & =\frac{6}{3} \\  & =\frac{12}{6} \\  & =\frac{24}{12} \\  & =⋯\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, setting  ${a}_{1}=6,$ the $n$th term ${a}_{n}$ of our sequence for $n\in Z$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{n-1} \\  & =6\cdot {2}^{n-1} \\  & =6\cdot {2}^{n}\cdot {2}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{6}{2}\cdot {2}^{n} \\  & =3\cdot {2}^{n}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can define our set using a constructive definition as follows:

$$
S=\{3\cdot {2}^{n}\,:\,n\in Z\}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "07b065de-bc57-5b1f-9638-2357e81c045e" :step/next {:db/id 17592186418465}} {:db/id 17592186418462 :step/content {:db/id 17592186198842 :question/answer-fields :question/math-academy-id "q-183325" :question/problem "Describe the set $S=\{5,6,7,...,50\}$ using a conditional definition.

$$
S=\{x\in {{field-1}}\,:\,{{field-2}}\le x\le {{field-3}}\}
$$" :question/worked-solution "The set $S$ contains all natural numbers between $5$ and $50$ (including $5$ and $50$).

Therefore, the set can be written as

$$
S=\{x\in N\,:\,5\le x\le 50\}.
$$

**Note**: This definition is not unique. For example:

- We can write $x\in Z.$ This gives

$$
S=\{x\in Z\,:\,5\le x\le 50\}.
$$

- We can write $4<x<51.$ This gives

$$
S=\{x\in N\,:\,4<x<51\},
$$

or, writing $x\in Z$ as before, we have

$$
S=\{x\in Z\,:\,4<x<51\}.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "8aac6117-dcf7-586f-a196-0f59c7458408" :step/next {:db/id 17592186418461}} {:db/id 17592186418463 :step/content {:db/id 17592186412792 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "8def1d3c-eb5a-566b-af12-d3ce42da3e13" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186412787} {:answer/id #uuid "9c500ffe-51a8-5905-8476-0b724f9d7bf5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186412788} {:answer/id #uuid "f774e7f6-8dc4-55a7-a225-c1111386f024" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186412789}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186412787} :answer-field/id #uuid "8b480447-2056-5cc5-bd5d-e625edb62fa3" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045494} :db/id 17592186412790} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0c80075a-23bd-565b-b792-75b9483248b2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "C" :db/id 17592186412783} {:answer/id #uuid "1fec48bf-7341-5e00-bf54-1e2e3c7d845f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "N" :db/id 17592186412784} {:answer/id #uuid "2ff79e69-0b12-56e7-9984-59ab4023180c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "Z" :db/id 17592186412785} {:answer/id #uuid "3b1ceaab-4f04-5722-81a1-b363e51746d5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "R" :db/id 17592186412786}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186412785} :answer-field/id #uuid "ddcd27c7-8319-5553-8fa5-9d996008549a" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045494} :db/id 17592186412791}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "1e8c26e7-e9d8-563e-b578-6100bf923d6c" :question/math-academy-id "q-183697" :question/problem "Describe the set $S=\{…,-2,-1,0,1,2,3\}$ using a conditional definition.

$$" :question/worked-solution "The set $S$ contains all integers less than $3,$ including $3.$

$\{-3,-\sqrt{5},\sqrt{5}\}=\{x\in R\,:\,3{x}^{3}\,+$
{{field-1}}
${x}^{2}\,-$
{{field-2}}
$x\,-$
{{field-3}}
$=0\}$" :question/worked-solution "The given set contains the roots $x\in R$ of some cubic polynomial $p(x).$

Since the cubic polynomial has roots ${x}_{1}=-3,$ ${x}_{2}=-\sqrt{5},$ and ${x}_{3}=\sqrt{5},$ and the coefficient of the cubic term is $a=3,$ we can write the polynomial as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}p(x) & =a(x-{x}_{1})(x-{x}_{2})(x-{x}_{3}) \\  & =(3)(x-(-3))(x-(-\sqrt{5}))(x-\sqrt{5}) \\  & =3(x+3)(x+\sqrt{5})(x-\sqrt{5}) \\  & =3(x+3)({x}^{2}-\sqrt{5}x+\sqrt{5}x-(\sqrt{5})^{2}) \\  & =3(x+3)({x}^{2}-5) \\  & =3({x}^{3}-5x+3{x}^{2}-15) \\  & =3{x}^{3}+9{x}^{2}-15x-45\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can express the given set as

$$
\{-3,-\sqrt{5},\sqrt{5}\}=\{x\in R\,:\,3{x}^{3}+9{x}^{2}-15x-45=0\}.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "a5125736-78d1-5780-b300-7ef91791e033"} {:db/id 17592186418465 :step/content {:db/id 17592186396254 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid $$" :question/worked-solution "The set $S$ contains all natural numbers between $5$ and $50$ (including $5$ and $50$).

Therefore, the set can be written as

$$
S=\{x\in N\,:\,5\le x\le 50\}.
$$

**Note**: This definition is not unique. For example:

- We can write $x\in Z.$ This gives

$$
S=\{x\in Z\,:\,5\le x\le 50\}.
$$

- We can write $4<x<51.$ This gives

$$
S=\{x\in N\,:\,4<x<51\},
$$

or, writing $x\in Z$ as before, we have

$$
S=\{x\in Z\,:\,4<x<51\}.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "8aac6117-dcf7-586f-a196-0f59c7458408" :step/next {:db/id 17592186418461}} {:db/id 17592186418461 :step/content {:db/id 17592186198844 :question/answer-fields "q-183328" :question/problem "Describe the set $S=\{…,3,6,12,24,48,...\}$ using a constructive definition.

*Hint: Take ${a}_{1}=6$ in the sequence that generates the elements of $S.$*

$$
S=\{{{field-1}}\,:\,n\in {{field-2}}\}
$$" :question/worked-solution "Notice that the elements of our set

$$
…,\,3,\,6,\,12,\,24,\,48,\,…
$$

form a two-way infinite geometric sequence with a common ratio $r=2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =2 \\  & =\frac{6}{3} \\  & =\frac{12}{6} \\  & =\frac{24}{12} \\  & =⋯\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, setting  ${a}_{1}=6,$ the $n$th term ${a}_{n}$ of our sequence for $n\in Z$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{n-1} \\  & =6\cdot {2}^{n-1} \\  & =6\cdot {2}^{n}\cdot {2}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{6}{2}\cdot {2}^{n} \\  & =3\cdot {2}^{n}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can define our set using a constructive definition as follows:

$$
S=\{3\cdot {2}^{n}\,:\,n\in Z\}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "07b065de-bc57-5b1f-9638-2357e81c045e" :step/next {:db/id 17592186418465}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "6756d5e9-8c2b-5648-9cef-d57cf02e8e50" :answer/type {:db/id :question/math-academy-id "q-183697" :question/problem "Describe the set $S=\{…,-2,-1,0,1,2,3\}$ using a conditional definition.

$$
S=\{x\in {{field-1}}\,:\,x<{{field-2}}\}
$$" :question/worked-solution "The set $S$ contains all integers less than $3,$ including $3.$

In other words, $S$ contains all integers less than $4,$  *excluding* $4.$ 

Therefore, the set can be written as

$$
S=\{x\in Z\,:\,x<4\}.
$$

**Note**: This definition is not unique. For example:

- We can write $x\le 3.$ This gives

$$
S=\{x\in Z\,:\,x\le 3\}.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "97d9e6fc-8a81-5514-9e30-4a41f4e00265" :step/next {:db/id 17592186418464}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "8def1d3c-eb5a-566b-af12-d3ce42da3e13" :answer/type {:db/id "250dc34e-ac8d-50ac-8f72-1123fa8a7b34" :question/math-academy-id "q-183751" :question/problem "Find the missing coefficients in the conditional definition of the set $\{-3,-\sqrt{5},\sqrt{5}\}$ given below.

$\{-3,-\sqrt{5},\sqrt{5}\}=\{x\in R\,:\,3{x}^{3}\,+$
{{field-1}}
${x}^{2}\,-$
{{field-2}}
$x\,-$
{{field-3}}
$=0\}$" :question/worked-solution "The given set contains the roots $x\in R$ of some cubic polynomial $p(x).$

Since the cubic polynomial has roots ${x}_{1}=-3,$ ${x}_{2}=-\sqrt{5},$ and ${x}_{3}=\sqrt{5},$ and the coefficient of the cubic term is $a=3,$ we can write the polynomial as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}p(x) & =a(x-{x}_{1})(x-{x}_{2})(x-{x}_{3}) \\  & =(3)(x-(-3))(x-(-\sqrt{5}))(x-\sqrt{5}) \\  & =3(x+3)(x+\sqrt{5})(x-\sqrt{5}) \\  & =3(x+3)({x}^{2}-\sqrt{5}x+\sqrt{5}x-(\sqrt{5})^{2}) \\  & =3(x+3)({x}^{2}-5) \\  & =3({x}^{3}-5x+3{x}^{2}-15) \\  & =3{x}^{3}+9{x}^{2}-15x-45\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can express the given set as

$$
\{-3,-\sqrt{5},\sqrt{5}\}=\{x\in R\,:\,3{x}^{3}+9{x}^{2}-15x-45=0\}.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "a5125736-78d1-5780-b300-7ef91791e033"} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "bcff3a1a-a2f3-5bdb-ac79-6dd44d5cc596" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "45" "q-183792" :question/problem "Describe the set $S=\{2,1,\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{4},...\}$ using a constructive definition.

$$
S=\{{{field-1}}\,:\,n\in {{field-2}}\}
$$" :question/worked-solution "Notice that the elements of our set

$$
2,\,1,\,\frac{1}{2},\,\frac{1}{4},\,…
$$

form an infinite geometric sequence with a common ratio $r=\frac{1}{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =\frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{\frac{1}{2}}{1} \\  & =\frac{\frac{1}{4}}{\frac{1}{2}} \\  & =⋯\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the $n$th term ${a}_{n}$ of our sequence for $n\in N,$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{n-1} \\  & =2\cdot {(\frac{1}{2})}^{n-1} \\  & =2\cdot {(\frac{1}{2})}^{n}\cdot {(\frac{1}{2})}^{-1} \\  & =4\cdot {(\frac{1}{2})}^{n}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can define our set using a constructive definition as follows:

$$
S=\{4\cdot {(\frac{1}{2})}^{n}\,:\,n\in N\}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "e1124dcc-a673-55f5-863e-080064a239ce"} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "c9cb22bc-c849-5803-89e4-d98877fc3515" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-6" Since the quadratic polynomial has roots ${q}_{1}=-\frac{1}{2}$ and ${q}_{2}=3,$ and the coefficient of the quadratic term is $a=4,$ we can write the polynomial as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}p(q) & =a(q-{q}_{1})(q-{q}_{2}) \\  & =4\cdot (q-(-\frac{1}{2}))(q-3) \\  & =4(q+\frac{1}{2})(q-3) \\  & =4({q}^{2}-\frac{5q}{2}-\frac{3}{2}) \\  & =4{q}^{2}-10q-6\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can express the given set as follows:

$$
\{-\frac{1}{2},3\}=\{q\in Q\,:\,4{q}^{2}-10q-6=0\}

Since the quadratic polynomial has roots ${z}_{1}=1-\text{i}$ and ${z}_{2}=1+\text{i},$ and the coefficient of the quadratic term is $a=2,$ we can write the polynomial as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(z) & =a(z-{z}_{1})(z-{z}_{2}) \\  & =2\cdot (z-(1-\text{i}))(z-(1+\text{i})) \\  & =2\cdot ({z}^{2}-(1-\text{i})z-(1+\text{i})z+(1-\text{i})(1+\text{i})) \\  & =2\cdot ({z}^{2}-(1-\text{i}+1+\text{i})z+((1)^{2}-(\text{i})^{2})) \\  & =2\cdot ({z}^{2}-(2)z+(1+1)) \\  & =2{z}^{2}-4z+4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can express the given set as follows:

$$
\{1\pm \text{i}\}=\{z\in C\,:\,2{z}^{2}-4z+4=0\}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "e3ae9ce9-3f42-51dc-87d2-39964c93e221" :step/next {:db/id 17592186435004}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1f70558b-9b80-5074-a897-55d56cf8c03f" :answer/type {:db/id
